en: Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! The Lalitavistara.
Om! Homage to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, and present, who reside in the infinite and boundless world-systems of the ten directions.
START Chapter 1:
The Introduction, the First. Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great saṅgha of twelve thousand bhikṣus,
such as the venerable Jñānakauṇḍinya and the venerable Aśvajit.
And with the Venerable Bāṣpa,
and with the Venerable Mahānāman,
and with the Venerable Bhadrika.
And with the venerable Yaśodeva,
the venerable Vimala,
and the venerable Subāhu.
And with the Venerable Pūrṇa,
the Venerable Gavāmpati,
and the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa.
And with the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa,
the Venerable Gayākāśyapa, and the Venerable Śāriputra.
And with the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa,
and the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
And with the venerable Kaphila,
the venerable Kauṇḍinya,
and the venerable Cunda.
And with the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
the venerable Aniruddha,
and the venerable Nandika.
And with the venerable Kaśphila,
and the venerable Subhūti,
and the venerable Revata.
And with the Venerable Khadiravanika,
the Venerable Amogharāja, and the Venerable Mahāpāraṇika.
And with the Venerable Bakkula,
the Venerable Nanda,
and the Venerable Rāhula.
Together with the venerable Svāgata,
the venerable Ānanda,
and twelve thousand bhikṣus headed by these, as well as thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas.
All of them were bound by only one more birth; they had emerged from all the perfections of the bodhisattvas; they sported with all the supernormal powers of the bodhisattvas;

they had attained all the dhāraṇīs and eloquence of the bodhisattvas; they had fully perfected all the vows of the bodhisattvas; they had reached the correct destination of all the bodhisattvas; and they had attained mastery over all the samādhis of the bodhisattvas.
They had attained mastery over all bodhisattvas, were strewn with the patient endurance of all bodhisattvas, and had fulfilled all the stages of all bodhisattvas.
They were as follows: the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya, and the bodhisattva mahāsattva Dharaṇīśvararāja.
and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Siṃhaketu,
and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Siddhārthamati;
And with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Praśāntacāritramati; and with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Pratisaṃvitprāpta; and with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Nityodyukta.
And with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākaruṇācandrin,
and thirty-two thousand Bodhisattvas headed by him.

Now at that time, the Blessed One was dwelling in dependence upon the great city of Śrāvastī, being honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the three assemblies—kings, princes, royal ministers, royal high officials, and royal attendants; by kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, ministers, and courtiers; by the people of the cities and the countryside; and by those of other sects, including śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, carakas, and parivrājakas.
The Blessed One is a recipient of abundant solid foods, soft foods, delicacies, and unwholesome requisites—robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
The Blessed One has attained the highest gain and the highest fame, yet he remains entirely unstained everywhere, like a lotus by water.
And the noble renown, report, and verses concerning the Blessed One have arisen in the world: "He is an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct."

The Sugata, the knower of the world, the supreme charioteer of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is endowed with the five eyes. Having himself realized, directly witnessed, and fully attained this world and the world beyond— including its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, as well as this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans— he [proclaims it].
He dwelt there; he taught the True Dharma— good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the correct meaning and phrasing, entirely complete, pure, and pristine—
and he fully revealed the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Now at that time, during the middle watch of the night, the Blessed One had entered the samādhi called the Array of the Buddha’s Ornaments.

As soon as the Blessed One had entered this samādhi called the Array of the Buddha’s Ornaments, at that very moment, from the opening of the uṣṇīṣa upon the crown of the Blessed One’s head, there issued forth a ray of light called the Ornament of the Light of Unobstructed Knowledge Recollecting Previous Buddhas.
Having illuminated all the celestial abodes of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, it exhorted immeasurable sons of the gods, headed by the divine son Maheśvara.
Then, emerging from the web of light-rays of the Tathāgata, these verses of exhortation issued forth:

Embrace the Sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, whose radiance is wisdom, who has destroyed darkness, who is a maker of light, whose brilliance is pure, whose supreme splendor is auspiciously stainless, whose body is tranquil, and whose mind is virtuous and peaceful.
Take refuge in the ocean of wisdom, the one of pure and great majesty, the Lord of Dharma, the all-knowing King of Sages;
the God beyond gods, worshipped by the lords of men, the Self-Become One in Dharma, the self-controlled. Lal_1.2 //
He who brought the difficult-to-tame mind under his control, whose intellect was released from the snares of Māra,
and for whom seeing and hearing him here are never in vain— he has ultimately reached the further shore of peaceful liberation.

With devotion, all of you approach him who has become the light, whose qualities are incomparable, who dispels darkness, who is the knower of the true path, whose activity is stilled, the Buddha of immeasurable wisdom.
He is the king of physicians, the giver of the medicine of immortality; he is the hero among debaters, who overcomes the power of evil factions;
he is the kinsman of the Dharma, skilled in the ultimate truth; he is the leader, the teacher of the unsurpassed path.
Thus it is said.
As soon as those sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm were touched by that ray of light— the illumination of unimpeded wisdom arising from the recollection of the Buddha—

and were exhorted by these verses, they became completely tranquil; rising from their meditative absorption, through the power of the Buddha, they recollected those Blessed Buddhas who had appeared throughout immeasurable, incalculable, and countless eons past.
And they recollected all those qualities and arrays of the Buddha-fields of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as well as their circles of assemblies and their teachings of the Dharma.
Then, when that night had become tranquil, the divine son of the Śuddhāvāsa host named Īśvara, along with Maheśvara, Nanda, Sunanda, Candana, Mahita, Praśānta, and Praśāntavinīteśvara—
these and many other divine sons of the Śuddhāvāsa host, possessing exceedingly transcendent complexions— [surrounded] the entire [assembly].
Having illuminated the Jeta Grove with a divine radiance, they approached the Blessed One;
having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, those sons of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm said this to the Blessed One: "There is, Blessed One..."

The Dharma discourse titled *Lalitavistara*, a sūtra, a great compendium of extensive teachings (*mahāvaipulya*), which reveals the roots of virtue of the Bodhisattva; which displays the intentional descent from the sublime Tuṣita heaven, his playful sports, and the excellence of his dwelling in the womb; which displays the majesty of his birthplace and noble lineage; and which [describes] the transcendence of all qualities of childish conduct and all worldly arts, crafts, scripts, mathematics, and seals.

It is the display of the skillful means of calculation, archery, and weaponry, as well as the display of the enjoyment of the objects of the inner harem—all of which are superior to those of all other beings;

it is the proclamation of the attainment of the fruit resulting from the completion of the conduct of all bodhisattvas; it is the playful sport of the bodhisattva that shatters the entire mandala of Māra; and it is the compendium of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata.
"This exposition of the Buddha-dharma according to the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been spoken previously by former Tathāgatas as well;
namely, by the Blessed One Padmottara, Dharmaketu, Dīpaṃkara, Guṇaketu, Mahākara, Ṛṣideva, Śrītejas, Satyaketu, Vajrasaṃhatana, and Sarvābhibhū."

And [there were] Hemavarṇa, Atyuccagāmin, Pravāhasāgara, Puṣpaketu, Vararūpa, Sulocana, Ṛṣigupta, Jinavaktra, Unnata, Puṣpita, Ūrṇatejas, Puṣkara, Suraśmi, Maṅgala, Sudarśana, Mahāsiṃhatejas, and Sthitabuddhidatta.
And with Vasantagandhin, Satyadharmavipulakīrti, Tiṣya, Puṣya, Lokasundara, Vistīrṇabheda, Ratnakīrti, Ugratejas, Brahmatejas, Sughoṣa, Supuṣpa,
Sumanojñaghoṣa, Suceṣṭarūpa, Prahasitanetra, and Guṇarāśi.

And it was previously spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Meghasvara, Sundaravarṇa, Āyustejas, Salīlagajagāmin, Lokābhilāṣita, Jitaśatru, Saṃpūjita, Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Kakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa.

The Blessed One might now also reveal it for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings— both gods and humans— for the purpose of exalting this Mahāyāna, for the purpose of refuting all rival proponents, for the purpose of exalting all bodhisattvas, for the purpose of overcoming all Māras, and for the sake of those persons who belong to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas.

"For the purpose of generating the undertaking of vigor, for the purpose of upholding the true Dharma, for the purpose of upholding the lineage of the Three Jewels, for the purpose of ensuring the non-interruption of the lineage of the Three Jewels, and for the purpose of fully manifesting the work of a Buddha.
Out of compassion for the world including its gods, the Blessed One consented to those sons of the gods by remaining silent.

Then, the sons of the gods, perceiving the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, were satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, scattered divine sandalwood powder, agallochum powder, and māndārava flowers over him, and vanished right there.
Then, at the end of that very night, the Blessed One approached the Karīra Grove, which was beautifully arrayed as a circular mandala.
Having approached, the Blessed One sat down upon the seat prepared for him, preceded by the host of bodhisattvas and the community of śrāvakas.
Once seated, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "In this way, monks, when the night has become tranquil, Īśvara..."

The son of the gods named Nāma-śuddhāvāsakāyika, Maheśvara, Nanda, Sunanda, Candana, Mahita, Praśānta, Vinīteśvara, and these and many other sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsakāyika realm, as previously described, vanished right there.

Then those bodhisattvas and great śrāvakas, having bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One: "It would be well, Blessed One, if you would teach that Dharma discourse named *Lalitavistara*.

That will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans, including those present here now."
And for the sake of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
the Blessed One, out of compassion for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, consented to those bodhisattva mahāsattvas and those great śrāvakas by remaining silent.
On this matter, it is said:
"O monks, on this very night, as I sat here today in comfort, free from passion,
having entered into auspicious meditative states with a one-pointed and concentrated mind— " *Lal_1.6*
Then the sons of the gods, possessed of great supernatural power, with serene complexions and radiant with stainless glory,
having illuminated this grove called Jeta with their splendor, joyfully approached my presence.
Maheśvara, Candana, Īśa, Nanda, Praśāntacitta, Mahita, Sunandana,
and the son of the gods named Śānta, as well as many other such tens of millions of deities.
Having bowed at my feet and performed a circumambulation, they stood here before me;
and with their hands joined in reverent salutation, they made this request of me with great respect.
O Sage, rich in the destruction of passion, this Vaipulya Sūtra is indeed a great foundation;
it was spoken by all the Tathāgatas of old for the sake of the welfare of the entire world. (Lal 1.10)
Therefore, even now, that Sage speaks well, desiring to gather the multitude of Bodhisattvas;
by proclaiming this supreme Mahāyāna, he subdues the arguments of adversaries and Māra.
He accepted the first request of the host of gods and their silent assent;
and all, satisfied, joyful, and exultant, having attained great delight, scattered flowers.
Therefore, O monks, all of you here listen to this Vaipulya Sūtra, the Great Nidāna,
which was spoken by all the Tathāgatas of old for the sake of the welfare of the entire world. (Lal 1.13)
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction," in the glorious Lalitavistara.
START Parivarta 2 (Vaidya 7):
The Second Chapter, "The Chapter on Encouragement."

In this regard, monks, what is the Dharma-discourse, the sūtra of great vaipulya, called the *Sulalitavistara*? Here, monks, it concerns the Bodhisattva while he was dwelling in the supreme Tuṣita abode, honored by those worthy of honor, having attained consecration, praised, extolled, lauded, and glorified by hundreds of thousands of gods, having received his empowerment, and having emerged through his former vows.

He whose awakening had fully realized all the qualities of a Buddha; who possessed the eye of wisdom that was vast and utterly pure; whose expansive awakening was ablaze with mindfulness, intelligence, realization, and fortitude;

who had attained the supreme perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and great skillful means; who was expert in the divine path of great loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; who had become face-to-face with the manifestation of the knowledge of the great superknowledges, free from attachment and obscuration; and who had reached the ultimate fulfillment of all the factors conducive to awakening—the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the limbs of awakening, and the path.

His body was adorned with the primary marks and secondary characteristics resulting from an immeasurable accumulation of merit; he had long followed [the path] by performing according to his word and speaking words that were not false; his mind was upright, free from crookedness, deceit, and obstruction; he was devoid of all pride, intoxication, arrogance, fear, and despondency; his heart was equal toward all sentient beings;
he had attended upon hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable Buddhas; and his face was gazed upon by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of many Bodhisattvas.
His fame was celebrated by the hosts of Śakra, Brahmā, Maheśvara, the World-Protectors, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and rākṣasas.

He was skilled in the knowledge of entering the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) that explain the distinctions of all words; he had attained infinite and boundless dhāraṇīs that serve as vessels for mindfulness and retention, preserving everything spoken by all the Buddhas without distraction;

and he possessed the great ship of the Dharma consisting of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the path (*mārga*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), and skillful means (*upāya*).

[He is] the great caravan leader who has accumulated the jewels of the Dharma through skillfulness and merit; whose intention is to cross to the further shore of the four floods; who has struck down the enemy of pride; who has thoroughly subdued all opposing disputants; who stands firm at the head of battle;

who slays the host of enemies that are the afflictions; who possesses the firm weapon of the supreme vajra of wisdom; and who has arisen from the resolute intention of the staff of great compassion rooted in the thought of awakening.

Of this great man-lotus, which has been sprinkled by the waters of profound vigor; whose pericarp is skill in means; whose filaments are the meditations on the factors of enlightenment; whose pollen is concentration; which is well-born in the stainless lake of the multitude of virtues; whose broad petals are as pure as the moon and free from the overflow of intoxication and pride; which possesses the fragrance of ethical conduct, learning, and serene faith that is unimpeded throughout the ten directions; which is mature in wisdom; which is unsullied by the eight worldly concerns; and which emits the sweet scent of the accumulated stores of merit and knowledge.

He who causes the hundred-petaled lotus of the perfectly pure mind to blossom by the rays of the sun of the knowledge of wisdom; who has recited the supreme mantra of the four bases of psychic power; whose claws and fangs are the extremely sharp nails of the four noble truths; whose vision is based upon the four divine abodes; whose head is well-gathered by the four means of attraction;

whose body has arisen in successive stages through the realization of the twelve-linked dependent origination; who is a lion of ignorance and wisdom with a well-formed mane of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; and who has yawned wide with the three gates of liberation.

He whose eye was perfectly purified by tranquility and insight; who dwelt in mountain caves and mountain grottoes as his abode for the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; whose tree of virtue was well-nourished in the grove of the discipline of the four modes of deportment; whose strength was cultivated through the practice of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; whose hair did not stand on end from the fear of existence or worldly prosperity; whose prowess was unshrinking; and who quelled the multitudes of the heretics, like a lion among a herd of deer.

He who utters the sound of selflessness with the roar of the great lion; the lion among men, whose radiance from the sphere of wisdom and the mandala of liberated meditation renders the host of fireflies that are the non-Buddhist teachers lusterless; he who dispels the cataracts of the darkness and gloom of ignorance; he of blazing strength and vigor; the sun among great beings, intensified by the splendor of merit among gods and humans; who has departed from the dark fortnight and is fully perfected in the bright fortnight; he of pleasing and beloved appearance.
He whose faculty of sight is unimpeded; who is adorned by a multitude of lights like hundreds of thousands of deities; whose mandala consists of the knowledge of meditative absorption and liberation;

who emits moonbeams of light rays of bliss from the factors of enlightenment; who awakens the night-lotuses of men awakened by the Buddha; who, like the great being-moon, is surrounded by the four assemblies as the four continents;
who is endowed with the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment; who applies his mind with equanimity toward all sentient beings; and whose intellect is unobstructed.

He was one who had perfected the vows and austerities of the ten paths of wholesome action; whose intention was to attain the most excellent and complete distinction; who set in motion the supreme and noble wheel of the jewel of the Dharma as an unimpeded King of Dharma; who was born into the lineage and family of the universal monarchs; who was filled with the jewels of all dharmas through the profound and unfathomable dependent origination; who never transgressed the shore of his conduct, wisdom, and vast, expansive undertakings, remaining insatiable in his hearing of the teachings; and whose eyes were like the interior of a great lotus.

He whose intellect was as vast as the ocean that sustains all; whose mind was equal to earth, water, fire, and air; who was firm in strength like Mount Meru and unshakable; who was free from both attachment and aversion;

whose buddhi was as pure, vast, and irresistible as the expanse of the sky; whose higher resolve (*adhyāśaya*) was perfectly purified; who had given gifts most excellently; who had performed his former practices well; who had fulfilled his obligations; who had made his word true; and who had sought out every root of merit.

For one whose latent tendencies have been perfumed, who has reached the final departure as it were of all roots of merit; who has brought forth a flow of all roots of merit accumulated over seven incalculable eons;

who has bestowed the seven kinds of giving; who has cultivated the five bases of meritorious action; who has practiced well-conducted behavior—threefold by body, fourfold by speech, and threefold by mind; and who has undertaken and cultivated the ten paths of wholesome action.
For one who has cultivated the correct application endowed with forty factors; who has made the correct vow endowed with forty factors;
who has entered upon the correct resolute intention endowed with forty factors; who has fulfilled the correct liberation endowed with forty factors;
who has straightened the correct inclination endowed with forty factors; and who has gone forth as a renunciant under four hundred thousand million billion Buddhas endowed with forty factors.
Having given gifts to five million five hundred thousand *koṭī-niyuta-śatasahasra* Buddhas; having performed services for three hundred and fifty million *pratyekabuddhas*;

having established immeasurable and incalculable beings on the path to heaven and liberation; and desiring to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—being bound by only one more birth, he, upon passing away from here, [will go] to the sublime abode of Tuṣita.

The supreme son of the gods named Śvetaketu, who was being honored by all the hosts of deities, having passed away from the world-system Raśmyāya and been reborn in the mortal realm, will before long realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

In that great celestial palace, he sat comfortably, which was supported by thirty-two thousand floors and adorned with railings, turrets, arches, windows, gabled chambers, and palace terraces; it was spread with canopies of raised parasols, banners, cloth streamers, and nets of jeweled bells, and strewn with a carpet of *māndārava* and great *māndārava* flowers; it resounded with the music of hundreds of thousands of millions of *apsarases*, and was beautified by jewel-trees such as the *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *kovidāra*, *mucilinda*, great *mucilinda*, *aśoka*, *nyagrodha*, *tinduka*, *āsana*, *karṇikāra*, *keśara*, and *sāla*.

It was covered with nets of gold, adorned with great full vases, and beautified by level arrangements; it was filled with the fragrance of flower-garlands of light and gazed upon by the eyes of hundreds of thousands of millions of deities facing toward it. It was a place for the great and vast chanting of the Dharma that cuts through the force of all sensual desires and afflictions, removes every trace of anger, hostility, pride, intoxication, and arrogance, and generates joy, serene faith, gladness, and expansive mindfulness.
While he was seated comfortably and this great discourse on the Dharma had commenced, amidst the sounding of eighty-four thousand musical instruments and songs,
these verses of exhortation issued forth from them through the accumulation of the Bodhisattva’s former virtuous karma:
(Vaidya 9)
Remember, O you who have accumulated a vast store of merit, you who possess mindfulness, intelligence, and resolve, and who radiate infinite wisdom!
You of incomparable strength and vast valor, remember also the prophecy of Dīpaṃkara.
Remember, O you of vast and stainless mind, who have abandoned the stains of the three impurities and whose pride and faults are stilled;
remember how your conduct of giving was characterized by a virtuous, stainless, and pure heart in the past.
Remember, O noble lady of excellent lineage, how you cultivated tranquility, moral discipline, vows, patience,
and self-control, as well as vigor, power, meditation, and wisdom for millions of billions of eons.
Remember, remember, O you of infinite fame, those millions of Buddhas who were fully honored;
having compassion for them all, this is the time—do not remain indifferent!

"Fall away, fall away! For many gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas—knowers of the process of passing away, destroyers of the afflictions of old age and death, and free from passion—are looking up expectantly."
Having enjoyed pleasures for a thousand eons, there is no satiety, just as with water in the ocean;
therefore, O Excellent One, be satisfied with wisdom and satisfy the people who have long been afflicted by thirst.
Moreover, O you of blameless fame, you delight in the Dharma and do not delight in sensual desires;
nevertheless, O one with stainless eyes, you have compassion for the world including the gods.
Moreover, even though millions of gods are never satiated by hearing the Dharma,
you should nevertheless look upon those who have fallen into the states of protection [the heavens] and those dwelling in the miserable realms.
Moreover, O one of stainless vision, although you see the Buddhas in the world throughout the ten directions and hear the Dharma from them, you too must distribute that supreme Dharma in the world.
Moreover, O glorious one, although the Tuṣita heaven is resplendent with the splendor of your merit,
nevertheless, O compassionate-minded one, rain down your rain upon the banner of Jambudvīpa.
Having transcended the realm of desire, all those various gods belonging to the realm of form rejoice, saying: "May he who has undertaken the vow of perfection touch enlightenment!"

"O Protector, you have struck down the deeds of Māra and conquered other heretics; by what means, O All-pervading One, will awakening be attained? This is the time—do not remain indifferent! (Lal 2.12)
O Hero, as the world is set ablaze by the fire of the afflictions, pervade it like a cloud and rain down a shower of nectar; extinguish the afflictions of gods and men.

O Physician, skilled in the elements, truthful physician who art true to your word, quickly establish those long afflicted by disease in the bliss of nirvāṇa through the application of the medicine of the three liberations.
Not having heard the lion’s roar, jackals howl without fear;
roar the lion’s roar of a Buddha and terrify the jackals of the rival sectarians!
With the lamp of wisdom in hand, arisen through the power of strength and vigor, having struck the earth with the palm of your excellent hand upon the circle of the ground, conquer Māra!
The four guardians look on, who shall present the bowl to you;
and millions of Śakras and Brahmās shall receive you at your birth.
Look down, O Abhiyaśas, you who are born of a lineage that is a jewel among families, you of noble descent;
staying there, O wise one, you shall behold the conduct of the Bodhisattva.
In whichever vessel this precious jewel remains, it becomes glorious;
O Jewel of Pure Intelligence, rain down your rain upon Jambudvīpa!
Thus, these verses, emerging from the sound of many kinds of musical instruments, urge him whose mind is compassionate: "This is the time; do not be indifferent! *Lal_2.20*
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Chapter on Encouragement," in the glorious Lalitavistara.
START Parivarta 3 (Vaidya 11).
The third chapter: "The Purity of Family."

Thus, monks, when the Bodhisattva was thus exhorted by the time for the Dharma, he emerged from that great celestial mansion and ascended the great palace named Dharmoccaya, where the Bodhisattva used to sit and teach the Dharma to the gods of the Tuṣita heaven.
Having ascended, he sat down upon the Lion Throne of the Sudharma Hall.
Then those sons of the gods who were of like nature with the Bodhisattva and had set out together on the same vehicle also ascended that very palace;
as did the Bodhisattvas from the ten directions who shared his conduct, as well as the sons of the gods.
They too, having ascended that palace, sat down each upon his own lion throne according to his rank;
they were accompanied by retinues of equal resolve, with sixty-eight thousand million followers, and were free from throngs of apsarases and ordinary sons of gods.
Thus, monks, after twelve years, the Bodhisattva was to descend into his mother’s womb.
Then the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm came to Jambudvīpa, concealed their divine splendor, and in the guise of brahmins, they taught the Vedas to the brahmins.
"He who has such an entry into the womb becomes endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man."
For one endowed with these, there are two destinies and no third: if he dwells at home,
he becomes a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), a conqueror of the four quarters, righteous, a king of dharma, and possessed of the seven jewels.
He possesses these seven jewels, namely:
the wheel-jewel, the elephant-jewel, the horse-jewel, the woman-jewel, the gem-jewel, the householder-jewel, and the counselor-jewel as the seventh.
In what manner is a wheel-turning monarch endowed with the precious wheel?

In this case, when a consecrated Kṣatriya king, on the fifteenth day of the Poṣadha observance, having bathed his head and observed the fast, has ascended to the upper terrace of his palace and is surrounded by his harem, a divine precious wheel appears in the eastern direction.

Having seen it— a thousand-spoked wheel, with a rim and a hub, adorned with gold-colored craftsmanship, seven palm-trees high, and appearing all around within the inner apartments of the consecrated Kṣatriya king—
he thinks: "I have indeed heard that for whichever consecrated Kṣatriya king this very divine Wheel-Treasure appears on the day of the *poṣadha*..."

On the fifteenth day, having bathed his head and observed the fast, while situated on the upper terrace of his palace and surrounded by the women of the harem, a divine wheel-treasure appears in the eastern direction;
he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin).
"Surely I am a wheel-turning monarch; what if I were now to examine the divine wheel-treasure?

Then the anointed Kṣatriya king, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and placed his right knee upon the ground, would reach out with his right hand for that divine wheel-treasure and address it thus: "Turn!"
"Venerable sir, does the divine wheel-treasure proceed by means of righteousness or unrighteousness?
"Then that divine wheel-treasure, set in motion by the anointed Kṣatriya king, proceeds rightly through the sky by means of supernatural power toward the east;
the Wheel-turning King follows it together with his fourfold army."
And on whichever spot of earth that divine wheel-treasure comes to rest, there the anointed Kṣatriya king establishes his residence together with his fourfold army.
Then, those kings who are regional rulers in the eastern direction—

Taking either a silver bowl filled with gold dust or a golden bowl filled with silver dust, they rise to meet the universal monarch and say: "Come, O Lord! Welcome to the Lord! This kingdom of yours is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, delightful, and crowded with many people."
"May Your Majesty dwell in your own conquered realm that you have now reached.
When this was said, the consecrated Kṣatriya king, the protector, spoke thus to those regional kings: "May you all govern your respective kingdoms according to the Dharma.
Come now, sirs, do not cause living beings to be killed."
Do not take what is not given;
do not engage in sexual misconduct;
do not speak falsely.
"Ensure that no unrighteousness arises within my realm, and do not take pleasure in those who practice unrighteousness.
In this way, indeed, an anointed Kṣatriya king conquers the eastern direction.

Having conquered the eastern direction and having plunged into the eastern ocean, he emerges from the eastern ocean. Having emerged from the eastern ocean, he proceeds correctly through the sky by means of his supernatural power toward the south.
The wheel-turning monarch follows along with his fourfold army.
In the same manner as before, he thus conquers the southern direction;
and just as he conquers the south, so too does he conquer the western and northern directions.
Having conquered the northern direction, he plunges into the northern ocean.
Having plunged into the northern ocean, he emerges from it;
having emerged, he returns by means of his supernatural power through the air directly to the royal capital, and stands unharmed above the gate of the inner apartments.
In such a manner is a consecrated Kṣatriya king endowed with the wheel-treasure.
In what manner is a wheel-turning monarch endowed with the elephant-treasure?
Here, for a consecrated Kṣatriya king, as previously described, the elephant-treasure appears:

entirely white, well-established on seven limbs, with a golden crest, a golden banner, and golden ornaments; covered with a golden net, possessing supernormal power, able to travel through the air, and capable of miraculous transformations.
That is to say, there is a dragon king named Bodhi.
And when a consecrated Kṣatriya king desires to examine that precious elephant,
he mounts that precious elephant at the time of sunrise and [traverses] this very great earth, which has the oceans as its moat.
Having wandered all around as far as the ocean's edge and returned to the royal capital, he experiences delight in governance.
In this manner, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with the elephant-treasure.
In what manner is a wheel-turning monarch endowed with the horse-treasure?
Now, for the consecrated Kṣatriya king, as before, there arises the horse-treasure:

entirely blue, with a black head, a mane like muñja grass, a respectful countenance, a golden banner, golden ornaments, covered with a golden net, possessing supernatural power, traveling through the air, and capable of miraculous transformations.
Namely, the king of horses named Bālāhaka.
And when the anointed Kṣatriya king desires to examine the horse-treasure,

he mounts the horse-treasure at the time of sunrise and, having traversed this very great earth— encircled by the ocean, bounded by the ocean, and encompassed on all sides— returns to the royal capital.
He experiences delight in governance;
in this manner, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with the horse-treasure.
In what manner is a wheel-turning monarch endowed with the jewel-treasure?

In this case, for a consecrated Kṣatriya king, as previously described, a jewel-treasure arises: it is pure blue beryl, eight-faceted, and well-polished. Furthermore, by the radiance of that jewel-treasure, the entire inner palace becomes suffused with light.
And when the consecrated Kṣatriya king desires to examine that jewel-gem,
then at the hour of midnight during the pitch-black darkness of the night, having hoisted that jewel-gem upon the top of a banner, he goes out to a park grounds to behold the beautiful landscape.
Furthermore, by the radiance of that precious gem, the entire fourfold army is illuminated for a distance of one *yojana* all around.
Moreover, those people who dwell in the vicinity of that precious gem, being suffused with that radiance, recognize one another.
They saw one another and said to one another: "Arise, gentle friends! Perform your labors and open your shops;
we thought the sun had risen during the day."
In this way, an anointed Kṣatriya king becomes endowed with such a precious jewel.
In what manner is a wheel-turning monarch endowed with the jewel of a woman?
Here, for a consecrated Kṣatriya king, as previously described, there arises the jewel of a woman:
she is a Kṣatriya of similar status, neither too tall nor too short, neither too stout nor too thin, neither too fair nor too dark, beautiful, gracious, and lovely to behold.
From all her pores the fragrance of sandalwood wafts forth,
and from her mouth the fragrance of the blue lotus wafts forth;
she is as pleasant to the touch as kācilindika cloth.
In the cold season her limbs have a warm touch,
and in the hot season they have a cool touch;
with the exception of the universal monarch, she does not feel passion for any other person even in her mind, much less with her body.
In this manner, a universal monarch is endowed with the jewel of a woman.
In what manner is a wheel-turning monarch endowed with the householder-treasure?
Here, for a consecrated Kṣatriya king, as before, the householder-treasure arises—one who is wise, discerning, intelligent, and possesses the divine eye.
With that divine eye, he perceives treasures within a league’s distance of his surroundings, including those that have owners.
He sees treasures that have no owner;
whatever those ownerless things may be, he uses them for the king, the universal monarch, to perform his necessary duties.
In this manner, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with the householder-treasure.
In what manner is a wheel-turning monarch endowed with the jewel of the general?
In this case, for a consecrated Kṣatriya king, as described before, there arises the jewel of the general— wise, discerning, and intelligent— who,
at the mere thought of the wheel-turning monarch, mobilizes whatever army needs to be mobilized.
In this manner, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with the jewel of the general.
He will be possessed of these seven jewels,
and he will have a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
Having conquered this entire great earth, bounded by the oceans, without exception, free from thorns, and without punishment or weapons, he dwells as its sovereign.
If he should go forth from the home to the homeless life,
he will be one who has vomited out desire and passion, a leader, a teacher of gods and humans, and a god without another god above him.
Likewise, other sons of the gods also came to Jambudvīpa and announced to the Pratyekabuddhas: "Friends, abandon this buddha-field!
In twelve years from now, the Bodhisattva will descend into his mother's womb."
Furthermore, monks, at that time in the great city of Rājagṛha, on the mountain Golāṅgulaparivartana, there dwelt a Pratyekabuddha named Mātaṅga.

Upon hearing that sound, he set out like mud upon a stone; having ascended into the air to the height of seven palm trees and entered the fire-element (*tejodhātu*), he attained parinirvāṇa like a meteor.
As for his bile, phlegm, sinews, bones, flesh, and blood—
All of that was consumed by his splendor;
only pure bodies fell upon the ground,
and even today they are known as the "footprints of the sages" (ṛṣipada).
Furthermore, monks, at that time five hundred pratyekabuddhas were dwelling in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in Vārāṇasī.

Having heard that sound as well, they rose into the air to the height of seven palm trees, entered the fire-element, and attained parinirvāṇa like meteors. Whatever bile, phlegm, flesh, bone, sinew, and blood they had, [all vanished].
All of that was completely consumed by his splendor;
only pure bodies fell to the ground. Because the sages (*ṛṣi*) had fallen there, from that time forth the name "Ṛṣipatana" (The Fall of the Sages) arose.
And because deer lived there, having been granted freedom from fear, the name "Mṛgadāva" (Deer Park) arose for that place after the deer park.
Thus, monks, while residing in the sublime Tuṣita abode, the Bodhisattva performed four great surveys.
What are these four?
Namely: the survey of the time, the survey of the continent, the survey of the region, and the survey of the family.

For what reason, monks, did the Bodhisattva observe the observation of the time? The Bodhisattva does not descend into his mother’s womb at the beginning of the world, during the period when beings are undergoing dissolution; rather, he descends only when the world has become manifest and well-established.
Birth is discerned, aging is discerned,
and sickness is discerned.
When death is discerned, then the Bodhisattva enters his mother's womb.
For what reason did the Bodhisattva perform the inspection of the continents?
It is because Bodhisattvas are not born in outlying continents,
nor in Pūrvavideha.
Not in Aparagodānīya, nor in Uttarakuru;
rather, they are reborn only in Jambudvīpa.
For what reason, monks, did the Bodhisattva survey the regions?

It is because Bodhisattvas are not born in borderlands where people are blind from birth, dull-witted, or like sheep and mutes— incapable of understanding the meaning of well-spoken or ill-spoken words.
Nevertheless, Bodhisattvas are born only in the central regions.
For what reason, monks, did the Bodhisattva survey the family?
Bodhisattvas are not born into low families—such as the families of outcastes (caṇḍāla), basket-makers (veṇukāra), chariot-makers (rathakāra), or scavengers (puṣkasa).
Rather, they are born into only two types of families: either the brahmin family or the kṣatriya family.
In that regard, when the world holds the brahmins in high esteem, they are reborn in a brahmin family;
when the world holds the kṣatriyas in high esteem, [they are reborn in a kṣatriya family].
At that time, they were reborn in a kṣatriya family; nowadays, monks, the world holds the kṣatriyas in high esteem. Therefore, bodhisattvas are reborn in a kṣatriya family.
Having fully realized that purpose, the Bodhisattva, while residing in his excellent palace in Tuṣita, performed the four great surveys.
Having observed this, he became silent.
Thus, monks, those sons of the gods questioned one another regarding the Bodhisattva: "In which jewel of a family and in what kind of mother will the Bodhisattva take his stand?
Thereupon, some said: "This is the Vaidehī family in the Magadha regions; it is prosperous, flourishing, secure, and well-supplied with food."
"This is a fitting womb for this Bodhisattva.
But others said, "That is not fitting.
Why is that? Because—" (Vaidya 15)

It is of pure maternal and paternal descent, yet it is unsteady, fickle, and unstable; it is moistened by meager merit rather than consecrated by vast merit; it is a mere adjunct to a noble lineage, lacking abundance of parks, lakes, and ponds—like a border settlement or a mountain hamlet. Therefore, it is not suitable for that purpose.
Others, however, said: "Furthermore, this family of the Kauśalas possesses great vehicles, a large retinue, and vast wealth;
it is therefore suitable for the Bodhisattva’s descent into the womb.
Others also said: "That too is unsuitable."
For what reason?
Because the Kauśala family was born from the death and rebirth of a Mātaṅga; it is not pure by descent from its mother and father.
Its inclinations are inferior, and it is neither of noble lineage nor arisen from immeasurable wealth, jewels, and treasures.
Therefore, that is not appropriate for it.
But others said, "This royal family of the Ikṣvākus is wealthy, prosperous, secure, and well-supplied with food;
this is a fitting place for the womb of this Bodhisattva.
Yet others spoke thus: "Even this is not fitting."
What is the reason?

It is as follows: the royal family of the Vaṃśas is vulgar and fierce, lacking radiant splendor; it is obscured by the birth of a low-born man and has not been produced by the power of the karma of its own mother and father;
moreover, the king there is a proponent of nihilism.
Therefore, that too is improper.

Others also said: "This great city of Vaiśālī is indeed prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, delightful, and teeming with many people; it is adorned with railings, turrets, gateways, windows, balconies, gabled houses, and palace terraces, and with its flowering flower-gardens and rows of groves, it possesses the splendor of the city of the gods."
"She is suitable for the conception of this Bodhisattva.
Others said, "She too is unsuitable.
For what reason?"
For instance: they do not speak to one another with justice, they do not practice the Dharma, and they do not observe the proper conduct toward superiors, those of middle rank, elders, and seniors.
Each one thinks to himself, "I am the king, I am the king," and none of them accepts the status of a disciple or the authority of the Dharma.
Therefore, that too is improper.
But others spoke thus: "This family of Pradyota possesses great strength and great vehicles, and has achieved victory at the head of enemy armies;
it is therefore suitable for the Bodhisattva’s descent into the womb.
Yet others spoke thus: "That too is unsuitable."
What is the reason? For they are fierce, fickle, violent, harsh, and reckless,
and they do not regard the consequences of their actions.
Therefore, even that was unsuitable for the conception of this Bodhisattva in a womb.
Others spoke thus: "This city of Mathurā is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants;
it is the capital of King Subāhu of the Kaṃsa clan, the lord of Śūrasena. It is a fitting place for this Bodhisattva to take up residence in the womb."
But others say: that too is unsuitable.
For what reason?
Because that king was born into a lineage of false views, a king who is a bandit.
It is not fitting for a Bodhisattva in his final existence to be born into a family of wrong views;
therefore, that [birth] as well would be unsuitable.

Others also said: "In this great city of Hastināpura, there is a king born of the lineage of the Pāṇḍava clan, who is heroic, valiant, endowed with excellent physical form, and a crusher of enemy armies; his family is a fitting vessel for the Bodhisattva’s descent into the womb."
Others also said: "That too is improper.
Why?
Because the family lineage has been rendered utterly turbulent by those born of the Pāṇḍava clan."
Yudhiṣṭhira is said to be the son of Dharma,
Bhīmasena of Vāyu, and Arjuna of Indra.
"Nakula and Sahadeva are the sons of the Aśvins"—
therefore, that family also was not a suitable birthplace for this Bodhisattva’s conception in the womb.

Others said: "This city of Mithilā is exceedingly beautiful; it is the residence of King Sumitra of Mithilā. That king is endowed with a vast force of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; he possesses abundant wealth in gold, silver, jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, bullion, and precious goods; his power and prowess are such that all neighboring kings fear him; he is well-favored by friends and devoted to the Dharma."
"That family is suitable for this Bodhisattva’s descent into the womb.
Others said, "That too is unsuitable.
There is that King Sumitra, who is endowed with such qualities."
However, he was too old to be capable of procreating, and moreover, he already had many sons;
therefore, that family also was not suitable for the conception of this Bodhisattva in its womb.
Thus, monks, those bodhisattvas and sons of gods, surveying all the various high and noble royal families throughout the sixteen provinces of Jambudvīpa, saw that they were all possessed of faults.

While they were thus engaged in reflection and mental attention, a son of the gods named Jñānaketudhvaja—who was irreversible from awakening and had made a firm resolve for this Mahāyāna—addressed that great assembly of bodhisattvas and gods: "Friends, let us approach this very bodhisattva and inquire: 'In what kind of family, endowed with what qualities, does a bodhisattva in his final existence take birth?'"

"Excellent! they all said, and with palms joined in reverence, they approached the Bodhisattva and asked: "In what kind of qualities is a jewel of a noble family endowed, such that a Bodhisattva in his final existence is born therein?"

Then the Bodhisattva, having surveyed that great assembly of Bodhisattvas and the host of gods, said this to them: "Friends, there are sixty-four qualities by which a family is perfected in which a Bodhisattva in his final existence is born. What are these sixty-four qualities? They are as follows:"
That family is renowned;
that family is noble and non-injurious;
and that family is endowed with a noble birth.
That family is endowed with a noble lineage;
that family is endowed with a succession of ancestors; and that family is endowed with a succession of men of high birth.
That family is endowed with a succession of distinguished men; that family is endowed with a succession of men of great power and influence; and that family possesses many women.
That family becomes one with many men; that family becomes fearless;
and that family becomes neither dejected nor dispirited.
That family is free from greed;
that family is possessed of ethical discipline;
and that family is possessed of wisdom.
That family enjoys its pleasures under the supervision of ministers; that family enjoys its pleasures with the establishment of productive crafts;
and that family possesses steadfast friends.
That family does not cause harm to living beings belonging to the animal realm;
that family is grateful and appreciative of what has been done for them;
and that family does not act according to its own whims.
And that family becomes one that does not fall into faults;
and that family becomes one that does not fall into delusion; and that family becomes one that does not fall into fear.
That family is fearful of blame;
that family dwells without delusion;
and that family is coarse in its begging.
And that family is devoted to ritual action;
that family is devoted to renunciation;
and that family is devoted to generosity.
And that family possesses refined intellect;
that family possesses firm valor;
and that family possesses powerful valor.
That family possesses excellent prowess;
that family honors the sages;
and that family honors the deities.
That family is one that honors shrines;
that family is one that honors deceased ancestors;
and that family is one free from unrequited enmity.
That family becomes one whose fame resounds throughout the ten directions; that family becomes one with a great retinue;
and that family becomes one with an indestructible retinue.
And that family possesses an unsurpassed retinue;
that family is the eldest of families;
and that family is the most excellent of families.
That family attains mastery over its lineage; that family becomes one of great authority;
and that family becomes one that respects its mother.
That family becomes one that knows its ancestors;
that family becomes one characterized by the state of a *śramaṇa*; and that family becomes one characterized by the state of a *brāhmaṇa*.
That family possesses abundant wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses;
that family possesses abundant gold, bullion, jewels, pearls, silver, and various articles of property;
and that family possesses abundant elephants, horses, camels, cattle, and sheep.
That family possesses an abundance of female and male slaves, laborers, and servants;
that family is invincible;
and that family achieves success in all its aims.
That family becomes a lineage of universal monarchs;
that family becomes one accumulated through the assistance of former roots of merit;
and that family becomes one arisen from the lineage of the bodhisattvas.
And that family is irreproachable with respect to all faults concerning claims of lineage within the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and among the generation of recluses and brahmins.
Friends, it is endowed with these sixty-four qualities in the family in which a Bodhisattva in his final existence is born.
Noble ones, that woman into whose womb a Bodhisattva in his final existence descends is endowed with thirty-two qualities.
What are these thirty-two?
Namely, the Bodhisattva in his final existence descends into the womb of a woman who is well-known.

She was well-selected, faultless in her conduct, endowed with noble birth, endowed with a good family, endowed with beauty, endowed with a fine name, endowed with perfect proportions of height and girth, childless, endowed with virtue, endowed with generosity, with a smiling face,
acting with circumspection, clear-minded, disciplined, confident, learned, wise, honest, and free from deceit.

Into the womb of a woman who is free from anger, devoid of envy, free from stinginess, steady, composed, not talkative, endowed with patience and gentleness, endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, possessing little passion, hatred, or delusion, free from the faults of womankind, devoted to her husband, and perfected in all qualities, the Bodhisattva in his final existence descends.
Friends, it is endowed with these thirty-two characteristics that woman into whose womb a Bodhisattva in his final existence descends.
Furthermore, friends, a Bodhisattva does not descend into his mother’s womb during the dark fortnight,
but rather during the bright fortnight.

Thus, on the fifteenth day, when it is full— the full moon— under the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism, while his mother is observing the Poṣadha fast, the Bodhisattva in his final existence descends into her womb.

Then indeed, those bodhisattvas and those sons of gods, having heard from the Bodhisattva this very purity of family and purity of mother, became reflective and contemplative, thinking: "Which family could be endowed with such qualities as have been described by this noble being?

As they were thus engaged in reflection and contemplation, this thought occurred to them: "This Śākya clan is indeed prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, delightful, and crowded with many people."

And King Śuddhodana was pure in his mother, pure in his father, and pure in his wife; he was endowed with an unblemished lineage, possessed of a handsome appearance and excellent discernment, and was radiant with the splendor of merit.

Born into the lineage of Mahāsaṃmata, descended from the noble family of the Cakravartin dynasty, he was endowed with immeasurable wealth, treasures, and granaries; he possessed right view regarding karma and was free from sinful views.
He was the sole sovereign over the entire Śākya realm, honored and revered by merchants, householders, ministers, and courtiers, and was of pleasing appearance.

He was handsome, neither too old nor too young, beautiful, endowed with all virtues, skilled in the arts, knowing the proper time, self-knowing, knowing the Dharma, knowing reality, knowing the world, and knowing the marks; he was a king of Dharma who governed by Dharma, and he was the great abode of Kapilavastu for those beings who had planted roots of merit.
Those who were born there were also of that very same nature.

And King Śuddhodana had a queen named Māyā, the daughter of Suprabuddha, the lord of the Śākyas; she was young and fresh, endowed with beauty and youth, childless, having neither sons nor daughters, beautiful in form, and as lovely to behold as a painting.

Like a celestial maiden, she was adorned with every ornament; free from the faults of womankind, she was truthful, gentle, not harsh, not rough, steady, blameless, possessing a voice like the cuckoo’s, and not prone to idle chatter. She spoke sweet and pleasant words; she was entirely devoid of anger, intoxication, pride, arrogance, and resentment; she was free from envy, spoke at the proper time, was perfected in generosity, possessed of virtuous conduct, contented with her husband, devoted to her husband, and free from thoughts or mental attention directed toward other men.

Her head, ears, and nose were well-proportioned; her hair was soft, glossy, and even; she had a beautiful forehead and lovely eyebrows, free from frowns, with a smiling face. She was the first to speak, possessed of smooth and sweet speech, receptive to advice, upright, straightforward, guileless, and free from deceit. Endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, she was not flighty, not fickle, not talkative, and did not speak incoherently; she was characterized by little passion, hatred, or delusion.

Endowed with patience and gentleness, her intellect was well-guarded through her hands, feet, and eyes; her hands and feet were soft and youthful, her touch as pleasant as *kācilindika* cloth, and her eyes were as pure as the petals of a fresh lotus or blue water-lily. Her nose was red and prominent, her limbs were well-proportioned like a staff bearing a rainbow, and she was well-disciplined with well-defined major and minor limbs. Her body was beyond reproach, her lips were like the *bimba* fruit, her teeth were beautiful, and her neck was elegantly tapered.

In this world, she was well-adorned, gracious, radiant with the splendor of the *vārṣikī* flower, possessed of most pure vision, with well-proportioned shoulders and arms that were tapering, well-formed, and beautiful;

her waist was like that of a bow, her flanks were unblemished, and the circle of her navel was deep. Her hips were rounded, broad, smooth, and firm; her stature was like that of one whose joints are as strong as a diamond (*vajra*). Her thighs were symmetrical and well-set like the trunks of elephants, her shanks were like those of the *aiṇeya* deer, and the palms of her hands and the soles of her feet were like the color of lac dye.

Delightful to the eye, with unimpeded visual faculty, lovely and pleasing to behold, distinguished by the form of a jewel among women, like a body fashioned by illusion, bearing the name and convention of "Māyā," skilled in the arts, and radiant like an apsaras in the Nandana grove, she dwelt in the midst of the inner apartments of the great king Śuddhodana.
She is a worthy mother for a Bodhisattva;
and this purity of lineage which has been proclaimed by the Bodhisattva is seen only in the Śākya clan.
In this regard, it is said:
On the lofty Dharmoccaya palace, the pure being sat upon the lion-throne of the Excellent Dharma;
the Seer was surrounded by the gods of the assembly and by the Bodhisattvas of great renown.

As they sat there, this thought arose: "Which family is pure and fully conscious, such that it would be a fitting birthplace for a Bodhisattva? Where are the mother and father of pure nature? (Lal 3.2)

Indeed, surveying the land called Jambudvīpa and reflecting upon all those kṣatriya royal families that were great-souled yet possessed of faults, they beheld the Śākya clan alone as free from defect.

Śuddhodana was of noble birth in the royal family, belonging to a lineage of lords of men with perfectly pure body; his realm was prosperous, flourishing, free from turmoil, full of reverence, and inhabited by virtuous and righteous people.
Other beings as well in the city named Kapila were all of pure intention and endowed with the Dharma;
adorned with gardens, groves, and monasteries, the birthplace shone in the city named Kapila.

All were endowed with the strength of great athletes, possessed vast elephants and the nine precious gems, and had reached the perfection of training in archery and weaponry; yet they would not harm another even for the sake of their own lives.
Among thousands of women, the chief consort of Śuddhodana was indeed preeminent;
delightful like a form fashioned by Māyā, she was called by the name Queen Māyā.
Possessing a beautiful form like a daughter of the gods, with well-proportioned limbs and pure, radiant body—
there is no god nor any human who, having seen me, could ever find satiety.
She was neither stained by passion nor corrupted by hatred; her speech was smooth, gentle, upright, and affectionate.
She was neither harsh nor coarse, but mild, with a smiling face and free from frowns.
Modest, bashful, and practicing the Dharma, she was free from pride, unarrogant, and steady;
she was without envy, neither deceitful nor guileful, devoted to renunciation, and possessed of a mind of loving-kindness.
Observant of her actions, free from improper conduct, established in truth, and well-restrained in body and mind— indeed,
none of the abundant web of faults found among women exists in her at all.
No maiden exists in the world of humans, nor in the world of Gandharvas, nor even in the world of gods, who is equal to Queen Māyā; for how could anyone else be a suitable mother for the Great Seer?
For five hundred births, not fewer, she was the mother of that Bodhisattva;
and Śuddhodana was his father in each of those instances. Therefore, the mother was endowed with such virtues as were appropriate for her role.
Abiding by her vows, she remained like an ascetic, practicing her religious observances as a companion in dharma;
permitted by the king and having received a boon, she said, "Enjoy sensual pleasures for thirty-two months."
In whatever place she stands, sits, lies down, or walks, that entire realm,
including the world of the gods, is illuminated by the radiance resulting from her excellence of virtuous deeds.
There is no one— whether among gods, asuras, or humans— who is able to look upon her with a mind of passion;
for she is endowed with noble qualities and is beloved by all in her modes of conduct, whether as a mother or a daughter.
By virtue of the auspicious karma of Queen Māyā, the vast royal family flourishes;
even the territories of neighboring kings cease their incursions, and the king’s fame and glory increase.
Just as Māyā was a worthy vessel for her likeness, so did the noble being shine forth most brilliantly;
behold how that daughter endowed with virtues, together with her compassionate mother Māyā, appeared thus beyond compare.

In Jambudvīpa, there is indeed no other woman capable of bearing the Supreme among Men, except for the Queen who is endowed with extraordinary virtues and possesses the strength of ten thousand elephants. (Lal 3.19)

For thus do those high-souled sons of the gods and the bodhisattvas of vast wisdom describe Māyā, endowed with virtues, as the worthy mother of the one who brings joy to the Śākya clan. *Lalitavistara* 3.20.
Thus [it is said].
Thus ends the third chapter of the Śrī Lalitavistara, titled "The Purification of the Family."
START Parivarta 4 (Vaidya 22).
The Fourth Chapter: The Entranceway to the Light of the Dharma.

Thus, monks, having surveyed the family of his birth, the Bodhisattva sat down in the great celestial palace named Uccadhvaja in the Tuṣita abode— which measured sixty-four yojanas in length and breadth— and there he taught the Dharma to the gods of the Tuṣita heaven.
The Bodhisattva ascended that great celestial palace (*mahāvimāna*). Having ascended, he addressed all the sons of the gods belonging to the Tuṣita realm: "Gentlemen, assemble!
You shall hear from the Bodhisattva for the last time a teaching on the Dharma—the instruction on the practice of recollection of the Dharma called 'The Application of the Manner of Passing Away'."
Upon hearing these words, all the sons of the gods belonging to the Tuṣita realm, together with their hosts of apsarases, assembled in that celestial palace.

There, the Bodhisattva established a mandala-platform equal in extent to the vast dimensions of a world-system of four great continents; it was so variegated, so beautiful to behold, so well-adorned, and so exceedingly radiant that all the gods of the desire realm and the sons of the gods of the form realm conceived the perception of a cemetery within their own magnificent celestial palaces.
There, the Bodhisattva sat upon a lion throne adorned by the natural outflow of the ripening of his own merit, which was inlaid with many jewels and gems.

It was prepared with many layers of flowers; it was perfumed with the scents of many divine fragrances; it was incensed with the smoke of many excellent and precious incenses; it was adorned with many-colored divine flower-garlands; its splendor blazed with the hundreds of thousands of rays produced by many mani-jewels;
it was covered by a lattice of many mani-jewels; it resounded with the tinkling of many lattices of small bells; and it echoed with the resonant sound of hundreds of thousands of jeweled bells.

It was completely covered by hundreds of thousands of nets made of many jewels; it was overspread by hundreds of thousands of multitudes of various gems; it was hung with hundreds of thousands of silk streamers; it was adorned with hundreds of thousands of garlands and wreaths of silk ribbons; it was celebrated with the songs, dances, and instrumental music of hundreds of thousands of apsarases;
it was praised in hundreds of thousands of ways for its manifold virtues; it was protected by hundreds of thousands of world-protectors; and it was venerated by hundreds of thousands of Śakras.

It was a place where hundreds of thousands of Brahmās bowed down, which was embraced by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Bodhisattvas, and which was attended upon by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas from the ten directions;
it had emerged as the natural outflow of the ripening of the merit and the equipment of the perfections accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable kalpas.
"Thus, monks, having sat upon the lion-throne endowed with such qualities, the Bodhisattva addressed that great assembly of gods: 'Behold, sirs, the Bodhisattva!'"
Behold this body, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits;
behold the immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions— east, south, west, north, below, above, and all around—

who dwell in the sublime Tuṣita heaven, all facing their final existence, surrounded by hosts of gods, and manifesting the gateway to the light of Dharma that gladdens the deities through the manner of their descent.

By the empowerment of the Bodhisattva, that entire assembly of gods beheld those Bodhisattvas; and having seen them, they bowed with palms joined toward where the Bodhisattva was and paid homage by prostrating with their five limbs touching the ground. And thus they uttered this exclamation: (Vaidya 23)
"Excellent! This empowerment of the Bodhisattva is inconceivable, for by a mere glance we have seen so many Bodhisattvas."

Then the Bodhisattva again addressed that great assembly of gods and spoke thus: "Therefore, friends, listen to this entrance into the light of the Dharma, which gladdens the gods and concerns the manner of passing away, which these Bodhisattvas are speaking to these sons of the gods.
Friends, this hundred and eight entrance into the light of the Dharma must necessarily be proclaimed by a Bodhisattva at the time of his passing away before the assembly of gods."
What are these one hundred and eight?
Namely, friends, faith is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to an unbreakable intention. Serenity is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the clarification of a turbid mind.
Joy is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to success. Rapture is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the purification of the mind.
Restraint of the body is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the complete purification of the three types of bodily action.

Restraint of speech is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the complete avoidance of the four faults of speech. Restraint of mind is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the abandonment of covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. Recollection of the Buddha is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the purification of the vision of the Buddha.

The recollection of the Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the purification of the teaching of the Dharma. The recollection of the Saṅgha is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to entering the right path. The recollection of relinquishment is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the casting off of all acquisitions.

The recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the fulfillment of one's aspirations. The recollection of the deities (*devatānusmṛti*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the development of a noble mind.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to surpassing all bases of meritorious action involving material substrates.
Compassion is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the supreme state of non-violence.
Joy is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the removal of all discontent. Equanimity is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the loathing of sensual desires.
Contemplation of impermanence is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the complete transcendence of passion for the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.

Contemplation of suffering is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the total severance of aspiration. Contemplation of selflessness is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to non-attachment to a self.
The contemplation of peace is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the absence of incitement toward attachment.
A sense of shame is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to internal tranquility. A sense of dread of blame is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to external tranquility.
Truth is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to not deceiving gods and humans.
Reality is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to not deceiving oneself. Practicing the Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to taking refuge in the Dharma.
Taking refuge in the Three Jewels is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the complete transcendence of the three lower realms.

Gratitude is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the non-wastage of roots of merit already performed. Reciprocity is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to being beyond the contempt of others.

Knowledge of the self is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the absence of self-exaltation. Knowledge of sentient beings is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to impartiality toward others. Knowledge of the Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to practice in accordance with the Dharma.

Knowledge of the proper time is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to unfailing vision. The destruction of pride is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the fulfillment of knowledge.
An unobstructed mind is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the protection of oneself and others.
Absence of malice is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to freedom from remorse.
Resolute faith is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to the perfection of non-doubt.
Contemplation of the foul is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to the abandonment of thoughts of sensual desire.

Non-malice is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the abandonment of thoughts of malice. Non-delusion is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the dispersal of all ignorance.
Seeking the Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to reliance upon the meaning.

The desire for the Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the attainment of the world. The pursuit of learning is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the thorough investigation of the Dharma through proper reflection.
Right application is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to right practice.
The full comprehension of name-and-form is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the complete transcendence of all attachments.

The uprooting of the view of causality is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the attainment of knowledge and resolute conviction. The abandonment of attraction and aversion is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the state of being neither elated nor dejected.
Skillfulness regarding the aggregates is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the full comprehension of suffering.

The equality of the elements is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the abandonment of the origin [of suffering]. The withdrawal from the sense bases is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the cultivation of the path.

The patient acceptance of non-arising (*anutpādakṣānti*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the direct realization of cessation (*nirodha*). Mindfulness directed toward the body (*kāyagatānusmṛti*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to physical seclusion (*kāyavivekatā*). Mindfulness directed toward feelings (*vedanāgatānusmṛti*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the complete subsiding of all that is felt (*sarvaveditapratipraśrabdhi*).
Mindfulness directed toward the mind is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the contemplation of the mind as being like an illusion.
Mindfulness directed toward the Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to knowledge free from darkness.
The four right efforts are gateways to the light of the Dharma; they lead to the abandonment of all unwholesome states and to the fulfillment of all wholesome states.
The four bases of psychic power are gateways to the light of the Dharma; they lead to lightness of body and mind.

The faculty of faith is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to not being led by others. The faculty of energy is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to well-considered knowledge.
The faculty of mindfulness is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the state of having well-performed actions.

The faculty of concentration is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the liberation of the mind. The faculty of wisdom is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the knowledge of analytical discernment.
The power of faith is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to the transcending of Māra’s forces.
The power of vigor is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to non-retrogression. The power of mindfulness is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to being unshakable.
The power of concentration is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to the abandonment of all discursive thoughts.

The power of wisdom is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to the absence of delusion. The factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to the thorough knowledge of phenomena as they truly are.

The factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the fulfillment of all phenomena. The factor of enlightenment that is vigor is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to a highly discerning intelligence.
The factor of enlightenment that is joy is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the attainment of meditative concentration.

The factor of enlightenment that is pliancy is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the state of having accomplished what was to be done. The factor of enlightenment that is concentration is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the realization of equality.
The factor of enlightenment that is equanimity is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to a sense of revulsion toward all rebirths.

Right view is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the attainment of the correct method. Right intention is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the abandonment of all conceptualization, discrimination, and mental construction.
Right speech is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the realization that all syllables, sounds, noises, and paths of speech are equal to echoes.

Right action is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the state of being free from the ripening of karma. Right livelihood is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the complete cessation of all seeking.
Right effort is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to reaching the further shore.

Right mindfulness is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the state of non-recollection and non-mental engagement. Right concentration is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the attainment of the unshakable concentration of the mind.
The thought of awakening is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the non-interruption of the lineage of the Three Jewels.

The resolute intention (*āśaya*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the absence of longing for the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). The superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to taking as one's object (*ālambana*) the sublime qualities of a Buddha and so forth.

Application is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the fulfillment of all wholesome qualities. The perfection of generosity is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the attainment of the primary and secondary marks, the purification of the Buddha-field, and the maturation of stingy beings. The perfection of ethical discipline is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the transcendence of all unfavorable conditions and miserable realms, and the maturation of beings of immoral conduct.

The perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the abandonment of all ill-will, harshness, faults, pride, intoxication, and arrogance, and to the maturing of sentient beings with malicious minds.
The perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the undertaking of the stage of all roots of merit and to the maturing of indolent sentient beings.

The perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the arising of all wisdoms and superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and to the maturing of sentient beings with distracted minds.

The perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the abandonment of the views of grasping at objects, which are the darkness and blindness of ignorance and delusion, and it serves to mature sentient beings of poor wisdom. Skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to manifesting modes of conduct according to the inclinations of sentient beings, and it serves to prevent the destruction of all the qualities of a Buddha. The four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*) are a gateway to the light of the Dharma; they lead to the gathering of sentient beings and, once awakening has been attained, to the thorough investigation of the Dharma.
