The ripening of sentient beings is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to non-attachment to one’s own happiness and to tirelessness.

The upholding of the true Dharma is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the abandonment of the afflictions of all sentient beings. The accumulation of merit is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to being a source of sustenance for all sentient beings.
The equipment of knowledge is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it conduces to the fulfillment of the ten powers.
The equipment of tranquility is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it conduces to the attainment of the samādhis of a Tathāgata.
The equipment of insight is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it conduces to the attainment of the eye of wisdom.
The entrance into the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the attainment of the Dharma-eye.

The entrance into the reliances (*pratiśaraṇa*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the purification of the Buddha-eye. The attainment of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*) is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the retention of everything spoken by all Buddhas.
The attainment of eloquence is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to the satisfaction of all sentient beings with well-spoken words.
Receptive patience toward the conformable Dharma is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to conformity with all the qualities of a Buddha.
Receptive patience toward the non-arising of phenomena is an entrance into the light of the Dharma; it leads to the attainment of the prophecy of enlightenment.

The stage of non-retrogression is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the complete fulfillment of all the qualities of a Buddha. The knowledge of the transition from one stage to another is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the consecration for the knowledge of the Omniscient One.

The stage of consecration is a gateway to the light of the Dharma; it leads to the descent into the womb, the birth, the renunciation, the practice of austerities, the approach to the seat of awakening, and the [defeat of] Māra.
This leads to the manifestation of the destruction [of Māra], the awakening to enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the great final nirvāṇa.
Friends, this is that one hundred and eightfold gateway to the light of the Dharma which must necessarily be proclaimed by a bodhisattva to the assembly of gods at the time of his passing away.

Moreover, monks, while this chapter on the "Entranceway to the Light of the Dharma" was being taught by the Bodhisattva, eighty-four thousand sons of the gods in that divine assembly conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and thirty-two thousand sons of the gods who had previously performed the necessary preparations attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
And for thirty-six million sons of the gods, the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena became purified;
and the entire sublime Tuṣita abode was covered knee-deep with divine flowers.
Thus, monks, at that time, in order to further gladden that assembly of gods, the Bodhisattva spoke this verse:
"When the Leader, the lion among men, descends from his abode in the sublime Tuṣita heaven..."
He addresses the gods: "Abandon all negligence!"
Whatever divine arrays of delights have been conceived through splendor by the glorious one—all this is the fruit of the cause of every virtuous deed; hear now of this karma.
Therefore, O grateful ones, having exhausted here this unprecedented accumulation of merit,
do not go again to the states of woe where there is fear and the experience of suffering.
And this Dharma which you have heard in my presence—having generated reverence for it, practice it therein; you will surely attain infinite happiness.
All sensual desires are impermanent, unstable, and not eternal; even eons are not so.
They are like illusions and mirages, as fleeting as lightning and foam.
There is no satisfaction through delights in the qualities of sensual pleasure, just as there is none after drinking salt water;
those who possess noble, supramundane, and stainless wisdom are truly satisfied.
The assembly with the apsarases is like waves;
their dwelling together is joined by mutual passion, just like a musical harmony.
In this conditioned world, there are no companions, no friends, no kinsmen, and no retinue;
nothing follows behind or accompanies one except for well-performed karma.
Therefore, united and complete, with minds of mutual loving-kindness and beneficial intent, you should practice the way of Dharma; those who have practiced conduct well do not suffer.
You should recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as heedfulness;
you who are devoted to learning, ethical conduct, and generosity, and endowed with patience and gentleness.
Examine these phenomena fundamentally as suffering, impermanent, and non-self;
they proceed through the conjunction of causes and conditions, being ownerless and insentient by nature.
Behold whatever supernatural power I possess, as well as my eloquence and the quality of my wisdom;
all this is due to the cause of every virtuous deed, through moral conduct, learning, and heedfulness.
"Instruct yourselves in my teaching through virtue, learning, and heedfulness;
through generosity, self-restraint, and self-control, for the sake of the welfare, benefit, and friendship of all beings."
Virtuous qualities cannot be accomplished merely by the sound of words;
you must undertake practice, and act exactly as you speak.
Do not leave the opportunity to others; always strive with diligent effort.
No one gives anything away after having done nothing, nor does success come to one who has not acted.
"Remember, O former ones, the suffering that has been experienced for a long time in saṃsāra; neither nirvāṇa nor dispassion has followed, for [our conduct] was fixed solely on falsehood. (Lal 4.16)
Therefore, having obtained for a moment a friend, a suitable dwelling place,
and the hearing of the sublime Dharma, you should pacify the afflictions such as passion.

Free from pride, intoxication, and arrogance, always upright and gentle in speech, and free from deceit— those who are intent upon the state of Nirvana should apply themselves to the realization of the Path.
Dispel all the darkness turbid with delusion by means of the lamp of wisdom;
tear asunder the web of faults along with their latent tendencies by means of the thunderbolt of knowledge.
I could speak much more on the Dharma connected with your welfare, yet you would not abide by it; that is not the fault of the Dharma.
"So that I may attain awakening and rain down the Dharma that leads to the deathless,
you who possess pure hearts, come once again to hear the sublime Dharma! (Lal 4.21)
Thus [it is said].
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Gateway to the Light of Dharma," in the glorious Lalitavistara.
START Chapter 5 (Vaidya 28): The Fifth Chapter, "The Moving About."

Thus, monks, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, gladdened, and taken leave of that great assembly of gods with this discourse on the Dharma, the Bodhisattva addressed the auspicious assembly of gods:
"Friends, I shall go to Jambudvīpa."

While I was formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, I invited sentient beings through the four means of attraction— by generosity, kind speech, purposeful action, and consistency between words and deeds. Therefore, friends, it would be improper for me and would constitute ingratitude if I were not to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Then those sons of the gods from the Tuṣita realm, weeping, grasped the feet of the Bodhisattva and said: "O Noble Being, this Tuṣita abode, deprived of you, will no longer shine.
Then the Bodhisattva spoke thus to that great assembly of gods: "This Bodhisattva Maitreya shall teach the Dharma to you.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva removed the turban and crown from his own head and placed them upon the head of the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
And he spoke thus: "O virtuous man, after me you shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Then the Bodhisattva, having seated himself in the Tuṣita abode, again addressed that great assembly of gods: "Friends, in what kind of form should I descend into my mother’s womb?
Thereupon some said, "Friends, in the form of a young brahmin."
Some said: "In the form of Śakra.
Some said: "In the form of Brahmā.
Some said: "In the form of a Mahārājika king."
Some said: "In the form of Vaiśravaṇa.
Some said: "In the form of a Gandharva.
Some said: "In the form of a Kinnara."
Some said: "In the form of a mahoraga.
Some said: "In the form of Maheśvara.
Some said: "In the form of the moon."
Some said, "In the form of the sun";
others said, "In the form of Garuḍa.

Therein was a son of the gods belonging to the Brahmakāyika realm named Ugratejas, who had passed away from a previous birth as a seer and was non-retrogressive in his progress toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
He spoke thus: "A Bodhisattva must descend into his mother's womb in such a form as appears in the recitations of the mantras, Vedas, and treatises of the Brahmins. Furthermore, what is that like?"
Of the size of a magnificent elephant, with six tusks, resembling a golden net, most beautiful, with a deep red head, and possessing a form that was radiant yet fading—
having heard this description, the brahmin, who knew the truth of the Vedic scriptures, was drawn toward him, thinking:
"From this [womb] shall surely come one endowed with the thirty-two marks."
Thus, monks, having observed the time for his birth, the Bodhisattva, while still residing in the sublime Tuṣita heaven, manifested eight portents within the excellent palace of King Śuddhodana.

What are these eight? They were as follows: [the palace] was free from grass, stumps, thorns, pebbles, and gravel; it was stainless, well-watered, well-swept, undisturbed by wind, free from darkness and dust, devoid of gadflies, flies, moths, reptiles, and serpents, and strewn with flowers.
That house became level like the palm of a hand;
this first omen appeared.

And those birds dwelling on the Himalaya, the king of mountains— namely, the patraguptas, parrots, sārikās, cuckoos, swans, cranes, peacocks, ruddy geese, kuṇālas, sparrows, and jīvaṃjīvakas— possessing variegated and beautiful wings and speaking with charming and pleasant voices,

came and, standing upon the terraces, turrets, archways, windows, balconies, gabled chambers, and palace roofs of King Śuddhodana’s excellent residence, being joyful and filled with gladness and cheerfulness, uttered their respective cries.
Thus, the second preliminary sign appeared.

And all those various trees bearing flowers and fruits that were out of season in King Śuddhodana’s delightful parks, delightful groves, and delightful gardens, all became fully blossomed and in full bloom.
This third omen appeared.

And all the lotus ponds belonging to King Śuddhodana, which were places for enjoying the water, became completely covered with lotuses having hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of petals, each as large as a cartwheel;
this fourth omen appeared.
Furthermore, whatever vessels of ghee, oil, honey, molasses, sugar, and so forth were in the excellent palace of King Śuddhodana, they did not diminish even as they were being consumed;
they appeared always completely full.
This was the fifth prior sign that appeared.

Furthermore, all the musical instruments in the great inner apartments of King Śuddhodana’s excellent and preeminent palace— such as kettledrums, clay drums, cymbals, flutes, lutes, reed-pipes, harps, and percussion instruments— all emitted pleasing sounds spontaneously, even without being struck. This sixth prior sign appeared.

Furthermore, all the vessels containing gold, silver, jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, and other gems that were in the most excellent and preeminent palace of King Śuddhodana, shone forth in this way— entirely uncovered, stainless, pure, and full.
This was the seventh preliminary sign that appeared.
That house was illuminated on all sides by a stainless and pure radiance that eclipsed the light of the sun and moon and produced a thrill of joy in both body and mind;
this eighth omen appeared.

And Queen Māyā, her limbs bathed and anointed, her arms adorned with various ornaments, wearing garments that were exceedingly smooth, graceful, and excellent, having attained joy, gladness, and serenity, surrounded and preceded by ten thousand women,
approached King Śuddhodana as he sat comfortably in the music pavilion and took her place at his right side.
Seated upon an auspicious throne inlaid with a net of jewels, her face smiling, her frown vanished, and her countenance beaming with laughter, she addressed King Śuddhodana with these verses:
"O virtuous protector of the earth, listen to me, O King! I entreat you, O Monarch; grant me this boon today."
Listen to my intention, which accords with the joy and gladness of my heart and mind; be joyful and uplifted.
"O Lord, I take up the vow of excellent conduct and fasting, the eightfold *poṣadha*, with a mind of loving-kindness toward the world;
abstaining from harming living beings and always pure in intention, I shall treat others with the same love as I do myself. (Lal 5.2)

O King, with a mind free from theft and devoid of pride and greed, I shall not practice sexual misconduct. Established in truth, free from slander, and having abandoned harsh speech, I shall not engage in idle chatter or any unwholesome conduct. (Lalita Vistara 5.3)
Having abandoned malice, hatred, stubbornness, delusion, and pride; having eliminated all covetousness and being content with my own wealth;
properly engaged, free from deceit and hypocrisy, and without envy—I shall practice these ten wholesome deeds as they are.
O Lord of Men, do not harbor a thirst of desire for me, who am devoted to moral precepts and vows and well-restrained.
O King, let there be no demerit for you for a long night; indeed, rejoice in my observance of moral conduct, vows, and fasting.

"O King, let this desire of mine be fulfilled quickly today: standing upon the roof-terrace of the palace while the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is present, surrounded always by my friends, may I rejoice in happiness upon a soft, fragrant bed strewn with flowers. (Lal 5.6)
Neither chamberlains nor common men, nor children, nor ordinary women shall stand before me;
nor shall there be anything unpleasant to my sight, nor sounds or smells, but only pleasant, sweet, and beautiful words that I may hear.

Release all those who are in confinement or bound; make men wealthy with goods and garments. For the sake of the happiness of this world, give clothing, food, drink, chariots, draft animals, and horse-carriages for seven nights.
In this city, let there be no disputes, quarrels, or words of anger; let people have minds of mutual friendliness and hearts of benevolence and gentleness.
Let the men, women, and children, together with the gods, rejoice like those who have reached the Nandana grove.

O King, let there be no royal punishments nor soldiers, nor likewise unjust penalties, nor oppression, nor threats or beatings; with a serene mind and a heart of benevolence and loving-kindness, look upon all people as if they were your only son. (Lal 5.10)
Having heard the king’s words, which were most exalted, he said: "Let all this be exactly as you desire.
Whatever intentions have been contemplated by your mind, whatever boon you ask for, that I grant to you."

Having commanded his own assembly, the best of kings said: "On the summit of the finest palace, create a display of supernatural power—beautifully strewn with flowers, fragrant with excellent incense, and adorned with parasols, banners, and rows of palm trees."
Then twenty thousand warriors, skilled in battle, wearing variegated armor, and grasping iron arrows, spears, shafts, darts, and swords,
surrounded Dhṛtarāṣṭra— who possessed a charming voice— and stood there out of compassion to protect the queen for her safety.
Surrounded by women like a celestial maiden, her limbs bathed, anointed, and adorned with excellent garments and ornaments,
the queen ascended and sat down amidst the delightful sounds of thousands of musical instruments being played, like a daughter-in-law of the Maruts.
Resting upon a delightful couch, well-spread with various flowers and divine feet made of great, highly precious, and wonderfully variegated jewels,
she stood there with her crest-jewels and gems slipping down, like a celestial maiden indeed dwelling in the Miśraka Grove.

Then, monks, the four great kings, Śakra the lord of the gods, the divine son Suyāma, Saṃtuṣita, Sunirmita, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Sārthavāha the son of Māra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, the priest Brahmottara, the priest Subrahmā, Prabhāvyūhābhāsvara, and Maheśvara— [The above is the translation of the provided Sanskrit fragment.]
The deities of the Śuddhāvāsa realm, those who have reached the ultimate limit, and those of the Akaniṣṭha realm— these and many hundreds of thousands of other gods—

assembled together and said to one another: "Friends, it would be improper for us, and it would be an act of ingratitude, if we were to abandon the Bodhisattva while he is alone and without a second."

"Friends, who among us is able to follow the Bodhisattva constantly and continuously— from his descent, his stay in the womb, his birth, youth, childhood play, his life in the inner apartments, his witnessing of theatrical performances, his renunciation, his practice of austerities, his approach to the seat of awakening, his subduing of Māra, his perfect awakening to enlightenment, and his turning of the wheel of Dharma,
until his great final nirvāṇa— with a mind intent on benefit, with an affectionate mind, with a dear mind, with a mind of loving-kindness, and with a gentle mind?"
At that time, he spoke this verse:
"Who would venture to follow him, who possesses such excellent form, with a mind constantly full of joy?
Who, by means of merit, splendor, fame, and speech, would desire to bind him himself?"

He who desires to constantly delight in divine pleasures in the city of the thirty-three gods, accompanied here by supreme apsarases and the qualities of sensual desire—[may he attain] that face like the stainless moon. *Lalita-vistara* 5.17.

Likewise, in the excellent Miśraka grove, delightful and divine in its nature, let him who possesses stainless splendor take his pleasure in the city of the gods amidst heaps of flowers resembling gold dust. Lal 5.18.
"Whoever desires to sport with celestial nymphs in the Citraratha grove or likewise in the Nandana garden, amidst Māndārava flowers strewn upon the ground—let him follow this Great Being. (Lal 5.19)
Whether he seeks sovereignty over the Yāma gods, or even lordship among the Tuṣita gods,
or desires to become worthy of worship throughout the entire world— he shall follow after this one of infinite fame.

Whoever wishes to sport in a beautiful city of emanations or in the celestial abodes of the Vaśavartin gods— let them follow this possessor of supreme virtues, for by his mere thought, all activities of enjoyment shall be accomplished.
May Māreśvara, whose mind is not corrupted and who has reached the further shore of all forms of sovereignty,
and Kāmeśvara, who has attained mastery over his senses— he too shall go together with the Benefactor.

Likewise, he whose mind is intent on transcending the realm of desire in order to dwell in the city of Brahmā, and who bears the splendorous power of the four immeasurables— may he follow after the Great Being this very day.
Or rather, let those among men who possess an expansive mind regarding the domain of the supreme Wheel-Turner,
follow him who is a mine of jewels, who bestows fearlessness and happiness, and who upholds vast merit.
Likewise, let this lord of the earth— the son of a merchant, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast stores,
having a retinue and having struck down the hosts of his enemies— go forth together with the Benefactor.
Possessing physical beauty, wealth, sovereignty, fame, renown, and virtuous strength,
with speech that is authoritative and a voice worthy of being heeded— he who has approached Brahmā and Īśvara shall become a wise man.

Whoever desires divine and human pleasures, or all the happiness within the three worlds, or the bliss of meditative concentration and the bliss of solitude—let them follow the Lord of Dharma. *Lalita-vistara* 5.27.
Whoever desires the abandonment of passion as well as hatred, and likewise the destruction of the afflictions—
he, with a mind that is calm, tranquil, and serene, should quickly follow the path of the tamed mind.
May those in training, those beyond training, and likewise the Pratyekajinas, in order to attain the omniscient knowledge of the All-Knowing One,
roar with the ten powers like lions and follow after the Sage, that ocean of virtues. (Lal 5.29)
May those whose minds are set on closing the path to the states of woe and opening the path to the six realms of existence for the sake of the Deathless,
follow the course of the Eightfold Path— the end-maker of the paths of rebirth.
O Compassionate One, whoever desires to worship the Sugata and to hear the Dharma from him,
and who has also attained the virtues residing in the Saṅgha— let them follow this Ocean of Virtue.
In order to bring about the destruction of the suffering of birth, old age, and death, and to liberate [beings] from the bonds of saṃsāra,
let him follow that Pure Being who practices with a gait as pure as the ultimate limit.

Desired, pleasing, and beloved by the entire world, endowed with excellent marks and accumulated with supreme virtues, let the one of lovely appearance approach the wise one in order to liberate both himself and others. *Lalita-vistara* 5.33.

The wise person who desires to attain liberation—which consists of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom, and which is profound, difficult to see, and hard to approach—should quickly follow the King of Physicians. *Lalita-vistara* 5.34.
And these various other qualities— birth, happiness, and likewise liberation—
for the sake of accomplishing perfection through all such virtues, let the wise man follow the vow of the perfected ones.
Thus it is said.
Upon hearing these words, eighty-four thousand gods of the Cāturmahārājika realm,
one hundred thousand gods of the Trayastriṃśa realm, one hundred thousand gods of the Yāma realm, one hundred thousand gods of the Tuṣita realm, one hundred thousand gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm,
one hundred thousand gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm, and sixty thousand gods of the Māra host who had been produced by their former virtuous karma [all rejoiced].
Sixty-eight thousand Brahmakāyika gods, and many hundreds of thousands of gods up to those of the Akaniṣṭha heaven, assembled there; and others as well. (Vaidya 35)
Furthermore, from the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions, many hundreds of thousands of deities assembled.
Among them, those sons of the gods who were most noble addressed that great assembly of deities with verses:
"Come, O lords of the immortals, listen to our words regarding this arrangement which is such as it truly is."
Having abandoned the lack of delight in wealth and sensual pleasures, we shall follow this supreme, pure being who experiences sublime meditative bliss.
We pay supreme worship to the Great-Souled One, who is worthy of honor, both as he steps forth and while remaining in the womb;
we guard the Sage who is well-protected by merits, whose mind does not become corrupted even when he encounters an opportunity for descent.

With songs, musical instruments, and excellent melodies, we shall proclaim the qualities and virtues of that ocean of merit, bringing great joy to gods and men; hearing which, people among the world will generate the supreme mind for enlightenment.
O King, we shall make the palace strewn with flowers and fragrant with the gentle scent of the finest black aloe-wood incense;
having smelled which, gods and men alike become exalted, free from fever, happy, and free from disease.

With māndārava flowers, as well as pārijāta, candra, and sucandra blossoms shining from their vessels, we shall scatter these flowers over the one named Kapila for the sake of worshiping him who has arisen from his former auspicious karma. *Lalita-vistara* 5.40.
As long as he dwells in the womb unsullied by the three stains, and until he is born as the one who brings an end to old age and death—
for that long, with serene minds, let us follow this intention and perform worship for the possessor of wisdom.
Great and well-attained is the gain for gods and humans, who shall behold this Kinsman of the Sun taking his seven steps,
being supported by the hands of Śakra and Brahmā, and being bathed with perfumed waters— this perfectly pure Being.
As long as he conforms to worldly ways and dwells in the inner palace, destroying the afflictions of desire;
and as long as he has not yet renounced everything and gone forth, so long shall we follow him with serene minds.
From the time he takes up the grass upon the great mandala of the earth until he touches enlightenment after having struck down Māra,
and while he is being entreated by tens of millions of Brahmās to turn the wheel [of Dharma]— during all that time, we shall perform vast worship for the Sugata.
When the work of a Buddha has been accomplished and millions of billions of beings in the triple-thousandfold world system have been led to the deathless state,
when they shall proceed upon the path to nirvāṇa and reach the state of coolness— until then, we all shall not abandon this great-souled Sage.
Thus [it is said].

Then, monks, when the celestial maidens who are sovereigns of the desire realm saw the perfection of the Bodhisattva’s form-body, this thought occurred to them: "What kind of maiden will she be who shall bear this most excellent, supreme, and pure being?
Filled with curiosity, they took up choice and superior flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, and robes.

Having attained divine, mind-made bodies, sustained by the empowerment of the ripening of their merit, at that very moment they vanished from the celestial palaces and appeared in the great city named Kapila, adorned with hundreds of thousands of gardens, in the palace of King Śuddhodana, within the Great Hall of Dhṛtarāṣṭra which shone like the abode of the immortals; there they stood, wearing garments of shimmering cloth, adorned with the pure and stainless splendor of their beauty.

With their arms paralyzed by divine ornaments, standing upon the excellent bed and pointing out Queen Māyā with a single finger, those who had gone into the expanse of the sky addressed one another in verses:
"Having seen the beautiful form of the Bodhisattva, [we long for] the apsaras dwelling in the city of the immortals."
For at that time, such was their thought: "O, what kind of woman indeed is the mother of the Bodhisattva! (Lal 5.46)
And they, with flowers and garlands held in their hands, approached the king’s palace full of longing;
taking flowers and likewise unguents, they paid homage with their ten fingers joined in the añjali gesture.

With their garments loosened and their forms bathed in water, they bowed with a finger of their right hand toward Queen Māyā as she lay upon her bed, saying: "Behold well this form, which is beyond that of ordinary women!"
(Vaidya 37) "We here imagine that these other celestial nymphs are most enchanting and beautiful; yet, beholding this queen, you look askance at these divine forms. (Lalita Vistara 5.49)
This mother of the most excellent of beings is like Rati herself, endowed with similar virtues;
just as a precious jewel rests in a fine vessel, so too, O Goddess, does she serve as the vessel for the God of Gods.
From the soles of his hands and feet up to the top of his body, his limbs were exceedingly beautiful, divine, and surpassing;
though he gazed with his eyes, there was no satiety, and his heart and mind rejoiced ever more.
Her excellent face shines like the moon in the sky, and her body glows with radiance;
she is as stainless as the sun and as brilliant as the moon, and likewise light issues forth from her very being.
Just as well-born gold shines with a brilliant luster, so too does the complexion of the goddess shine;
her hair, resembling a swarm of excellent bees, is soft and possesses a fragrant scent at its roots.
Likewise, his eyes resemble lotus petals; his teeth are as pure as stars in the sky;
and his broad sides, O slender-waisted one, are like a bow, with flesh rising up so that no joints are visible.
His thighs and calves resemble the trunks of elephants, and his knees are well-formed and rise up in a smooth, gradual curve;
his palms and soles are even and deep red—clearly, she is indeed a daughter of the gods and nothing else.
Having thus observed the Goddess in these many ways, and having scattered flowers and performed a circumambulation,
Yaśovatī, the beloved mother of the Jina, returned in an instant to the city of the gods.
Then the four guardians of the four directions—Śakra, Suyāma, and likewise Nirmita—as well as the hosts of gods, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, asuras, mahoragas, and kinnaras, spoke: Lal_5.57 //
Go before the Supreme among Men, the Best of Beings, and provide him protection and guard;
do not harbor malice toward the world, nor cause harm to human beings.

Wherever Māyādevī was in that excellent palace, there they all stood together with their entire retinue in the expanse of the sky, weapons such as swords, bows, arrows, spears, and scimitars in hand, gazing down.
Knowing that the time for his passing had come, the sons of the gods approached Māyā with joyful hearts,
carrying flowers and ointments, and paying homage with their ten fingers joined in reverent salutation.
Depart, depart indeed, O Lord of Men, for you are of pure being; this is now the time for you, O Lion of Speakers!
Having generated compassion and pity for all the world, we entreat you for the sake of the gift of the Dharma.
Thus [it is said].

Then, monks, at the time of the Bodhisattva’s descent from his existence, many hundreds of thousands of Bodhisattvas— all bound to only one more birth and dwelling in the sublime Tuṣita abode— approached the Bodhisattva from the eastern direction in order to perform acts of worship for him.

Thus, from each of the ten directions, many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas— all of whom were bound to only one more birth and were dwelling in the sublime Tuṣita heaven— approached the Bodhisattva for the purpose of making offerings to him.
Likewise, from the gods of the Four Great Kings, eighty-four hundred thousand apsarases [approached], and so too from the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

From the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, eighty-four hundred thousand apsarases approached the Bodhisattva with the playing of various musical instruments and songs for the purpose of honoring the Bodhisattva.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva, having sat upon the Śrīgarbha lion-throne— which had arisen from all merit and was visible to all gods and nāgas—
in the great peaked pavilion, surrounded and honored by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, gods, nāgas, and yakṣas, [departed] from the excellent Tuṣita abode.
He moved, monks.

And as the Bodhisattva moved, monks, such a radiance was emitted from his body that by this radiance this trichiliocosm, so vast and extensive, was illuminated with a great, noble, and magnificent light such as had never been seen before.
It became completely suffused with a radiance that surpassed divine splendor.

Even those intermediate spaces between worlds— void, filled with ruin, darkness, and gloom, where even these two, the moon and the sun, though possessing such great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), such great majesty (*mahānubhāva*), and such great authority (*maheśākhya*), cannot with their light overcome their light, nor their color their color, nor their brilliance their brilliance— [were illuminated].
The splendor did not scorch, nor did it blaze;
yet the beings born there could not even see their own outstretched arms.
Nevertheless, at that time, a great and sublime radiance appeared.
And those beings who had been reborn there, being suffused by that very radiance, clearly saw one another;
they recognized one another and said:
"Indeed, friends, it seems other beings have also been reborn here!"
And this great trichiliocosm world-system underwent six types of movement and eighteen great omens: it shook, it trembled, it quaked; it swayed, it trembled violently, it quaked violently.
It shook, it shook violently, it shook intensely;
it trembled, it trembled violently, it trembled intensely;
it resounded, it resounded loudly, it resounded intensely.
He roared, he roared forth, he roared completely;
at the end he bowed down,
and in the middle he rose up.
It sank down in the middle and rose up at the edges;
it sank down in the eastern direction, and so forth.
The western direction rose up,
the western direction sank down,
and the eastern direction rose up.
It sank down in the southern direction and rose up in the northern direction;
it sank down in the northern direction.

In the southern direction, the earth rose up. At that time, sounds were heard that were gladdening, satisfying, lovable, inspiring confidence, beautiful to behold, refreshing, beyond description, inexhaustible, agreeable, and not causing terror.
At that moment, no sentient being experienced any affliction, terror, fear, or paralysis.
Furthermore, at that moment, the radiance of the sun and moon, as well as that of Brahmā, Śakra, and the world-protectors, was no longer perceived.
And all sentient beings born in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama became free from suffering and were endowed with every happiness.
And no sentient being was afflicted by passion, or hatred, or delusion, or envy, or avarice.
Whether it be conceit or hypocrisy, intoxication or anger, malice or burning anguish.
At that moment, all sentient beings became possessed of minds of loving-kindness and benevolence, regarding one another as their own parents.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of divine and human musical instruments, though unstruck, emitted delightful sounds.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods bore that great celestial palace upon their hands, shoulders, and heads.

And those hundreds of thousands of apsarases, having each performed their own musical concert, stood before, behind, to the left, and to the right of the Bodhisattva, and praised him with the sound of their singing:
"For you who have accumulated the merit of past deeds, for you who have arisen from virtue practiced for a long night!"
Today, a vast worship is being performed for you, who have been purified by the method of the true Dharma.
In the past, for many millions of eons, you gave gifts of your beloved sons and daughters;
that is the fruit of such practice of generosity by which these divine flowers have been rained down.
O Lord, having weighed his own flesh on a scale, he gave it away for the sake of that dear bird;
as the fruit of that practice of giving, he obtained food and drink in the world of hungry ghosts.
In former times, for many millions of eons, you maintained ethical discipline with unbroken vows;
that is the fruit of such practice of virtue, by which the unfavorable states and the lower realms have been purified.
In the past, for many millions of eons, you cultivated patience as the causal basis for awakening;
that is the fruit of your practice of patience: that gods and humans have come to possess a mind of loving-kindness.
In former times, for many millions of eons, you cultivated supreme and untiring vigor;
that is the fruit of your practice of vigor, by which your body shines like Mount Meru.
In the past, for many millions of eons, you practiced meditation in order to eliminate the afflictions;
that is the fruit of your practice of meditation, by which the afflictions do not oppress the world.
In the past, for many millions of eons, you cultivated wisdom that cuts through the afflictions;
that is the fruit of your practice of wisdom, by which this supreme radiance shines forth.
Armed with the armor of loving-kindness, you are the destroyer of the afflictions; you have arisen out of compassion for all beings.
Having attained supreme joy and equanimity, you are the Sugata who has become Brahma—homage be to you!

O Sage, whose wisdom is like the light of a torch, arisen from splendor, purifier of all faults, darkness, and delusion; you who have become the eye for the leaders of the triple-thousand world system, the guide upon the path—to you, we pay homage! (Lal 5.71)

Skilled in the supreme super-knowledges of the bases of psychic power, seeing the truth and trained in the ultimate goal, you have crossed over and ferry other living beings across; O Sugata, who act as a boatman, homage be to you!
Skilled in all supreme means and higher knowledges, you manifest passing away and the non-passing away of passing away;
you move in accordance with the arising of worldly phenomena, yet you are not defiled by the world anywhere.
Supreme and inconceivable is the gain for those whom you shall visit with your sight and hearing;
how much more so for one who hears this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā)—such a person will generate vast faith and joy.
Though formerly you dwelt in the Tuṣita abode, you have now arisen in this city in Jambudvīpa;
you shall awaken inconceivable millions of billions of living beings who are fast asleep due to their afflictions.
Today this city shall become prosperous and flourishing, crowded with tens of millions of deities;
it shall resound with the music of celestial nymphs, and the royal household shall hear its sweet strains.
Filled with the splendor of merit through her auspicious deeds, that woman was endowed with supreme beauty;
for her son is thus prosperous, outshining the three worlds with his glory.
No longer shall there be greed, faults, quarrels, or disputes among the embodied beings in this supreme city;
through the majesty of that future Best of Men, all shall possess minds of loving-kindness and be full of reverence.
The royal lineage of the king shall flourish, originating from a universal monarch of noble descent;
the city named Kapila shall become exceedingly prosperous and filled with treasuries of jewels.
The yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, guhyakas, and the hosts of gods and dānavas, including Indra—
those who stand as protectors of the Best of Men, for them liberation will soon come to pass.
Having accumulated merit by praising the Leader and having established love and reverence toward him, we dedicate all this toward awakening; may we quickly become like you, O Best of Men!
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Departure," in the glorious Lalitavistara.
START Parivarta 6 (Vaidya 43):
The Sixth Chapter, "The Descent into the Womb."
Thus, monks, when the cold season had passed and the month of Vaiśākha had arrived,

during the most excellent of seasons— the time of spring— when the best of trees were covered with leaves and the finest flowers were in full bloom, when cold, heat, darkness, and dust had vanished, and the ground was well-settled with soft green grass; at that time of the season, on the fifteenth day, the Eldest of the Three Worlds, honored by the world, looked out.

On the full moon day, while his mother had taken the *poṣadha* vows, the Bodhisattva— descending from the sublime Tuṣita abode, mindful and self-possessed— entered his mother’s right womb in the form of a pale white elephant calf with six tusks, its head marked by the color of an *indragopaka* insect and its tusks striped with gold, with all limbs and members complete and all faculties unimpaired.
And he descended, always moving to the right and never to the left.
Queen Māyā, while sleeping peacefully upon her bed, saw this dream:
a six-tusked elephant, resembling snow and silver, with beautiful feet, lovely tusks, and a deep red head.
The preeminent elephant, with his graceful gait and limbs and joints as firm as adamant, has entered her womb.
Never before have I seen, heard, or even experienced such happiness as this;
it is like the state of physical and mental bliss when one is absorbed in meditative concentration.
Then Queen Māyā, her ornaments and garments loosened, her body and mind refreshed, having attained joy, gladness, and serene faith, rose from the surface of her excellent bed.
Surrounded and escorted by a host of women, she descended from the pinnacle of the magnificent palace and proceeded toward the Aśoka grove.
Having sat comfortably in the Aśoka grove, she sent a messenger to King Śuddhodana, saying: "May the King come; the Queen desires to see him."

Then King Śuddhodana, having heard those words, with a mind filled with joy and his body trembling, rose from his auspicious throne and, surrounded by his ministers, merchants, courtiers, and kinsmen, approached the Aśoka grove; yet he was unable to enter the Aśoka grove,
for he felt as though his own body had become exceedingly heavy.

Standing at the gate of the Aśoka grove, he reflected for a moment and at that time spoke this verse: “I do not recall ever being so heavy-bodied as I am today when standing upon the head of one intoxicated by battle. Today I am unable to enter my own family home; what purpose would there be for me here, and whom could I ask? (Lal 6.3)
Thus it is said.

Then, indeed, the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm, having manifested half their bodies while remaining in the expanse of the sky, addressed the king with a verse: "Endowed with the virtues of vows and asceticism, worthy of worship in the three worlds, you have attained loving-kindness and compassion, and are consecrated by merit and wisdom."
Having descended from the Tuṣita heaven, the high-souled Bodhisattva has been conceived in the womb of Māyā as the son of you, O King.
Then, joining his ten fingers and shaking his head, the king entered, intent on showing honor.
Māyā, beholding him, spoke words brought forth by pride and arrogance: "Tell me, what shall I do for you? Speak, what is your purpose? *Lalita-vistara* 6.5.
The Goddess said: "Resembling snow and silver, surpassing the sun and moon, with beautiful feet and well-proportioned limbs, the great-souled one with six tusks,
a noble elephant with firm joints, adamantine in nature and handsome— having entered my womb, hear now the reason for this."
Free from darkness, I behold the three thousandfold world-system shining brightly, where millions of gods, both moving and resting, offer praise.
I have no fault of stubbornness, nor anger, nor delusion; endowed with the bliss of meditative concentration, I know my mind to be peaceful.
"Excellent, O King! Quickly summon those brahmins who are experts in the recitation of the Vedas and skilled in the rituals;
for they shall interpret my dream according to its true meaning. Will this bring me prosperity or will it be a calamity for my lineage?"
Having heard these words, O Brahmin, the king immediately summoned those who had mastered the Vedas and were learned in the recitation of the scriptures.
Standing before the Brahmins, he said: "A dream was seen by me; hear now its significance."
The brahmins said: "Speak, O Queen; what kind of dream have you seen?
Having heard it, we shall know."

The Goddess said: "Resembling snow and silver, surpassing the moon and sun, with beautiful feet and well-proportioned limbs, the great-souled one with six tusks, a noble elephant with firm joints, adamantine in nature and handsome— having entered my womb, listen now to the reason for this."
Having heard these words, the brahmins spoke thus: "A vast and inconceivable joy [fills us]; there is no evil for our family!
O son, you have given birth to one whose limbs are adorned with the marks, a high-souled universal monarch (cakravartin) born of a royal lineage."
Having previously abandoned his kingdom of desire and his home, he has gone forth into homelessness, indifferent [to worldly ties] and compassionate toward all the world.
He shall become a Buddha, a field of merit for the three worlds, and shall satisfy the entire world with the supreme nectar of immortality.
Having delivered their gentle words, partaken of the king’s meal,
and accepted the garments, the brahmins then departed from there.

Thus, monks, King Śuddhodana, having heard this from the brahmins who were experts in marks and omens, masters of the five sciences, and reciters of the manuals on dreams, was thrilled, satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheer; he gratified those brahmins with abundant food— both solid and soft, as well as delicacies— and after providing them with garments, he dismissed them.

At that time, in the great city of Kapilavastu, he caused alms to be distributed at the four city gates and at all the city squares and crossroads: food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink,
and clothing to those seeking clothing.
Vehicles to those who desire vehicles;
likewise, perfumes, garlands, ointments, beds, dwellings, and the means of livelihood to those who desire such things—all for the purpose of performing acts of worship toward a Bodhisattva.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana: "In which house might Queen Māyā dwell in comfort, free from affliction?
At that very moment, the four Great Kings approached King Śuddhodana and said to him: "O King, be of little concern; remain at ease and maintain equanimity."
For we are indeed constructing the dwelling for the Bodhisattva.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, approached King Śuddhodana and said this:
"The palaces of the world-protectors are inferior; those of the Thirty-three are supreme."
"I shall give a palace equal to Vaijayanta to the Bodhisattva."
Then the divine son Suyāma approached King Śuddhodana and said to him:
"Tens of millions of Śakras were struck with wonder upon seeing my palace;
I shall give this glorious palace of Suyāma to the Bodhisattva."
Then the divine son Saṃtuṣita approached King Śuddhodana and said to him:
"I shall give to the Bodhisattva that very same delightful palace where he formerly dwelt among the Tuṣitas, O you of great renown."
Then the divine son Sunirmita approached King Śuddhodana and spoke thus: "O King, for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva, I shall bring a magnificent, mind-made palace composed of jewels."
Then the son of the gods from the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm approached King Śuddhodana and said to him:
"Whatever beautiful celestial palaces there are anywhere within the realm of desire,
their radiance is eclipsed by the splendor of my own palace."
"I shall bestow upon you that glorious, auspicious mansion made of jewels; O King, I will bring it here for the sake of worshipping the Bodhisattva. (Lal 6.20)
I shall present a vast place, strewn with celestial flowers and perfumed with divine fragrances,
where the Goddess shall dwell.
Thus, monks, for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva, all the lords of the gods in the realm of desire had their respective residences constructed in the great and excellent city named Kapila.
King Śuddhodana, too, had a superior residence prepared, which surpassed that of humans yet did not reach the level of the divine.
There, through the power of the Great Array Samādhi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva manifested Queen Māyā within all those houses.
And the Bodhisattva, having entered within, sat cross-legged on the right side of Queen Māyā’s womb.
And all those lords of gods each perceived it thus: "The mother of the Bodhisattva dwells in my very house, and nowhere else."
In this regard, it is said:
Established in the Great Array Samādhi, he emanates inconceivable emanations.
The intentions of all the gods were fulfilled, and at that time, the king’s own desire was also completely realized.

Then, indeed, it occurred to some sons of the gods in that divine assembly: "Even those gods belonging to the realm of the Four Great Kings, having entered into human bodies, become weary of them and depart;
how much more so for other, most exalted gods, whether of the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, or Tuṣita realms?

How then can the Bodhisattva—who has risen above the entire world, who is pure, free from the stench of impurity, and a jewel among beings—having passed away from the Tuṣita host of gods, remain for ten months within the foul-smelling human body?"
"Abiding in the mother's womb."

Then, indeed, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Blessed One, how the Tathāgata has described the female sex as so utterly loathsome and so prone to passion;
yet, Blessed One, this is even more wonderful:

how is it that the Blessed One, who has transcended all the world, while formerly still a bodhisattva, having passed away from the Tuṣita host of gods, [descended] into a human body [which is foul-smelling]?"
"He has been conceived in the mother's right side, in her womb.
"Lord, I do not venture to say this, exactly as it was previously prophesied by the Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, do you wish to see the Ratnavyūha, the enjoyment of the Bodhisattva, which served as the enjoyment of the Bodhisattva while he was in his mother’s womb?
Ānanda said: "Now is the time for this, O Blessed One; now is the occasion, O Sugata."
May the Tathāgata show us that enjoyment of the Bodhisattva, seeing which we shall experience joy.
Then the Blessed One performed such a sign that Brahmā Sahāpati, together with sixty-eight hundred thousand Brahmās, vanished from the Brahma-world and appeared before the Blessed One.
Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and circumambulated the Blessed One three times, he stood to one side with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One, knowing full well, addressed Brahmā Sahāpati: "Brahmā, have you taken possession of that ten-month-long enjoyment of a Bodhisattva which formerly belonged to my mother when I was a Bodhisattva dwelling in her womb?
Brahmā replied: "So it is, Blessed One."
"So it is, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "Where is he now, O Brahmā? Show him to us."
And Brahmā said, "Lord, he is in the Brahma-world.
The Blessed One said, "In that case, Brahmā, show that enjoyment of the Bodhisattva which has been kept for ten months; they will come to know how much it is conditioned."
Then Brahmā Sahāpati said this to those brahmins: "Gentlemen, wait for a moment until we bring the jewel-adorned palace, the possession of the Bodhisattva."
Then Brahmā Sahāpati, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, vanished from before the Blessed One and in that very instant reappeared in the Brahma-world.
Then Brahmā Sahāpati said this to the divine son Subrahmā: "Go, friend, from this Brahma-world as far as the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods; raise a cry and let forth a proclamation:
'We shall bring the jewel-arrayed enjoyment of the Bodhisattva into the presence of the Tathāgata.'"
"Whoever among you desires to see him, let him come quickly."

Then Brahmā Sahāpati, together with eighty-four hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of gods, took up that jeweled array, the possession of the Bodhisattva, and having placed it upon a great Brahma-palace three hundred yojanas in height, [he departed] with many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of gods.
Having surrounded Jambudvīpa on all sides, he caused it to descend.
At that time, moreover, there was a great assembly of the gods of the desire realm who were about to go into the presence of the Blessed One.

Furthermore, that jeweled array, the possession of the Bodhisattva, had been prepared with divine garments, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine flowers, divine musical instruments, and divine articles of enjoyment.
He was surrounded by such great and powerful deities that Śakra, the lord of the gods, standing upon Sumeru (or in the ocean),
could only observe him from afar, having placed his palm like a parasol over his face, looking with a downward gaze or by means of a sidelong glance;
yet he was not even able to see him clearly.
Why is that? For the brahmins are gods of great majesty;
how much more so then Śakra, the lord of the gods, compared to the others—the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin!
They indeed fell into delusion.
Then the Blessed One caused that divine sound of music to vanish.
Why was that? Because as soon as they heard it, the humans of Jambudvīpa would fall into a state of madness.
Then the four great kings approached Śakra, the lord of the gods, and said to him: "O Lord of the gods, what shall we do? We are unable to see the Ratnavyūha, the enjoyment-asset of the Bodhisattva.
He said to them: "What can I do, sirs?"
"I too am unable to see him.
However, friends, we shall see him once he has been brought into the presence of the Blessed One.
Then they said, "In that case, O Indra, Lord of the Gods, act in such a way that his appearance may be swift."
Śakra said: "Wait a moment, friends, until the sons of the gods who have surpassed even the most transcendent ones pay their respects to the Blessed One.
Standing to one side with their heads slightly raised, they gaze upon the Blessed One."
Then Brahmā Sahāpati, together with those eighty-four hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of gods, took that jeweled array—the enjoyment of the Bodhisattva—and approached where the Blessed One was.
Now, that jeweled array, the enjoyment of the Bodhisattva, was beautiful, pleasing, and lovely to behold; it was square and had four pillars.
And above it was adorned with a gabled chamber;
its height was such that it was like that of a child six months old.
Furthermore, in the center of that gabled pavilion, a couch was arranged like a wooden board for a child six months old.

Moreover, this jeweled array, the possession of the Bodhisattva, possessed such color and form that there is nothing in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās that is its equal in either shape or color.
Indeed, when the gods saw him, they were struck with wonder;
their eyes grew dim.
And when he was brought into the presence of the Tathāgata, he shone, glowed, and radiated intensely.
Just as, for example, gold that has been twice refined and well-finished by a skilled smith is free from all impurities and defects,
even so did that gabled hall shine forth at that time.

Furthermore, in that very place for the Bodhisattva’s enjoyment, a couch was prepared; in the world with its gods, there was nothing equal to it in either color or shape, except for the shell-like neck of the Bodhisattva.
Indeed, the robe that had been worn by Mahābrahmā did not shine at all before the Bodhisattva’s cross-legged seat, just like a black woolen blanket beaten by wind and rain.
Furthermore, that gabled pavilion was made of uragasāra sandalwood, for which a single gold floor would suffice as the price for a thousandfold world-system.
That gabled chamber was smeared all over with such uragasāra sandalwood.
A second gabled chamber exactly like it was made, which stood within that first gabled chamber, unattached and unbound.
A third gabled chamber exactly like it was also made, which stood within that second gabled chamber, unattached and unbound.
And that couch was situated within that third fragrant gabled chamber, completely covered.
Furthermore, the color of that uragasāra sandalwood was like this: it was just like the hue of a noble blue beryl.
Moreover, above that fragrant gabled chamber, all around, there were as many flowers as exist that surpass those of the divine realm.
All those things arose within that gabled hall, having been obtained through the ripening of the Bodhisattva’s former roots of merit.
Furthermore, that jeweled array, the possession of the Bodhisattva, was of solid essence, indestructible, and like a diamond; yet its touch was as pleasant as the touch of kācilindika cloth.
Moreover, within that jeweled array, the possession of the Bodhisattva, all the various celestial mansions of the gods belonging to the realm of desire were clearly visible.

On the very night the Bodhisattva entered his mother’s womb, on that same night, from the lower water-element downward, he split the great earth for six million eight hundred thousand *yojanas* and caused a lotus to emerge as far as the Brahma-world.
And no one saw that lotus except for the Charioteer, the Best of Men, and Mahābrahmā of the hundred-thousand-fold world system.
And whatever vitality, essence, or flavor there was in this trichiliocosm,
all of that came to abide as a drop of honey within that great lotus.
Mahābrahmā placed it in a beautiful vessel of vaidūrya and presented it to the Bodhisattva.
Taking it, the Bodhisattva consumed it out of compassion for Mahābrahmā.

There was no being whatsoever in the realm of sentient beings who, having consumed that drop of vital energy, could digest it properly and with ease, except for a Bodhisattva in his final existence who has fulfilled all the stages of a Bodhisattva.
As the ripening of what karma did that drop of vital energy (*ojas*) present itself to the Bodhisattva?

Indeed, for a long time, while formerly practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva gave medicine to sick beings, fulfilled the hopes of hundreds of thousands of beings, and did not abandon those who had come to him for refuge.

Having constantly offered the finest flowers, the finest fruits, and likewise the finest essences to the Tathāgatas, to the shrines of the Tathāgatas, to the Saṅghas of the Tathāgata’s disciples, and to his mother and father, and only afterwards consuming them himself—
through the ripening of that karma, Mahābrahmā presented that drop of honey to the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, whatever exceedingly transcendent places for the manifestation of the delights of illusory qualities there were in that gabled hall,
they all appeared within it through the ripening of the Bodhisattva’s past karma.
Furthermore, within that jeweled array of enjoyments for bodhisattvas, a pair of garments named "Hundred-Thousandfold Array" appeared.
There was no being whatsoever to be found among the classes of beings to whom those would appear, except for a bodhisattva in his final existence.
And there were none of those most sublime forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or textures that were not visible within that gabled chamber.

If the enjoyment of the gabled hall is thus well-enjoyed, thus perfectly accomplished, thus well-finished both inside and out, and thus soft— just as, for example, the pleasant touch of kācilindika cloth is merely a point of illustration,
for no actual comparison for it exists.

Indeed, this is the nature of things for a bodhisattva: by virtue of his previous vow, this intention must necessarily lead the bodhisattva mahāsattva to take birth in the human world, to go forth from home, to realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
and to turn the wheel of Dharma.
In the womb of whichever mother he is to take birth, a peaked pavilion arrayed with jewels is first manifested within her right side;
subsequently, the Bodhisattva, descending from the Tuṣita heaven, comes to be born seated cross-legged within that pavilion.
For the body of a Bodhisattva in his final existence does not develop through the stages of the embryo— namely, the *kalala*, *arbuda*, *ghana*, and *peśī*—
but rather appears already fully seated, endowed with all the primary and secondary limbs and marks.
Furthermore, Queen Māyā, the mother of the Bodhisattva, while in her dream, perceived that a great elephant, a noble tusker, had entered her womb.

Furthermore, while he was thus seated, Śakra, the lord of the gods, the four great kings, the twenty-eight great yakṣa generals, and the one named Guhyakādhipati— from the yakṣa clan from which Vajrapāṇi originated— having learned that the Bodhisattva had entered his mother’s womb, remained constantly and continuously following him.
Furthermore, there were four goddesses who were attendants of the Bodhisattva—namely, Utkhalī, Samutkhalī, Dhvajavatī, and Prabhāvatī.
Having learned that the Bodhisattva had entered his mother’s womb, they too constantly and continuously protected him.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, also, having learned that the Bodhisattva was in his mother’s womb, followed him constantly and continuously together with about five hundred sons of the gods.

Furthermore, while the Bodhisattva was in his mother’s womb, his body became such that it was visible even from a distance of one *yojana*, and even from as far as five *yojanas*, like a great mass of fire on a mountain peak in the pitch-black darkness of night.
In the very same way, the physical form of the Bodhisattva, having been produced while in his mother’s womb, was luminous, handsome, serene, and beautiful to behold;
seated cross-legged in that peaked pavilion, he shone exceedingly,
like noble gold set upon lapis lazuli.
The Bodhisattva’s mother, standing in deep contemplation, beheld the Bodhisattva within her womb.
Just as great flashes of lightning issuing from a massive bank of clouds produce a vast radiance,
even so the Bodhisattva, while remaining in his mother’s womb, illuminated that first jeweled gabled chamber with his splendor, brilliance, and color.
Having illuminated it, he illuminated the second fragrant gabled chamber; having illuminated the second fragrant gabled chamber, he illuminated the third jeweled gabled chamber;
and having illuminated the third jeweled gabled chamber, he illuminated the entire body of his mother.
Having illuminated that, it illuminated the seat upon which he was sitting;
having illuminated that, it illuminated the entire house;
having illuminated the entire house, it emerged from above the house and illuminated the eastern direction.

In this way, the Bodhisattva dwelling within his mother’s womb illuminated the south, the west, the north, below, above, and all ten directions for the distance of one krośa in each direction with his splendor, majesty, and beauty.
Furthermore,

monks, at the time of forenoon, the four great kings and the twenty-eight great yakṣa generals, together with about five hundred yakṣas, came for the purpose of seeing and paying homage to the Bodhisattva.
For the purpose of attending upon him and hearing the Dharma,
the Bodhisattva, perceiving that they had arrived, raised his right hand and indicated seats for them with a single finger.
Those world-protectors and others sat down upon the seats as they had been assigned.
They beheld the Bodhisattva within his mother’s womb, his body like refined gold, moving his hand, shifting it, raising it, and setting it down.
Having attained joy, gladness, and serene faith, they paid homage to the Bodhisattva.
Knowing that they were seated, the Bodhisattva instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma.
And whenever they desired to depart, the Bodhisattva, knowing their thoughts by his own mind alone, would raise his right hand and move it; having moved it, he would stroke them,
yet he did not cause his mother any pain.
Then it occurred to those four Great Kings: "We have been dismissed by the Bodhisattva.
Having circumambulated the Bodhisattva and the Bodhisattva’s mother three times to the right, they departed.
This was the cause and this was the condition why, when the night had become tranquil, the Bodhisattva moved and stroked his right hand.
Having reflected and being fully mindful, he would again place that hand down.
Furthermore, whenever any women, men, boys, or girls came to see the Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva would greet them first.
Afterwards, the mother of the Bodhisattva.
Thus, monks, while the Bodhisattva was within his mother’s womb, he was skilled in greeting sentient beings.
No one—whether a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, a human, or a non-human—was able to greet the Bodhisattva first;
rather, it was the Bodhisattva himself who greeted them first.
Afterwards, the mother of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, when the forenoon had passed and the time of midday had arrived, Śakra, the lord of the gods, went forth;
and the sons of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven also went out and came to behold, worship, attend upon, and hear the Dharma from the Bodhisattva.
Seeing them approaching from afar, the Bodhisattva extended his right golden-colored arm and greeted Śakra, lord of the gods, and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
with a single finger, he indicated the seats for them.
And, monks, Śakra, lord of the gods, was unable to obstruct the command of the Bodhisattva.
Śakra, lord of the gods, and the other sons of the gods sat down upon the seats as they had been prepared.
Knowing that they were seated, the Bodhisattva instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma.
And toward whichever side the Bodhisattva extended his hand, the Bodhisattva’s mother would turn her face in that direction;
then it occurred to them: "The Bodhisattva is conversing with us."
And each one perceived thus: "The Bodhisattva is conversing with me alone; he is greeting me alone."
Furthermore, in that gabled chamber, the reflection of Śakra, the lord of the gods, and of the Trāyastriṃśa deities was clearly visible.
Indeed, nowhere else is the enjoyment of a Bodhisattva so perfectly pure as it is for a Bodhisattva dwelling within his mother’s womb.
And when, monks, Śakra, lord of the gods, and the other sons of the gods desired to depart,
the Bodhisattva, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, raised his right hand and waved it.
Having waved and considered this, he again, mindful and clearly comprehending, set it down.
And he did not cause his mother any distress.
Then, it occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods, and to the other gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three: "We have been dismissed by the Bodhisattva.
Having circumambulated the Bodhisattva and the Bodhisattva’s mother three times to the right, they departed.
And furthermore, monks, when the time of midday had passed and the time of evening had arrived,
Brahmā Sahāpati, surrounded and escorted by many hundreds of thousands of gods belonging to the Brahma-realm, took that divine drop of vital energy and approached the Bodhisattva.
O monks, the Bodhisattva turned his attention toward Brahmā Sahāpati and his retinue as they were coming to see, worship, attend upon him, and hear the Dharma.
Then the Bodhisattva raised his right hand, which was golden in color, and greeted Brahmā Sahāpati and the gods of the Brahma-realm.
With a single finger, he pointed out the seats.
And, monks, Brahmā Sahāpati had no power to resist the command of the Bodhisattva.
Monks, Brahmā Sahāpati and the other sons of the gods belonging to the Brahmā realm sat down upon the seats as they had been prepared.
Knowing that they were seated, the Bodhisattva instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma.
And toward whichever direction the Bodhisattva moved his hand,
Queen Māyā turned her face in that very direction.
Then, for each one of them individually, this thought arose: "The Bodhisattva is conversing with me; he is greeting me alone.
And when Brahmā Sahāpati and the other gods of the Brahma-realm desired to depart, they perceived it thus.
Then the Bodhisattva, knowing with his own mind the reflection in their minds, raised his right golden-colored arm and moved it; having moved it, he examined it;
and having moved it and examined it, he moved his hand in a manner that was discouraging.
And he did not cause his mother any distress.
Then, it occurred to Brahmā Sahāpati and the other sons of the gods belonging to the Brahmakāyika realm: "We have been dismissed by the Bodhisattva.
Having circumambulated the Bodhisattva and the Bodhisattva’s mother three times to the right, they departed once more.
And the Bodhisattva, mindful and clearly comprehending, placed his hand down.

Furthermore, monks, many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas came from the east, south, west, north, below, above, and from all ten directions, in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Bodhisattva, and to hear the Dharma and chant together in the communal recitation of the Dharma.
As those bodhisattvas arrived one after another, the Bodhisattva emitted light from his body and miraculously manifested lion-thrones adorned with arrays of light.
Having manifested them, he had those bodhisattvas sit upon those seats.
Knowing that they were seated, he questioned and cross-examined them concerning the detailed classification of this very Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva.
And no one else saw them, except for those sons of the gods who were of a similar lot.
Monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, by which the Bodhisattva emitted light from his body during the tranquil night.
Furthermore, monks, while the Bodhisattva was in her womb, Queen Māyā did not perceive any heaviness of body; rather, she experienced only lightness, softness, and ease.
Nor did she experience any pains arising from the womb.
He was not consumed by the fever of passion, nor by the fever of hatred, nor by the fever of delusion.
He did not entertain thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, or thoughts of cruelty.
Nor did he perceive or see cold or heat, hunger or thirst, darkness or dust, or even affliction.
Furthermore, no unpleasant forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tactile objects came within her range of perception;
nor did she see any evil dreams. Neither feminine guile, nor deceit, nor envy, nor the afflictions of womanhood troubled her.
Furthermore, at that time, the mother of the Bodhisattva was one who had undertaken the five precepts, was virtuous, and was established in the ten paths of wholesome action.
No lustful thought toward any man arose in the mother of the Bodhisattva, nor did any man’s thought of lust arise toward the mother of the Bodhisattva.

And whoever— whether gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, or those possessed by spirits— among women, men, boys, or girls, were in the great preeminent city named Kapila or in other regions,
they all became healthy and regained their mindfulness at the mere sight of the Bodhisattva’s mother;
and those non-human beings departed immediately.
And whatever beings there were who were afflicted by various diseases,
suffering from ailments born of wind, bile, phlegm, or their combination,
whether from diseases of the eye, or of the ear, or of the nose, or of the tongue, or of the lips, or of the teeth—
They were afflicted by diseases such as throat ailments, goiters, scrofula, leprosy, vitiligo, wasting, insanity, epilepsy, fever, swellings of the neck, pustules, erysipelas, and eczema; for them,
the Bodhisattva’s mother placed her right hand upon their heads.
As soon as they placed their hands [upon them], they became free from disease and went to their respective homes.
Finally, Queen Māyā would even pick up a blade of grass or a shrub from the surface of the earth and give it to sick beings;
upon receiving it, they became healthy and free from affliction.
And when Queen Māyā looked toward her own right side,
she saw the Bodhisattva within her womb,
just as the reflection of a face is seen in a perfectly pure mirror-disk.
And having seen it, she became satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness.
Furthermore, monks, while the Bodhisattva was dwelling in his mother’s womb, divine musical instruments were constantly and continuously produced by his power and resounded day and night;
and divine flowers rained down from above.
At the proper time the gods sent down rain;
at the proper time the winds blew;
and at the proper time the seasons and the constellations revolved.
He experienced a kingdom that was secure, well-supplied with food, and filled with joyful people;
and all the Śākyas and other beings in the great, excellent city named Kapila ate and drank.
They took their pleasure, they played, and they enjoyed themselves.
They gave gifts and performed meritorious deeds,
and they spent their time enjoying the pleasures of play at intervals during the four-month period, as if it were the Kaumudī festival.
King Śuddhodana, too, having attained the holy life and ceased his royal duties, followed the Dharma alone, being perfectly pure as if he had entered a forest of asceticism.
Monks, endowed with such a miraculous feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), the Bodhisattva remained within his mother’s womb.

Then, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, will you behold the jeweled array (*ratnavyūha*), the enjoyment of the Bodhisattva, wherein the Bodhisattva dwelt within his mother’s womb?"
He spoke;
he said: "May I see it, Blessed One! May I see it, Sugata!
Then the Tathāgata revealed it to the Venerable Ānanda, to Śakra, the lord of the gods, to the four world-protectors, and to other gods and humans.
Upon seeing this, they became contented, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness.
And that Brahmā Sahāpati, having once again raised it up in the Brahma-world, established it for the purpose of a shrine (caitya).

Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks once again: "In this way, monks, while the Bodhisattva was in the womb for ten months, thirty-six nayutas of gods and humans were brought to maturity in the three vehicles.
Regarding this, it is said:"
While the Bodhisattva, the supreme being, remained within his mother’s womb, the earth with its forests shook in six ways;
a golden light was released, all states of woe were purified, and the hosts of gods were filled with joy, for he shall become a treasury of the Dharma.
A magnificent great palace, beautifully constructed and adorned with many jewels, where the Hero, the Guide, ascends and dwells;
it shines, filled with the finest sandalwood incense, such that a single karṣa of it is worth as much as the jewels filling the three-thousandfold world system.
Having burst through the great trichiliocosm, a drop of lotus-essence emerged from Guṇākara.
For seven nights, it rose up in the Brahma-world with the splendor of merit; having taken that drop of Brahma-essence, the Bodhisattva named it.
There is no one among all sentient beings who, having eaten it, could digest it—save for a Bodhisattva as vast as a Brahma-eon.
Having consumed this drop of vital essence consisting of the merit and splendor of many eons, sentient beings proceed with their bodies and minds purified by wisdom.

Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors, having come at the three times of day to honor the Leader, the Bodhisattva, and having paid homage and made offerings, they listened to the sublime Dharma; then, having performed circumambulations, they all departed as they had come.
Bodhisattvas who desire the Dharma come from various world-systems; they are seen seated upon thrones of radiant splendor.
And having heard one another’s teaching of the supreme, most excellent vehicle,
they all go forth with joyful hearts, proclaiming a garland of praises.

And those women who were suffering from the possession of spirits—distraught in mind, naked, and smeared with dust—all regained their senses upon seeing Māyā; endowed with mindfulness and understanding, they went back to their respective homes.
Those who are afflicted by wind, bile, or phlegm, or by the combination of the humors; those tormented by diseases of the eyes, ears, body, or mind;
and those struck by various forms and kinds of maladies—when I place my hand upon their heads through my power of illusion, they shall become free from old age.
Or again, having taken a tuft of grass from the ground, he gives it as a magical illusion; all those who are afflicted become free from disease.
Having attained happiness and remaining unchanging, they go from house to house; while the King of Physicians, the source of medicine, is established within the womb.
At that time, when Queen Māyā beheld her own body, she saw the Bodhisattva established within her womb;
just as the moon in the sky is surrounded by stars, so too was the Protector adorned with the marks of a Bodhisattva.
Neither passion, nor hatred, nor delusion afflicts him; neither sensual desire, nor envy, nor malice.
With a contented mind, a joyful mind, established in gladness and cheerfulness, hunger, thirst, cold, and heat do not afflict him at all.
And divine musical instruments, though never struck, resound perpetually; they rain down beautiful, supreme, fragrant celestial flowers.
O King, behold! Humans and non-humans alike do not harass or harm one another there. (Lal 6.34)
Beings rejoice and play, and they offer food and drink; with hearts joyful and content, they proclaim sounds of "Ānanda! (bliss).
O Lord, at that time the earth was free from dust and calm; when the god sent down rain, grasses, flowers, and medicinal herbs grew forth in that season.
For seven nights in Rājagṛha, a rain of the finest jewels fell, so that poor beings took them and gave gifts, enjoyed them, and ate;
there was not a single being who was poor or suffering, and all beings rejoiced as if in the Nandana grove atop Mount Meru.
And that king of the Śākyas, having observed the fast on the day of the Poṣadha, performed no affairs of state, but made his sphere of activity solely the Dharma.
Having entered the grove of asceticism, he asked Queen Māyā: "What kind of physical bliss does the Supreme Being experience?"
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Descent into the Womb," in the Noble Lalitavistara.
START Parivarta 7 (Vaidya 57):
The Seventh Chapter, "Birth" (Janmaparivarta).
Thus, monks, when ten months had passed and the time for the Bodhisattva’s birth was at hand, thirty-two preliminary signs appeared in King Śuddhodana’s palace garden.
What were these thirty-two?
All the flowers became buds and did not bloom.
In the lotus ponds, blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-blooming water lilies, and white lotuses had emerged and formed buds, yet they did not blossom.
At that time, the trees bearing flowers and fruit rose from the surface of the earth, but though they were fully grown, they did not bear fruit.
And eight jewel-trees appeared.
And twenty hundred-thousand treasuries of jewels were seen springing up and remaining suspended in the air;
within the inner apartments, jewel-sprouts appeared,
and fragrant oils and perfumed waters, both cold and warm, began to flow forth.
And from the slopes of the Himavat mountain, lion cubs came again and again, roaring as they circumambulated the excellent city named Kapila and stood at the gates;
they did not harm any living being whatsoever.
Five hundred white elephant calves arrived and, with their trunks, touched the feet of King Śuddhodana.

Young divine boys wearing girdles were seen moving from lap to lap within the inner apartments of King Śuddhodana. Naga maidens with half their bodies visible in the expanse of the sky were seen hanging down, holding various articles for worship.
And ten thousand naga maidens were seen stationed in the sky, holding peacock-feather fans in their hands.
