Ten thousand full jars were seen circumambulating the great city of Kapilavastu;
ten thousand celestial maidens were seen standing with fragrant water-pitchers held over their heads;
and ten thousand celestial maidens were seen standing holding parasols, banners, and flags.
Many hundreds of thousands of apsarases were seen standing there waiting, with conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, and small drums attached to bells;
all the winds stood still and did not blow,
and all the rivers and springs ceased to flow.
The celestial mansions of the moon and sun, as well as the hosts of lunar mansions and luminaries, ceased their movement;
the constellation Puṣya became conjoined with the moon;
and King Śuddhodana’s palace became completely enveloped by a net of jewels.
The Vaiśvānara fire did not blaze;
and upon the gables, palaces, archways, gates, and ledges, various precious gems were seen hanging down; and the stores of fine cloth and the treasuries of diverse jewels were seen covered over.
The cries of crows, owls, vultures, wolves, and jackals vanished; instead,
the sounds of "well-born, well-born" were heard,
and all worldly activities throughout every land ceased.

The uneven regions of the earth, with their highs and lows, became level and even; and all the streets, squares, crossroads, roads, and market entrances shone brilliantly, strewn with flowers as if polished by the palms of hands.
Furthermore, all pregnant women gave birth easily and in perfect comfort.
And all the deities of the śāla groves appeared, manifesting their upper bodies from within the leaves and standing in a posture of bowing;
these thirty-two preliminary signs thus became manifest.

Then, indeed, Queen Māyā, knowing that the time for the Bodhisattva’s birth had arrived, approached King Śuddhodana during the first watch of the night through the very power and majesty of the Bodhisattva,
and addressed him in verses:
"O Lord, listen to what I say, my thought: after a very long time, the desire for a pleasure grove has arisen in me.
If you have no anger, no fault, and no delusion, may I quickly go to the grounds of the pleasure grove."

"You are exhausted here by your asceticism, devoted to a mind of dharma; and I have long been pregnant with a pure being. O best of trees, the śāla trees have awakened and blossomed; it is fitting that the gods should now go to the pleasure grove."
The preeminent season of spring, the adornment of women, resounds with the humming of excellent bees and the songs of cuckoos and peacocks;
it is pure, radiant, and variegated as the pollen of flowers swirls about. Grant us your permission graciously; let us go, do not delay!
Having heard these words of the queen, the lord of kings was pleased and, with a joyful heart, spoke to his courtiers:
"Harness the mounts— horses, elephants, and chariots— in rows."
Adorn Lumbinī, which is enriched with preeminent virtues!
Yoke twenty thousand elephants resembling Mount Nīla, with the hue of clouds;
let them be variegated with jewels and gold, covered with golden nets, their flanks beautiful with bells, and each a lordly elephant possessing six tusks.
"Yoke twenty thousand horses that resemble snow and silver, with hair like muñja grass and beautiful manes;
let them be royal steeds with golden-hued flanks, draped with networks of tiny bells, and possessing a speed as swift as the wind."

"Quickly mobilize twenty thousand men of the host, skilled in battle, heroes eager for combat, with swords, bows, arrows, spears, nooses, and scimitars in their hands; protect me along with my retinue with great vigilance."
"Have Lumbinī sprinkled with jewels and gold; clothe all the trees with various garments and gems.
Make it as variegated with diverse flowers as the Nandana grove of the gods. Having performed all this, report it to me quickly. (Lal 7.8)
Having heard these words, the attendants in an instant made the mounts ready and Lumbinī was adorned.
The attendants said:
"Victory, victory to you, O Lord of Men! May you live long; everything has been done as commanded. O Compassionate One, wait for the King."
And that lord of men, having become joyful in heart, entered his excellent palace and spoke thus to the women:
"Whosoever is dear to me and desires my pleasure, let her fulfill my command by adorning her own body."
Put on, full of joy, garments that are excellent, fragrant, sweet-smelling, multicolored, soft, and beautiful;
let pearl necklaces fall upon your breasts, and today display all your various ornaments.
"Prepare the tuṇa, paṇava, mṛdaṅga, vīṇā, veṇu, and mukuṇḍa instruments, and hundreds of thousands of delightful musical instruments!
O celestial maidens, bring forth great joy; having heard this sweet sound, even the gods will long for it. (Lal 7.12)
"Let Queen Māyā remain in that excellent single chariot, and let no other man or woman mount it there.
Let women clad in various armor drive that chariot, so that she shall hear nothing disagreeable or unpleasant. (Lal 7.13)
The magnificent and diverse splendor of the army—consisting of horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry—is heard at the king’s gate with a loud clamor;
indeed, the sound is like that of an agitated ocean. * * * * Lal_7.14 //
When Māyā had departed from her home and reached the threshold of the gate, hundreds of thousands of bells were struck for the sake of auspiciousness.
And that chariot was variegated and adorned by the king, as well as by thousands of gods with divine lion-thrones;
there were four jewel-trees endowed with leaves and flowers, and the delightful calls of swans, cranes, and peacocks resounded.
Upraised were the parasols, banners, and victory-flags, and the chariot was covered with nets of tiny bells and divine cloths;
the daughters of the gods gazed upon that chariot in the sky, praising it while making heard its divine and sweet sound.

When Māyā sat down upon the front of the lion throne, the three-thousandfold world-system shook in six ways; the gods scattered flowers and waved their garments in the sky, crying, "Today, the most excellent one in the world is born in Lumbinī! *Lalitavistara* 7.18.
The four guardians of the world drive that chariot, while Indra, the lord of the thirty-three gods, clears the path;
Brahmā goes before them warding off evil beings, and hundreds of thousands of immortals bow with palms joined in reverence.

The king, with a joyful heart, beheld that array, and it occurred to him: "Clearly this is a god of gods, for whom the four guardians, Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods perform such vast worship; clearly this one is of pure nature."
O Deva, there is no being in the three worlds—neither gods, nor nāgas, nor Śakra, nor Brahmā, nor the world-protectors—who could endure this worship;
his head would shatter and his life would perish. But this one, the Supreme Deity, endures all worship.
Then, monks, Queen Māyā was surrounded by eighty-four thousand horse-chariots adorned with every ornament,
and eighty-four thousand elephant-chariots adorned with every ornament; she was escorted by eighty-four thousand foot-soldiers who were brave,
heroic, handsome in form, well-armored, and clad in firm mail, as well as sixty thousand...
She was preceded by thousands of Śākya maidens and protected by forty thousand Śākyas born of King Śuddhodana’s own kinsmen— elders, youths, and those of middle age—
and she was surrounded by sixty thousand women of King Śuddhodana’s harem, who were performing songs, instrumental music, and the harmonious playing of various musical instruments and cymbals.
She was surrounded by eighty-four thousand celestial maidens,

eighty-four thousand naga maidens, eighty-four thousand gandharva maidens, eighty-four thousand kinnara maidens, and eighty-four thousand asura maidens, all adorned with various magnificent ornaments.
She went forth, followed by women singing various songs, playing instruments, and speaking in diverse tongues;
and the entire Lumbinī grove was sprinkled with scented water and strewn with celestial flowers.
Furthermore, all the trees in that excellent grove produced leaves, flowers, and fruits out of season.
And that forest was likewise adorned by the gods, just as the Miśrakāvana grove of the gods is adorned.
Then, having entered the Lumbinī grove, Queen Māyā descended from that excellent chariot; surrounded by the daughters of men and gods, she wandered from tree to tree,
strolled from forest to forest, and gazed from tree to tree, until in due course she reached that great fig tree (*plakṣa*),
the most excellent and supreme of precious trees, with its well-proportioned branches bearing leaves and flower-clusters.
It was blossomed with various divine and human flowers; it was draped with garments of various colors and possessed various fragrances of the most excellent and sublime scents;

it blazed with the diverse radiance of various jewels; it was adorned with roots, trunks, branches, and leaves made of every kind of gem; its well-proportioned and extensive branches spread over a ground surface as smooth as the palm of a hand, covered with well-distributed, broad blue grass resembling the neck of a peacock and possessing a soft touch like *kācilindika* cloth.
Standing upon the surface of the earth, having been previously inhabited by the mothers of former Victors, and celebrated in song by the celestial choruses— pure, stainless,

and radiant— he approached that Plakṣa tree while being hailed by hundreds of thousands of Śuddhāvāsa deities whose minds were tranquil and who bowed their heads with their matted locks and crowns hanging down in prostration.
Then, by the majestic power of the Bodhisattva, that *plakṣa* tree bent down and bowed.

Then Queen Māyā, like a flash of lightning in the expanse of the sky, extended her right arm, grasped a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, and stood gracefully gazing into the sky while stretching her limbs.
At that moment, six million apsarases descended from the gods of the desire realm and attended upon Queen Māyā, performing services for her.

Furthermore, endowed with such a miraculous display of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), the Bodhisattva remained within his mother’s womb. At the completion of ten full months, he emerged from his mother’s right side— mindful, clearly conscious, and unsullied by the impurities of the womb— unlike any other who is said to be "defiled by the impurities of the womb."

Moreover, monks, at that time Śakra, the lord of the gods, and Brahmā Sahāpati stood before him; filled with supreme reverence, they—mindful and clearly conscious—received the Bodhisattva in all his limbs and members, as he was enveloped in divine Kāśika cloth.

The peaked pavilion in which the Bodhisattva remained while dwelling in his mother’s womb was lifted up by Brahmā Sahāpati and the gods of the Brahma-realm, who brought it to the Brahma-world for the purpose of making it a shrine and for worship.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva was not held by any human being.
Then, at that time, the deities received the Bodhisattva first of all.
Then, as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, he descended onto the earth.
Immediately upon his descent, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva split the great earth, and a great lotus appeared.
And the two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda, with their upper bodies half-emerged from the surface of the sky, [stood there].

Standing there, two streams of water— one cool and one warm— burst forth and bathed the Bodhisattva. Led by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, many hundreds of thousands of other sons of the gods bathed the newborn Bodhisattva with various scented waters and scattered loose flowers over him.
And in the sky, two yak-tail whisks and a jewel parasol appeared.
Standing upon that great lotus, he surveyed the four directions;
having surveyed the four directions—
He surveyed with the lion’s gaze, the gaze of a Great Being.

Furthermore, at that time, the Bodhisattva, by means of his divine eye— which had appeared through the ripening of his former roots of merit and was unimpeded— beheld the entire great trichiliocosm, including its cities, towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals, together with its gods and humans.
He understood the mental conduct of all sentient beings;

having understood it, he surveyed them, thinking: "Is there any sentient being who is my equal in terms of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, or the practice of the roots of virtue?
And when the Bodhisattva did not see any sentient being in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system who was his equal, [he proceeded further].
Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva— like a lion, free from fear and terror, undaunted, and unshaken—

recalling and reflecting upon his well-considered resolve, and having known the mental activities of all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva, remaining unattached, took seven steps toward the eastern direction, [thinking]: "I shall be the precursor of all roots of virtue and all dharmas."

As he stepped forth, in the sky above, a vast, divine white parasol unattached [to any support] and beautiful yak-tail whisks followed him as he went. And wherever the Bodhisattva lifted his foot, there lotuses appeared.
Facing the southern direction, he took seven steps, thinking: "I shall be one worthy of offerings among gods and humans."
Facing the western direction, he took seven steps;
standing on the seventh step, like a lion, he uttered these words of joy: "I am the eldest in the world; I am the most excellent in the world.
This is my final birth."
"I shall bring an end to the suffering of birth, old age, and death.

Facing the northern direction, he took seven steps and declared: "I shall be unsurpassed among all sentient beings. Facing the downward direction, he took seven steps and declared: "I shall slay Māra and the army of Māra."
And for the sake of extinguishing the fires of hell for all those in the hells, I shall rain down a simultaneous shower from the Cloud of Dharma, by which they will become endowed with happiness.
He then took seven steps toward the upper direction.
And he looked upward, thinking, "I shall become one to be looked up to by all sentient beings.
As soon as these words were spoken by the Bodhisattva,
at that very moment, this great trichiliocosm was made known by his voice.
This is the nature of the superknowledges born from the maturation of karma for a bodhisattva.
When a Bodhisattva is born in his final existence,

and when he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, at those times he possesses such miraculous feats of supernatural power (ṛddhiprātihārya) that, O monks, at that very moment all sentient beings have the hairs on their bodies standing on end with joy.
And there occurred in the world a great earthquake, terrifying and hair-raising;
and divine and human musical instruments, though unstruck, resounded;
and [flowers] belonging to all seasons...
At that time, the trees in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were in full bloom and bore fruit;
from the pure expanse of the sky, the sound of clouds was heard,
and from the cloudless sky, a very fine, subtle rain fell gently.
Gentle, fragrant breezes blew, possessing a most pleasant touch and intermingled with various divine flowers of many colors, garments, ornaments, and powdered perfumes.
All directions shone forth, exceedingly clear, as darkness, dust, smoke, and mist had vanished.
And from above, from the sky, the deep, resonant voices of the Great Brahmās were heard, though they remained invisible.
The radiance of all the moons, suns, Śakras, Brahmās, and world-protectors was eclipsed;

and the entire trichiliocosm great trichiliocosm world-system became suffused with a supramundane light of many hundreds of thousands of colors, which possessed a touch of supreme bliss and generated bliss in the bodies and minds of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, all sentient beings became endowed with absolute happiness;

they were freed from all passion, hatred, delusion, pride, discontent, despondency, fear, greed, envy, and stinginess, and they abstained from all unwholesome actions. The diseases of sick beings were pacified, and the hunger and thirst of hungry and thirsty beings were relieved.
The intoxication of beings who were drunk with liquor has subsided;
those who were insane have regained their mindfulness;
and those beings who were deprived of sight have regained their vision.
Beings with impaired hearing regained their sense of hearing;
those with missing limbs or defective faculties became possessed of unimpaired faculties;
and the poor obtained wealth.
Those bound in fetters were released from their bonds;
from Āvīci downward, at that time, all the sufferings of every kind experienced by the beings in the hells were stilled.
Likewise, the suffering of the animals in the animal realm, such as devouring one another, [was stilled].
The suffering of hunger, thirst, and so forth of the beings in the world of Yama was completely stilled.

And when the Bodhisattva, immediately upon birth, took seven steps, at that moment— due to his attainment of the nature of reality through the practice of well-performed conduct over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons, and by virtue of his great heroism and great power— the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, residing in the world-systems of the ten directions, empowered that spot of earth so that it became composed of diamond.
Monks, the Bodhisattva, endowed with such great strength and impetus as soon as he was born, took seven steps in that direction where the great earth did not sink;
and at that time, all the intermediate spaces between the worlds were suffused with a great radiance.
At that time, there was a great sound of singing and dancing;
and at that time, immeasurable clouds of flowers, powders, perfumes, garlands, jewels, ornaments, and garments rained down from above.
Furthermore, all sentient beings were endowed with supreme happiness.
In brief, that activity was inconceivable when the Bodhisattva, who has transcended all worlds, appeared in the world.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "O Blessed One, the Tathāgata has become a source of wonder for all sentient beings."
Even while still a bodhisattva, he was endowed with marvelous qualities;
how much more so now that he has thus awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
O Blessed One, I, this very person, [would go] four or five times, ten times, even fifty times, a hundred times, or even many hundreds of thousands of times to the Blessed Buddha.
I go for refuge.

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "Furthermore, Ānanda, in a future time there will indeed be certain monks who are undeveloped in body, undeveloped in mind, undeveloped in virtue, and undeveloped in wisdom— fools."

Those who are unwise, conceited, agitated, arrogant, unrestrained, distracted in mind, overcome by doubt, full of skepticism, lacking faith, stains upon the ascetic life, and mere counterfeits of ascetics—
they will not have faith in this such purity of the Bodhisattva’s descent into the womb.

Gathering together in a secluded place, they will say to one another: "Behold, sirs, this lack of honor! While the Bodhisattva was in his mother’s womb—indeed, mixed with the mass of excrement and urine—such was his splendor!
And yet, it is said that when he emerged from his mother’s right side, he was entirely unsullied by the impurities of the womb."
How is this to be applied?
Those deluded persons will not understand that the body of beings who have performed wholesome deeds does not arise from the excrement, urine, or mucus of others;
indeed, the descent into the womb of such noble beings is truly auspicious.

Furthermore, it is out of compassion for sentient beings that a bodhisattva takes birth in the human world while still in the womb; he does not set the wheel of Dharma in motion while remaining as a deity.
Why is that? It is so that, Ānanda, sentient beings do not fall into indolence.
"The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has become a god,
whereas we are merely human beings;
we are not capable of fulfilling that state," they might think, and thus fall into indolence.
Furthermore, Ānanda, it will not occur to those deluded men, those thieves of the Dharma, that "that being is indeed inconceivable;
we must not treat him as an authority.
On the contrary, at that time, they will not even believe in the miraculous power of the Buddha's supernormal transformations.
How much more so, Ānanda, for a Tathāgata who has become a Bodhisattva, regarding the miraculous displays of a Bodhisattva!

Behold, Ānanda, how much demerit those deluded men will accumulate, who—overcome by gain, honor, and fame; clinging to excrement; overcome by gain and honor; and being of such a base nature—will reject the Buddha-dharmas.
Ānanda said: "O Blessed One, may it not be so; may there not be such monks in a future time who will reject these very auspicious discourses and oppose them."
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, they will reject such sūtras as these, they will speak against them, and they will perform many other kinds of evil deeds.
Furthermore, they will have no interest in the life of a śramaṇa."
Ānanda said: "But, Blessed One, what will be the destination of those such unworthy persons? What will be their future state?

The Blessed One replied: "They will go to that same destination as one who causes the awakening of a Buddha to disappear, and who reviles the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present."

Then, indeed, the venerable Ānanda, his hair standing on end with joy, said, "Homage to the Buddha! and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "O Blessed One, my body fainted upon hearing of this conduct of those wicked men."
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, their conduct will not be consistent;
indeed, those beings will be of inconsistent conduct."
They will fall into the great Avīci hell because of that improper conduct.
Why is that?
Ānanda, whatever monks or nuns, laymen or laywomen, having heard such sūtras as these, do not resolve upon them, do not have faith in them, and do not understand them.
Having passed away, they will fall into the great Avīci hell.
Ānanda, let them not treat the Tathāgata with disrespect.
For what reason?
"Ānanda, the Tathāgata is indeed immeasurable, profound, vast, and difficult to fathom.
Ānanda, for whichever beings, upon hearing such sūtras as these, joy and gladness shall arise, they have gained a great benefit through their attainment of serene faith."
Their life is not in vain,
their human existence is not in vain,
and they have practiced virtuous conduct.
They have taken up the essence,
they have been liberated from the three lower realms,
and they shall become sons of the Tathāgata.
And they have accomplished all their tasks;
their attainment of faith has not been in vain,
and they have properly distributed the alms of the kingdom.
And they have been inspired by those supreme beings;
the snares of Māra have been severed by them;
and the wilderness of the forest of saṃsāra has been crossed by them.
The arrow of sorrow has been extracted by them,
the basis for joy has been attained by them,
and the goings for refuge have been well-grasped by them.
They are worthy of offerings and deserving of worship;
their appearance in the world is rare;
and they, being worthy of offerings, should be upheld.
For what reason?
Because they, in this entire world, have faith in this very Dharma of the Tathāgata, which is thus contrary to the whole world.
Ānanda, those beings are not endowed with inferior roots of merit.
And those beings, Ānanda, will become my friends bound by only one more birth.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, someone may become dear and pleasing merely through hearing, but not through seeing.
"Ānanda, there is someone who is dear and pleasing even by sight, but certainly not by hearing. Ānanda, there is someone who is dear and pleasing both by sight and by hearing.
Regarding those [beings], Ānanda, for whom I might be dear and pleasing either by sight or by hearing, you should reach the conclusion that they are not bound to me by only one more birth."
They have been seen by the Tathāgata;
they are to be liberated by the Tathāgata;
they are sharers in an equal portion of qualities.
They are partakers of the qualities of a Tathāgata;
they are to be made lay followers by the Tathāgata;
they have gone for refuge to the Tathāgata.
They have been taken into the care of the Tathāgata.
Indeed, Ānanda, even in the past, while I was still practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, whatever beings afflicted by fear came to me and begged for fearlessness,
I granted fearlessness to those beings.
How much more so now that I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment! Ānanda, you should apply yourself to faith;
this is what the Tathāgata makes known.
Ānanda, when the Tathāgata has done what was to be done for you,
the thorn of pride has been extracted by the Tathāgata.
Ānanda, do people not travel even hundreds of yojanas just to hear of a friend?

Having gone [to them], they become happy upon seeing a friend not seen before; how much more so for those who, relying on me, plant roots of merit! Ānanda, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas will know: "These beings were former friends of the Tathāgatas."
"These [beings] are our friends as well.
Why, Ānanda, is a friend dear and pleasing to a friend?
Because that [friend] also...
It becomes dear;
that which is dear to a friend, even that friend's friend, becomes dear and pleasing as well.
Therefore, Ānanda, I announce and declare to you:
generate even a mere measure of faith;
we shall entrust [this teaching] to you.
"Knowing that those future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones will also fulfill our aspirations according to our wishes, we shall regard them as our friends as well.
Ānanda, it is just as if some man had an only son who was young and quick to grasp what is right."
And that man would have many friends;
when his father has passed away, he would not suffer, being well-supported by his father’s friends.
In the same way, Ānanda, whoever shall have faith in me, them I accept.
They are like my friends;
they have come to me for refuge,
and the Tathāgata has many friends.
And those friends of the Tathāgata speak what is true, not what is false;
I entrust them to those who speak the truth—
those who are the future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who are the friends of the Tathāgata.
"Ānanda, one should apply oneself to faith.
In this regard, I exhort you."

Thus, when the Bodhisattva was born, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of apsarases dwelling in the expanse of the sky showered Queen Māyā with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, garments, and ornaments.
On this matter, it is said:

At that moment, sixty thousand celestial nymphs of the gods, possessing voices as melodious as Mañjughoṣa, with the radiance of pure, stainless, and purified gold and the splendor of the moon and sun,
approached Lumbinī and spoke to Queen Māyā.
Do not give way to despair; be content, for we are your attendants.
"Speak! What is to be done? What shall we do? And by what means is your business to be accomplished?
We are your most capable attendants, established in a state of loving devotion.
Furthermore, be uplifted and filled with joy; do not give way to weariness."
Today the Goddess has given birth to a swift one, the supreme physician who destroys old age and death.
Just as these *śāla* trees are in full bloom and covered with blossoms,
and just as thousands of gods stand at his side waving their arms,
and just as this earth, together with its oceans, trembles in six ways;
And in every heaven you proclaimed, "You have fathered a son who is transcendent among men."
Just as a pure radiance shines forth, beautiful and golden-hued,
and just as hundreds of delightful musical instruments resound in the sky without being struck,
so too do hundreds of thousands of pure, auspicious gods, free from passion, [appear].
With joyful hearts, they bowed today to the one who brings benefit to all the world.
Śakra, Brahmā, Pāla, and whatever other deities there were,
standing by his side with hearts full of joy and satisfaction, bowed their arms;
and that lion among men, of pure vows, [pierced]—
Having emerged from the womb,
the Leader, whose vows were pure and who resembled a mountain of gold, went forth.
Both Śakra and Brahmā received the Sage with their hands;
a hundred thousand realms trembled, and a beautiful radiance was released.
Moreover, beings in the three lower realms are happy and there is no more suffering;
furthermore, hundreds of thousands of immortals scatter flowers and whirl them through the sky.
Endowed with the power of vigor, the earth, whose nature is like a diamond, remained steadfast;
there a beautiful and variegated lotus rose up, upon which the Leader stood with his feet, marked by the signs of the wheel.
Having taken seven steps, he with the voice of Brahmā uttered the most excellent sound:
"I shall be the supreme physician, the best of beings, who destroys old age and death."
Standing in the expanse of the sky, Brahmottama and Śakradevottama, the supreme among gods,
bathed the Leader with pure, radiant, and serene waters of fragrant perfumes;
moreover, the kings of the nagas, remaining in the intermediate space, released two auspicious streams of water, one cool and one warm.
Hundreds of thousands of immortals bathed the Leader with perfumed waters.
And the world-protectors, greatly agitated, supported [the earth] with their beautiful hands;
this triple-thousandfold world-system, including all that is moving and unmoving, trembled.
Radiant light was released and the lower realms were purified;
those afflictions and sufferings were stilled when the Guide of the World was born.
When this Leader of Men was born, the Maruts scattered flowers;
the hero, endowed with strength and valor, took seven steps.
Wherever he places his feet upon the ground, auspicious and excellent lotuses,
adorned with every kind of jewel, sprout up from the earth.
When he had taken seven steps and uttered a voice like that of Brahmā,
he rose up like a supreme physician who destroys old age and death.
Having fearlessly surveyed the directions, he then uttered words full of meaning:
"I am the eldest of the entire world, the most excellent (the Guide in the world); and this birth of mine is the last. (Lal 7.35)
And a laugh was released by the Leader of Men, along with the world-protectors, the Maruts, and Indra;
he who acts for the benefit of the world was consecrated by those with serene minds with excellent fragrant waters. *Lalita-vistara* 7.36.
Moreover, all the lords of serpents together bathed him with streams of intense fragrant spray;
other millions of gods also stood by.
In the intermediate space, they bathed the Self-Existent One, the Victor supreme in fragrance.
And white, vast parasols, yak-tail whisks, and beautiful garments—
gods who had gone into the sky were bathing that bull among men.
Five hundred women of noble lineage gave birth.
A man, having gone quickly, joyfully said to Śuddhodana: "O King, a great increase of fortune has occurred; a son adorned with the marks of excellence has been born!"
This manifest Lord of Universal Monarchs has increased the glory of the great jewel of his lineage;
and there shall be no rival enemy in Jambudvīpa, for he shall hold the single umbrella of sovereignty.
The second person, having gone to King Śuddhodana and established [the child] within him, grew up gradually and extensively, O Lord, in the royal family of the Śākyas.
Twenty-five thousand sons were born in the houses of the Śākyas;
all were endowed with strength, equal in vigor, and invincible by others.
Another man said: "O Lord, hear my joyful cry!
Eight hundred sons of maidservants, headed by Chandaka, have been born;
moreover, ten thousand horses, the companions of Kaṇṭhaka, have been born."
The foremost among excellent horses were golden-hued, with beautiful manes, and most noble.
And twenty thousand frontier kings, as well as regional rulers, followed at the soles of the king's feet, saying: "Excellent, O Lord! Victory to you!
Grant us your command; we shall go—what shall we do, O King?"
O Lord, you have attained mastery here; we are your servants, O Victorious One!
And twenty thousand excellent elephants, radiant with nets of gold, approached the king’s palace swiftly, trumpeting in the sky;
sixty hundred [elephants] were born, headed by Kṛṣṇa, Śabala, Vatsa, and Gopāmukha.
This auspicious news has also reached the supreme God of Gods: that prosperity has come to the king’s house.
Moreover, O King, go and see for yourself, O Lord (the Lord of the splendor of merit), all those thousands of men and gods who are filled with joy upon seeing the virtues that have arisen.
Having set out for the supreme enlightenment free from sorrow, may you quickly become Jinas on this earth.
Thus [it is said].
Thus, monks, at the moment the Bodhisattva was born, the distribution of gifts proceeded even more extensively;
five hundred women of noble family gave birth,
and ten thousand maidens, headed by Yaśovatī, were born.
There were eight hundred female slaves and eight hundred male slaves headed by Chandaka;
ten thousand mares and ten thousand colts headed by Kaṇṭhaka;
and five thousand female elephants and five thousand male elephants were born.
All of those were planted by King Śuddhodana and given for the prince’s play.

In the midst of four hundred thousand million continents, a *aśvattha* tree-staff appeared upon a spot of earth, and within the inner continent (*antardvīpa*), a sandalwood grove appeared through the very power of the Bodhisattva for the Bodhisattva’s enjoyment.
Furthermore, five hundred gardens appeared all around the city for the Bodhisattva’s enjoyment.
And five thousand treasures, having risen up from the surface of the earth, revealed their faces.
Thus, whatever purposes King Śuddhodana had intended, they all became fulfilled according to his intentions; they were completely accomplished.
Then this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana: "What name shall I give to the prince?
Then it occurred to him: "As soon as he was born, all my purposes were fully accomplished;
therefore, I shall give him the name Sarvārthasiddha (Accomplisher of All Aims)."
Then the king, having honored the Bodhisattva with great reverence, gave him the name Sarvārthasiddha, saying, "Let this prince be known by the name Sarvārthasiddha."
Thus, monks, when the Bodhisattva was born, the side of his mother’s womb remained uninjured and unimpaired, as it was before, so it was after.
Three wells of flowing water appeared, as well as lotus ponds of fragrant oil.

Five thousand celestial nymphs, carrying oils perfumed with divine scents, approached the mother of the Bodhisattva and, having greeted her on the occasion of this auspicious birth, inquired whether she was free from fatigue and whether her body was at ease.
Five thousand celestial nymphs, carrying divine ointments, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother and, as she had given birth to one so well-born, inquired whether her body was free from fatigue.

Five thousand celestial nymphs, carrying jars filled with divine scented water, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother and, as she had given birth to one so well-born, inquired whether her body was free from fatigue.

Five thousand apsarases, carrying divine ointments, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother and inquired whether she had given birth well and whether her body was free from fatigue. Five thousand apsarases, carrying divine garments for a child, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother and inquired whether she had given birth well and whether her body was free from fatigue.
Five thousand apsarases, bearing divine ornaments for children, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother and inquired whether she had given birth auspiciously and whether her body was free from fatigue.

Five thousand apsarases, with the sounding of divine musical instruments and songs, approached the Bodhisattva’s mother and inquired whether she had given birth auspiciously and whether her body was free from fatigue.

And as many non-Buddhist seers possessing the five superknowledges as were here in Jambudvīpa, they all came through the expanse of the sky, stood before King Śuddhodana, and proclaimed cries of victory and prosperity.
Thus, monks, as soon as he was born, for seven nights the Bodhisattva was honored, revered, and esteemed in the Lumbinī grove with divine and human musical instruments, cymbals, and drums.
He was honored,
and various kinds of food— hard foods, soft foods, and delicacies—
were distributed.
And all the hosts of Śākyas gathered together, raised shouts of joy, gave gifts,
and performed meritorious deeds.
And thirty-two hundred thousand brahmins were satisfied day after day;
whatever each of them required, that was given to them.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, and Brahmā, having manifested in the form of young brahmins within that assembly of brahmins, sat upon the foremost seats and recited this auspicious verse:
Just as the states of woe have become peaceful and the entire world has become happy,
he has surely been born as one who brings happiness and will establish the world in bliss.
Just as the light of the sun, the moon, and the gods, though free from darkness,
does not shine when overwhelmed [by another light], this is surely born from the radiance of merit.
Just as those without eyes see and those deprived of hearing hear,
so shall he who possesses mindfulness become a shrine for the world, even though he is like one who is insane.
Just as the afflictions do not oppress this world born of loving-kindness,
he will undoubtedly become worthy of worship by millions of Brahmās.
Since the śāla trees are in full bloom and the earth stands so level,
it is certain that he will become an omniscient one, worthy of worship by the entire world.
Just as the world is undisturbed and as the great lotus has arisen,
there is no doubt that he of great majesty will become the Lord of the World.
And just as gentle breezes, perfumed with divine fragrances,
soothe the ailments of sentient beings, so shall he become the King of Physicians.
Just as these gods of the realm of form, free from passion,
pay homage with palms joined, he shall become one worthy of offerings.
Just as humans see the gods and the gods see humans, they will not harm one another; he shall become a caravan leader.
Just as the fire has been extinguished and all the rivers have stood still,
and the earth trembles subtly— he shall become a seer of reality.
Thus it is said.
Thus, monks, seven days after the Bodhisattva was born, his mother, Queen Māyā, passed away;
having passed away, she was reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Now, monks, it might occur to you that Queen Māyā died because of some fault of the Bodhisattva. But this is not so.
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?
Because that was the maximum limit of her lifespan.
Monks, even for the Bodhisattvas of the past, their mothers passed away seven nights after they were born.
For what reason?
Because when a Bodhisattva has grown and his faculties are fully developed, the heart of his mother would burst as he departs from home.
"Thus, monks, on the seventh day, with a grand array exactly like that with which Queen Māyā had previously departed from the great city of Kapilavastu for the pleasure gardens,
the Bodhisattva entered the great city of Kapilavastu with a magnificent array a hundred thousand times more vast."
And as he entered, five thousand full jars filled with scented water were carried before him;
likewise, five thousand maidens carrying peacock-feather fans went before him,
and five thousand maidens carrying palm-leaf fans went before him.
Five thousand maidens, carrying water-pitchers filled with scented water, went before him, sprinkling the path;
and five thousand maidens, carrying various caskets, went before him.
And five thousand maidens, holding various multicolored hanging garlands,
went before him; and five thousand maidens, holding auspicious jewel ornaments, went before him, clearing the path.
Five thousand maidens carrying auspicious thrones went before him; five thousand brahmins carrying bells went before him, proclaiming auspicious sounds;
and twenty thousand elephants adorned with every ornament went before him.
Twenty thousand horses, covered with golden ornaments and adorned with every kind of decoration, went before him.
Eighty thousand chariots, beautifully adorned with raised parasols, banners, flags, and networks of tinkling bells, followed behind the Bodhisattva.
Forty thousand foot soldiers—brave, heroic, handsome in form, and clad in firm, armored mail—followed the Bodhisattva as he proceeded.

And from the expanse of the sky, immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of millions of sons of the gods from the desire realm and the form realm, possessing various supernormal powers, followed the Bodhisattva while performing worship with many kinds of diverse arrays. And upon that most excellent, supreme chariot, the Bodhisattva was mounted.
He was adorned by many deities of the desire realm with magnificent arrays.
Twenty thousand celestial maidens, adorned with every ornament and supported by jeweled cords, drew that chariot.
Between every two apsarases stood one human maiden, and between every two human maidens stood one apsaras.
And the apsarases did not smell the raw odor of human women,
nor did humans fall into negligence upon seeing the form of the apsarases, all this being due to the majestic power of the Bodhisattva.
Thus, monks, in the excellent city named Kapila, five hundred Śākyas, numbering about five hundred, had each constructed a house for the sake of the Bodhisattva.

As the Bodhisattva was entering the city, they stood at the doors of their respective houses with palms joined in reverence, bodies bowed low, and full of respect, saying: "Enter here, O Sarvārthasiddha! Enter here, O God beyond gods!"
"Enter here, O pure being!
Enter here, O best of charioteers!
Enter here, O bringer of joy and gladness!"
Enter here, O you of blameless fame!
Enter here, O you who see in all directions! Enter here, O you who are equal to the unequaled!
"Come in here, O bearer of incomparable qualities and splendor, whose body is beautifully adorned with the primary and secondary marks!
From that time forward, the prince came to be known here by the name Sarvārthasiddha, "One Who Has Accomplished All Aims."
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana, in order to comply with all of them, had the Bodhisattva enter every house; then, after the lapse of four months, he brought the Bodhisattva back into his own palace.
And there was a hall named Nānāratnavyūha.
The Bodhisattva ascended that great palace.

There, the elder Śākyas assembled and deliberated thus: "Who indeed is capable of protecting, playing with, and cherishing the Bodhisattva, with a mind of welfare, a mind of loving-kindness, and a mind of virtue?"
And because of their gentle-mindedness:
there, about five hundred Śākya women each spoke thus: "I shall attend upon the Prince."
Thereupon, the elderly Śākya men and women said this: "All these brides are new, young, and youthful, intoxicated by the pride of their beauty and youth;
they are not capable of attending to the Bodhisattva from time to time.
Furthermore, this Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī is the prince’s maternal aunt."
"She is capable of raising the prince in perfect happiness and supporting King Śuddhodana.
Thus, they all together encouraged Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.

In this way, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī raised the prince. For the sake of the Bodhisattva, thirty-two nurses were appointed there: eight as body-nurses (*aṅgadhātrī*) and eight as milk-nurses (*kṣīradhātrī*).
There were eight nurses for cleansing and eight nurses for play.
Then King Śuddhodana, having assembled the entire Śākya clan, reflected thus: "Will this prince indeed become a universal monarch (cakravartin), or will he go forth into the religious life?
At that time, on the slopes of Himavat, the king of mountains, there lived a great seer named Asita, possessed of the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā), together with his nephew Naradatta.
He beheld many wonderful, marvelous, and miraculous portents occurring as soon as the Bodhisattva was born.
He saw sons of the gods stationed in the expanse of the sky proclaiming the word "Buddha" and waving their garments here and there, wandering about in great joy.
This thought occurred to him: "What if I were now to look out?"

Surveying the entire Jambudvīpa with his divine eye, he saw that in the great preeminent city named Kapila, in the house of King Śuddhodana, a prince had been born, resplendent with the majesty of a hundred merits, honored by all the world, and whose body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Having seen him, he addressed the young brahmin Naradatta: "Know, young man, that a great jewel has appeared in Jambudvīpa!"

In the great city of Kapilavastu, in the palace of King Śuddhodana, a prince was born, radiant with the splendor of a hundred merits, honored by all the world, and endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. If he should dwell in the midst of a household,
he will become a Cakravartin king of the four divisions, a conqueror, righteous, a king of Dharma who has attained the power and prowess of his subjects, and one possessed of the seven jewels.
He possesses these seven jewels, namely:
the wheel-jewel, the elephant-jewel, the horse-jewel, the gem-jewel, the woman-jewel, the householder-jewel, and the counselor-jewel;
thus he is fully endowed with the seven jewels.
He shall have a thousand sons who will be heroes, warriors, possessed of excellent forms, and crushers of enemy armies.

Having overcome and conquered this entire circle of the great earth, which is girt by the oceans, through his own power of righteousness— without rod or weapon— he shall rule the kingdom with sovereign authority and lordship.

"If, however, he shall go forth from the home to the homeless life, he will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha— a leader, one who leads others rather than being led by them, a teacher, a fully enlightened one in the world.
Therefore, let us now approach him to see him."

Then the great seer Asita, together with his nephew Naradatta, rose up and leaped into the air like a royal swan; he proceeded toward the great city of Kapilavastu, and having arrived there, he withdrew his supernormal power and entered the great city of Kapilavastu on foot.
He went to the residence of King Śuddhodana and stood at the gate of King Śuddhodana’s house.

"Thus, monks, the great seer Asita saw many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered at the gate of King Śuddhodana’s palace. Then the great seer Asita approached the doorkeeper and said: 'Go, my good man, to King Śuddhodana.'"
"Announce at the gate that a seer is standing there. "Very well," the gatekeeper replied to the great seer Asita, and having done so, he approached King Śuddhodana.
Having approached him with palms joined in reverence, he said to King Śuddhodana: "Your Majesty, you should know that an aged, elderly, and advanced seer is standing at the gate."
And he spoke thus: "I desire to see the king.
Then King Śuddhodana, having prepared a seat for the great seer Asita, said to that man, "Let the seer enter.
Thereupon, that man, having departed from the royal palace, said to the great seer Asita, "Please enter."
Then the great seer Asita approached King Śuddhodana;
having approached and stood before him, he spoke thus to King Śuddhodana: "Victory, victory to you, O Great King! May you long protect your life!"
"Rule the kingdom according to the Dharma."
Then King Śuddhodana, having offered the great seer Asita water for his feet, a respectful reception, and worship, received him with great care and courtesy and invited him to a seat.
Perceiving that he was comfortably seated, the king, full of reverence and deep satisfaction, spoke thus: "O Seer, I do not recall seeing you before. For what purpose have you come here?"
"What was the purpose?
When this was asked, the great seer Asita said this to King Śuddhodana: "Great King, a son has been born to you; I have come here desiring to see him."
The king said, "The prince is sleeping, O Great Seer;
wait for a moment until he awakens."
The seer said: "Great King, such great persons do not sleep for long;
such virtuous persons are habitually wakeful."
Thus, monks, out of compassion for the great seer Asita, the Bodhisattva made a sign of waking.
Then King Śuddhodana, having carefully and firmly grasped Prince Sarvārthasiddha with both hands, brought him into the presence of the great seer Asita.
Indeed, upon beholding the Bodhisattva, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and a body exquisitely adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, the great seer Asita—

Seeing him with a body surpassing that of Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors, with a splendor exceeding hundreds of thousands of suns, and beautiful in every limb, he uttered this exclamation: "Oh, what a marvelous person has appeared in the world!
Oh, what a most marvelous person has appeared in the world! Then, rising from his seat with palms joined in reverence, he [gazed] at the Bodhisattva.
Having prostrated at his feet and circumambulated the Bodhisattva, he took him in his arms and stood gazing upon him.
He beheld the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) possessed by the Bodhisattva, for a person endowed with these has only two possible destinies and no other:

if he dwells in the midst of a household, he becomes a fourfold-limbed Universal Monarch (*cakravartin* king), as previously described, up to and including the exercise of sovereign power and lordship.
"If, however, he goes forth from the home to the homeless life, he will become a Tathāgata, a Samyaksaṃbuddha of far-reaching renown.
Upon seeing him, he wept, shedding tears and sighing deeply.
King Śuddhodana saw the great seer Asita weeping, shedding tears, and sighing deeply.

Upon seeing him, his hair standing on end with joy, yet with a distressed mind, he spoke thus to the great seer Asita in great haste: "What is this, O Seer? Why do you weep, shed tears, and sigh so deeply?"
May there indeed be no misfortune whatsoever for the prince.
When this had been said, the great seer Asita spoke thus to King Śuddhodana: "Great King, I do not weep for the sake of the prince, nor is there any misfortune concerning him.
Rather, it is myself that I weep for."
For what reason?
Because, Great King, I am old, aged, and advanced in years;
yet this Prince Sarvārthasiddha will certainly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

And having attained supreme enlightenment, he will set in motion the wheel of Dharma that has never been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma;
for the benefit and happiness of the world including the devas, he will teach the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end.
He will fully proclaim to sentient beings the holy life (*brahmacarya*)—which is meaningful in itself, well-expressed in its phrasing, solitary, complete, pure, and purified.
Having heard this Dharma from him, sentient beings subject to birth will be liberated from birth;
likewise, they will be liberated from old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
He will bring refreshment by raining down the water of the True Dharma upon sentient beings scorched by the fires of passion, hatred, and delusion.
He will lead by the straight path to the way of Nirvana those beings who have entered into various graspings of wrong views and have set out upon evil paths.
He will effect their release from bondage for those confined in the prison-cage of saṃsāra and bound by the fetters of the afflictions.
He will produce the eye of wisdom for those beings whose eyes are shrouded by the cataracts of the darkness of ignorance;
he will extract the thorn of the afflictions for those beings pierced by the thorns of the defilements.
Great King, it is just as the udumbara flower appears in the world only once in a great while.
In the same way, Great King, only once in a great while, after many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, do Buddha-Bhagavāns arise in the world.
This prince will certainly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and having awakened, he will ferry hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings to the further shore across the ocean of saṃsāra.
"And he will establish [beings] in the deathless;
yet we shall not behold that jewel of a Buddha.
It is for this reason, Great King, that I weep with a dejected mind and sigh deeply, thinking that I shall not attain success even in this state of health.
For indeed, O Great King, it is stated in our mantra-veda scriptures: "The prince Sarvārthasiddha ought not to dwell within the household.
Why is that?
Because, O Great King, the prince Sarvārthasiddha is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man."
By which thirty-two? They are as follows:
Great King, Prince Sarvārthasiddha has a protuberance on his head (*uṣṇīṣaśīrṣa*).
Great King, by this first mark of a great man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), Prince Sarvārthasiddha is endowed.
His hair is curled to the right, as dark as a streak of crushed collyrium or a peacock’s plumage;
his forehead is even and broad;
and, O Great King, between the eyebrows of Prince Sarvārthasiddha there has grown an *ūrṇā*, radiant like snow or silver.
His eyelashes are like those of a cow;
his eyes are deep blue;
he has forty even teeth.
The Prince Sarvārthasiddha, O Great King, has teeth that are closely set and teeth that are white; he possesses the voice of Brahmā.
Possessing a sense of taste that is supreme among tastes; having a broad and thin tongue; and having a jaw like that of a lion.
He has well-rounded shoulders; he has seven prominent features; his shoulders are broad and well-filled.
His skin has a subtle, golden hue;
he stands with his arms hanging down so that they reach his knees without bending;
and the upper half of his body is like that of a lion.
Great King, Prince Sarvārthasiddha is well-proportioned like a banyan tree; his body hairs grow one by one,
and each hair points upward, curls to the right, and is fine.
His private organ is concealed in a sheath; his thighs are well-rounded;
and his shanks are like those of the king of the eṇeya deer.
He has long fingers; his heels are broad and his feet are level; his ankles are concealed within the folds of his feet.
His hands and feet are soft and youthful;
his fingers and toes are webbed;
and, O Great King, on the soles of the feet of Prince Sarvārthasiddha, long lines were formed, marked with wheels that were radiant, brilliant, and white.
"O Great King, Prince Sarvārthasiddha has feet that are well-set and level upon a thousand-spoked wheel with a rim and a hub.
O Great King, by this thirty-second mark of a great man, Prince Sarvārthasiddha is endowed."
Moreover, Great King, such marks as these do not belong to universal monarchs;
rather, it is the Bodhisattvas who possess such marks.
Furthermore, Great King, there truly exist eighty secondary marks upon the body of Prince Sarvārthasiddha;
endowed with these, Prince Sarvārthasiddha ought not to dwell in the midst of a household.
He will certainly go forth into the homeless life for the sake of renunciation.
And what, O Great King, are those eighty secondary marks? They are as follows: Prince Sarvārthasiddha has high nails;

he has copper-colored nails; he has glossy nails; his fingers are rounded; his fingers are beautifully tapered; his veins are hidden; his ankles are hidden; his joints are firm; his feet are even and level; and his heels are broad and long.

Great King, Prince Sarvārthasiddha has glossy lines on his palms, symmetrical lines on his palms, deep lines on his palms, straight lines on his palms, and orderly lines on his palms; he has lips like the *bimba* fruit, a voice that is not loud or harsh, a tongue that is soft, tender, and copper-colored, and a sweet, charming resonance with the sound of an elephant’s roar and the thundering of clouds.
And, Great King, Prince Sarvārthasiddha has fully developed secondary characteristics:

his arms are long; he is endowed with pure limbs and a fine physical constitution; his body is soft, expansive, and noble; his limbs are well-proportioned, symmetrical, and beautifully articulated; and his kneecaps are broad, vast, and perfectly rounded.
And, O Great King, Prince Sarvārthasiddha has rounded limbs;

his limbs are well-polished; his limbs are straight like those of a bull; his limbs are symmetrical; he has a deep navel; his navel is not crooked; his navel is symmetrical; his conduct is pure; he is as pleasing on all sides as a bull; and he possesses a supreme, utterly pure radiance, free from darkness, which shines forth in every direction.
And, O Great King, Prince Sarvārthasiddha has a gait slow and majestic like that of an elephant;
he has a gait with the stride of a lion, a gait with the stride of a bull, and a gait with the stride of a swan; his gait turns toward the right;
he has rounded hips, polished hips, and straight hips; and he has a belly like a bow, free from the defects of protuberances, dark spots, or blemishes on his body.
And the prince Sarvārthasiddha, O Great King, has rounded fangs;

he has sharp fangs and well-proportioned fangs; he has a prominent nose, pure eyes, stainless eyes, smiling eyes, wide eyes, expansive eyes, large eyes, and eyes resembling the petals of the blue lotus; and his eyebrows, O Great King, are joined together.

The prince Sarvārthasiddha, O Great King, has beautiful eyebrows— variegated, dark, well-knit, and symmetrical; he has full cheeks, even cheeks, cheeks free from defects, a face unmarred by frowning, and his sense faculties are well-known and perfectly complete.

The prince Sarvārthasiddha, O Great King, has a well-proportioned face and forehead; his head is perfectly formed; his hair is black, even, well-joined, fragrant, not coarse, not disordered, regular, beautifully curled, and shaped like the *śrīvatsa*, the *svastika*, the *nandyāvarta*, and the *vardhamāna*.
"Prince Sarvārthasiddha!
Great King, these are those eighty secondary marks of Prince Sarvārthasiddha,
endowed with which Prince Sarvārthasiddha ought not to dwell in the midst of a household."
He will certainly go forth into homelessness for the sake of the religious life.
Then King Śuddhodana, having heard this prophecy concerning the prince from the great seer Asita,
was satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheer; rising from his seat, he prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva and spoke this verse:
You are saluted by the gods together with Indra, and you are honored by the sages;
O Physician of the entire world, I too salute you, O Lord. (Lal 7.55)
Thus, monks, King Śuddhodana satisfied the great seer Asita together with his nephew Naradatta with suitable food.
Having satisfied them and provided them with clothing, he circumambulated them.
Then the great seer Asita departed from that very spot, traveling through the sky by means of his supernatural power.
He approached his own hermitage.

Then, having moved from that place, the great seer Asita said this to the young man Naradatta: "Naradatta, when you hear that a Buddha has appeared in the world, then you should go and go forth in his teaching.
That will lead to your welfare, benefit, and happiness for a long time."
In this regard, it is said:
Having seen the hosts of gods situated in the vault of the sky proclaiming the name of the Buddha,
the divine seer Asita, dwelling in a mountain cave, attained supreme joy.
"O sir, what is this word 'Buddha' that brings such joy to living beings?
My body has become refreshed and my mind has reached a state of supreme peace and happiness. (Lal_7.56)
Is he a god, or perhaps an asura? Could he be Garuḍa or a kinnara?
What is this "Buddha"—this unprecedented term that brings such joy and delight?
With divine vision, he gazes upon the ten directions: the mountains, the earth, and the oceans.
Furthermore, he beholds many kinds of wonders upon the earth, on the mountains, and in the ocean.
This radiant and beautiful luster shines forth, gladdening the body,
just like the glossy sprouts of coral upon a mountain peak;
and just as trees are laden with fine blossoms and adorned with various fruits.
It is evident that the beautiful Ratnodbhava will soon appear within the three worlds.
The entire earth shone like the palm of a hand— level and stainless— and the gods, their minds filled with joy, whirled their garments through the sky;
just as wondrous jewels float upon the ocean, the abode of the Naga kings.
It is clearly evident, O jewel among Jinas, that the source of the mine of Dharma has arisen in the land of Jambūdvīpa.
Just as the lower realms have become peaceful and free from suffering, and beings are endowed with happiness;
and just as the hosts of gods dwelling in the vault of the sky proceed filled with joy.
And just as one might hear the smooth, charming sound of divine music,
so too is the appearance of this Jewel in the three worlds, of which these are the omens.
With his divine eye, Asita surveyed this land called Jambudvīpa; he beheld that one born in the palace of Śuddhodana in the excellent city named Kapila,
endowed with the splendor of merit and the marks of excellence, and possessed of the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
Having seen this, he was delighted; with an uplifted mind, his strength was increased.
Exerting himself with haste and a mind filled with great wonder, he arrived at the excellent city named Kapila accompanied by his disciples and stood at the king's gate; there,
the aged seer beheld many tens of millions of billions of living beings following after him.
The charioteer said to the king, "Inform him quickly that a seer stands at the gate."
Having heard this, he quickly entered the royal palace and announced to the king at the gate: "Your Majesty, a great ascetic stands here—an aged and decrepit seer.
That most excellent of seers desires to enter the king's residence."
"O best of kings, let the command be given; I shall grant them entrance."
The king said, "Prepare a seat for him," and "Go, grant him entrance.
Hearing the charioteer's words, Asita was delighted, filled with affection and happiness,
like a thirsty man who longs for cool water or one who has first eaten his meal.
In that same way, the excellent sage, filled with joy, desired to see that supreme being.
"Victory to you, O King! he said joyfully, "May you protect the world for a long time.
Having increased his prosperity, seated with a subdued mind, his senses calmed and his heart gentle, the king indeed saluted him and, being very composed, asked: "What is the reason?"
"O Lord of Kings, you have come to my abode; therefore, tell me quickly, O Sage."

"O King, your son has been born with excellent form, having reached the perfection of greatness and possessing mighty splendor; he is armored with the thirty-two marks of excellence and endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa. O Lord of Men, it is my desire to see that infant, Sarvārthasiddha."
"For this purpose alone have I come, O King; I have no other business. (Lal 7.66)
"Excellent! Welcome! You have come as a petitioner; I am pleased by the sight of you.
This prince, the granter of boons, is currently asleep and cannot be seen at this time."
"Come here for a moment, O virtuous one, so that you may see him who is as stainless as the full moon on the night of the full moon, adorned by a multitude of stars."
And when that excellent charioteer, Paripūrṇacandraprabha, had awakened, the king received him— whose body was like fire and whose radiance surpassed the sun—
and said: "Behold, O Sage, one honored by gods and men, resembling the finest image of gold!"
And Asita, having seen those two beautiful feet of his, marked with wheels, [was filled with wonder].
Then, rising up with palms joined in reverence, he who was skilled in the great self and the scriptures took him by the feet and paid homage; as he gazed intently,
he beheld one clad in the armor of excellent marks, possessing the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
Shaking his head, he who was skilled in the Vedas and the Śāstras perceived two possible courses for him.
"Will he become a powerful universal monarch, or a Buddha, the supreme one in the world?
Having shed tears with a body and mind deeply distressed, and sighing profoundly, this best of kings became anxious: 'Why does this brahmin weep?'"
"May this Asita indeed see no obstacle for me, Sarvārthasiddha."
"Speak the truth; why do you weep, O Sage? Is there some good or some evil [to come]?
There is no sin, nor is there any obstacle here for you, O Sarvārthasiddha.
I grieve greatly for myself, O Lord of Men, for I am worn out and decrepit."
When he shall become a Buddha, honored by the world, and when he shall preach the Dharma.
I weep because I shall not see her whose mind has attained joy, in whose body there exist the thirty-two stainless, supreme marks;
know this, O King: for her there are only two destinies, no third.
He will become either a powerful universal monarch or a Buddha, the supreme being in the world.
"This Buddha does not seek after the qualities of sensual pleasure";
having heard this prophecy from the seer, the king obtained joy and happiness.
Then, rising up with palms joined in reverence, he paid homage at his feet.
You have been highly honored by the gods and praised by the ṛṣis as one possessed of great strength.
I pay homage to you, the excellent caravan leader, who is honored by the entire world in the three realms of existence;
and Asita, being joyful, said to his nephew: "Listen with delight as I speak."
When you hear that the Buddhas have attained enlightenment and that they turn the wheel for the sake of the world, go forth quickly into the teaching of this Sage; thus you shall attain nirvāṇa.
Having bowed at his feet and performed a circumambulation, that best of sages said:
"O King, you have attained vast and well-gained blessings, for such a son as this is yours;
he shall satisfy the world, including its gods and humans, through the Dharma."
Having departed from the city named Kapila, the best of seers dwelt in his own hermitage in the forest.
Thus it is said.

Thus, monks, as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, the divine son Maheśvara addressed the divine sons of the Śuddhāvāsa realm and said: "Friends, he who has practiced well through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons by means of giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, wisdom, skillful means, learning, conduct, vows, and austerities;

he who is endowed with great loving-kindness, great compassion, and great sympathetic joy; whose mind has emerged from equanimity; and who is devoted to the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings."

He was well-armored with the mail of firm vigor, arisen from the roots of merit planted under previous Victors, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits, possessing the prowess of well-executed resolve, the crusher of enemy armies, endowed with a perfectly pure and stainless intention, one whose conduct was well-practiced,

the great banner and standard of wisdom, the destroyer of Māra’s forces, the caravan leader of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, and the performer of the great sacrifice honored by gods and humans.
With the intention of emerging through a perfectly accumulated store of merit, bringing an end to birth, old age, and death, one born of noble birth, arisen from the royal Ikṣvāku lineage,
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who awakens the world has appeared in the human realm. Before long, he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Come, let us go to pay homage to him, to honor him, to worship him, and to praise him, for the sake of cutting through the pride, intoxication, and arrogance of other sons of the gods who are overcome by conceit.
When they see us paying homage, they too will bow to the Bodhisattva, honor him, and worship him.
This will lead to their welfare, benefit, and happiness for a long time, even unto the attainment of the Deathless."
And the victory and prosperity of King Śuddhodana shall be proclaimed;
and having prophesied concerning the Bodhisattva through an explanation of the truth, we shall return once more.
Then indeed, the divine son Maheśvara, surrounded and escorted by twelve hundred thousand divine sons,
having illuminated the entire great city of Kapilavastu with his radiance, approached the residence of King Śuddhodana.
Having arrived and informed the gatekeeper, and being permitted by the king, he entered the royal palace and [approached] the Bodhisattva.

Having prostrated with his head at [the Bodhisattva’s] feet, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, he placed the Bodhisattva upon his lap and comforted King Śuddhodana, saying: "Be satisfied, Great King, and be supremely joyful!
For what reason? Because—"
Just as, Great King, the body of the Bodhisattva is adorned with the primary marks and secondary signs,

and just as the prince surpasses the world of gods, humans, and asuras by his complexion, splendor, fame, and majesty, so it is certain, Great King, that the Bodhisattva will attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Thus, monks, the divine son Maheśvara, together with the divine sons belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm, having performed a great act of worship and service for the Bodhisattva and having prophesied the Bodhisattva’s true destiny, returned once more to his own abode.
Regarding this, it is said:
Having learned that he who was born is an ocean of virtues, the exalted Lord of the Gods and the Maruts spoke.
The hearing of whose name is very difficult to obtain even in many millions of eons—come now, let us go to worship that Lord of Sages!
A full twelve thousand pure Maruts, adorned with crests of precious jewels, possessed of noble deportment and wearing long-hanging crests,
quickly approached the excellent city named Kapila and stood at the gate of the king.
With voices most pleasing, they said to the gatekeeper: "Announce us to the king once we have entered his palace.
Having heard these words, the doorkeeper entered the house and, bowing low with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the king.

Victory to you, O Lord! May you eternally protect this long life. Standing at the gate are those of vast merit and pure radiance, beautifully adorned with crests of precious jewels, possessed of noble deportment, with faces like the full moon and a luster as stainless as the moon.

O King, we saw no shadow of them anywhere, nor did we hear any sound as they lifted their feet; yet as they moved across the earth, they raised no dust, and the people who gazed upon them could never reach satiety. (Lal 7.80)

The radiance of their bodies shines forth most extensively, and their speech is as pleasing as nothing among humans; it is profound, smooth, well-fashioned, and well-articulated. Indeed, I have a doubt: these hosts of gods are surely not human beings.
Holding excellent flowers, garlands, ointments, and silk ribbons in their hands, they waited expectantly with reverence;
"Without doubt, O King, these gods have come from the heavens to behold the prince and to worship the God of Gods."
Having heard these words, the king was exceedingly uplifted and said: "Go, tell them: 'May you enter the house.
For such supernatural power as this does not belong to mere humans, nor do the virtues you describe, nor such a manner of deportment. (Lalita-vistara 7.83)
The doorkeeper, with palms joined like a flower bud, spoke thus as if moved by the wind: "May you enter; you have been granted permission by the lord of men.
With hearts joyful and content, holding excellent garlands in their hands, they entered the king’s palace, which was like the abode of the immortals.
Seeing that most excellent of goddesses entering his home, the king rose up and, joining his palms in reverence, said:
"These seats with jeweled feet are prepared; please sit here, O Lord, out of compassion for us."
Free from pride and arrogance, they stood upon their seats; O King, listen to the purpose for which we have come here:
a son has been born to you with a body purified by immense merit, whose feet are well-formed, and we desire to behold him.

"We are knowers of the ritual, O best of kings, who understand the characteristics of the excellent marks; for us, such is the way it is—what the destiny shall be and what the application [of signs] will be.
Therefore, O noble king, cast aside your grief; let us behold your body adorned with the various wonderful marks."
Surrounded by throngs of women, the king, filled with joy, took up the incomparable prince, whose complexion was like the radiance of a blazing flame;
leading him toward the supreme gods with their beautifully hanging topknots, he departed from the gate, causing the three thousandfold world-system to tremble.
As soon as those best of gods saw the copper-colored nails of the Leader, which possessed the pure luster of stainless petals,
they rose up quickly with their beautiful, hanging topknots and bowed their heads to the feet of the one of stainless radiance.

Just as his marks are, and just as they have been shown and characterized; just as Puṇyatejas-Śrī has gazed upon his crown; and just as his gaze, his eyes, and the stainless light of the circle of hair between his brows are—without doubt he will touch enlightenment, having conquered Māra. (Lal 7.90)

Those who perceive reality as it is praise him who has become the embodiment of virtue, the meditator who dispels the darkness of afflictions through his qualities; for the appearance of this jewel among beings, who abandons the battle of birth, old age, death, and affliction, occurs only after a very long time.
The entire triple world is ablaze, scorched by the three fires arising from the fire-drill of conceptualization, passion, and sense objects.
O steadfast Cloud of Dharma, having pervaded the triple-thousandfold world system with the nectar-water of your wisdom, you shall extinguish the heat of the afflictions.
O you who speak with loving-kindness, endowed with compassion, whose speech is gentle, whose resonance is fashioned with the voice of Brahmā, and whose words are charming;
O Lord, you who cause the command to be known throughout the triple-thousand world system, quickly release the great Buddha-voice for the sake of the world!
The hosts of false teachers have been broken; those of perverted views, submerged in the bonds of craving for existence, remained at the peak of becoming.
But having heard the Dharma—that existence is empty and dependent upon causes—they fled like a pack of jackals before a lion.
Having pierced the veil of ignorance and the rising smoke of the great afflictions for the sake of the people, you shall shine with certainty;
with the gaze of the lightning of knowledge, the radiance of wisdom, and the light of insight, you shall dispel the great darkness throughout the entire world.
Great gain has been well-attained by gods and humans, since such a marvelous and pure being has appeared here;
for through this jewel of a being, the awakener, the paths to the lower realms will be closed and the paths to the celestial realms will flourish.

Having rained down celestial flowers upon this place called Kapila, and having performed circumambulations and offered praise with reverence, those hosts of gods departed gracefully through the sky, uttering the words, "A Buddha! A truly awakened one!"
Thus [it is said].
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Birth," in the glorious Lalitavistara.
START Parivarta 8 (Vaidya 83):
The eighth chapter, "The Presentation at the Temple."
Thus, monks, on the very night that the Bodhisattva was born, twenty thousand maidens born into the families of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, merchants, householders,
and great śāla-clans were given by their parents to the Bodhisattva for his attendance and service;
and twenty thousand maidens were also given by King Śuddhodana to the Bodhisattva for his attendance and service.
And twenty thousand maidens were given by friends, ministers, sons, kinsmen, and blood relatives for the purpose of attending upon and serving the Bodhisattva;
and twenty thousand maidens were given by the assembly of ministers for the purpose of attending upon and serving the Bodhisattva.
Then, monks, the elderly Śākya men and women, having assembled and approached King Śuddhodana, said this: "May Your Majesty know that the prince should be brought to the temple.
The king said, "Very well; let the prince be brought."
Therefore, let the city be adorned;
let the streets, squares, crossroads, marketplaces, and thoroughfares be decorated.
Let those who are inauspicious—those who are one-eyed, hunchbacked, deaf, blind, mute, deformed, misshapen, or deficient in their faculties—be removed.
Let auspicious objects be brought forward;
let the drums of merit be sounded;
let the auspicious bells be struck.
Let the gates of this preeminent city be beautifully adorned;
let the most delightful musical instruments, cymbals, and percussion be sounded;
and let all the subordinate kings be assembled.
Let the guild-masters, householders, ministers, gatekeepers, and courtiers assemble!
Let the maidens' chariots be readied!
Let the full water-jars be brought forward!
"Let the Brahmins who have completed their studies be assembled;
let the temples be adorned.
And so, monks, everything was done exactly as previously described.
Then King Śuddhodana, having entered his own palace, addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and said: "Let the prince be adorned; he shall be led to the temple of the gods.
Having assented with "So be it," Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī adorned the prince.
Then the prince, being adorned, with a smiling face and free from frowns, spoke thus to his maternal aunt in a most sweet voice: "Mother, where will you lead me?
She replied, "To a temple, my son.
Thereupon the prince, displaying a smile and with a cheerful countenance, addressed his maternal aunt in verses:

When I was born here, the triple-thousandfold world system trembled; Śakra, Brahmā, the asuras, and the mahoragas, as well as the moon, the sun, Vaiśravaṇa, and Kumāra, prostrated with their heads at my feet and paid homage.
"Who else is there, O Mother, a god superior to me, more distinguished than I, for whom you would have such affection for me today?
I am the God beyond gods, the most supreme among all gods; there is no god equal to me, so how could there be one superior? (Lal 8.2)
"Mother, I shall go with the thought of conforming to the world; seeing my miraculous transformations, the people will be uplifted.
The painters will show the utmost reverence, and gods and men alike will know: 'This is the God of Gods himself. (Lal 8.3)
