Thus, monks, while all castes were present with hymns and auspicious recitations, and while the streets, squares, crossroads, and market entrances were adorned with immeasurable ornaments, King Śuddhodana— having decorated the prince’s chariot within the inner palace—
was surrounded by brahmins, merchants, guild-leaders, householders, ministers, provincial governors, gatekeepers, courtiers, friends, and kinsmen.

Honored by a path perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, crowded with horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry, and adorned with raised parasols, banners, and flags, and accompanied by the sounding of various musical instruments, he went along taking the prince with him;
hundreds of thousands of deities drew the Bodhisattva’s chariot.

And many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sons of gods and apsarases, stationed in the expanse of the sky, rained down showers of flowers and played musical instruments. Thus, King Śuddhodana, with a great royal array, great royal majesty, and great royal power, took the prince and entered the temple of the gods.
As soon as the Bodhisattva placed the soles of his right feet upon that temple,
those inanimate statues of gods— namely, the images of Śiva, Skanda, Nārāyaṇa, Kubera, Candra, Sūrya, Vaiśravaṇa, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), and so forth—
all rose from their respective places and prostrated themselves at the soles of the Bodhisattva’s feet.
There, hundreds of thousands of gods and humans let out hundreds of thousands of shouts, led by cries of "Hīhī" and "Kilakila," and they waved their garments;
and the entire great city of Kapilavastu shook in six ways.
Divine flowers rained down,
and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded without being struck.
And as for those deities whose images they were—
They all, having revealed their own true forms, spoke these verses:
"Neither Mount Meru, the king of mountains and best of peaks, would ever bend before a mustard seed;
nor would the ocean, the abode of the naga kings, ever bend before the water in a cow's hoofprint."
O maker of light, with the radiance of the moon and sun; O firefly, we do not bow to you.
Why, O deity, do we not bow to the one born of the family of wisdom and merit, the possessor of virtues?
Just as there might be water in a mustard seed or a cow’s footprint, or like fireflies,
so too are all the gods and humans in the triple-thousand world-system who rely on pride;
whereas the Self-Arisen One, the Supreme, is like Mount Meru, the ocean, the moon, and the sun in this world.
For by worshipping him, the world obtains gain, as well as heaven and likewise liberation.

Furthermore, monks, while this entry into the divine palace was being displayed by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the minds of three million two hundred thousand sons of gods were set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, why the Bodhisattva remained in equanimity while being led into the divine palace.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Chapter on the Presentation at the Temple."
START Parivarta 9 (Vaidya 85):
The Ninth Chapter, "The Ornament" (Ābharaṇa-parivarta).
Then, monks, a brahmin named Udayana, the royal chaplain and father of Udāyin,

surrounded by about five hundred brahmins, approached King Śuddhodana under the constellation Citrā, when the moon was in the asterism Hastottarā, and spoke thus: "May Your Majesty be informed that ornaments should be prepared for the prince."
The king said to him: "Very well; let it be done thoroughly."

Thereupon, King Śuddhodana and about five hundred Śākyas had some five hundred kinds of ornaments fashioned. They were as follows: ornaments for the hands, ornaments for the feet, ornaments for the head, ornaments for the neck, ornaments for the fingers, earrings, armlets, girdles, golden threads, networks of small bells, and nets of jewels set with precious gems.

Having had sandals adorned with various jewels, necklaces, bracelets, earrings, and crowns made, those Śākyas approached King Śuddhodana while the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism was occurring and said to him, "Come, Your Majesty, let the prince be adorned. The king replied,
"The prince has already been sufficiently adorned and honored by you."
I also had all the ornaments made for the prince.
They said, "Let the prince fasten our ornaments upon his body for seven times seven days and nights."
"Then our exertion will become fruitful."
There, when the night had passed and the sun had risen, the Bodhisattva went out to the garden named Vimalavyūha.
There, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī held the Bodhisattva in her arms,
and eighty thousand women came forth to meet him and gazed upon the face of the Bodhisattva.
Ten thousand maidens came forth to meet the Bodhisattva and gazed upon his face; five thousand brahmins also came forth to meet him and gazed upon his face.
Therein were the ornaments that had been commissioned by Bhadrika, the Śākya king.
They were fastened upon the body of the Bodhisattva;
as soon as they were fastened, they were eclipsed by the radiance of the Bodhisattva’s body and did not shine.
They did not glow, they did not shine;
just as, for example, a lump of soot placed before Jāmbūnada gold does not gleam, does not glow, and does not shine.
In the same way, those ornaments, not touched by the radiance of the Bodhisattva’s body, did not shine, did not glow, and did not gleam. Likewise,
whatever variety of ornament was fastened upon the Bodhisattva’s body became dimmed, just like a lump of soot.
Thereupon, the garden deity named Vimalā manifested a gross physical form, stood before him, and addressed King Śuddhodana and that great assembly of Śākyas with these verses:
"May this entire trichiliocosm, including its cities and market towns, be filled with a beautiful and stainless accumulation of gold."
A single kārṣāpaṇa coin, when compared to gold from Jambū, appears diminished; it does not shine, for it is devoid of the splendor and luster of that gold. // Lal_9.1 //
Furthermore, this entire earth, filled with the splendor of modesty, would become like Jāmbūnada gold when the Leader emits light from a single pore;
it would not shine, nor burn, nor gleam, nor exert its own radiance.
The radiance from the Sugata’s body does not become like ink.
Adorned by his own splendor and filled with hundreds of virtues, these ornaments do not outshine him of the utterly pure body;
nor do the radiance of the moon and sun, nor the light of the stars, nor the brilliance of jewels.
The radiance of Śakra and Brahmā does not shine in the presence of that mass of glory.
For her whose body is adorned with the marks produced by the fruits of former virtues—what need has she for these transient ornaments made by others?
Remove these ornaments, O fool; do not cause distress to one who brings enlightenment.
This one does not desire artificial ornaments; he brings about supreme intelligence.
"Give these most beautiful and stainless ornaments to the servant;
Chandaka, who was born together with him, has been well-adorned by them in this auspicious royal family.
The Śākyas became joyful, astonished, and delighted in their hearts.
And there will be supreme and vast prosperity for the one who brings joy to the Śākya clan.
Having spoken thus, that deity scattered divine flowers over the Bodhisattva and vanished right there.
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the Śrī Lalitavistara, titled "The Chapter on Ornaments."
START Parivarta 10 (Vaidya 87):
The Tenth Chapter, "The Manifestation at the Writing School" (Lipiśālāsaṃdarśana-parivarta).
Thus, monks, when the prince had grown up,
he was led to the writing school amidst hundreds of thousands of auspicious ceremonies, surrounded and escorted by ten thousand boys,
and by ten thousand chariots filled with various kinds of food— hard, soft, and flavorful— as well as with silver and gold.
By means of this, it was scattered and distributed throughout the streets, squares, roads, and market entrances of the great city of Kapilavastu;
while hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded and a great rain of flowers fell,
hundreds of thousands of maidens adorned with every ornament stood upon the balconies, turrets, gateways, windows, and the terraces of the gabled chambers and palaces.
Gazing upon the Bodhisattva, they scattered flowers.

And eight thousand celestial maidens, adorned with ornaments and fine jewels that had slipped from their places, holding precious *bhadraṃkara* vessels, went before the Bodhisattva, clearing the path as they proceeded.
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, appearing with only half their bodies, suspended garlands of flowers and silk ribbons from the expanse of the sky.
And all the Śākya clansmen, placing King Śuddhodana at their head, walked before the Bodhisattva. In such a magnificent array, the Bodhisattva was led to the writing school.
As soon as the Bodhisattva had entered the writing school,
the teacher of children named Viśvāmitra, unable to endure the Bodhisattva’s splendor and majesty, sank down upon the surface of the earth and fell with his face turned downward.
Seeing him fallen in that manner, a son of the gods from the Tuṣita realm named Śubhāṅga took hold of him with his right palm and raised him up.
Having raised him up, he stood in the expanse of the sky and addressed King Śuddhodana and that great multitude of people with these verses:
"Whatever treatises circulate in the world of men—calculation, writing, and arithmetic, as well as the systems of the elements;

Thus, monks, as those boys were being taught the alphabet, by the very power of the Bodhisattva, hundreds of thousands of incalculable gateways to the Dharma issued forth from the very first syllables.

I shall choose her for the prince."
Then King Śuddhodana had sorrowless vessels made of gold, silver, and various precious gems.

Having had them made, he caused a proclamation by the ringing of bells to be made throughout the great city of Kapilavastu: "On the seventh day, the prince will grant an audience and distribute sorrowless vessels to the young maidens."
In that regard, all the young girls must assemble in the assembly hall.
Thus, monks, on the seventh day, the Bodhisattva approached the assembly hall and sat down upon the auspicious throne.
King Śuddhodana also stationed invisible men with the command: "Whichever girl the prince’s eye should rest upon, report her to me."

Thus, monks, all the young girls who were in the great city of Kapilavastu went to the assembly hall where the Bodhisattva was, in order to see the Bodhisattva and to receive the vessels of the Ashoka tree.
Thus, monks, the Bodhisattva bestowed those baskets of *aśoka* flowers upon the maidens who had approached him;
yet those maidens were unable to endure the Bodhisattva’s splendor and majesty.
Taking those baskets of ashoka flowers, they departed very quickly.
Then the daughter of Daṇḍapāṇi the Śākya, a Śākya maiden named Gopā, surrounded and escorted by a retinue of female servants, approached the assembly hall where the Bodhisattva was;
having approached, she stood to one side, gazing at the Bodhisattva with unblinking eyes.

When the Bodhisattva had given away all the articles free from sorrow, she approached the Bodhisattva with a smiling face and said to him: "Prince, what have I taken from you that you should treat me with such contempt?
He replied: "I do not treat you with contempt."
"But indeed, you have come from behind me.
Then, having removed a finger-ring worth many hundreds of thousands, he gave it to her.
She said, "O Prince, am I worthy of this from you?
He replied, "These are my own ornaments; take them.
She said, "We shall not adorn the Prince [with these]."
"We shall adorn the prince," having said this, the maiden departed.
Then those secret agents approached King Śuddhodana and reported this account: "Your Majesty, the daughter of the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi, a Śākya maiden named Gopā, has captured the prince's eye;
for a moment, there was conversation between them."
Having heard these words, King Śuddhodana dispatched the domestic priest of the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi as an envoy with this message: "Let your daughter be given to my prince."
Daṇḍapāṇi said, "Noble sir, the prince has been raised in luxury at home.
Furthermore, this is our family custom: a daughter must be given to one who is skilled in the arts, not to one who is unskilled.
And the prince is not skilled in the arts; he does not know the rules for the sword, the bow, weaponry, combat, or wrestling."
"How can I give my daughter to one who is ignorant of the arts?
This was reported to the king.
Then this thought occurred to the king: "For a second time, I have been urged by what is consistent with righteousness."
Even when I asked, "Why do the Śākya youths not come to attend upon the prince? I was told then as well: "Why should we attend upon Maṇḍaka?
Now, too, he sat there lost in thought, reflecting that it was exactly the same.
The Bodhisattva heard this account;
having heard it, he approached King Śuddhodana and, upon arriving, spoke thus: "Your Majesty, why do you remain here with such a dejected mind?"
The king said, "Enough of this, prince.
The prince replied, "Your Majesty, it must certainly be told by all means.
Thus the Bodhisattva questioned King Śuddhodana even up to three times.
(Vaidya 101) Then King Śuddhodana informed the Bodhisattva of this matter.
Having heard it, the Bodhisattva said: "Your Majesty, is there anyone else here in this city who is capable of displaying his skill in craftsmanship alongside me?"
Then King Śuddhodana, with a smiling countenance, said this to the Bodhisattva: "My son, are you able to demonstrate your craft once more?
He replied, "Certainly, I am able, O King.
"In that case, let all those skilled in the arts be assembled."
Before whom I shall demonstrate my own craft.
Then King Śuddhodana caused a proclamation by the sounding of bells to be made in the great city of Kapilavastu: "On the seventh day, the prince will display his own artistic skills;
all those skilled in the arts must assemble there."
On the seventh day, about five hundred Śākya youths assembled there.

And Gopā, the daughter of the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi, was established as the banner of victory with these words: "Whosoever among you shall be victorious here in swordsmanship, archery, skill in the arts of war, and wrestling, she shall be his."
There, Prince Devadatta emerged from the city at the very forefront;
and a white elephant of great stature was being led into the city for the sake of the Bodhisattva.
There, Prince Devadatta was intoxicated with envy and with the pride of the Śākya power.
Seizing that noble elephant by its trunk with his left hand, he struck it with a single blow of his right palm, and it was killed instantly.
Immediately after him, Prince Sundarananda went forth.
He saw that elephant-king slain at the city gate;
having seen it, he asked, "By whom was this killed?"
There, the great multitude of people said, "By Devadatta! He replied, "This is not the fault of Devadatta. Seizing that noble elephant by the tail, he dragged it away from the city gate.
Immediately thereafter, the Bodhisattva, mounted upon his chariot, went forth.
The Bodhisattva saw that elephant slain;
having seen it, he asked, "By whom was this killed?"
They said, "By Devadatta.
He said, "Devadatta acted improperly.
But by whom was he dragged away from this city gate?"
They said, "By Sundarananda. He said, "This is excellent on the part of Sundarananda;
however, this being is of great body."
"This [corpse], being soaked, will cause a foul stench to pervade the entire city."

Then the prince, having extended one foot of the chariot onto the ground, seized that great elephant by its tail with his big toe and hurled it across seven walls and seven moats, casting it a *krośa* outside the city.
At the spot where that elephant fell, a great pit was formed, which is even now called "Hastigarta" (the Elephant Pit).
There, hundreds of thousands of gods and humans let out hundreds of thousands of cries of "Alas!", shouts of joy, and roars;
they also waved their garments.
And the sons of the gods situated in the expanse of the sky spoke these two verses:

Just as one with the gait of a lordly elephant in rut, having crossed over the seven moats of the city with the sole of his big toe, cast that lordly elephant outside of his own city— so indeed is this [the Buddha].
Without a doubt, this one of excellent wisdom, by the power of his pride, will cast those whose bodies are raised high outside the city of saṃsāra, using the power of his insight.

Thus, five hundred Śākya youths departed from the city and proceeded to a certain spot on the earth where the Śākya youths were displaying their artistic skills; King Śuddhodana, as well as the elderly Śākyas and a great multitude of people, also proceeded to that spot on the earth, desiring to witness the superior craftsmanship of the Bodhisattva and the other Śākya youths.
There, from the very beginning, those Śākya youths who were skilled in the methods of writing competed in calligraphy with the Bodhisattva.

There, the Śākyas appointed the teacher Viśvāmitra as a witness, saying: "Observe this: which prince here excels in the knowledge of writing, whether in terms of the written form itself or in the mastery of many scripts?"

Then the teacher Viśvāmitra, appearing in person before the Bodhisattva and displaying a smile regarding his knowledge of scripts, spoke these two verses: "In the world of humans, in the world of gods, in the world of gandharvas, and even in the world of the lords of asuras—
whatever scripts exist in all the worlds, this pure being has reached the further shore of them all."
Neither you nor I know the names of those scripts, nor even their letters;
only this Moon among Men knows them, and he shall emerge victorious here before our very eyes.
The Śākyas said, "Let the prince first be distinguished in the knowledge of scripts;
as for the knowledge of numbers, the prince must be further distinguished and tested.
In that regard, there was a Śākya mathematician named Arjuna, a high official who had reached the furthest shore of numerical calculation.
He was appointed as the witness: "Observe which prince here excels in the knowledge of calculation. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva set forth his problem, and one Śākya prince presented his solution.
And he did not reach [the end].
Even when one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, and even up to five hundred Śākya youths simultaneously threw [the dice] at the same time,
they did not reach [the end].
Then the Bodhisattva said, "Recite it yourselves; I shall deposit it.
Thereupon, one Śākya youth recited it for the Bodhisattva.
And yet he could not complete them;
for two, three, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and even up to five hundred Śākya youths recited simultaneously,
yet they could not finish them as the Bodhisattva was laying them down.
The Bodhisattva said: "Enough, enough with this dispute!
Now all of you, becoming one, designate me;
I shall deposit it."
There, about five hundred Śākya youths recited their previous lives one after another, yet the Bodhisattva remained undeluded as he recounted his own.
In this manner, all the Śākya youths were inexhaustible [in their recounting].
Now, the Bodhisattva is also one who has reached the limit.
Then Arjuna, the chief of the mathematicians, filled with wonder, spoke these two verses: "Excellent is the swiftness of the Buddha's knowledge in responding to inquiries!
These five hundred men have been surpassed in the path of calculation."
Such is this wisdom, intelligence, knowledge, mindfulness, and discernment;
yet even now, this ocean of knowledge continues to study mathematics.
Thereupon, the entire assembly of Śākyas was struck with wonder and filled with supreme amazement. With one voice, they uttered these words: "Victory! Victory, O Prince Sarvārthasiddha!

Then, all rising from their seats and joining their palms in reverence, they paid homage to the Bodhisattva and said this to King Śuddhodana: "It is a gain for you, Great King; it is a most excellent attainment."
For you have a son whose eloquence consists of such swift, light, rapid, and agile inquiries.

Then King Śuddhodana said this to the Bodhisattva: "My son, are you able to enter into the method of calculation and the skill in numerical knowledge together with Arjuna, the great minister of accountants?
"In that case, let it be calculated.
Then Arjuna, the great minister of accountants, said this to the Bodhisattva: "Do you know, O Prince, the method of calculation called 'One Hundred Times Ten Million Plus' (*koṭiśatottarā*)?"
The Bodhisattva said, "I am able, O Lord.
He said, "I know this.
He asked, "Furthermore, how is the method of calculation exceeding a hundred koṭis to be entered?"
The Bodhisattva said: "One hundred koṭis is called an ayuta; one hundred ayutas is called a niyuta;
one hundred niyutas is called a kaṅkara."
One hundred *kaṅkara*s are called a *vivara*;
one hundred *vivaras* are called an *akṣobhya*;
and one hundred *akṣobhyas* are called a *vivāha*.
One hundred *vivāhas* are called an *utsaṅga*;
one hundred *utsaṅgas* are called a *bahula*;
one hundred *bahulas* are called a *nāgabala*.
One hundred *nāgabala*s are called a *tiṭilambha*.
One hundred *tiṭilambha*s are called a *vyavasthānaprajñapti*.
One hundred *vyavasthānaprajñapti*s are called a *hetuhila*.
One hundred *hetuhilās* are called a *karakūṇa*.
One hundred *karakūṇas* are called a *hetvindriya*.
One hundred *hetvindriyas* are called a *samāptalambha*.
One hundred *samāptalambhas* is called a *gaṇanāgati*. One hundred *gaṇanāgatis* is called a *niravadya*.
One hundred *niravadyas* is called a *mudrābala*.
One hundred *mudrābalas* is called a *sarvabala*.
One hundred *sarvabalas* is called a *visaṃjñāgati*. One hundred *visaṃjñāgatis* is called a *sarvasaṃjñā*.
One hundred *sarvasaṃjñā* are called a *vibhūtaṅgama*;
one hundred *vibhūtaṅgama* are called a *tallakṣaṇa*.
Indeed, by this calculation of *tallakṣaṇa*, even Sumeru, the king of mountains, would be exhausted by the act of casting down [a single grain] at each unit of a *lakṣa*.

Beyond this is the calculation called Dhvajāgravatī (Flag-Pinnacle), in which even as many [units] as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā would reach exhaustion through the process of depositing marks.
Beyond this is the calculation called Dhvajāgraniśāmaṇī (Jewel of the Flag-Pinnacle).
Beyond this is that which is called Vāhanaprajñapti; beyond this is that which is called Iṅga;
and beyond this is that which is called Kuruṭu.
Beyond that is the calculation called *kuruṭāvi*; beyond that is the calculation called *sarvanikṣepā*,
in which calculation ten [units] equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā would be exhausted by the act of depositing them as *lakṣas*.
Beyond this is the calculation called *agrasārā*,
wherein one hundred *koṭīs* of deposits equal to the sands of the Ganges River would be exhausted.
Beyond even that is the calculation following the entry of atoms (*paramāṇurajaḥ*).

Except for the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattva who has reached the supreme, excellent seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and is facing the consecration into all dharmas, there is no other being whatsoever to be found among the classes of beings who understands this calculation, except for me or someone like me.
Thus is the Bodhisattva in his final existence who has departed from the household life.
Arjuna asked: "O Prince, how is the calculation of the entry into atoms to be understood?
The Bodhisattva replied: "Seven atoms constitute one minute particle (*aṇu*)."
Seven atoms (aṇu) make one minute particle (truti);
seven minute particles make one mote in a sunbeam (vātāyanarajas);
and seven motes in a sunbeam make one rabbit-hair particle (śaśarajas).
Seven rabbit-hairs make one sheep’s hair;
seven sheep’s hairs make one cow’s hair;
seven cow’s hairs make one nit-mite’s hair.
Seven *likṣā*s make one mustard seed (*sarṣapa*);
seven mustard seeds make one barley grain (*yava*);
and seven barley grains make one finger-joint (*aṅgulīparva*).
Twelve finger-joints make a span (vitasti);
two spans make a cubit (hasta);
four cubits make a bow (dhanu).
One thousand bows is the distance of a *mārgadhvajākrośa*;
four *krośas* make one *yojana*. Among you, who knows the total measure of a *yojana*?
"How many are those atoms?
Arjuna replied, "O Prince, I myself have fallen into confusion;
how much more so then for others who possess little intelligence?"
"Let the prince explain: how many atoms are there in a mass of one yojana?

The Bodhisattva replied: "In that regard, a mass of one yojana consists of one *akṣobhya-nayuta* of atoms, plus thirty *koṭī-nayuta-śata-sahasras*, sixty *koṭī-śatas*, and thirty-two *koṭis*, and five [more]."
One million two hundred and twenty thousand— that is the total number of *yojanas* in the placement of a single atom-dust.
By this measure of entry, this Jambudvīpa is seven thousand *yojanas*,
and Godānīya is eight thousand *yojanas*.
Pūrvavideha is nine thousand yojanas;
Uttarakuru Island is ten thousand yojanas.

With this as the entry point, taking this four-continent world system as the foremost, there are one hundred full koṭis of four-continent world systems, wherein there are one hundred koṭis of great oceans.
a hundred koṭis of Cakravālas and Mahācakravālas, a hundred koṭis of Sumeru mountains, kings of mountains, and a hundred koṭis of the gods of the Four Great Kings;
A hundred koṭis of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, a hundred koṭis of the Yāma gods, and a hundred koṭis of the Tuṣita gods.
a hundred koṭis of Nirmāṇarati gods,
a hundred koṭis of Paranirmitavaśavartin gods,
and a hundred koṭis of Brahmakāyika gods;
One hundred koṭis of Brahmapurohitas,
one hundred koṭis of Brahmapārṣadyas,
and one hundred koṭis of Mahābrahmās.
One hundred koṭis of Parīttābhas, one hundred koṭis of Apramāṇābhas,
and one hundred koṭis of Ābhāsvaras.
One hundred koṭis of Parīttaśubhas,
one hundred koṭis of Apramāṇaśubhas,
and one hundred koṭis of Śubhakṛtsnas.
One hundred koṭis of Anabhrakas,
one hundred koṭis of Puṇyaprasavas,
and one hundred koṭis of Bṛhatphalas.
One hundred *kīṭīs* of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*),
one hundred *koṭīs* of the Abṛha deities,
and one hundred *koṭīs* of the Atapa deities.
One hundred koṭis of Sudṛśa gods, one hundred koṭis of Sudarśana gods, and one hundred koṭis of Akaniṣṭha gods.
This is called the trichiliocosm, great trichiliocosm world-system, vast and extensive.
It contains as many hundreds of yojanas as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, great trichiliocosm world-system,
and as many thousands of yojanas.
As many as there are ten million *yojanas*, as many as there are billions (*nayuta*) of *yojanas*—and so on, in detail—as far as there are calculations of the finest essence of *yojanas*:
how many atoms (*paramāṇu-rajas*) are these? Thus he says.
For this calculation of theirs has transcended all reckonings; therefore, it is called "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*).
Thus, there are incalculable numbers of atoms (*paramāṇu-rajas*) that exist within a triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).

Now, while this chapter on calculation was being expounded by the Bodhisattva, Arjuna the chief minister of accounts and the entire Śākya community became satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with wonder and amazement;
they all stood there, each offering his own garment.
They covered the Bodhisattva with the remaining garments and ornaments.
Then Arjuna, the great minister of astrology, spoke these verses:
"Hundreds of koṭis, ayutas, nayutas, as well as niyutas, kaṅkaras, and likewise bimbaras;
Akṣobhiṇī is supreme knowledge; for me there is no purpose beyond this. Therefore, the calculation of that incomparable knowledge lies further still.

Moreover, O Śākyas: one could, with a single *huṃ* sound, cast down all the atoms of the three-thousandfold world system, its grasses, forests, herbs, and drops of water; what wonder, then, that he does so with five hundred?
There, hundreds of thousands of gods and humans let out hundreds of thousands of cries of "Alas!", shouts of joy, and roars of exultation.
And the sons of the gods situated in the vault of the sky spoke these verses:
"As many beings as there are in their entirety throughout the three times, and all the minds, mental factors, perceptions, and discursive thoughts..."
Whether inferior or sublime, contracted or expanded—he understands them all within a single movement of thought.
Thus, monks, all the Śākya princes were surpassed;
the Bodhisattva alone excelled.
Immediately thereafter, in leaping, bounding, and running, the Bodhisattva alone excelled in every respect.
And the sons of the gods situated in the expanse of the sky spoke this verse:
"Through the virtue of his vows and austerities, through self-restraint, patience, self-control, and the power of loving-kindness, for ten million eons;
now hear the excellence of that speed, which has made his body and mind light. (Lal 12.26)
While you look on from here within the house, this essence of beings travels in an instant to the ten directions;
performing worship of immeasurable Victors with jewels, gold, and various wonders throughout infinite world-systems.
Furthermore, you do not even understand his coming and going, for he has attained such supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Who could feel wonder here that he moves so swiftly? He is peerless; show him respect.
Having done this, the Bodhisattva alone was distinguished.
Thereupon the Śākyas said, "In battles, the prince must first be distinguished and tested.
Then the Bodhisattva stood to one side,
while those five hundred Śākya youths fought simultaneously.
Thus, thirty-two Śākya youths stood ready for the wrestling match. Then Nanda and Ānanda approached the Bodhisattva for the wrestling match.
As soon as those two were touched by the Bodhisattva’s hand,
they fell to the surface of the earth, unable to endure the Bodhisattva’s strength and splendor.
Immediately thereafter, Prince Devadatta— arrogant, conceited, powerful, and intoxicated with the pride of being a Śākya— [remained standing].
And then, competing with the Bodhisattva, Devadatta, undaunted, circled the entire arena clockwise and,
displaying his prowess, rushed toward the Bodhisattva. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, remaining entirely unperturbed and without haste, playfully seized Prince Devadatta with his right hand.

Having seized him and whirled him three times in the expanse of the sky, he cast him down upon the surface of the earth with a mind of loving-kindness and an intent not to harm, for the purpose of subduing his pride;
yet it did not injure his body.
Then the Bodhisattva also said: "Enough, enough with this dispute!
Let all of you now become one and come together for the contest."
Then they all became joyful and rushed toward the Bodhisattva.

As soon as they were touched by the Bodhisattva, being unable to endure his splendor, majesty, physical strength, and power, they fell to the surface of the earth the very moment they were touched by him.
There, hundreds of thousands of gods and humans raised hundreds of thousands of shouts of "Hīhī! and cries of joy and exultation.
And the sons of the gods situated in the expanse of the sky, having rained down a great shower of flowers, spoke this verse in a single voice:
"However many millions of beings there may be in the ten directions, even if they were all like wicked wrestlers or great giants,
should they fall upon the Bull among Men in a single instant, they would collapse to the surface of the earth at the mere touch."

Mount Meru, Sumeru, as well as the Vajraka and Cakravāla mountains, and whatever other mountains exist anywhere in the ten directions—one might take them in one's hands and reduce them to powder like ink; what wonder is there in this regarding the insubstantial human body?

On the tip of the banner of this most excellent king of trees, he has struck down with the power of loving-kindness Māra—the great wicked wrestler, the kinsman of Darkness—along with his army, his forces, and his horses; indeed, he shall now touch unsurpassed, peaceful awakening.
Thus [it is said].
Having done this, the Bodhisattva alone was distinguished.
Then Daṇḍapāṇi said this to the Śākya princes: "This has been tested and seen;
come now, demonstrate your skill in archery.
There, at a distance of two *krośas*, an iron drum had been set up as a target for Ānanda.
Immediately following this, an iron drum was placed four *krośas* away from Devadatta;
an iron drum was placed two *yojanas* away from Daṇḍapāṇi;
and an iron drum was placed ten *krośas* away from the Bodhisattva.
Immediately after that, seven palm trees and an iron image of a boar equipped with a mechanical device were set up. There, Ānanda struck a drum from a distance of two *krośas*,
but beyond that point he was unable to do so.
Devadatta struck a drum located four krośas away, but he was unable to strike one further than that.
Sundarananda struck a drum located six krośas away.
He was unable to go further.
When a drum situated two yojanas away was struck by Daṇḍapāṇi, it was pierced,
yet he still could not go further.
There, whatever bow the Bodhisattva drew, that very one would snap.
Then the Bodhisattva said: "O King, is there anything else here in this city—a bow that could withstand my stringing and my physical strength and power?"
The king said, "There was, my son. The prince asked, "Where is that, Your Majesty?
The king said, "Your father’s grandfather, my son, was named Siṃhahanu."
The very bow of his is now being honored with perfumes and garlands in the temple;
yet no one at all was able to string that bow, much less draw it.
The Bodhisattva said, "O King, let that bow be brought here."
We shall desire to know.
When that bow was brought forward,
all the Śākya princes, despite exerting themselves with the utmost effort, were unable even to string the bow, let alone draw it. Thereupon, that bow was presented to the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi.
Then Daṇḍapāṇi the Śākya, exerting all his physical strength and power, began to string that bow,
but he was not able to do so;
finally, it was presented to the Bodhisattva.

Then the Bodhisattva, having taken it up, without even rising from his seat and remaining in the half-lotus posture, took hold of it with his left hand and strung it with the tip of a single finger of his right hand.
As that bow was being strung, the entire great city of Kapilavastu was made aware of it by the sound.
The entire population of the city became agitated and asked one another, "Whose is this kind of sound?
Others said to them, "It is said that Prince Siddhārtha has strung his grandfather’s bow;
this is its sound."
There, hundreds of thousands of gods and humans let out hundreds of thousands of cries of "Alas!", shouts of joy, and roars of exultation.
And the sons of the gods situated in the vault of the sky addressed King Śuddhodana and that great multitude with this verse:
"Just as this bow was drawn by the Sage, yet he has neither risen from his seat nor touched the ground."
Without doubt, the Sage, having conquered the army of Māra, will quickly fulfill his intention.
Thus, monks, the Bodhisattva, having strung that bow and taken up an arrow, discharged it with such power and strength that it pierced through Ānanda’s drum,
Devadatta’s, and all those as far as Sundarananda’s and Daṇḍapāṇi’s;
it then passed right through his own iron drum located ten *krośas* away, and further pierced seven palm trees and a boar statue equipped with mechanical devices.
That arrow, having entered the surface of the earth, became invisible.
In the very spot where that arrow had pierced and entered the ground, a well was formed,
which even today is called "Arrow Well" (Śarakūpa).
There, hundreds of thousands of gods and humans let out hundreds of thousands of cries of "Hīhī," shouts of joy, and roars of exultation;
and the entire Śākya host was struck with wonder and filled with amazement, exclaiming, "O,
how wonderful!"
"And yet, he has not even undergone formal training, yet such is his skill in the arts!
Then the sons of the gods situated in the expanse of the sky said this to King Śuddhodana and that great multitude of people: 'O men, what is there to marvel at here? Why is that? "

Seated here upon the seat of former Buddhas on this circle of the earth, having taken up the bow of tranquility and struck down the enemy of the afflictions with the arrows of emptiness and selflessness, and having shattered the net of views, he shall attain supreme, auspicious, stainless, and sorrowless enlightenment.
Having spoken thus, those sons of the gods scattered divine flowers over the Bodhisattva and departed.

Thus, having surpassed [others] as before in leaping, in the arts of writing, seals, calculation, and numbers, in the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), in running, jumping, swimming, and in the use of missiles; in the management of elephants, riding horses, and driving chariots; in the handling of bows, in steadiness and strength, in great valor, in the exercise of the arms, in the grasping of the elephant goad, in the grasping of the noose, in entering the garden, in exiting, in retreating, in the clenching of the fist, in the positioning of the feet, in the tying of the topknot, and in the art of cutting.
In piercing, splitting, cleaving, unerring hitting, hitting vital points, hitting by sound, firm striking,
in the game of dice, in composing poetry, in books, in painting, in form, in the art of sculpture, in learning, in the work of fire, in the lute, in instrumental music,
in dancing, in singing, in reciting, in narration, in comedy, in graceful movement, in drama, in mimicry, in the stringing of garlands, and in massage.

In gemology, in the coloring of cloth, in the art of illusion, in the study of dreams, in the cries of omens, in the characteristics of women, in the characteristics of men, in the characteristics of horses, in the characteristics of elephants, in the characteristics of cattle, in the characteristics of goats, in the characteristics of mixed breeds, in the characteristics of householders and lords,
in glossaries, in the Vedas, in the Purāṇas, in the Itihāsas, in grammar, in etymology, in phonetics, in prosody, in the ritual manuals for sacrifice, in astrology, and in Sāṃkhya.

In yoga, ritual practice (*kriyākalpa*), the arts of love (*vaiśika*), the Vaiśeṣika philosophy, the science of wealth (*arthavidyā*), the teachings of Bṛhaspati, the *āmbhīrya* and *āsurya* systems, the cries of beasts and birds, the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), water-machines, work with beeswax, needlework, basket-weaving, leaf-cutting, the compounding of perfumes—
in all such branches of activity (*sarvakarmakalā*) belonging to the worldly and other realms, including those that transcend the divine and the human— the Bodhisattva is everywhere [skilled].
Thus was he distinguished.
Then, at that time, Daṇḍapāṇi the Śākya gave his own daughter, Gopā the Śākya maiden, to the Bodhisattva;
and she was formally requested by King Śuddhodana in due course for the Bodhisattva.

There, moreover, the Bodhisattva, having entered into the midst of eighty-four thousand women, manifested himself as one who was enjoying, sporting, and diverting himself for the sake of experiencing the world.
Among those eighty-four thousand women, Gopā, the Śākya maiden, was consecrated as the chief queen of them all.

Furthermore, Gopā, the Śākya maiden, did not cover her face upon seeing anyone—not her mother-in-law, nor her father-in-law, nor the household folk. They were suspicious of her and reflected: "A newlywed bride indeed remains modestly withdrawn."
"Furthermore, this [nature] is always manifest.

Then Gopā, the Śākya maiden, having heard this fundamental truth, stood before all the members of the household and spoke these verses: "The Noble One shines when manifest, whether seated, standing, or walking."
Or like a precious jewel shining and radiant at the top of a banner.
Whether going, the Noble One shines; whether coming, he also shines.
Whether standing or sitting, the Noble One shines everywhere. (Lal 12.35)
The Noble One shines while speaking, and he shines even when silent; just as the kalaviṅka bird is beautiful whether by its appearance or its song. (Lal 12.36)
Clad in garments of kuśa grass or coarse cloth, his body emaciated,
that virtuous man, adorned by his own qualities, shines with his own inner splendor.
The noble one in whom no evil exists shines in every way;
how much soever he may be adorned, the fool who practices evil does not shine.

Those who are sinful within their own hearts, yet whose speech is as sweet as nectar poured from a jar, while their inner nature is as harsh as a rough mountain rock— meeting such people is as unpleasant as the sight of a venomous serpent.
O gentle ones, all bow down to you, and everything comes to you; like a sacred ford, you are the source of sustenance for all.
Noble ones, you are always like jars filled with curd and milk; for those such as you, the vision of the pure self is a supreme blessing.

Those who have for a long time avoided evil friends and have been embraced by the jewels of virtuous friends—having abandoned evil and established themselves in the Buddha-dharma—their [vision] is fruitful, auspicious, and beautiful to behold. Lal_12.41.
For those who are restrained in body and whose bodily faults are well-restrained, who are restrained in speech and whose words are never scattered,
whose senses are guarded, who are perfectly composed, and whose minds are serene— why should one conceal the face of such as these?

Even if one were to cover their body with thousands of garments, if their mind is exposed and lacks both modesty and shame; if they possess neither such virtues nor truthful speech—those who are thus naked wander in the world as the most naked of all. (Lal 12.43)
Those women who are guarded in mind and constantly restrained in their senses, who do not find pleasure in the thoughts of other beings but are devoted to their own husbands,
and who are as radiant and open as the sun and the moon— why should such women cover their faces? (Lal 12.44)
Moreover: "The great-souled sages, who are skilled in knowing the thoughts of others, as well as the hosts of gods, know my intention;
since my restraint of moral conduct and virtue is such that I am never heedless, what need have I for veiling my face? (Lal 12.45)
Monks, King Śuddhodana heard these very verses and this inspired exposition from Gopā, the Śākya maiden.

Having heard them, he was satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; he [presented her] with a pair of fine garments inlaid with many jewels, a pearl necklace worth hundreds of thousands of millions, and a [necklace] set with noble red pearls.
Having clothed the Śākya maiden Gopā in a golden necklace, he uttered this inspired utterance:

"Just as my son is adorned with virtues, so too does the maiden shine with her own qualities. These two pure beings have come together; they are united like clarified butter with the cream of clarified butter."
Thus [it is said].
(In due course, with the bodhisattvas at their head, they departed for their own city as before.)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the Śrī Lalitavistara, titled "The Display of Skills."
START Chapter 13 (Vaidya 111):
The Thirteenth Chapter, "The Exhortation."

Thus, monks, while the Bodhisattva was in the midst of his inner apartments, many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors arrived, uttering cries of self-rejoicing;
they were those who had applied themselves with zeal for the purpose of honoring the Bodhisattva.

Then, monks, at another time, it occurred to many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors: "Alas, this True Man has delayed in the inner apartments far too long!
And these beings whom he has matured over a long period through the four means of attraction—through generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial action, and consistency of purpose—"
When he has attained awakening, those who understand the Dharma he teaches will, at that very moment, find all those vessels of the Dharma vanished;
and the Bodhisattva, having subsequently gone forth, will realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.

Then, full of reverence and longing, they joined their palms in salutation and paid homage to the Bodhisattva. With such an intention, they remained gazing at him, thinking: "When indeed will that time come when we shall see this most excellent, pure Being departing from home;
and having departed, sitting down at the foot of that great king of trees, subduing Māra together with his host, and [attaining] the unsurpassed..."
Having fully awakened to perfect enlightenment, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with the four grounds of self-confidence of a Tathāgata,

and endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, he was turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma— threefold and twelve-fold— by means of the great miraculous play of a Buddha, according to the inclinations of the world of gods, humans, and asuras.
"Delighting them with well-spoken words."
In this regard, monks, for a long time, throughout incalculable eons, the Bodhisattva was constantly and continuously independent of others' guidance.

Regarding all mundane and supramundane phenomena, he was himself his own teacher in all practices of the roots of virtue. For a long time, he was one who knew the right time, the proper occasion, and the appropriate moment;
he was unfallen and possessed the five superknowledges.

Sporting with the bases of psychic power, skilled in all the faculties, knowing the proper and improper time, and seeking the right moment, he did not transgress the boundary he had reached, just like the great ocean.
Endowed with the power of the knowledge of the superknowledges (*abhijñājñānabala*), he himself knew everything:
"This is the time for exertion," [and so forth].
This is the time for restraint; this is the time for gathering;
this is the time for favor.
This is the time for equanimity;
this is the time for speaking; this is the time for remaining silent.
This is the time for departure,
this is the time for going forth,
this is the time for private study.
This is the time for appropriate mental attention;
this is the time for seclusion; this is the time to approach the assembly of kṣatriyas... [and so on] ... up to: this is the time to approach the assembly of brahmins and householders.
This is the time to approach the assembly of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen;
this is the time for teaching the Dharma;
this is the time for seclusion.
In all circumstances, the Bodhisattva was at all times one who knew the proper time and sought the right occasion.
Furthermore, monks, it is the natural law for Bodhisattvas in their final existence that the Buddhas,

the Blessed Ones, residing in the world-systems of the ten directions, must necessarily address them while they are in the midst of their inner apartments with such Dharma-gates as these, through the sounds of songs and musical instruments.
They are to be exhorted.
In this regard, it is said:
"Whatever beings there are in the worlds of the ten directions, they especially delight there in these musical instruments;
these verses, sung with sweet melody, urge on the most excellent among the best of men."
Previously, having seen sentient beings burdened by hundreds of sufferings, you made this vow:
"I shall become a shelter, a protection, a refuge for the world, a supreme benefactor and lord. (Lal 13.2)
O virtuous hero, remember your former conduct and the vow you made for the benefit of the world;
now is the time, this is the hour, this is your moment—go forth, O most excellent of the best of seers!
"For whose sake, O best of givers, you previously sacrificed various riches, as well as your head, hands, and feet—
you shall become a Buddha, a tamer of men and gods, the foremost in the world, and one perfected with hundreds of virtues."
Through ethical discipline you have practiced vows and austerities; through patience you act for the welfare of the world;
through vigor you are accumulated with auspicious qualities; and in meditation and wisdom, you are not equaled by anyone in the three realms.
O Sugata, you are clearly manifest in loving-kindness toward those who are possessed by anger, thick with the impurities of stubbornness;
you have manifold compassion for the ignorant, for those in falsehood, and for those devoid of virtuous qualities.
Having accumulated merit and wisdom, with a self purified by the auspicious, you shine forth free from dust through your mastery of meditation;
you illuminate these ten directions like the stainless moon released from the clouds.

These and many other kinds of beautiful sounds from musical instruments, possessing the resonance of the voice of a Jina, urge the one honored by gods and men: "Arise! This is your time to go forth! *Lal_13.8*
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, monks, in that most excellent and preeminent house—which was enriched with every kind of requisite, conducive to dwelling in happiness according to one’s wishes, radiant like a celestial palace in the city of the immortals, and possessed of the finest balconies, turrets, gateways, windows, chambers, gabled halls, and palaces; which was beautifully divided by various patterns of diverse ornaments made of all kinds of jewels; and which was adorned with raised parasols, banners, flags, and many nets of jeweled bells—there the Bodhisattva dwelt.

It was adorned with hundreds of thousands of hanging silk streamers, inlaid with various jewels, and draped with strings of pearls; it was beautified by walkways made of variegated silk and gems, hung with clusters of silk ribbons and garlands, perfumed by incense burners, covered with canopies of fine cotton cloth,
and strewn with lotuses, white lilies, and clusters of fresh water-lilies from all seasons— flowers that were most fragrant and exceedingly beautiful.

It abounded in various forms of enjoyment and architectural arrangements, resounded with the sweet warbling of diverse flocks of birds such as partridges, parrots, mainas, cuckoos, swans, peacocks, ruddy geese, kunālas, kalaviṅkas, and jīvajīvakas; its ground was composed of blue beryl, providing for all manner of enjoyment and structural beauty, displaying the reflections of all forms, and delighting the eyes so that one could never look upon it enough.

While the Bodhisattva was dwelling in that preeminent and excellent palace which generates supreme joy and gladness—a magnificent and noble refuge and abode—he remained with limbs stainless, pure, and immaculate; wearing unfading garlands and ornaments; his body anointed with the finest fragrant perfumes and unguents;

his person clothed in white, auspicious, spotless, pure, stainless garments; and reclining upon a couch fashioned from the most beautiful parts of many celestial fabrics, fine, well-arranged, soft, and pleasant to the touch like *kācilindika* wool.

He was like one surrounded on all sides by the wives of the immortals, his conduct marked by faultless, agreeable appearance and auspicious refinements; he dwelt amidst a beautiful inner court and was awakened by the performance of various musical instruments and songs— resounding with the sweet sounds of conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, small drums, flutes, lutes, *vallakī* lutes, *saṃpatāḍaka*, *kipala*, *nakula*, and *sughoṣaka* drums, as well as the melodious flute— and by those throngs of women who awakened the Bodhisattva with the resonant sounds of flutes played in smooth, sweet, and charming tones.

By the empowerment of those Blessed Buddhas residing in the ten directions, from the sounds and resonances of those bamboo flutes and musical instruments, these verses of exhortation to the bodhisattva issued forth:
Those women, with joyful minds and serene hearts, played sweet and enchanting music from their flutes;
and through the inspiration [of the Buddhas], they sang these verses concerning the Supreme Victors dwelling in the ten directions, which were of various, manifold, and wonderful forms.

O Hero, in the past you made this vow: "Having seen these people who are always without a protector, I shall bring them across old age, death, and other sufferings, after awakening to the supreme, ageless state free from sorrow. *Lalita-vistara* 13.10.

Therefore, O virtuous one, depart quickly from this excellent city and go to that region of the earth where the ancient seers practiced, so that you may awaken to the incomparable wisdom of the Victors.
In the past, you gave away various treasures of wealth, as well as your hands, feet, and your own dear self;
today is the time for you, O Great Sage, to distribute the infinite flood of Dharma to the world.
O auspicious one, your virtuous conduct was pure, unbroken, excellent, and constant throughout the past;
O Great Seer, by such conduct you are peerless, for you grieve for the world afflicted by various defilements.
For hundreds of lifetimes you have practiced patience; you have endured the various harsh words spoken by the world.
O Lord of Men, since your self is devoted to patience, forgiveness, and self-control, set your mind upon renunciation. (Lal 13.14)
Your vigor is firm, immovable, and unshakable; O Sugata, it was vast in the past.
Having subdued the deceitful Namuci along with his army, you shall dry up the three entire lower realms.
For whose sake you have practiced vows and austerities, having meditated upon the defilements and afflictions of the Kali age—
O Cloud, satisfy us who have long been thirsty and without a protector with a flood of the water of nectar!
Reflecting upon that former supreme mountain, having quickly departed from this excellent city,
and having realized the deathless state free from sorrow, I shall satisfy those afflicted by thirst with the nectar of immortality.
You are skilled in attending upon wisdom; your knowledge is vast, expansive, and infinite.
O you of auspicious and beautiful luster, spread the radiance of wisdom for those who are deluded and standing on the path of doubt.

Abide in loving-kindness; you have practiced it for a hundred lives. O Best One, abide in compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Whatever sublime conduct you yourself have practiced, distribute that very same conduct to the world.

Thus, from the splendors of the Jinas in the ten directions, verses variegated with the flowers of virtue resounded in various ways from musical instruments, exhorting the Prince as he lay upon his bed.
When again the joyful, delightful women, most beautiful and sweet-voiced,
played upon their musical instruments, then the Jinas, the tamers of gods and men in the ten directions, caused their supreme speech to resound through those instruments.
O benefactor of many virtues, you have performed [deeds] for the sake of the multitude; having conquered your own qualities, you wander through the realms of existence.
Remember, remember your former practice of vows and austerities! Go quickly to the excellent tree and touch the state of immortality.

O Lord of Men, those humans and gods who are parched with thirst and devoid of the qualities of the Jinas have their hopes fixed upon you, for you are capable of bestowing the essence of the deathless nectar.
O possessor of the ten powers, honored by the wise, quickly distribute this nectar among them.

O Friend, you who delight in the qualities of a Jina and act for the benefit of the world, you renounced wealth, jewels, and gold in your city; you renounced dear sons, the earth with its towns and villages; and you even renounced your own head, hands, feet, and eyes.
Formerly, when you were a king, O son of the best of men, a man came before you and spoke these words:
"Give me this earth with its cities and towns. At that time, you abandoned it joyfully, and your mind was not disturbed. (Lal 13.25)
Formerly, O King, when you were a brahmin, you served your elders and did no harm to others;
you established many people in wholesome conduct, and having passed away from there, you went to a state of existence dwelling in the city of the gods.
Formerly, when you were a prince and that best of sages was present, the king of the Kali age became enraged and cut off your body-hair;
yet, though the ancestral rites were performed upon you, your mind was not disturbed, and then milk flowed from your palms and feet.

Furthermore, O son of a seer, when you were formerly in the city, devoted to your vows and bearing a heavy burden while dwelling in the abode of the excellent mountain, the king struck you with an arrow made of poison; yet, O King, your compassion for him then was such that your mind was not disturbed.
Formerly, O bearer of virtues, when you were the lord of beasts, a man was being swept away by the many waters of a mountain river;
though he placed his enemy upon your back and set him on dry land for his benefit, you felt no agitation of mind. (Lalita Vistara 13.29)
O best of men, in the past you abandoned your son when the jewel fell into the vast ocean;
having crossed over and exhausted that great sea, you then obtained that precious gem, O firm-strengthed bull among men.
"O twice-born one, formerly you were a supreme man, a most excellent seer; come now, become my refuge.
The seer replied, "O best of the twice-born, when my enemy approached me, you abandoned your own body, yet you do not abandon me, O twice-born one. (Lal 13.31)
The seer Syāma approached him in his former dwelling among the trees and spoke with interest: "How many fruits are on this tree? Let me count them.
Having thoroughly understood and well-calculated them, just as there were shoots there, so too did he compose his words for you without error.

O noble-born one, bearer of excellent virtues, though you dwell in this city tree, it has not decayed; remembering your former deeds, the Lord of Maruts rejoices, recollecting your qualities, and bestows glory upon this supreme tree just as he did upon the previous ones.
Thus, O possessor of many virtues, who walks upon the path of virtue, your practice of vows and asceticism has been peerless;
now is the time for you to abandon the earth and its cities—quickly establish the world in the virtues and conduct of a Jina.

When the jewels of women, clad in beautiful garments and their limbs adorned, played most excellent and delightful musical instruments, then from the sounds of those instruments there issued forth sweet vocal tones, resonant with the splendor of the Jinas from the ten directions, as these various verses were proclaimed: Lal_13.35.
In former times, for many eons, you made this vow: "O Lamp of the World,
when the world is swallowed by old age and death, I shall become its protector."
Remember your former vow, O Lion among Men;
this is the time, O Lord of Bipeds, for you to go forth from here.
Throughout ten million lifetimes, you have given here many various gifts:
much wealth, gold, jewels, auspicious garments variegated with gems,
as well as hands, feet, eyes, beloved sons, and a prosperous kingdom.
What has been renounced by you is not subject to the fault of stinginess toward those who beg.

In this world, you were King Śiśu, Śaśiketu, Sudaṃṣṭra, Kṛpa, Karuṇāmanas, Maṇicūḍa, Candrapradīpa, and others such as Dṛḍhaśūra, Rājasunetra, and many millions of kings; you delighted in giving while manifesting various miraculous transformations.
For many eons you practiced the conduct of a Sugata; your purity of morality was like a stainless jewel.
While practicing there, you protected your morality as a yak protects its tail; through delighting in morality, you have brought vast benefit here in this world.
"O excellent elephant, you have been pierced here by arrows in this place seized by enemies; O Kṛpa, let compassion arise for this most fierce [battle] which obscures your splendor!
You have abandoned your beautiful, auspicious tusks, yet you do not abandon your virtue"—with these and many other such words, she performed many displays of virtue for you. (Lal 13.40)

O Man, in former times, many who were harmful to the world, accompanied by thousands of sufferings and harsh words, as well as execution and imprisonment—those whom you served with all happiness while devoted to patience—became your executioners here; yet that was endured by you.
O Lord, when you were among the bears in your dwelling on the preeminent mountain,
and the moon was like water [to them], you took hold of a man terrified by fear and attended to him with various fruits, roots, and every comfort.
The executioner Laghu brought him before you, and you granted him his life.
Your vigor was firmly established, immovable, and unshakable; through various vows and ascetic practices, you sought the knowledge of qualities for the sake of awakening.
Kṛtaka has become weak and Namuci is under your control; this is the time for you, O Lion among Men, to go forth from here by the power of your heroism.
In this city, you were formerly an excellent horse, golden-hued and light as a diamond in the sky; out of compassion, you went to the island of the rākṣasīs and,
taking hold of those people who had fallen into calamity, you established them in safety.
Thus, O Hero, many such primary miraculous transformations have been performed by you.
Having subdued the mind— which is swift, fickle, and longing for delight in sense objects— through self-restraint, tranquility, and discipline that strike down the afflictions,
you, O foremost of meditators, have perfected your own virtues here for the sake of the world while delighting in meditation.
This is the time for you, O supreme being, to display your miraculous power of meditation here.
In former times, you were a well-established seer, delighting in meditation; when men were bereft of kings, you took them as subjects and consecrated them in the kingdom.
You generated them in the ten wholesome paths and established them on the paths of Brahmā; when those men passed away, they all went then to the abode of Brahmā.
O Knower of the various movements in every direction, you who know the proper methods, who understand the conduct of others in the world, the knowledge of sounds, and the knowledge of the senses;
O Master of the principles of discipline, who possesses diverse mental power and has reached the further shore—you, O Son of a King, this is the time for your departure from here.
Seeing you, former generations—fallen into wrong views and fallen into various sufferings and many hardships due to old age and death—were indeed in a state of distress.
You, who bring about the end of existence and non-existence, have followed the straight path; having destroyed the darkness, you have accomplished a great benefit for the world here.
Thus, with various beautiful and virtuous verses of diverse kinds,
Jinatejā urged the Hero with musical instruments:
"Having seen the masses of people here filled with suffering, do not remain indifferent!"
O Excellent Buddha, this is the time for you to go forth from here.

Adorned with various garments, jewels, necklaces, perfumes, and garlands, the women—filled with serene minds and born of love—were overjoyed as they awakened the Supreme Being with the sounding of musical instruments. Through the power of the Jina, a single form of verse issued forth from the instruments: (Vaidya 119) Lal_13.50 //
For whose sake you have practiced giving for many eons, renouncing what is difficult to give,
and cultivated morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom—
now the time has arrived for that purpose of benefiting the world.
O Leader, quickly contemplate the thought of renunciation; do not delay!
In former times, you gave away treasuries of jewels and ornaments of gold and silver, and you performed various kinds of sacrifices in those various births.
You renounced your wife, sons, daughters, your body, your kingdom, and your life—immeasurable things difficult to give up—for the sake of awakening. Lal_13.52.
O King of noble merit, you were formerly the renowned Viśrutaśrī,
Nimiṃdhara, Nimi, Kṛṣṇabandhu, Brahmadatta, and Kesarī.
Sahasrayajña, Dharmacintin, Arcimat, Dṛḍhadhanus,
Sucintitārtha, and Dīnasattva— by these, that which is difficult to renounce was abandoned.
Sutasoma, of blazing heroism and meritorious rays, you were he who possessed great generosity and strength; you were the grateful one,
the royal sage with the form of the moon, the hero who increases truth.
O King, you are a seeker of well-spoken words, possessed of excellent wisdom, and gentle.

Candraprabha, Viśeṣagāmin, Reṇubhū, Diśāmpati, Pradānaśūra, Kāśirāja, Ratnacūḍa, Śāntaga, and other lords of kings by whom things difficult to give were renounced; just as they rained down the rain of renunciation, so does this one rain down the Dharma.
O Essence of Beings, in the past you have seen Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and for them you performed immeasurable and inconceivable worship of the Buddhas.
While seeking the supreme, foremost enlightenment for the sake of liberating sentient beings, that time has now arrived; O Hero, go forth from this best of cities.
In your first [birth], you worshipped Amoghadarśin with *śāla* flowers; with a serene mind, you gazed upon Virocana for a moment.
You gave a single *harītakī* fruit to Dundubhisvara, and having taken up a blade of grass, you maintained it; thus was the house of sandalwood seen by you.
As he entered the city, Reṇu saw a handful of powder being thrown; he gave a cry of "Well done! to the Lord of Dharma as he was preaching the Dharma.
"Homage, homage to Samantadarśin! he said upon seeing him, and with joy, Mahārciskandhin threw a golden garland at him.

Dharmadhvaja [was the Buddha] when [the bodhisattva] was a giver of garments; Rodha [was the Buddha] when he was a handful of *muṅga* grass; Aśokapuṣpin [was the Buddha] when he was a vessel of gruel; Jñānaketu [was the Buddha] when he was a charioteer; Ratnaśikhī [was the Buddha] when he was a giver of lamps; Padmayoni [was the Buddha] when he was medicinal herbs; Sarvābhibhū [was the Buddha] when he was a pearl necklace; and Sāgara [was the Buddha] when he was a giver of lotuses.

Vitāna gave a canopy; Padmagarbha, a lion skin for a seat; Śālendrarāja gave ghee; Puṣpita abandoned milk; Yaśodatta gave a kurunṭaka flower; Satyadarśin offered food; Jñānameru prostrated his body; and Nāgadatta gave a robe. (Lal 13.60)
Atyuccagāmin, Candanāgri, Tīkṣṇaloha, Muṣṭinā, Mahāviyūha, Padmadāni, Raśmirāja, and Ratnabhi;
Śākyamuni, Suvarṇamuṣṭi, Indraketu, and Sūryānana were praised; and Vataṃsaka was adorned with a golden band by Sūmatī.

Nāgābhibhū [offered] a gift of jewels; Puṣya [offered] a spread of fine cloth; Bhaiṣajyarāja [offered] a precious parasol; Siṃhaketu [offered] a seat; Guṇāgradhārin [offered] a net of jewels; Sarvavādin [offered] to Kāśyapa [a gift of] the finest incense; Arciketu [offered] powdered incense; and [he offered it] at a shrine of flowers.

Akṣobhyarāja offered a gabled pavilion; Mālya was honored by the world; Tagaraśikhin renounced his kingdom; Sarvagandhin was invincible; Mahāpradīpa sacrificed himself; Bhūṣaṇa [offered] lotuses; Padmottara [offered] various flowers; Dharmaketu acted as a lamp with blue lotuses. Lal_13.63.

"O Essence of Beings, remember those other Buddhas whom you worshipped in the past with various and manifold offerings; remember those past Buddhas and the worship rendered to those Teachers. Do not neglect these helpless beings who are filled with grief; go forth! (Lal 13.64)
Upon merely seeing Dīpaṃkara, he attained supreme patience; he obtained the five infallible higher knowledges and the conformable [powers].
Thereafter, for incalculable eons throughout all world-systems, he performed inconceivable worship of each and every Buddha.

"Those immeasurable eons have passed away, and those Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa; even all your own former existences and their names—where have they gone? All phenomena are subject to the nature of exhaustion and destruction; there is nothing eternal in the conditioned. Worldly desires, kingdoms, and enjoyments are impermanent; therefore, go forth from this supreme city."

Old age, sickness, and death arrive—terrible and of great dread—like a fire of fierce brilliance and terror at the end of an eon. All conditioned phenomena have the nature of ending in decay; nothing within the compounded is permanent.
Having undergone great hardship, the virtuous being has gone forth.

When the host of women sought to awaken the lord of men, who was lying in a comfortable sleep, with the sounds of lutes, flutes, and various musical instruments, then this sound of music issued forth: Lal_13.68.
The three realms of existence are ablaze with the sufferings of old age and disease; this world is ignited by the fire of death and is without a protector.
Always deluded within the refuge of cyclic existence, the world wanders like a bee trapped inside a jar.
The three realms of existence are unstable, resembling autumn clouds; birth and death in the world are like a theatrical performance.
Life in the world passes with swift and rapid speed, like a mountain river, or like lightning in the sky.
On earth, in the city of the gods, and on the path of the three lower realms, the ignorant masses, under the power of the thirst for existence and ignorance,
revolve through the five destinies like the spinning of a potter’s wheel. (Lalita-vistara 13.71)

O noose of the Kali age, this world is besprinkled with things of lovely form, with pleasant sounds, with auspicious fragrances and tastes, and with the supreme happiness of touch— just like a monkey caught in the snare of a deer-hunter.
The qualities of sensual desire are accompanied by fear, fraught with danger, and always productive of enmity; they bring much sorrow and affliction.
They are like the edge of a sword, resembling poisonous leaves, and are abandoned by noble beings just as one avoids a jar of excrement.

The qualities of sensual desire always cause the loss of mindfulness, produce darkness, and give rise to fear; they are the constant root of suffering and the means by which the creeper of craving for existence grows. They are inherently fearful and provide no refuge. (Lal 13.74)
Just as a blazing pit of fire is full of terror, so have these sensual desires been understood by the noble ones;
they are like a great mire, like the edge of a sword, and like the blade of a razor smeared with honey.
Just as jars of excrement, so are these sensual desires known by the wise;
they are like spears, like the flesh of a human corpse, and like the skulls of dogs with their mouths full of filth. (Lal 13.76)
These qualities of sensual pleasure are like the moon reflected in water, like a reflection, or like an echo in the mountains;
they are like a mirage, like a theatrical performance, and likewise like a dream—so have they been understood by the noble ones.
These qualities of sensual pleasure are momentary and insubstantial; they are like illusions and mirages, false and unreal.
Like bubbles and foam upon the water, they are deceptive and arise from conceptual construction—thus have they been understood by the wise.
In the first stage of life, possessing excellent form and considered dear and beloved, they practice this childhood sport;
yet when the body's vigor is destroyed by the sufferings of old age and disease, they abandon him like deer a dried-up river.
This childhood conduct is considered dear and desirable when one possesses wealth, grain, many goods, and power;
yet they abandon one who has lost his wealth and fallen into distress, just as men leave a desolate wilderness.
Just as a flowering tree or a fruit-bearing tree brings joy to people, so too does one who delights in giving;
yet when that seeker of alms becomes destitute of wealth and afflicted by old age, he then becomes unpleasant, like a vulture.
A lord who is powerful in wealth, endowed with excellent form, and who brings delight to the senses through the company of beloved ones,
becomes as disagreeable as death itself when he is afflicted by the sufferings of old age and disease and his fortune has perished.
Worn out by old age and past the prime of life, one becomes like a tree struck by lightning;
like a house decayed by age and full of danger, O Sage, quickly speak of the escape from old age.
Old age withers the multitude of men and women, just as the māluva creeper dries up a dense grove of sāl trees;
old age robs one of vigor, prowess, and speed, like a man sunk in the mud.
Old age makes the beautiful form ugly; old age robs one of splendor, strength, and stamina;
old age always takes away happiness and brings about humiliation; old age brings death and robs one of vitality.
The world is afflicted by hundreds of various diseases and the intense suffering of manifold ailments, like deer scorched by fire;
behold this world overcome by old age and sickness, and quickly teach the way out of suffering.

Just as in the cold season a great mass of snow robs the vigor of grasses, shrubs, forests, and medicinal herbs, so too do disease and old age rob one of vitality; the faculties, physical form, and strength decline.
It causes the destruction of wealth, grain, and great possessions; it brings about affliction, accompanied by disease and old age;
it acts as an obstacle and creates hatred for what is dear; it produces a burning heat like the sun in the sky. (Lal 13.88)

Death, passing away, decease, and the end of life; constant separation from beloved things and people; and the non-returning and non-reuniting—these are like the leaves and fruits of a tree or the current of a river.
Death brings those who have mastery under its power; death carries one away as a river sweeps away a log.
A man goes forth without a companion, alone and helpless, followed by the fruit of his own karma.
Death devours hundreds of living beings, as a sea-monster seizes creatures in the water;
it swallows the host of beings as Garuḍa swallows the serpent, as the king of beasts swallows the elephant, and as fire consumes grass, herbs, and the multitude of living things.
You made a vow to liberate this world from hundreds of such manifold faults;
remember that former course of your vow, for now is the time for you to go forth.
When the throng of women, filled with great joy, awakened the Great Sage with musical instruments,
then various verses issued forth from the sound of those instruments through the power of the Sugata.
All that is conditioned is fragile and does not endure for long, existing like a bubble in the sky;
this time has arrived for you, O observer of noble vows—it is the moment for your renunciation.
Formations are impermanent and unstable; they are by nature fragile like an unbaked clay pot.
They are like borrowed goods belonging to another, like a city of sand, existing only for a moment.
Formations are subject to destruction, like plaster washed away by the rainy season;
they are dependent on conditions and inherently weak, like a riverbank with its sand.
Formations are like a lamp, characterized by rapid arising and ceasing;
they are unstable like the wind, and as insubstantial and weak as a mass of foam.
Formations are inactive and empty; when examined, they are like the trunk of a plantain tree.
Like an illusion, they delude the mind; they are said to be like a fist used to deceive children.
Everything comprised within conditioned phenomena proceeds by means of causes and conditions;
through mutual dependence upon causes, this is not understood by foolish people.

Just as a rope made of balvaja grass is twisted by the power of effort depending upon muñja grass, and thus the water-wheel with its mechanism revolves— yet individually, each part lacks the capacity for such movement. (Lal 13.100)
Likewise, that which exists within all the factors of existence depends upon mutual accumulation;
yet, as it occurs within each individual factor, it is not perceived from the perspective of either the prior or the subsequent limit.
Just as when a seed exists there is a sprout, yet that which is the seed is not itself the sprout;
it is neither different from it nor identical to it—such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), characterized by neither annihilation nor permanence.
Volitional formations have ignorance as their condition; yet in reality, those volitional formations do not exist within that ignorance.
For both volitional formations and ignorance are empty, being of a single nature and devoid of activity.
From a seal, a counter-seal is seen, yet no transference of the seal is perceived;
it is neither there, nor is it eternal; thus, conditioned phenomena are neither annihilated nor eternal.
Dependent upon the eye and visible forms, visual consciousness arises here;
yet the form does not reside in the eye, nor is there any transfer of the form into the eye.
These phenomena are selfless and impure, yet they are imagined as having a self and being pure;
from such a perverted and unreal conceptualization, visual consciousness arises.
The yogi perceives the arising and ceasing of consciousness, its production and its passing away;
he sees that which has gone nowhere and come from nowhere as empty and like an illusion. *Lal 13.107*

Just as fire is produced from the lower fire-stick, the upper fire-stick, and the exertion of the hands— arising through these conditions— the fire, having accomplished its purpose, quickly ceases. (Lal 13.108)
Then, if some wise person searches for where this has come from or where it goes,
searching through all the intermediate and cardinal directions, neither its coming nor its going can be found.

The aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, as well as the elements of craving and ignorance, have karma as their condition; yet this collection is merely a designation for a "sentient being," and that [being] is not found in the ultimate sense.
Syllables arise in dependence upon the throat, the lips, the palate, and the movement of the tongue;
yet they do not reside in the throat nor in the palate, for not even a single syllable can be apprehended.
And that speech issues forth from the assembly of conditions by the power of mind and intellect;
mind and speech are invisible and formless, and are not perceived either externally or internally.
The wise one, perceiving the arising and passing away of speech, sounds, and voices,
then sees all words as momentary, hollow, and like an echo.

Just as, through the conjunction of three factors—the strings, the wood, and the exertion of the hand—sound issues forth from instruments such as the *tuṇava*, the lute, and the *sughoṣaka*, arising from them; so it is with this.
Then, if some wise person searches for where this [sound] has come from or where it goes,
searching through all the intermediate and cardinal directions, the coming and going of the sound cannot be found. (Lal 13.115)
Thus, through causes and conditions, the entire realm of conditioned phenomena proceeds;
yet the yogi, by seeing reality as it is, perceives that conditioned phenomena are empty and devoid of agency.
