The aggregates, sense-bases, and elements are empty; the internal is empty and the external is empty.
They are devoid of a sentient being or a self, without abode, and have the nature and characteristics of the space of phenomena.
Such is the characteristic of the Dharma as it was realized by you yourself upon seeing the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; awaken now all beings, including gods and humans, just as you have awakened for yourself.
The world is scorched by the passions of attachment and aversion, which are falsely imagined through perversion;
O Leader, release a stream of nectar, cooled like the water from the clouds of compassion! (Lal 13.119)
For the sake of you, the wise have bestowed gifts throughout many millions of eons;
indeed, having attained supreme enlightenment, they will gather the noble wealth for all living beings.
O Noble One, remember that former conduct when you were poor, destitute, and suffering; O Charioteer of Beings, do not neglect them, but bestow upon them the accumulation of the noble wealth.
Since you have always well-guarded your moral conduct for the sake of closing off the realms of misery,
I shall show the supreme gateway to the nectar of heaven to many millions of beings.

Remember that former conduct; having closed the gates to the realms of hell, open the gates to heaven and the deathless nectar! By means of your supernatural power, fulfill the intention of those who possess virtue.
In you, patience has always been well-guarded for the sake of pacifying resentment and anger in embodied beings.
O ocean of existence, I shall ferry sentient beings across and establish them in a state that is auspicious, secure, and free from fever.
Recall that former conduct, which was agitated by enmity, malice, and cruelty;
do not remain indifferent toward those who practice violence, but establish this world upon the ground of patience.
Having fully prepared this ship of Dharma for the sake of which I have cultivated vigor within you,
I shall ferry the world across the ocean of existence and establish it in a state that is auspicious, secure, and free from feverish affliction.
Recall that former conduct; the world is deluded as if by the four floods.
With light vigor, strength, and prowess, you shall deliver the beings who are without a leader.
You have cultivated meditation and the subduing of the afflictions for the sake of which you possess such gentleness;
I shall establish those with wandering senses and ordinary faculties upon the noble path of the mind.
Remember that former conduct; this world is here entangled in the webs of affliction.
Do not neglect those oppressed by afflictions; establish these people in one-pointed concentration.
O Wise One, in the past you cultivated wisdom for the sake of this world shrouded in the blinding darkness of delusion and ignorance;
now, as a gift, you shall provide the eye that perceives reality for the beholding of the many hundreds of dharmas.
Remember that former conduct in this world shrouded by the blinding darkness of delusion and ignorance;
bestow your excellent wisdom, its sublime radiance, and the stainless, pure eye of Dharma.
From the sound of the musical instruments and the singing of the women, such a verse issued forth;
having heard it, they abandoned sloth and directed their minds toward supreme, foremost enlightenment.
Thus it is said.
Thus, monks, even while in the midst of the inner apartments, the Bodhisattva was not deprived of hearing the Dharma,
nor was he deprived of mental attention to the Dharma.
For what reason?

For thus, monks, for a long time the Bodhisattva was full of reverence; with resolute intention toward the teachings and the preachers of the Dharma, he was a seeker of the Dharma, a lover of the Dharma, and one who delighted in the joy of the Dharma; insatiable in his search for the Dharma, he proclaimed the teachings exactly as he had heard them.
He is the unsurpassed great master of the gift of Dharma;
he teaches the Dharma without worldly motives and is free from stinginess regarding the gift of Dharma;
he is devoid of the "teacher's fist" and has practiced in accordance with the Dharma, being a hero in the practice of the Dharma.

He has the Dharma as his abode, the Dharma as his protection, the Dharma as his refuge, the Dharma as his resort, and the Dharma as his ultimate goal; he is absorbed in the contemplation of the Dharma, has emerged through patience, practices the perfection of wisdom, and has reached the mastery of skillful means.
In that regard, monks, the Bodhisattva, through the play of his great skill in means, displayed various modes of conduct to the entire harem according to their individual inclinations;
and following the natural law of conforming to the world— just as previous Bodhisattvas who had transcended the worldly realm did—
he, having long understood the faults of sensual desire, nevertheless manifested the enjoyment of desires against his own will for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
Having displayed a sovereignty over the world that is peerless, distinguished by the power of the accumulation of merit from the gathering of immeasurable roots of virtue;

having displayed the bliss of sensual pleasure, which is more delightful than the highest delights and consists of the most excellent, exquisite, diverse, and manifold forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures that transcend those of gods and humans;
and having displayed mastery over one's own mind because there is no limit to all the objects of sensual delight within one's own domain;
Having matured those beings who had accumulated roots of merit through the assistance of the power of his former vows by dwelling together with them in a state of equality,

and because his mind was unstained by the impurities of the afflictions of all the world even while situated in the midst of his harem, the Bodhisattva, observing the time for the maturation of the realm of beings as he had previously invited them, at that moment recollected his former vow to a still greater degree.
He brought the qualities of a Buddha to manifestation,
brought forth the power of his vows,
and entered into great compassion for all sentient beings.
He reflected upon the liberation of sentient beings;
he contemplated that all prosperities end in calamity;
and he thoroughly examined how cyclic existence is filled with many misfortunes and fears.
He cut through the snares of Māra’s strife and released himself from the continuity of saṃsāra,
directing his mind toward nirvāṇa.
In that regard, monks, the Bodhisattva, having thoroughly understood the defects of saṃsāra from its very beginning, was through his resolute intention (adhyāśaya) indifferent to the conditioned;
he was indifferent to all forms of grasping and acquisition, oriented toward the Buddha-dharma and nirvāṇa, turned away from saṃsāra, and delighted in the sphere of the Tathāgatas.

He remained unmingled with the sphere of Māra’s domain, seeing the faults of existence as ablaze, intent on escaping the triple world, and skilled in the departure from the defects and miseries of saṃsāra.

Desirous of going forth, intent on renunciation, inclined toward solitude, leaning toward solitude, tending toward solitude, facing the wilderness and remote forests, longing for seclusion and tranquility, established in the welfare of himself and others, a hero in the practice of the unsurpassed, desiring the benefit, welfare, happiness, and security of the world, compassionate toward the world, seeking its well-being, dwelling in loving-kindness, and possessed of great compassion.
He was skilled in the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), constantly and perpetually possessing a mind free from weariness, and expert in the ripening and disciplining of sentient beings.

His mental attention was imbued with love for all beings as if they were his only son; he was one who renounced all things without regard, delighting in the distribution of gifts, dedicated to relinquishment, open-handed, a hero in generosity, a performer of sacrifices, one whose merit was fully abundant, and whose merit was well-collected.

With a mind well-restrained, free from the stains of attachment and stinginess, he is an unsurpassed great lord of giving; having given, he does not expect a karmic result, for he is a hero in generosity. He has risen up to subdue all hostile afflictions, headed by desire, great desire, greed, hatred, intoxication, pride, delusion, and stinginess. Unwavering due to the continuous production of the mind set on omniscience, he is well-armored with the great armor of the mind of renunciation and is compassionate toward the world.
Like a well-wisher, his heroism was armored and clad in mail; he possessed the strength, prowess, and valor of great compassion focused on the liberation of sentient beings as its objective.

His weapon was the renunciation of an irreversible equanimity toward all beings, satisfying the intentions and inclinations of sentient beings according to their desires. Having become a vessel for enlightenment, he pierced the Dharma at the opportune moment and made the vow of dedicating [merit] toward awakening. With his banner never lowered, he practiced the relinquishment of giving that purifies the three spheres.

He possesses the firm weapon of the supreme vajra of wisdom; he has thoroughly subdued the adversaries that are the afflictions; he is established in the practice of ethical discipline, virtuous qualities, and proper conduct;

his physical, vocal, and mental actions are well-guarded; he perceives even the slightest fault with fear; his ethical discipline is perfectly pure; his mind is stainless, immaculate, and free from defilement;
and his mind is undisturbed by any ill-spoken words, offensive speech, paths of verbal abuse, reviling, disparagement, beating, threatening, killing, binding, imprisonment, or any such suffering.
With an unperturbed mind, endowed with patience and gentleness, unharmed, uninjured, and free from malice, he exerts ardent vigor for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings;

possessing firm resolve, he undertakes the accumulation of all roots of merit and wholesome qualities without turning back; being mindful, well-possessed of clear comprehension, well-composed, and undistracted in mind, he applies his attention one-pointedly to meditative concentration, is skilled in the discernment of phenomena, has attained illumination, and is free from the darkness of ignorance.

With a mind cultivated through the aspects of impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and impurity; with mental attention thoroughly refined by the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, and the noble truths—all the dharmas conducive to awakening; with an intellect purified by calm abiding and insight; seeing dependent origination and the truths; through the realization of the truths, no longer dependent on others; sporting in the bliss of the three liberations; he has entered the way of all dharmas as being like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, the moon reflected in water, an echo, and a reflection.

Thus, monks, such was the mental disposition of the Bodhisattva: he dwelt in this manner in the Dharma, he dwelt in this manner in the greatness of his virtues, and he dwelt in this manner devoted to the welfare of sentient beings. Furthermore, at that time, being exhorted by these verses issued from the musical instruments and songs empowered by the Buddhas of the ten directions, he [recollected] the inner apartments of the previous Bodhisattvas who had reached their final existence.
He brought four gateways of the Dharma into manifestation.
What are these four? Namely: generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful action, and consistency of purpose.

He brought before him the Dharma-door called "the purification of the accomplishment of the application of the four means of attraction. He brought before him the Dharma-door called "the domain of irreversibility through the empowerment of the vow for the mind of omniscience, which is never lost and shares the same intention as the lineage of the Three Jewels. And he brought before him the Dharma-door called "the entry into great compassion, the resolute intention of not abandoning any sentient being."

He brought before him a Dharma-door called the Great Array of the Accumulation of the Specific Power of Saṃsāra through the Knowledge that Ascertains the Meaning of the Distinctions in All the Terms of the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment.
Having brought these four Dharma-doors before him, at that time the Bodhisattva performed such a miraculous feat (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) for the sake of maturing his entire harem.

By means of such a miraculous feat (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) performed through the power of the Bodhisattva, hundreds of thousands of such gateways of the Dharma (*dharmamukha*) issued forth from those sounds of musical chanting. They were as follows:
with noble zeal (*udārachanda*), with intention (*āśaya*), with resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), and with compassion (*karuṇā*) for living beings.
A mind arises for the sake of supreme, foremost enlightenment, and from the musical instruments, sounds emerge.
Faith, clarity, resolve, reverence, freedom from pride, and bowing before one's teachers;
inquiring after them, seeking what is wholesome, mindfulness, and cultivation—these were the sounds that went forth.

From it issued forth the sound of generosity, self-restraint, and the virtues of discipline; likewise the sound of patience and the sound of vigor; the sound of the accomplishment of meditative concentration and absorption; and the sound of wisdom and skillful means.
The word for loving-kindness, the word for compassion, the word for sympathetic joy, and the word for equanimity;
the word for supernormal knowledge, and the word for maturing sentient beings through the determination of the four means of attraction—all these words issued forth.

The words "foundations of mindfulness" and their classifications, as well as the "right efforts," the "bases of psychic power," the "five faculties," the distinctions of the "five powers," and the word "factors of enlightenment"—these issued forth from the musical instruments. *Lalita-vistara* 13.137.

The distinctions of the power of the eightfold path, the sounds of tranquility and insight, the words of impermanence, suffering, affliction, and non-self, and the words of the affliction of impurity— all these issued forth from the musical instruments. (Lal 13.138)

The word "dispassion," the word "seclusion," the word "knowledge of destruction," the word "non-arising," the word "non-cessation," and the word "nirvana without substrate" issued forth from the musical instruments.
From such musical sounds as these, the power of the word of awakening issued forth;
hearing which, all the women who had been trained set their aspirations for awakening toward the Supreme Being.

Thus, monks, while staying in the midst of the inner apartments, the Bodhisattva brought those eighty-four thousand women to maturity for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, as well as many hundreds of thousands of deities who had gathered there.

Likewise, at the time of his Great Departure, there was a son of the gods belonging to the Tuṣita host named Hrīdeva; surrounded and escorted by thirty-two thousand sons of the gods, he approached the palace where the Bodhisattva was staying during the tranquility of the night for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Having approached, while still situated in the expanse of the sky, he addressed the Bodhisattva in verses:

"O one of great fame, you have displayed your passing away and manifested your birth; O lion among men, you have shown yourself in the inner apartments, acting in accordance with the ways of the world."
"Many gods and humans in the world have been brought to maturity by attaining the Dharma;
today is the time and the occasion—reflect upon the thought of renunciation. (Lal 13.142)
For one who is bound cannot liberate others, nor can a blind man show the path;
but one who is liberated can liberate others, and one with sight can show the path.
Those beings who are slaves to desire, whose trust is fixed on home, wealth, sons, and wives—
when they are being instructed by you, may they conceive a longing for the thought of renunciation.
Having renounced sovereignty, the play of desire, the four continents, and the seven jewels, the world of men and gods, knowing that you have gone forth, would surely yearn for you.
Moreover, although you dwell in the states of meditative bliss and are not attached to sensual desires,
nevertheless, awaken those hundreds of gods and humans who have long been asleep.
This youth has already passed away like a mountain river with its swift and trembling current;
for one whose youth has gone, the thought of renunciation does not shine.
Therefore, it is well that you should go forth now while in the first stage of youth and in the prime of life;
fulfill your vow and accomplish the purpose of the hosts of gods.
There is no satisfaction in the pleasures of the sensory qualities, just as there is no satiation of the salt ocean by waters;
those alone are satisfied whose noble, supramundane, and stainless wisdom exists.
"You are dear and pleasing here to King Śuddhodana and to the kingdom; O you whose face resembles a hundred-petaled lotus, contemplate the thought of renunciation."
O Unequaled Hero, quickly establish on the path of liberation those who are bound by firm fetters, lacking refuge, and scorched by the fires of the afflictions, O Peaceful One.
O Physician, skilled in the elements, quickly establish in the bliss of nirvana those beings long afflicted by disease, using the application of the medicine of the Dharma.
Blinded by deepest darkness, sightless, and bound by the net of views agitated by delusion—
quickly purify the eye of the lamp of wisdom for men and gods!
Many gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas gaze upward, thinking:
"We shall see him when he has attained awakening, and we shall hear the unsurpassed Dharma."
And the king of serpents shall behold his own abode illuminated by your splendor;
he will perform infinite worship, fulfilling his vow and aspiration.
The four world-protectors, together with their armies, wait upon you;
O Banner of Enlightenment, we shall give four bowls to you whose mind is fulfilled.
The Brahmā, moving in perfect tranquility and possessing loving speech and compassion, gazes upon him, thinking:
"I shall serve the Lord of Men as he turns the unsurpassed wheel."
And the deities who ripen awakening, having resided upon the seat of awakening, thought:
"This truth shall arise; I shall behold him as he awakens to enlightenment."
For it is true that Bodhisattvas manifest activities within the inner apartments;
you should be their leader, lest you become their follower.
O you of lovely speech and gentle voice, remember the prophecy of Dīpaṃkara;
utter the sound of the Conqueror’s voice, which is true, such as it is, and not false.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter of the Śrī Lalitavistara, titled "The Chapter on the Exhortation."
START Chapter 14 (Vaidya 135): The Fourteenth Chapter, "The Dream."

Thus, monks, being thus exhorted by that son of the gods, the Bodhisattva caused King Śuddhodana to see this dream: namely, that King Śuddhodana, while asleep and having entered the state of dreaming at night during the time of profound stillness, saw the Bodhisattva departing, surrounded by a host of deities.
He saw that [the prince], having gone forth, had become a renunciant and was clad in saffron-colored robes.
Having awakened, he asked the chamberlain very urgently: "Is the prince in the inner apartments?
He replied: "He is, Your Majesty."
Then, a dart of grief entered the heart of King Śuddhodana within the inner apartments: "This prince will certainly go forth into the homeless life, since these preliminary signs are now being seen."
This thought occurred to him: "The prince must certainly never be allowed to go out to the park grounds.
Delighting in the midst of a company of women, he will find pleasure right here and will not go forth."
Then King Śuddhodana had three palaces built for the prince's enjoyment, corresponding to the seasons: one for summer, one for the rainy season, and one for winter.
Among them, that which was for summer was exclusively cool; that which was for the rainy season was temperate.
That which was for the winter season was naturally warm;
and for each palace, they raised five hundred men at a time onto the staircases and lowered them down again.
As they were being lifted up and set down in that manner, their sound was heard for half a *yojana*: "May it not be that the prince departs without our knowledge!
The fortune-tellers and interpreters of omens had predicted, "The prince will depart through the Gate of Auspiciousness.
Thereupon, the king had massive door-panels made for the Gate of Auspiciousness.
And for each single door-panel, five hundred men opened it and closed it;
and their sound traveled for half a yojana.
And she provided him with five kinds of sensual pleasures suited to his taste;
and young women always attended upon him with song, instrumental music, and dance.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva said to the charioteer: "Quickly, charioteer, harness the chariot;
I shall go to the pleasure grove.
Thereupon, the charioteer approached King Śuddhodana and spoke thus: "Your Majesty, the prince intends to depart for the pleasure grove."
Then this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana: "Never before have I allowed the prince to go out to the park grounds to see the beautiful landscape.
What if I were now to have the prince go out to the park grounds?"
Then the prince, surrounded by a host of women, will experience pleasure and will not go forth.

Then King Śuddhodana, out of affection and great respect for the Bodhisattva, had a proclamation made by the sounding of bells throughout the city: "On the seventh day, the prince will go forth to the pleasure gardens (in order to see the beautiful lands). Therefore, you must remove all things that are unpleasant; let not the prince behold anything disagreeable."
And all delightful objects that provide sensory pleasure should be brought forth.
Then, on the seventh day, the entire city was adorned; the park grounds were beautified, covered with canopies of various colored fabrics, and decorated with parasols, banners, and flags.
And by whichever path the Bodhisattva was to depart, [it too was likewise prepared].

That road was sprinkled, swept, drenched with scented water, strewn with loose flowers, perfumed by various incense burners, adorned with full water-jars, lined with tall plantain trees, covered with canopies of various colorful cloths, and hung with nets of jeweled bells and strings of pearls and half-strings of pearls.
A retinue arrayed in a fourfold army was prepared and intent upon decorating the prince’s inner apartments.
Then the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm resolved to bring the Bodhisattva back;
for as the Bodhisattva was departing for the park grounds through the eastern city gate with a great procession,
by the power of the Bodhisattva, the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm caused an old man to appear on that path.

An old man appeared before him on the road, decrepit and advanced in years, his body covered with visible veins, with broken teeth and a frame wrinkled by folds; his hair was white, he was hunchbacked and bent like a rafter, broken down and leaning upon a staff; afflicted and past his youth, with a throat rasping with a harsh cough, he trembled as he leaned on his staff with his body slumped forward, his every limb and member clearly displayed.
Then the Bodhisattva, knowing full well, said this to the charioteer:
"O charioteer, what kind of man is this—weak, with little strength, his flesh, blood, skin, and sinews withered away?
With white hair, sparse teeth, and a body emaciated in form, he walks leaning on a staff, stumbling in misery?"
The charioteer said: "O Lord, this man is indeed overcome by old age; his faculties are decayed, he is deeply miserable, and deprived of strength and vigor.
Despised by his kinsmen and having become helpless, incapable of performing his duties, he is cast aside like a piece of wood in the forest."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Is this his family custom? Speak for his benefit, or rather, speak for the sake of the entire world, for such is his condition.
Speak these words quickly and according to the truth; having heard them, I shall here reflect upon their meaning with proper discernment."
The charioteer said:
"O Lord, this is neither the law of his family nor the law of the kingdom; old age assails the youth of all the world.
Even for you, the assembly of mother, father, kinsmen, and relatives is not exempt from old age; for there is no other destiny for living beings."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Alas, charioteer! The intellect of ignorant, foolish people is deluded; intoxicated by youth, they do not perceive old age."
"Turn my chariot back quickly; I shall enter once more. Of what use are these pleasures of play to me, who am already overtaken by old age?"
Then the Bodhisattva, having turned back his excellent chariot, entered the city once again.

Thus, monks, at a later time, as the Bodhisattva was departing for the pleasure gardens by way of the southern city gate with a great retinue, he saw on the road a man afflicted by disease, overcome by a parched belly, with a weak body, submerged in his own urine and excrement, without protection or refuge, breathing in and out with great difficulty.

And having seen him, the Bodhisattva, though already knowing [the answer], spoke thus to the charioteer: "What is this man, O charioteer, whose limbs are withered and discolored, whose senses are all impaired,
who breathes heavily, whose entire body is parched, whose belly is distended, who has fallen into distress, and who remains in his own loathsome urine and excrement?"
The charioteer said:
"O Lord, this man is indeed extremely ill, overcome by the fear of disease; he has reached the end of life.
He is devoid of the nectar of health, stripped of strength, and without protection, island, refuge, or resort."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Health is like play in a dream, and this fear of disease is of such a terrible form.
What wise person, having seen this condition, would give rise to delight in play or the perception of it as beautiful?"
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva, having turned back his excellent chariot, entered the supreme city once again.

Thus, monks, at another time, as the Bodhisattva was departing for the pleasure gardens by way of the western city gate with a great retinue, he saw a man who had died and passed away, laid upon a bier, covered with a cloth canopy, surrounded by a multitude of kinsmen, all of whom were weeping, wailing, and lamenting, with disheveled hair and dust strewn over their heads, beating their breasts.
Seeing them striking [him], crying out, and following behind him,
the Bodhisattva, though already knowing [the situation], spoke thus to the charioteer:
(Vaidya 138)
"Charioteer, who is this man being carried on a litter, with his hair and nails disheveled and dust upon his head?
They attend to him as he lies there, beating their breasts and uttering various words of lamentation."
The charioteer said: "O Lord, this man is indeed dead; he shall no longer see his mother and father, nor his sons and wife, having abandoned his wealth, home, and parents."
Having reached the other world, he will indeed never again see the assembly of friends and kinsmen.

The Bodhisattva said: "Fie upon youth, which is assailed by old age! Fie upon health, which is struck down by manifold diseases! Fie upon the life of the wise man, which does not endure for long! Fie upon the learned man’s attachment to pleasures! (Lal 14.11)
If there were no old age, no sickness, and no death,
even so it would be a great suffering to bear the five aggregates; how much more so when old age, sickness, and death are constantly attached to one?
"It is well; having returned, I shall contemplate liberation."
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva, having turned back that excellent chariot, entered the city once again.
Thus, monks, at another time when the Bodhisattva was departing for the pleasure gardens by way of the northern city gate, those very sons of the gods, through the power of the Bodhisattva himself,
manifested a monk on that path.
The Bodhisattva saw that monk— peaceful, self-controlled, restrained, living the holy life, with eyes not wandering.

He stood on the path looking only a yoke’s length ahead, endowed with a pleasing deportment, endowed with a pleasing manner of advancing and retreating, endowed with a pleasing way of looking forward and looking aside, endowed with a pleasing way of bending and stretching his limbs, and endowed with a pleasing manner of carrying his outer robe, bowl, and inner robes.

And having seen him, the Bodhisattva, knowing full well, spoke thus to the charioteer: "O charioteer, who is this man whose mind is peaceful and perfectly tranquil, who walks with eyes cast down, looking only a yoke's length ahead; who is clothed in saffron-colored robes, whose conduct is most serene, who carries an alms-bowl, and who is neither agitated nor arrogant? (Lal 14.13)
The charioteer said:
"O Lord, this man is one called a *bhikṣu*; having abandoned the delights of sensual pleasure, he conducts himself with perfect discipline."
Having attained the going-forth and seeking peace for himself, free from passion and hatred, he follows the practice of begging for alms.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Excellent! This is well-spoken and it pleases me; that which is called 'renunciation' is always praised by the wise.
In it lies one's own welfare and the welfare of other beings, as well as a happy life and the fruit of ambrosia, most sweet."
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva, having turned back that excellent chariot, entered the supreme city once again.

Thus, monks, when King Śuddhodana saw and heard such an exhortation regarding the Bodhisattva, he, to an even greater degree, had ramparts constructed and moats dug for the purpose of guarding the Bodhisattva.
He caused the gates to be made secure,
stationed guards,
and urged on the brave warriors.
He harnessed the mounts and had them don their armor; for the sake of protecting the Bodhisattva, he stationed four great military arrays at the four crossroads of the city gates.

Those who guarded him day and night, thinking, "May the Bodhisattva not go forth," were given this command in the inner apartments: "Never interrupt the musical performances; all forms of pleasure and play must be provided."
Display the deceits of women and entreat the prince so that, with his heart deeply attached, he does not go forth into the homeless life.
In this regard, it is said:
At the gate stand men skilled in battle, sword-armed in hand; there are elephants, horses, and chariots, and rows of armored men mounted upon the great serpents.
Moats, watchtowers, and gateways were constructed, and a great wall was raised;
the gates were fastened with very firm bolts and released with a sound that echoed for a league.
All the Śākya clansmen, with dejected minds, guarded [the city] day and night;
and the great sound of that vast army was heard as a loud clamor.
The city was thrown into turmoil, its people terrified and trembling in mind, lest the Compassionate One depart.
Let it not be that this lineage of one born of the Śākya clan should be severed upon his departure.
And he commanded the young women: "Never interrupt the musical performance; maintain the setting and persistently engage their minds with pleasures and delights."
Or those who, through the illusion of women, display many various gestures and employ great protection to create obstacles, thinking, "Let not the gentle one depart."
At the time of her departure, O excellent charioteer, these omens appeared before us:
the swans, cranes, peacocks, mynas, and parrots did not utter a sound from the palaces, the windows, the noble archways, or the palm-tree balconies.
With drooping tongues and deeply dejected minds, they meditate unhappily with their heads cast downward.
The lotuses in the ponds and lotus-pools lose their luster and wither;
the trees, stripped of their leaves and flowers, do not bloom again; and then, the strings of the vīṇās, vallakīs, and flutes suddenly snap.
And even when struck by hand, the kettledrums and clay drums do not sound among the musicians.
The entire city was in a state of agitation, and overcome by deep sleep,
not a single person’s mind was inclined toward dancing,
singing, or pleasure; even the king, with an exceedingly dejected heart, remained lost in anxious reflection.
Alas, what a pity! May the vast prosperity of the Śākya clan not be utterly consumed by fire.
While the cowherd and the king were both resting upon a single bed,
the cowherd beheld these dreams at the hour of midnight:
this entire earth trembled, along with its mountains, peaks, and valleys.
The trees, stirred by the wind, were uprooted from their foundations like sovereign kings.
The sun and moon fell from the sky to the earth, adorned with their celestial lights;
his hair was seen shorn, the crown shattered on his right arm,
his hands likewise cut off, and his feet severed— he saw himself naked.
Likewise, her pearl necklace and the gems of her girdle were seen shattered upon herself.
The four legs of the bed were seen severed upon the surface of the earth;
the beautiful, glorious, and radiant parasol-staff was seen broken by the king.
All the ornaments were scattered and fallen; they fainted from the water.
Adorned with her husband's ornaments, wearing his garments and crown, she lay upon the bed in a state of agitation.
He sees a meteor emerging from the city; he sees the city overcome by darkness and its beautiful jeweled lattice-work shattered in his dream.
A long strand of pearls fell down, and the great ocean was seen to be agitated; then Mount Meru, the king of mountains, shook from its very foundation.
Having seen such dreams as these within her sleep, the daughter of the Śākyas awoke with tearful eyes and spoke to her husband:
"O Lord, tell me, what indeed will become of me? For such are the dreams I have seen."
My memory has become confused, and I see nothing again; my mind is afflicted by grief.
Having heard that voice, which was like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, like a drum, and like the Brahma-voice—a beautiful sound—he addressed the cowherd: "Be joyful; no evil exists for you.
Such dreams belong to those beings who have performed meritorious deeds in the past."
Who else but he, who is not subject to manifold sufferings, can perceive these as if they were dreams?
When you were seen, the earth trembled and the mountain peaks fell upon the ground;
all the gods, nāgas, rākṣasas, and hosts of spirits paid you the highest and most excellent worship.
Since you saw the roots of the trees uprooted and saw your hair being shorn with the right hand,
O cowherd, you shall soon cut through the web of afflictions and uproot the web of views from conditioned existence.

"O Gopā, since you saw the sun and moon falling within your sight, and the stars and luminaries falling down, you shall soon slay the enemies that are the afflictions; you will become worthy of worship and praise in the world."
Since you have seen him with his pearl necklace cast off, his body naked and broken, and all his limbs shattered—
you will soon, O cowherd girl, abandon this female body and before long you shall indeed become a man.
"O Gopā, that couch which you saw with its legs broken, and the parasol with its jewel-adorned handle shattered—
having swiftly crossed the four floods, you shall soon behold me as the sole sovereign umbrella over the three worlds."
"O Gopā, when you saw my ornaments, crest-jewel, and garments being carried away from my couch,
look quickly at me now— my body adorned with the marks of a great man, praised by all the worlds. (Lal_14.33)
"O Gopā, you have seen hundreds of millions of lamps that went out once they left the city, leaving that town in darkness;
I shall quickly create the light of wisdom for all the world, which is blinded by the darkness of delusion and ignorance."
O cowherd, that pearl necklace you saw broken and the variegated golden thread severed—
having swiftly cut through the net of afflictions, he has pulled out the thread of perception from the conditioned.

"Since you, O Gopā, always show such regard and offer worship with the highest reverence, there shall be no miserable rebirth for you, nor any sorrow; quickly, indeed, you shall attain joy and gladness."
In the past, I gave sublime gifts, practiced excellent conduct, and cultivated constant patience;
therefore, all those who find faith in me shall obtain joy and gladness.
For infinite millions of eons, I have cultivated the sublime path to enlightenment;
therefore, for all those who place their faith in me, the three lower realms are severed.
"Find joy and do not give way to sorrow; find contentment and cultivate gladness.
Soon you shall obtain joy and rapture; endure this, O Gopā, for these signs of yours are auspicious. (Lal 14.39)
Thus, filled with the splendor of merit and containing the essence of glorious majesty, these signs were seen in dreams beforehand—
those which appear when the time for renunciation arrives for the Bull-like Men who have accumulated stores of virtuous deeds from the past.

Thus he appeared, shaking the waters with his four great oceans from his hands and feet, making this entire earth his variegated bed and Mount Meru, the best of mountains, his pillow for his head. *Lalita-vistara* 14.41.
Then, in a dream, you were seen in the world emitting a radiance that dispelled the dense, great darkness;
a parasol rose up from the earth and spread across the three worlds, and by its light being touched, the sufferings of the states of woe were stilled.
Dark-hued, auspicious, clever, and drawing the footprints of living beings—these four-colored birds were a marvel, yet they were all of one color.
They trampled upon dung-heaps and the most wretched, loathsome places, yet they wandered there unsullied.
Furthermore, in a dream he saw a river filled with water, with many millions of billions of beings being carried away;
having fashioned a boat and crossed over, and having ferried others across, he established them on a supreme, fearless, and sorrowless dry land.
Again, he sees many who are afflicted, touched by disease, devoid of the splendor of health, and bereft of strength;
becoming a physician, he bestows many medicines and liberates millions of beings touched by manifold illnesses.

Indeed, seated upon the lion-throne on the summit of Mount Sumeru, while his disciples and the immortals stood with palms joined in reverence, he beheld himself victorious in the midst of battle; and the immortals in the sky uttered cries of "Joy! (Ānanda).
The Bodhisattva saw such dreams, which signify the auspicious fulfillment of his beautiful vows;
hearing them, gods and men were filled with joy, knowing that before long he would become the god of gods among men.
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Chapter on the Dreams."
START Chapter 15 (Vaidya 144):
The Fifteenth Chapter, "The Great Departure" (Abhiniṣkramaṇa).

Then, monks, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "It would be improper for me, and it would be an act of ingratitude, if I were to depart without having informed the great king Śuddhodana and without my father's permission.
At night, when all was quiet, he descended from his own residence palace and stood upon the roof-terrace of King Śuddhodana’s palace.
Furthermore, as soon as the Bodhisattva was established there, that entire palace became suffused with light.
Having awakened, the king beheld that radiance; seeing it, he addressed the chamberlain in great haste: "Ho, chamberlain! Has the sun risen, by which this light shines so brightly?"
The chamberlain said: "Even now, not even half of the night has passed. Moreover, O Lord— The sun’s radiance makes the shadows of trees and walls scorching, and it produces heat upon the body.
At the time of dawn, the swans, peacocks, parrots, cuckoos, and ruddy geese utter their respective cries."
"O god among men, this light is pleasant, delightful, refreshing, and auspicious; it causes no burning heat.
It overcomes walls and trees, yet there is no shadow. Without a doubt, one who possesses virtues has arrived here today. (Lal 15.2)
The king looked toward the ten directions in dejection, and then he beheld that lotus-eyed one of pure being.
Desiring to rise from his bed, he was unable to do so; possessed of excellent and pure intellect, he conceived a sense of reverence for his father.
Standing before the king, he said: "Do not create further obstacles, nor indeed cause me distress.
O King, the time for my renunciation has arrived; alas, forgive me, O Lord, along with your kin and your kingdom."
With eyes filled with tears, the king said to him: "Is there some purpose in your returning?
What boon do you ask of me? Speak, and I shall grant it all; favor me, the royal family, and this kingdom."
Then the Bodhisattva, speaking with sweet discourse, said: "O King, I desire four boons; grant them to me.
If you are able to give them to me under my authority, then I shall always remain there in the palace and will not go forth. (Lal 15.6)
"O Lord, I desire that old age may not overcome me; may I remain forever established in youth with a beautiful complexion,
and having attained health, may disease never befall me."
May there be immeasurable life and may there be no death; may there be abundant prosperity and never misfortune.
Having heard these words, the king was deeply afflicted by grief: "O Prince, you ask for what is impossible; I have no power in this matter.
Even the sages, throughout the duration of an eon, have never been liberated from the fear of old age, sickness, death, and calamity."

"Since you now, O King, grant us these four boons—freedom from the fear of old age, sickness, death, and calamity—well then, listen, O Lord of Men, to one further boon: may there be no rebirth for me once I have passed away from this state."
Upon hearing these words of the bull among men, she thinned out her craving and severed her affection for her son.
"I rejoice in you who bring benefit to the world; may your intention for liberation be fulfilled, and may whatever purpose you have set for yourself be accomplished."
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva returned, ascended to his own palace, and sat down upon his couch;
yet no one perceived either his departure or his arrival.
Thus, monks, at the end of that night, King Śuddhodana assembled the entire Śākya clan and announced this matter to them: "The prince will go forth into the homeless life;
what shall we do?
The Śākyas said, "O King, we shall provide protection."
Why is that? On one hand there is this great multitude of Śākyas, and on the other he is all alone. What power does he have to go forth by force?
Thereupon, those Śākyas and King Śuddhodana [prepared] five hundred Śākyan youths who were skilled in weapons and well-trained.

For the sake of protecting the Bodhisattva, those trained in archery and weaponry and endowed with the strength of great wrestlers were stationed at the eastern city gate. Each Śākya youth was accompanied by a retinue of five hundred chariots,
and each chariot was stationed with a retinue of five hundred infantrymen.
For the sake of protecting the Bodhisattva,

likewise at the southern, western, and northern city gates, five hundred Śākya youths were stationed— skilled in weapons, well-trained, educated in archery, and endowed with the strength of great athletes.
Each individual Śākya youth was accompanied by a retinue of five hundred chariots.
And for the protection of the Bodhisattva, each chariot was stationed with an entourage of five hundred foot soldiers.
The elder Śākyas, both men and women, stood at all the crossroads, junctions, marketplaces, and main streets for the purpose of guarding him.
And King Śuddhodana, surrounded and escorted by five hundred Śākya youths, remained awake at the gate of his own palace, mounted upon horses and elephants.
And Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī addressed the group of maidservants:
"Light the pure lamps; place all the precious jewels upon the tops of the banners.
Hang down the necklaces and let them illuminate this entire house."
Perform the musical concert and remain vigilant and tireless throughout this night;
guard the prince so that he may not depart unperceived. (Lal 15.12)
With rows of armors in hand, and grasping swords, bows, arrows, spears, and javelins,
all of you must exert great effort for the sake of protecting my beloved son!
Securely fasten all the gates with bolts, making them firm with strong panels;
do not open them at an improper time, lest the Supreme Being depart from here.
Fashion necklaces of gems and strings of pearls, facial ornaments, crescent moons with chains,
girdles, earrings, rings well-fashioned, and anklets.
If he should suddenly emerge, moving like a rutting elephant,
then you must exert such prowess that he may meet with no obstacle.
"O women who bear strength, surround the bed of Vimala;
do not be overcome by drowsiness, but guard him with your eyes like so many moths."
Cover this palace of the king with a net of jewels for its protection;
and you, O Veṇuravas, roar out through this night and guard her who is free from passion.
Awaken one another; do not dwell in negligence, but protect this night.
Do not indeed go forth into homelessness, abandoning both the kingdom and the realm.
"If he were to depart for the royal palace, this entire city would become joyless,
and the long-enduring lineage of kings would be cut off.
Then, O monks, twenty-eight great yakṣa generals, led by the general Pāñcika...
And having assembled five hundred sons of Hāritī in one place, they deliberated thus: "Friends, today the Bodhisattva will go forth;
you must apply yourselves with zeal to perform acts of worship for him."
And the four Great Kings, having entered the royal capital of Alakavatī, addressed that great assembly of yakṣas: "Friends, today the Bodhisattva will go forth;
he must be escorted out by you, supported by the best of horses."
And that assembly of yakṣas said:
"O Vajradṛḍha, his body is indestructible and like that of Nārāyaṇa; he is heavy, endowed with the power of heroism, unshakable, and the supreme among all beings.

It might be possible for someone to uproot Mahāmeru, the best of mountains, and hold it in the sky; but the Meru of the Conqueror’s qualities, heavy and resting upon merit and wisdom, cannot be moved anywhere by mountains."
Vaiśravaṇa said:
"Know those men who are arrogant with pride to be heavy; know those who abide in love and reverence to be light.
Apply yourselves with resolute intention and reverence, for you will find them as light as a tuft of cotton by the hand of a bird."
"I shall go before you, and you must carry the horse;
thus, through the Bodhisattva’s departure from the world, we shall accumulate great merit."
Then, monks, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven: "Friends, today the Bodhisattva will go forth;
therefore, you all must be eager to perform acts of worship."
There, a son of the gods named Śāntamati spoke thus: "I, for my part, will cause all the women, men, boys, and girls in the great city of Kapilavastu to fall into a deep sleep.
A son of the gods named Lalitavyūha spoke thus: "I, too, will make the sounds of all horses, elephants, donkeys, camels, oxen, buffaloes, women, men, boys, and girls disappear.
A son of the gods named Vyūhamati spoke thus: "I [will create] in the expanse of the sky a space measuring the width of seven chariots..."

I shall prepare an array of the road, surrounded by jeweled railings, blazing with the light of sun-crystal gems, with parasols, banners, and flags raised aloft, strewn with various flowers, and perfumed by various incense burners—
by which path the Bodhisattva will go forth.

The nāga king named Airāvaṇa spoke thus: "I, too, shall construct upon my own trunk a peaked pavilion measuring thirty-two yojanas in size, wherein the apsarases, having mounted it, shall go while performing service and attendance for the Bodhisattva with the sounding of musical instruments and songs, and with great singing and instrumental music.
And Śakra, the lord of the gods, himself said: "I shall open the gates."
"And I shall show you the path.
The divine son Dharmacārin said, "I shall display the transformed inner apartments. The divine son Saṃcodaka said, "I shall rouse the Bodhisattva from his bed."
There, the nāga king named Varuṇa, the nāga king Manasvin, the nāga king Sāgara, the nāga king Anavatapta,
and the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda spoke thus: "We too, for the sake of making an offering to the Bodhisattva, shall manifest a cloud that rains according to the season."
We shall rain down a shower of powdered uragasāra sandalwood.
Thus, monks, this very resolve and intention was conceived and determined by the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas.
While the Bodhisattva had entered into such reflection on the Dharma, reclining at ease in the music halls, amidst the inner apartments,
contemplating the conduct of former Buddhas and considering the welfare of all sentient beings, four points of his former vows became manifest before him.

What are the four? Formerly, desiring the sovereignty of the Self-Existent Ones and aspiring toward omniscience, I donned this armor: "Having seen sentient beings suffering—alas! for one cast into the great prison-fetters of saṃsāra—"

"Having broken through the prison of saṃsāra for the world's inhabitants, may I raise the cry of liberation from bondage; and may I release those beings who are bound by the tight shackles of craving.
This was the first point of his former vow that became manifest.

"Alas! May I bring forth the great light of the Dharma and provide the lamp of knowledge for this world, which is cast into the dense thicket of the great darkness of ignorance within saṃsāra, whose eyes are shrouded by the cataracts of the film of nescience, and which is bereft of the eye of wisdom, blinded by the darkness of the delusion of ignorance."

And by means of the application of the medicinal herb consisting of the knowledge of the bliss of the three liberations, conjoined with the knowledge of skillful means and wisdom, may I remove the turbidity of the great cataract-film of darkness—the blindness and gloom of all ignorance—and purify the eye of wisdom; this second point of my former vow then became manifest.

"Alas! May I cause the felling of the banner of the conceit 'I am' for this world—which has its banner of pride raised high, which is obsessed with the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' whose mind follows the grasping at a self, which is overturned by the perversions of perception, thought, and view, and which is seized by non-inclusion—by means of the instruction of the Noble Path.
Thus, this third phrase of his former vow became manifest.

"O, that I might proclaim the Dharma— which brings tranquility and satisfies with wisdom— to this world that is unpeaceful, overwhelmed by sloth, shrouded by its own qualities, caught in the cycle of coming and going, wandering from this world to the next and from the next world back to this, transmigrating and never turning away from *saṃsāra*, and mounted upon the wheel of a whirling firebrand!"
Thus, this fourth point of his former vow became manifest;
these four points of his former vow became manifest.
And at that moment, the divine son Dharmacārin and the divine sons belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host manifested the inner apartments with disfigured and decomposed forms.
Having displayed this distorted and loathsome appearance, they stood in the expanse of the sky and addressed the Bodhisattva in verses;
then those sons of the gods, possessed of great supernatural power, spoke to him whose long eyes were like blossomed lotuses:
How can delight arise in you while you are stationed in the midst of a cremation ground?
Then, urged by the lords of the gods, he gazed upon that inner apartment for a moment;
he sent forth his vision and beheld that loathsome place, thinking, "I have come to dwell in the midst of a cemetery."
Indeed, the Bodhisattva beheld the entire assembly of women;
looking about,
he saw that some had their garments disarrayed, some had their hair disheveled, some had their ornaments scattered, and some had their diadems fallen off.
Some had their shoulders slumped; some had their limbs distorted; some had their faces askew; some had their eyes rolled back;

some were drooling with saliva; some were gasping for breath; some were laughing; some were moaning; some were prattling; some were gnashing their teeth; some had pale faces; some had disfigured forms; and some had their arms hanging limp.

Some had their feet scattered about; some had their heads bared; some had their heads covered; some had their faces turned upside down; some had their bodies shattered; some had their limbs contorted; some were hunched over, making a *khura-khurā* sound; some, embracing a mṛdaṅga drum, had their heads and bodies twisted; some had their hands still holding vīṇās, vallakīs, and other instruments; and some were biting flutes with their teeth.

Some were clattering their teeth; some had musical instruments dragged away by kimpalas and nakulas; some had their eyes rolling with the opening and closing of their lids; and some had their mouths wide open.
Beholding the inner apartments thus distorted and lying upon the surface of the earth, the Bodhisattva conceived the perception that it was a cemetery.
In this regard, it is said:
Having seen her, the Lord of the World was distressed; sighing piteously, he spoke these words:
"Alas! Having fallen into such hardship, how could she find delight among a host of rākṣasīs? (Lal 15.26)
Enveloped by the darkness of extreme delusion, O dull-witted one, perceiving as virtues those qualities which are devoid of virtue,
you shall never attain liberation, just like a bird trapped within a cage.

Then the Bodhisattva, once again surveying the inner apartments through this gateway of the light of the Dharma, lamented for sentient beings with a cry of great compassion: "In this world, those fools are slaughtered like condemned criminals at a place of execution;
in this world, those ignorant fools are attached to it as if to variegated jars filled with impurities."
Here those fools sink like elephants in the midst of water;
here those fools are imprisoned like thieves in the midst of a jail;
here those fools take delight like boars in the midst of filth.
Here these fools are obsessed, like dogs amidst a skeleton;
here these fools have fallen, like moths into the flames of a lamp;
here these fools are bound, like monkeys by sticky resin.
Here these fools are scorched like lotuses drawn up by a net;
here these fools are roasted like rams on the stakes of a slaughterer;
here these fools, having committed evil deeds, hang suspended like those upon the point of a stake.
Here these fools sink away like aged elephants in the mud;
here these fools perish like a shattered ship upon the great ocean;
here these fools fall headlong like those born blind into a vast abyss.
In this world, those fools go to exhaustion like water situated in the depths of the underworld;
in this world, those fools smoke like the great earth at the dissolution of an eon;
by these [afflictions], fools are whirled around like a potter’s wheel that has been set spinning.
Here these fools wander about like those born blind inside a mountain;
here these fools revolve like dogs tied to a tiger.
Here these fools wither away like grass and forest trees in the summer season;
here these fools decline like the moon in the dark fortnight;
by these [passions] fools are devoured like serpents by Garuḍa.
By these, fools are swallowed, like a ship by a great sea-monster;
by these, fools are plundered, like a caravan by a band of thieves;
by these, fools are shattered, like sal trees by the wind.
By these [senses], fools are struck down, like living beings by venomous glances;
perceiving them as mere tastes, fools of childish nature are wounded, as if by razor-edges smeared with honey;
by these fools are carried away, like logs of wood by floods of water.
By these fools play like children with their own urine and excrement;
by these fools are turned around like elephants with a goad;
by these fools are bound like simpletons by rogues.
"In this world, those fools exhaust their roots of merit, like gamblers squandering their wealth;
by these [pleasures], fools are devoured, like merchants by ogresses.
Having thus scrutinized the inner apartments through these thirty-two aspects, the Bodhisattva cultivated the perception of the foulness of the body.

Reflecting thus, he cultivated the perception of repulsiveness, generated the perception of loathsomeness, analyzed his own body, clearly saw the defects of the body, and cast off attachment to the body. Dispelling the perception of beauty and entering into the perception of foulness,
he beheld [his body] from the soles of the feet below up to the crown of the head above as something constantly arisen from impurity, produced from impurity, and flowing with impurity.
And at that time, he spoke this verse:
"Grown in the field of karma, born from the water of craving, made into the notion of a self-body,
moistened by tears, sweat, and phlegm, transformed by urine, and crowded with drops of blood."
It is filled with urine, pus, fat, blood, and brains, as well as with impurities; it constantly flows with all manner of impure things and is foul-smelling in its various forms.
It is a mass of bones, teeth, nails, hair, and body-hair, covered by skin and bristling with down;
it is filled within with these weak things—spleen, liver, lungs, and tongue;
it resembles a machine bound together by marrow and sinews, made to appear beautiful only by the flesh.

Having seen this abode of living beings— strewn with various diseases, turbid with grief, tormented by hunger and thirst, full of many cavities, and subject to death and old age— who indeed, being wise, would consider his own body anything other than an enemy? (Lal 15.29)
And in this way, the Bodhisattva dwelt with mindfulness directed toward the body in relation to the body.
And the sons of the gods situated in the expanse of the sky said this to the son of the gods Dharmacārin: "What is this, friends?
Siddhārtha delays and gazes upon the inner apartments;
he displays his body and agitates their hearts."
Furthermore, he fixes his gaze upon it, thinking:
"Or rather, this [ocean] is as deep as the swift-flowing ocean; it is impossible to grasp its measure."
Or rather, let it not be that the mind of one who is unattached becomes attached to sense objects;
let it not be that, unurged by the immortals, he forgets his former vow.
Dharmacārī said: "Why do you speak thus?
Was it not the case that while you were previously practicing for awakening before his very eyes, you possessed such detachment?"
If he had no attachment even when renouncing the life of a householder, how much less, my friends, could there be any attachment now for him who stands in his final existence?

Then, monks, the Bodhisattva—firmly resolved, with a heart stirred by spiritual urgency, and with an intellect determined—gracefully and without delay descended from his cross-legged seat; standing in the Hall of Music facing the east, he lowered the jeweled lattice with his right hand.

Standing atop the pinnacle of the palace, he joined his palms with ten fingers together, focused his mind upon all the Buddhas, and having paid homage to all the Buddhas, he gazed toward the expanse of the sky.
There he beheld the Lord of the Immortals (Indra), who possesses a thousand eyes, situated in the sky and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of gods.

He stood bowing with his body bent low, paying homage to the Bodhisattva who was holding flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, ear-ornaments, jewels, necklaces, and wreaths;
and he saw the four world-protectors, surrounded by hosts of yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and nāgas, all clad in firm, armored mail and wearing protective armor.
He saw [the gods] standing and bowing to the Bodhisattva, their hands holding swords, bows, arrows, spears, lances, and tridents, with their topknots hanging down from jeweled crowns;
he saw the two sons of the gods, Candrasūryāvati, standing on his left and right sides.
The constellation Puṣya, the lord of the stars, had appeared, and the time of midnight had arrived. Having seen this, the Bodhisattva addressed Chandaka:
“Chandaka, do not delay, O fickle one! Give me the king of horses, adorned with ornaments.
All auspicious success shall come to me; the accomplishment of my purpose will surely be realized today. (Lal 15.30)
Then Chandaka, having heard these words, with a troubled mind spoke thus:
"Where will you go, O lion among kings, with your blossoming brows and beautiful lotus-petal eyes, you who are like the full autumn moon that gladdens the night-lotuses?"
Your face is like a fully blossomed lotus, tender as a fresh nalinī flower;
you possess the splendor of refined gold, nectar, the rising sun, and the stainless moon;
your radiant majesty blazes forth like the light of a flame, a fire-gem, and lightning.
She walks with the playful gait of an elephant in rut;
her beautiful feet possess the stride of a bull, a lion-king, and a swan.
The Bodhisattva said: "Chandaka, for whose sake I previously gave away my hands, feet, eyes, as well as my head,
my son, my beloved wife, my kingdom, wealth, gold, and garments— "
They possess the speed and force of elephants and horses filled with jewels, as swift as the wind in their prowess and strength.
For many hundreds of billions of nayutas of eons, I have guarded my morality, cultivated patience, and remained devoted to vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
But now that I have touched the auspicious peace of awakening, the time has arrived for me to liberate all beings who are trapped within the cage of old age and death.
Chandaka said: "Noble son, I have heard how as soon as you were born, you were presented for inspection to the Brahmins skilled in signs.
They prophesied before King Śuddhodana: 'Your Majesty, there is prosperity for the royal house.
[The Prince] asked: 'In what way? They replied:"
"O Prince, this son born to you is endowed with the marks of a hundred merits and is radiant with the splendor of virtue;
he shall become a universal monarch, lord of the four continents, possessed of the seven treasures."
But if, beholding the world in suffering, he abandons the inner apartments and goes forth,
having attained awakening— the state free from old age and death— he will satisfy this multitude of beings with the waters of the Dharma.
"Ah, noble son, that prophecy certainly exists; it is not non-existent.
However, listen first to my words, for I desire your welfare. He asked, "What is it?"

He said: "Your Majesty, it is for this purpose that some here undertake various kinds of vows and austerities—wearing skins, matted hair, crowns, rags, and bark garments, with long nails, hair, and beards—and endure various forms of bodily mortification and torment;
they undertake intense vows and austerities."
"What is it? [They replied: "May we obtain the prosperity of gods and humans.
"And that prosperity, noble son, has been obtained by you;
as well as this kingdom, which is wealthy, flourishing, secure, abundant in food, delightful, and crowded with many people and inhabitants."
These gardens are most excellent and sublime, adorned with various kinds of flowers and fruits, and resounding with the warbling of flocks of diverse birds.

The lotus ponds are graced by blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-blooming water lilies, and white lotuses; they echo with the cries of swans, peacocks, cuckoos, ruddy geese, cranes, curlews, and sarus cranes.

Their banks are lined with flowering mango, ashoka, campaka, kurabaka, tilaka, and kesara trees, as well as various other species, and they are further embellished by groves of trees made of diverse precious gems.

They are laid out like a chessboard, surrounded by jeweled railings, covered with nets of jewels, and provide enjoyment according to the seasons, being pleasant to dwell in during summer, the rainy season, autumn, and winter.

And these great palaces, resembling autumn clouds and like Mount Kailāsa, are equal to the Vaijayanta palace and to the secure Sudharma hall; they are free from sorrow and possess such splendor, adorned with terraces, turrets, gateways, windows, balconies, gabled chambers, and palace floors.

And this inner apartment, noble son, is stirred by networks of jeweled bells; it is well-trained in the performance of songs accompanied by instrumental music—such as the *tuṇava*, *paṇava*, lute, flute, *saṃpatāḍa*, *avacara*, *kimpala*, *nakula*, *sughoṣaka*, mṛdaṅga drum, and kettle-drum—and in dancing, singing, and musical ensembles;
it is filled with laughter, graceful movements, play, delight, and sweet attentions.
And you, O Lord, are a youth whose prime has not yet passed; you are new, young, tender-bodied, a child with black hair. You have not yet sported with sensual pleasures;
therefore, take your delight for now like the lord of the immortals, the thousand-eyed sovereign of the thirty-three gods.
Thereafter, having grown old, we shall go forth from home;
and at that time, he spoke this verse:
"May they take delight, like the Lord of the Immortals in the world of the Thirty-three, with those who know the ways of pleasure."
"After we have grown older, we shall undertake vows and ascetic practices."
The Bodhisattva said: "Enough, Chandaka!
These sensual pleasures are indeed impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to change, fleeting, and fickle; they are like the current of a mountain river.

Like drops of dew, they do not last long; they are deceptive, as unsubstantial as an empty fist, as weak as the trunk of a plantain tree, prone to breaking like an unbaked vessel, and like autumn clouds—they exist for but a moment."
They do not endure;

they last but a short time like lightning in the sky. Like poisoned food, they result in suffering at their conclusion; like the *mālutā* creeper, they grant no happiness. Painted by the intellects of the foolish, they are like water bubbles, quickly vanishing like illusions or mirages, arising from the perversion of perception.
They are like illusions, produced by the distortions of the mind;
they are like dreams, failing to bring satisfaction due to their association with the grasping of distorted views. Like the ocean, they are difficult to fill; like salt water, they provoke thirst.
Like the head of a serpent, they are difficult to touch; like a great precipice, they are avoided by the wise.

Knowing them to be full of fear, full of refuge-seeking, fraught with danger, and full of fault, they are shunned by the prudent, censured by the learned, and loathed by the noble. They are avoided by the enlightened, yet embraced by the ignorant and frequented by fools.
And at that time, he spoke this verse:
"Like the head of a serpent avoided by the wise, like an impure jar of excrement despised, knowing that desires are the destroyers of all that is auspicious, I find no delight in them. (Lal 15.40)
Then Chandaka, crying out like one pierced by an arrow, with tearful eyes and in great distress, spoke these words:
"O God, for whose sake certain people here undertake various intense vows—wearing deerskins and matted hair, with long hair, nails, and beards, and clad in rags; [for his sake I have come]."

Some wore bark garments with emaciated limbs, having undertaken various vows; others subsisted on vegetables, wild rice, or *gardūla* grass; some remained standing on their tiptoes, while others adopted the vow of cows.

But rather, may we become supreme and distinguished in the world as excellent universal monarchs, or likewise as world-protectors; or may we go forth as Śakras, wielders of the thunderbolt, lords of the gods, or as emanated beings;
and in the Brahma-world, may we long for the bliss of meditative concentration.
O best of men, this kingdom of yours is vast, prosperous, and well-supplied with food; it is adorned with raised pleasure groves, gardens, and palaces equal to the Vaijayanta palace itself.
It is filled with the sounds of women’s voices, flutes, and lutes, joined with songs, instrumental music, delights, dances, and performances, all perfectly mastered.
Enjoy these sensual pleasures; do not depart, O gentle one!
The Bodhisattva said: "Chandaka, listen! In former lives, for the sake of sensual desires, I was subjected to hundreds of sufferings—imprisonment, confinement, beating, and threats."
Yet his mind did not become disenchanted with the conditioned.

Formerly, fallen under the power of negligence, agitated by delusion, shrouded in the net of views, and become blind, these phenomena—due to ignorance—were characterized by the grasping at the notion of a self and were transcended by feelings. (Lal 15.45)
Arising as flickering and unstable, they are impermanent like clouds, similar to lightning;
like drops of dew, they are empty, hollow, essence-less, selfless, and by nature void in every respect.
And my mind does not take delight in sense-objects; O Chandaka, give me Kaṇṭhaka, the best of kings among horses, adorned with trappings.
May all those auspicious signs that I previously envisioned be fulfilled for me.
I shall become the All-Conqueror, the Lord of all phenomena, the King of Dharma, the Sage.
Chandaka said:
"Do you not look with indifference upon this woman, whose eyes are like the petals of a blooming lotus, adorned with variegated necklaces and precious gems,
shining as she lies upon her bed like a flash of lightning released from a thick cloud in the sky?"

And you shall leave behind these flutes, drums, sweet-sounding instruments, clay drums, and bamboo pipes used for musical performance; as well as the cries of the *cakora* and *kalaviṅka* birds, and the songs of the *kinnarīs* according to their natural melodies. *Lal_15.49*

Why do you disregard the *sumana* flowers, the *utpala*, the *vārṣika*, and the *campaka*, as well as fragrant garlands and heaps of virtuous blossoms, the finest black aloe-wood incense, and these excellent unguents? *Lal_15.50*

O Lord, you do not disregard fragrant scents, exquisite and well-prepared flavors, nor likewise the side dishes and foods, nor the well-refined drinking juices mixed with sugar; where will you go? (Lal 15.51)

O Lord, why do you disregard her who, in the cold, wears warm ointments and garments, and in the heat, wears fine sandalwood paste, and who is adorned with beautiful and excellent Kashi silk robes? Where will you go?
"O King, these five strands of sensual pleasure are indeed abundant here as they are among the deities in heaven;
therefore, enjoy yourself for now, endowed with the happiness of delight, for only then will the Bull of the Śākyas depart for the forest."
The Bodhisattva said:
"For immeasurable and infinite eons, I have enjoyed various kinds of desirable objects—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches;
whether divine or human, there was never any satisfaction."
When I was a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), endowed with the seven jewels, I exercised sovereignty over the four continents as the son of the best of kings;

I even exercised the lordship of Suyāma, the king of the gods of the Thirty-three, from which realm I passed away and came here to this created world among the *nirmāṇarati* gods, possessing a supreme, personal splendor that I enjoyed in the past.

In the city of the gods, I exercised sovereign power as the lord of Māra; I enjoyed abundant desires, yet I was not satisfied. How much less could I find satisfaction today by associating with the lowly? This is simply impossible.
Moreover—
Chandaka, I behold this world suffering, situated in the midst of the wilderness of sorrow that is saṃsāra,
and perpetually being swept away amidst the thicket of the serpents of the afflictions.

For those who are without refuge or resort, oppressed by the darkness of delusion and ignorance, tormented by the fears of old age, sickness, and death, and struck down by the sufferings of birth and assailed by enemies—I shall here assemble the ship of Dharma. It is constructed from the timber of great renunciation, ethical discipline, vows, patience, vigor, and power; it is held together with the essential core of adamantine resolute intentions, and is thus firm.

Having myself boarded this boat and descended into the flood of saṃsāra, I shall ferry across the infinite world. My mind is thus resolved: [I shall cross] that which is difficult to traverse, agitated by the grief of saṃsāra, the wilderness, the waves of anger, the crocodiles of passion, and the whirlpools of enmity. *Lalita-vistara* 15.55.
Having crossed this ocean of existence by means of my own self— an ocean filled with the crocodiles of enmity and false views, and the rākṣasas of the afflictions—
and having myself crossed over, I shall establish the infinite world upon the auspicious shore that is free from old age and death.
Then Chandaka, weeping even more profusely, spoke thus: "O Lord, is this the firm resolve of your determination?
The Bodhisattva said:
"Listen, Chandaka, to my resolve, which is exerted for the sake of liberation and for the welfare and benefit of sentient beings."
Unwavering, immovable, and imperishable, it is as firm and difficult to shake as the king of mountains, Meru.
Chandaka said, "What kind of resolve is the Noble Son's?
The Bodhisattva replied,
"Even if there were a rain of thunderbolts, axes, spears, and arrows, and blazing streaks of lightning, and molten iron;"
Even if flaming mountain peaks were to fall upon my head, I would never again conceive a longing for home.
Then the immortals, stationed in the sky, let out shouts of joy and released a rain of flowers:
"Victory to you, O Lord who possesses supreme intelligence, the bestower of fearlessness upon the world! (Lal 15.59)
The mind of the Best of Men is not stained, just as the sky is not affected by darkness, dust, or comets;
he is unsullied by the pleasures of the sense objects, pure like a newly blossomed lotus arisen from the water.

Then, monks, having understood the Bodhisattva’s resolve, the divine son Śāntamati and the divine son Lalitavyūha caused all the men, women, boys, and girls in the great city of Kapilavastu to fall into a deep sleep,
and they caused all sounds to vanish.

Then, monks, the Bodhisattva, perceiving that all the people of the city were fast asleep and knowing that the hour of midnight had arrived, and knowing that Puṣya, the lord of constellations, was in conjunction, and realizing that the time for his departure had come,
addressed Chandaka: "Chandaka, do not weary me now."
Give me Kaṇṭhaka, having adorned him well; do not delay.
As soon as these words were uttered by the Bodhisattva,

at that very moment the four world-protectors, having heard the Bodhisattva’s speech, went to their respective abodes and, for the purpose of honoring the Bodhisattva, quickly, very quickly returned with their own individual arrays.
They were coming toward the great city of Kapilavastu.

There, the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the gandharvas, arrived from the eastern direction together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gandharvas, accompanied by the sounding of various musical instruments and songs.
Having arrived, he circumambulated the great city of Kapilavastu and, remaining stationed in the eastern direction from which he had come, paid homage to the Bodhisattva.

From the southern direction, the Great King Virūḍhaka arrived together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kumbhāṇḍas, who had various pearl necklaces hanging from their hands, who held various precious jewels, and who carried jars filled with various kinds of fragrant water.
Having arrived, he circumambulated the great city of Kapilavastu and, remaining in the southern direction just as he had come, stood there paying homage to the Bodhisattva.

From the western direction, the great king Virūpākṣa arrived together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nāgas, who hung various pearl necklaces from their hands, held various precious jewels, and blew gentle, fragrant winds arising from clouds of rain consisting of perfumed powders and flowers.
Having arrived, he circumambulated the great city of Kapilavastu and, remaining in the western direction from which he had come, stood there paying homage to the Bodhisattva.

From the northern direction, O Great King, Kubera arrived together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yakṣas, who were carrying jyotīrasa jewel-lamps, holding torches in their hands, and bearing various weapons such as bows, swords, arrows, spears, javelins, tridents, discuses, *kaṇayas*, and slings; they were all firmly armored, equipped, and clad in mail.
Having arrived at the great city of Kapilavastu and circumambulated it, he remained stationed toward the northern direction from which he had come, paying homage to the Bodhisattva.

And Śakra, the lord of the gods, arrived together with the Trāyastriṃśa gods, carrying divine flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, ear-ornaments, and jewelry.
Having arrived and circumambulated the great city of Kapilavastu, he and his retinue remained in the sky above, just as they had come, paying homage to the Bodhisattva.

Thus, monks, having heard the words of the Bodhisattva, Chandaka, his eyes filled with tears, spoke thus to the Bodhisattva: "Noble Son, you are one who knows the right time, the right hour, and the right occasion;
yet this is an improper time and an untimely moment to depart.
Therefore, what do you command?"
The Bodhisattva said, "Chandaka,
this is that time.
Chandaka asked, "Of what, noble son, is this the time?"
The Bodhisattva said:

"That which I have long sought while striving for the welfare of sentient beings—that moment has now arrived: having attained awakening, the state free from old age and death, I shall liberate the world."
This is the nature of things here.
In this regard, it is said: The guardians of the earth and the atmosphere, as well as Śakra, the lord of the gods, together with the yakṣas;
the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmita gods, and likewise the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
The wise Varuṇa, the Naga king Anavatapta, and likewise Māgara—
all these were intent upon honoring the Bull among Men at the time of his renunciation.
And those gods who dwell in the realm of form, moving in tranquility and engaged in the sphere of meditative concentration,
were also intent upon honoring the Best of Men, who is worthy of worship by the three worlds.
"Pure beings who have come from the ten directions as my companions while practicing their former conduct—
may we behold the renunciation of the Jina, and I shall perform worship for him in a fitting manner."
