And that high-souled lord of the Guhyakas, with his vajra blazing, stood in the sky;
his limbs armored and possessed of strength, heroism, and prowess, he held a flaming vajra in his hand.
The moon and the sun, both sons of the gods, stood well-established to his right and left;
joining their ten fingers in reverent salutation, they proclaimed the sound of renunciation.
And the constellation Puṣya, together with his retinue, manifested a magnificent physical form; standing before that Supreme among Men, he let forth a delightful and resonant voice.
Today all your auspicious omens have been realized; the Puṣya asterism is joined with the favorable moment for departure.
I too shall go together with you.
Become unsurpassed, O destroyer of passion!
The inciting son of the gods exhorted him: "Arise quickly, O you who have risen through strength and heroism!
Deliver all sentient beings struck down by sufferings; the time for your renunciation has arrived."
Thousands of millions of deities have gathered, raining down delightful flowers;
and he, seated upon his excellent couch and surrounded by the gods, shines with blazing splendor.
In the city, the women, boys, men, and girls—
all of them lay down with weary minds, fallen from their normal postures;
so too did the elephants, horses, oxen, mynas, parrots, cranes, and peacocks.
All of them, their minds utterly exhausted, lay asleep; they did not see his form.
And those sons of the Śākyas who were stationed at that excellent gateway, bearing firm vajra-spears upon elephants, horses, and chariots—
they too were put to sleep; the king, the princes, and all the royal attendants fell fast asleep.
Moreover, these groups of women, sleeping with their garments disarrayed and their bodies bared, do not appear in your mind.
And he, possessing the voice of Brahmā, with a charming tone and a resonance like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, went forth during the night at the hour of midnight and said to Chandaka:
"Well done, Chandaka! Give me Kaṇṭhaka, well-adorned and beautiful."
Do not create an obstacle for me; grant it quickly if you hold me dear.
"Where will you go, O best of charioteers of beings? What business do you have with horses?
Knowing the time and knowing the occasion, you who practice the Dharma—this is not the time to go anywhere. Your gates are closed and secured with firm bolts; who will open them for you?"
Then, by the power of his intention, Śakra opened those gates with his mind;
seeing this, Chandaka was filled with joy, yet again he became sorrowful and shed tears, crying:
"Alas! Woe is me, my companion! What shall I do? To which direction shall I run?"
The speech uttered by the one who possesses fierce splendor cannot be endured.
What is that powerful fourfold army doing here on the ground? Alas! O King, O Prince, O ruler of men, do you not perceive this?
The assembly of women lay thus asleep, and Yaśovatī was put to sleep by the deities; "Alas!
Fie! His vow, which was previously conceived, is now being fulfilled. *Lalitavistara* 15.75.
The gods, their minds filled with joy, spoke to Chandaka:
"Excellent, Chandaka! Give us the noble Kaṇṭhaka; do not cause distress to the Leader.
Tens of millions of drums, conchs, mṛdaṅgas, and trumpets were sounded by the gods and asuras.
This excellent city, put to sleep by the deities, does not even perceive this.
Behold, Chandaka, the stainless atmosphere; divine radiance shines forth.
Behold the many millions of bodhisattvas who have arrived to offer worship.
Behold Śakra, the lord of Śacī, surrounded by his hosts, shining as he stands at the gate.
And also the gods, the asuras, and the hosts of kinnaras who had come for the purpose of worship.
Having heard those words of the deities, Chandaka spoke to Kaṇṭhaka:
"The supreme charioteer of beings is coming here; you must neigh now!
Having thus prepared him—who was the color of a rain cloud, with hooves like gold, and well-adorned—[he mounted].
Weeping and dejected, he brought the ship of the ocean of virtues [to the shore].
This horse of yours, endowed with excellent marks, beneficial, well-born, and auspicious—go! May the aspiration that you previously contemplated be fulfilled for you!
May those who create obstacles for you go to peace; may their vows be accomplished!
May you be the bestower of happiness upon the entire world, as well as of heaven and peace.
When he arose from his bed and mounted that supreme king of horses, which resembled the full orb of the moon, the entire earth shook in six ways;
then the Pālas placed their pure hands, like stainless lotuses, upon the noble horse.
Both Śakra and Brahmā appeared before him, for this indeed is the path.

A brilliant, pure, and stainless radiance was released by him, illuminating the entire earth; all states of woe were stilled, beings became happy, and they were no longer oppressed by afflictions at that time.
Flowers rained down, tens of millions of musical instruments resounded, and the gods and asuras offered praise.
Having circumambulated the excellent city, they all departed filled with joy.
When the Great Being was departing, the tutelary deity of the supreme city approached with a dejected mind;
standing before him with a piteous and sorrowful heart, she addressed these words to the lotus-faced one: *Lalita-vistara* 15.82.
Confounded by darkness, every city and town on earth does not shine when deprived of you;
there is no pleasure or delight for me here now that this palace has been abandoned by you.
Furthermore, O you of infinite fame, I shall no longer hear within the inner apartments the sweet sound of the flute from the flocks of birds,
nor the auspicious sounds and the resonance of songs that awaken you.
"May the hosts of gods and *siddhas* perform worship for you day and night, as they do at the new moon festival;
yet they shall no longer smell that divine fragrance once you have departed, having destroyed the multitude of afflictions."

Like a withered garland cast aside, so indeed does this palace appear to me today, abandoned by you; now that you have departed, it seems to me like a deserted theatrical stage, its splendor and glory no longer present.
"You take away the vigor and strength in every city, yet this [palace] does not shine; it is like a wilderness.
Today the word of the seers has proven false, for by them he was prophesied on earth as one possessing the power of a universal monarch."
The strength on earth is weak; the Śākya force is powerless. The lineage here in this royal family is severed;
hope has perished within this Śākya host now that you, the great tree of merit, have departed.
"I myself shall go as your refuge, just as you, stainless and pure, are departing. Furthermore, O Compassionate One, having given rise to pity and mercy, please look upon this palace of yours."
Having surveyed his palace, the wise one uttered these words in a sweet voice:
"I shall not enter the city of Kapila until I have attained that which brings an end to birth and death."
I shall not perform standing, sitting, lying down, or walking toward Kapilavastu until I have attained supreme enlightenment— the excellent state that is ageless, deathless, and immortal.
When that Bodhisattva, the foremost in the world, was departing, the Apsarases praised him as he traveled through the sky:
"He is the one most worthy of offerings; he is the great field of merit, the field for those seeking merit, the giver of the fruit of immortality."
Through many millions of eons, he has accumulated this awakening by means of generosity, self-control, and restraint, out of compassion for sentient beings.
He is pure in morality, firm in his vows, and unbroken in his conduct; as a guardian of morality, he seeks neither sensual pleasures nor enjoyments.
This one has always been a proponent of patience; though his limbs were being cut member by member, he felt neither anger nor resentment, for the sake of protecting all beings.
This one has always been possessed of vigor, untiring for tens of millions of eons; he has fully accomplished awakening and has sacrificed tens of millions of yakṣas.
Constantly meditating in dhyāna with a calm and tranquil mind, having meditated, he will liberate millions of beings from all afflictions.
This wise one, free from attachment and liberated from conceptual constructions, with a mind released from constructs, shall become a self-arisen Victor.
He is ever possessed of a mind of loving-kindness, having reached the further shore of compassion; he meditates with joy and equanimity, knowing the ritual of the Brahma-path.
He is the god beyond gods, worthy of worship by the deities, his mind pure, stainless, and auspicious, having reached the further shore of millions of virtues.

A refuge for those afflicted by fear, a lamp for those without eyes, a shelter for those who are distressed, and a physician for those long ill; like a king is the King of Dharma, like Indra the thousand-eyed, he is Brahmā, the self-existent, with body tranquil and mind stilled. (Lal 15.97)
He is steadfast, possessed of abundant wisdom, a hero with a secluded mind, a champion who destroys the afflictions, the conqueror of the unconquered, and one who has vanquished his enemies.
He is a lion who has abandoned fear, an elephant whose mind is well-tamed, a bull preeminent among the herd, patient, and one whose anger has been eliminated.
The moon illuminates; the sun brings forth radiance; the torch produces light, being free from all darkness.
The lotus is unstained; the flower has well-cultivated petals.
The Teacher is unshakable like Mount Meru; he is like the earth, the source of jewels, upon which all depend for their livelihood.

By him the Māra of the afflictions has been conquered; by him the Māra of the aggregates has been conquered; by him the Māra of death has been conquered; his Māra of the sons of gods has been struck down.
This great caravan leader will, before long, teach the most excellent Eightfold Path to those who have set out upon wrong paths.
The Victor, the Self-Existent One, who destroys old age, death, and the afflictions, and is liberated from the darkness of ignorance, shall become renowned throughout the earth and heavens; he,
the immeasurable one who bears the form of a supreme person, is beyond praise, yet is praised.
Whatever merit we have gained from praising you, O Lion among Speakers, may it be as you have directed.

Thus, monks, having gone forth, the Bodhisattva passed beyond the Śākyas, passed beyond the Kroḍyas, and passed beyond the Mallas; at six yojanas from the town of Anuvaineya belonging to the Maineyas, it was night for the Bodhisattva. Then the Bodhisattva, having dismounted from Kaṇṭhaka and stood upon the surface of the earth, dismissed that great assembly of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
Having dismissed him, this thought occurred to him: "I shall entrust these ornaments and Kaṇṭhaka into the hands of Chandaka."
Then the Bodhisattva addressed Chandaka, saying: "Go, Chandaka;
take these ornaments and Kaṇṭhaka, and return.
And at the place where Chandaka turned back, a shrine was established.
Even today, that shrine is known as "The Turning Back of Chandaka."
Again, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "How indeed can there be both the top-knot and the going forth?
Having cut off his top-knot with a sword, he cast it into the air.
And she was taken up by the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven for the purpose of worship;
even today, the festival of the crest (cūḍāmaha) continues among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven,
and a shrine (caitya) was established there as well.
And even today, it is known as "the receiving of his topknot."
Once again, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "How indeed can there be both the life of renunciation and Kāśī garments?
If I could obtain saffron-colored robes suitable for dwelling in the forest, it would be excellent."
Then, this thought occurred to the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm: "The Bodhisattva has need of saffron robes.
Thereupon, one son of the gods, having made his divine form disappear, stood before the Bodhisattva in the guise of a hunter, clothed in saffron garments.
Then the Bodhisattva said to him: "Friend, if you would give me these saffron robes..."
"I shall give these Kāśī garments to you.
He replied, "These garments suit you;
these are for me."
The Bodhisattva said, "I entreat you.
Then, that son of the gods in the form of a hunter gave the saffron-colored robes to the Bodhisattva; he took the garments from Kāśī.
Then that son of the gods, filled with reverence, took those garments upon his head with both hands and departed from that very spot for the world of the gods in order to worship them.
Chandaka saw this,
and he too established a shrine there.
Even today, that shrine is known simply as "The Taking of the Saṃghāṭī."

And when the Bodhisattva had cut off his top-knot and donned the saffron robes, at that moment hundreds of thousands of sons of gods—elated, satisfied, uplifted, joyful, supremely delighted, and filled with gladness and cheer—raised a great sound of "Hīhī! and "Kilikilā! and shouts of exultation, crying out:
"Friends, Prince Siddhārtha has gone forth into the religious life!"
Having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he will turn the wheel of Dharma;
he will liberate countless beings subject to birth from birth,
and having liberated them from old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair, he will deliver them from the ocean of saṃsāra.

"He will establish them in the supreme, transcendental realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)— which is secure, fearless, sorrowless, free from affliction, auspicious, stainless, and immortal. And that sound, through a succession of sounds, rose up as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Then, when the women of the inner apartments, not seeing the prince, searched through the summer, rainy-season, and winter palaces, as well as the seats and the houses, and still did not see him,
they raised a cry of lamentation like female ospreys gathered together.
There, some women, afflicted by supreme grief, cried out, "Alas, our father!"
Some cried out, "O brother! others, "O husband! some cried out, "Alas, my protector! and others, "Alas, my lord!"
Some wept with various outpourings of endearing words; some wept by writhing their bodies in various ways;
and some by dragging their heads along the ground.
Some wept while gazing at one another’s faces;
some wept by rolling their eyes; some wept while covering their own faces with their garments.
Some were slapping their thighs with their hands,
while others were beating their chests with their hands.
Some were weeping while slapping their arms with their hands, some their heads, and others were scattering dust over their heads as they cried.
Some had disheveled hair,
some were tearing out their hair,
and some, with arms upraised, cried out loudly.
Some, like does pierced by poisoned arrows, ran about suddenly and wept;
others, trembling like plantain trees shaken by the wind, wept as they shook.
Some, having fallen upon the surface of the earth with but little life remaining, wept while rolling on the ground like fish cast out from a net; others,
suddenly collapsing to the earth like trees cut at their roots, wept.

Hearing that sound, the king addressed the Śākyas: "What is this loud noise being heard in the inner apartments? The Śākyas, having understood the situation, replied: "Your Majesty, it is said that the prince is not to be seen in the inner apartments. The king said: "Quickly close the city gates!"
"We shall search for the prince within.
They searched both inside and outside;
searching inside and outside, they did not see him.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī also, lamenting, rolled upon the ground and said this to King Śuddhodana: "O Great King, quickly reunite me with my son!"
Then the king dispatched horse-messengers to the four quarters with the command:
"Go, and do not return until you have seen the prince."
The soothsayers and astrologers had predicted: "The Bodhisattva will depart through the Auspicious Gate.
As they were going out by way of the Auspicious Gate, they saw a rain of flowers falling upon the road. They thought to themselves: "By this path the Prince has gone forth."
Having gone only a short distance, they saw that son of a god approaching with the Kāśika garments of the Bodhisattva placed upon his head.
This thought occurred to them: "These indeed are the prince’s Kāśika garments;
surely it was for the sake of these garments that the prince was deprived of life by him."
"Seize him! they cried. Once more they looked, and they saw Chandaka coming behind him, carrying Kaṇṭhaka and the ornaments.
Then they said to one another: "O friends, do not commit such a rash act!
Here comes Chandaka, bringing Kaṇṭhaka;
let us question him first."
They questioned Chandaka:
"O Chandaka, could it be that the prince has been deprived of life by this very man for the sake of the Kāśika garments?
Chandaka said: "Certainly not."
Moreover, he gave saffron-colored robes to the prince,
and the prince gave these Kāśī garments to him.
Then that son of the gods, placing those garments upon his head with both hands, departed from there for the world of the gods in order to worship them.
And so they questioned Chandaka further: "What do you think, Chandaka? Shall we go?
Is it possible to turn the Prince back?
He replied: "Certainly not."
The prince is irreversible, possessing firm vigor and prowess;
and thus he spoke: "I shall not enter the great city of Kapilavastu again until I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
And exactly as it has been spoken by the prince, so shall it come to pass.
Why is that? Because the prince is irreversible, possessing firm vigor and prowess.
Then Chandaka, taking Kaṇṭhaka and the ornaments, entered the inner apartments.
Thereafter, after a long time, those ornaments were fastened upon the Śākya princes Bhadrika, Mahānāman, and Aniruddha;
others [wore them] for the sake of bodies possessing the compactness of Mahānārāyaṇa.
Those who possessed the Nārāyaṇa constitution were unable to bear them.
When no one at all was able to bear them, it occurred to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: "As long as I am looking at these ornaments..."
"Only then will sorrow depart from my heart,
when I cast these ornaments into the lotus pond.
Thereupon, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī cast those ornaments into the lotus pond.
Even today, it is known by the name "The Ornamentation Pond."
In this regard, it is said:
When the wise Bodhisattva, the hero, had departed, the entire city of Kapilavastu was awakened;
everyone thought the prince was still lying in bed, and they congratulated one another with joy and delight.

The cowherds and likewise the women of the harem woke up, but though they looked at the bed, they did not see the Bodhisattva. A cry was let out in the king’s palace: "Alas, we have been deceived! Where has the Bodhisattva gone? *Lalita-vistara* 15.103.
Having heard this, the king collapsed upon the surface of the earth and cried out, "Alas! My only son!
Then, many hundreds of Śākyans comforted him, as he stood motionless like one drenched by a jar of water.
Gopā, falling from her bed onto the surface of the earth, tore out her hair and cast off her ornaments, crying:
"Alas! A most unfortunate thing has been spoken by the Leader in my city; before long there will be separation from all that is dear."

Beautiful in form, lovely, with limbs adorned by stainless purity, translucent, pure, dear and pleasing to the world—blessed, praiseworthy, and worthy of worship in heaven and on earth—where have you gone, leaving me behind as I lay asleep? (Lal 15.106)
I shall drink no water, nor honey, nor indulge in negligence; I shall sleep upon the ground and wear matted locks and a crown.
Having abandoned bathing, I shall practice vows and austerities until I behold the Bodhisattva who possesses all virtues.

All the gardens were devoid of fruit, leaves, and flowers; the pure necklaces became like darkness, dust, and grime; the palace was no longer beautiful, and the city appeared like a wilderness—this was because it had been abandoned by that bull among the best of men. (Lal 15.108)
"Alas for the songs and instrumental music, so sweet and melodious! Alas for the women's quarters with their loosened ornaments!
Alas for the sky clearly illuminated by nets of gold! Deprived of the Possessor of Virtues, I shall never behold these things again."
And his maternal aunt, having fallen into extreme distress, comforted her, saying: "Do not weep, O Śākyan maiden!
For it was previously declared by that bull among the best of men: 'I shall effect liberation from old age and death for the world.'"
And that great seer, having practiced thousands of virtues, traveled six yojanas during the remainder of the night;
he gave his excellent horse and ornaments to Chandaka, saying, "Chandaka, take these and go to the city of Kapila."
"Ask my parents in my name that the prince has departed, and do not grieve further.
Having awakened to enlightenment, I shall return here again; having heard the Dharma, you will become peaceful in mind."
Chanda replied weeping to the Leader: "I have neither the power, strength, nor prowess [to stop him].
The host of my kinsmen, the best of men, would slay me; where has the Bodhisattva, the possessor of virtues, been led by Chanda?"
The Bodhisattva replied to Chanda: "Let them be satisfied, even though they are my circle of kinsmen;
they will always regard you as their teacher and will conduct themselves toward you with love for me."
Having taken the excellent horse and the ornaments, Chandaka arrived at the park of the bull among the best of men.
The park-keeper, filled with joy and impetuous excitement, uttered a cry of "Ānanda! to the Śākyas.
"This prince, his excellent horse, and Chandaka have reached the park; there is no longer any need for grief.
Having heard this, the king, surrounded by the Śākyas, was filled with joy and great excitement upon reaching the park.
Having learned that the Bodhisattva was firm in resolve, Gopā was neither joyful nor did she believe his words;
she thought it impossible that the prince could return here again without having attained enlightenment.
But having seen the excellent horse and Chandaka, the king let out a cry and collapsed upon the surface of the earth:
"Alas, my son, so skilled in song and instrumental music! Where have you gone, abandoning the entire kingdom? (Lal 15.118)
Speak these words to me truly here, O Chanda: what was the purpose, and where has the Bodhisattva gone?
By whom was he led out, by whom were the gates opened, and how was worship offered to him by the hosts of gods?

Chanda spoke: "Listen to me, O lord of kings! While the city, including its children and the elderly, sleeps at night, that Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa said to me: 'Chanda, give me quickly the king of horses.'"
Thus I awaken the multitudes of men and the assembly of women; yet, sleeping and fast asleep, they do not hear my voice.
Weeping, I gave away the king of horses: "Alas, go, O benefactor, wherever you desire!"
Śakra opened the gates equipped with mechanical devices, and the four guardians clung to the hooves of the horse.
When the hero mounted, the three thousandfold world-system trembled; he traversed this vast path in the sky.
A radiance was released, dispelling the thick darkness; flowers fell and hundreds of musical instruments resounded.
The gods and likewise the apsarases offered praise as he traveled through the sky, surrounded by hosts of deities. (Lal 15.123)
Having taken the horse and the ornaments, Chandaka went to the inner apartments weeping.
But when Gopā saw the excellent horse and Chandaka, she fainted and collapsed upon the surface of the earth.
All the vast multitudes of women exerted themselves, taking water to bathe the Śākya maiden,
lest she should pass away overcome by grief through the great separation from her two beloveds.
Having summoned her strength, the deeply distressed Śākya maiden clung to the neck of the noble horse, the king of steeds;
recollecting their former amorous play, she lamented with various cries, overcome by grief.
Alas, you who produce joy for me! Alas, my bull among men, with a face like the stainless moon!
Alas, my one of beautiful form! Alas, my possessor of excellent marks, bearer of stainless splendor!
Alas, my one of blameless limbs, well-born, with proportions that rise in perfect symmetry, peerless!
Alas, my bearer of the highest virtues, honored by men and gods, supremely compassionate!
"Alas for me! My men, endowed with strength and possessing the power of Nārāyaṇa, who have destroyed the hosts of enemies;
alas for me! My horses, with beautiful, resonant neighs, whose voices are like the song of the kalaviṅka bird and as sweet as the sound of Brahmā. (Lal 15.129)
Alas, my one of infinite fame, arisen from a hundred merits, the bearer of stainless merit!
Alas, my one of infinite splendor, adorned with a multitude of virtues, who brings joy to the hosts of sages!
"Alas, my one of noble birth, born in the most excellent Lumbinī grove amidst the humming songs of bees!
Alas, my one whose fame resounds through heaven and earth, honored by all, the great tree of vast wisdom! (Lal 15.131)
"Alas for my one whose lips are the finest of flavors, like the *bimba* fruit, with eyes like lotuses and a complexion like gold!
Alas for my one with perfectly pure teeth, whose teeth are as bright as cow’s milk and snow! (Lal 15.132)
"Alas for me! My face was adorned with a beautiful nose, lovely eyebrows, and a pure ūrṇā-hair situated between the brows.
Alas for me! My shoulders were well-rounded, my waist like a bow, and my shanks and hips were as round as those of an antelope. (Lal 15.133)

"Alas! My thighs are like the trunks of elephants, my hands and feet are pure and beautiful, and my nails are copper-colored"—thus did his ornaments, fashioned through merit, bring joy to the king. (Lal 15.134)
Alas, for me there were songs and instrumental music, excellent flowers and ointments during the most auspicious of seasons!
Alas, for me there were the scents of flowers and the inner apartments, which brought joy with their songs and instrumental music!
"Alas, Kaṇṭhaka! O well-born steed, where have you led my lord’s companion?
Alas, Chandaka! You are pitiless; why did you not wake me as the best of men was departing?"
This Benefactor goes forth with but a single voice; why do you not speak within this interval?
Today, from this preeminent city, the compassionate Charioteer who tames men departs.
How did the Benefactor go, and by whom was he led out from this royal palace?
To which direction did he follow, and who is the blessed forest-deity that became his companion?
"O Chandā, my eyes were plucked out while I was in extreme suffering, yet you gave me back my sight;
therefore, O Chandā, all people should always praise and honor parents."
Having abandoned even those, he departed; how much more so this delight in women?
Alas! Separation from loved ones is like the nature of a theatrical stage; they are impermanent.
"By grasping at perceptions, fools who rely on the perversion of views undergo birth and death;
for that very reason, he has declared that within conditioned phenomena subject to aging and death, there is no friend whatsoever."
May his aspiration be fulfilled; may he touch the supreme, most excellent enlightenment at the best of trees.
Having awakened to stainless enlightenment, may he return once more to this preeminent city.
Having heard Gopikā’s words, Chandaka, with a most dejected mind and a throat choked with tears, spoke these words: "Excellent, Gopikā! Listen to my speech. (Lal 15.143)
In the middle of the night, in secret, while the entire host of women was fast asleep, he, arisen through a hundredfold merit, then spoke to me: "Give me Kaṇṭhaka."
Having heard those words, I then looked at you as you lay there desiring sleep; I let out a loud cry there: "Arise, O cowherd woman! Your beloved is going away!"
The deity silenced that speech; not even a single woman was awakened.
Weeping and having adorned herself, she gave the horse-king to the Best of Men. *Lalita-vistara* 15.146.
Kaṇṭhaka, possessed of fierce majesty, neighed, and his sound traveled for the distance of a krośa;
yet no one heard it within the supreme city, for the deities had cast a spell of sleep upon them.
The earth, struck by the hooves of Kaṇṭhaka, was covered with gold, silver, and millions of jewels;
it resounded with a sweet, formidable, and beautiful noise, yet no humans heard it.
At that moment, the moon was joined with the Puṣya constellation and stood in the sky;
millions of gods in the air, with palms joined, bowed their heads in salutation.

Attended by hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, the four world-protectors of great supernatural power placed the hooves of Kaṇṭhaka upon their hands, which were as pure and stainless as the filaments of a lotus.
And that Puṇyaśatatejaudgata ascended like a noble white lotus or a *varṣikā* flower;
the earth shook in six ways, and the Buddha-field was suffused with stainless light.
Śakra, the teacher of the gods and lord of Śacī, opened his own gate;
honored by millions of billions of deities and worshipped by immortals and nāgas, he proceeded within it.
In this world, birth is merely a designation; Kaṇṭhaka carries the Lord of the World through the midst of the sky.
So too do the hosts of gods and dānavas, along with Indra, carry the Sugata as he proceeds.
The Apsarases, skilled in song and instrumental music, proclaiming the virtues of the Bodhisattva,
bestowed strength upon Kaṇṭhaka and let forth a sweet and enchanting sound.
"Kaṇṭhaka, carry the Leader of the World swiftly, swiftly; do not feel weariness!
I have no fear of the miserable states or evil rebirths, having taken hold of the Lord of the World."
Each deity individually rejoiced, thinking, "I am the vehicle for the Leader of the World," yet there was not even the slightest space that was not trampled by the feet of tens of millions of gods.
Behold, Kaṇṭhaka, this path established in the midst of the sky, wonderful and beautiful,
adorned with various jeweled railings, and perfumed with the finest divine incense.
"Kaṇṭhaka, by virtue of this auspicious deed, you shall be reborn as Sunirmita in the abode of the Thirty-three;
surrounded and honored by apsarases, you will delight in divine sensual pleasures."
"Excellent, O Gopī! Do not weep any longer; be content and supremely joyful.
Before long you shall behold the Supreme among Men, having attained awakening and honored by the immortals."
Those men who perform deeds of merit should never be wept for;
he who has arisen with the splendor of a hundredfold merits should be rejoiced for, not wept for.
O Gopikā, even in seven nights one could not describe that array which was manifested there by the King, who is honored by gods and men. (Lal 15.161)
"O benefactor of the world, it is a supreme and inconceivable gain for you that you have appeared;
my own perception persists only toward myself, for you shall indeed become the Supreme among Men."
Thus [it is said].
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Departure."
START Chapter 16 (Vaidya 174): The Sixteenth Chapter, "The Visit of Bimbisāra"

In this way, monks, through the empowerment of the Bodhisattva, Chandaka dispelled the grief of King Śuddhodana, of Gopā the Śākya maiden, of the entire harem, and of the whole Śākya clan by means of these words of consolation.

Thus, monks, the Bodhisattva, having given the Kāśika garments to the son of the gods who was in the form of a hunter and having taken the saffron robes from him, himself undertook the going forth out of conformity with the world, out of compassion for sentient beings,
and for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
Then the Bodhisattva approached the hermitage of the Śākya brahmin woman;
she invited the Bodhisattva to stay and take a meal.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva went to the hermitage of the brahmin woman Padmā.
She, too, invited the Bodhisattva to stay and to take a meal.
From there, he went to the hermitage of the brahmin seer Raivata;
he too invited the Bodhisattva in the same manner.
Likewise, Rājaka, the son of Datṛmadaṇḍika, also invited the Bodhisattva in the same way.
Thus, monks, the Bodhisattva gradually arrived at the great city of Vaiśālī.
Now at that time, Ārāḍa Kālāma was residing near Vaiśālī together with a great community of disciples, three hundred in number.
He was teaching the Dharma to his disciples for the sake of practicing the vow associated with the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Seeing the Bodhisattva approaching from afar, he was struck with wonder and addressed his disciples: "Behold, behold, sirs, this form of his!"
They said, "Indeed, we see it thus;
this is truly most wonderful."

Then, monks, I approached Ārāḍa Kālāma and said this to him: "Venerable Ārāḍa Kālāma, I would practice the holy life under you. He replied: "Practice it, O Gautama, in such a teaching of the Dharma wherein a faithful son of good family attains realization with little difficulty."

Then, monks, this occurred to me: "I have zeal, I have energy, I have mindfulness, I have concentration, and I have wisdom; what if I were to dwell alone, heedful, ardent, and resolute, for the sake of attaining and realizing that very Dharma?"
Then indeed, monks, dwelling alone, heedful, ardent, and resolute, I realized that Dharma with very little difficulty and directly experienced it.
Then, monks, I approached Ārāḍa Kālāma and said this to him: "O Ārāḍa, has such a Dharma been realized and personally attained by you?
He replied: "It is so, O Gautama.
I said to him: "O sir, this very Dharma has also been realized and attained by me."
He said: "In that case, O Gautama, that Dharma which I know, you also know; and that which you know,"
I too know him;
therefore, let us both together look after this community of disciples.
Thus, monks, Ārāḍa Kālāma honored me with the highest honor and established me as one of equal status among his disciples.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: "This dharma of Ārāḍa is indeed not conducive to liberation, nor does it lead forth;
to what end, then, could it lead to the complete destruction of suffering?"
"What if I were to go forth from here, seeking further beyond this?"
Then indeed, monks, having dwelt in Vaiśālī for as long as I desired, I set out for the Magadha country.
While wandering on tour through Magadha, I proceeded toward Rājagṛha, the city of the people of Magadha, and approached Pāṇḍava, the king of mountains.
There, on the side of Pāṇḍava, the king of mountains, I stayed alone, without a second, without a companion, protected by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods.

Then, having dressed early in the morning and taken my bowl and robes, I entered the great city of Rājagṛha for alms through the Tapoda gate, with graceful deportment— graceful in advancing and retreating,

in looking ahead and looking aside, in drawing in and extending [the limbs]— and with the carrying of my outer cloak, inner robe, bowl, and robes that was pleasing to behold, with senses unscattered and not wandering outward.

Moving with a mind-made body like one carrying a vessel of oil, looking ahead only the distance of a yoke, the people of Rājagṛha were filled with wonder upon seeing me there, thinking: "Could this be Brahmā? Or Śakra, the lord of the gods? Or perhaps Vaiśravaṇa? Or some mountain deity?
Regarding this, it is said:
Then the Bodhisattva Vimaladhara, possessing infinite splendor, having himself gone forth into homelessness here,
dwelt on the side of Pāṇḍava, the king of mountains, peaceful, self-controlled, and possessed of noble deportment.
Knowing that the night had passed, the Bodhisattva, having put on his most beautiful robes and taking up his alms-bowl with humble demeanor, entered Rājagṛha for alms-food.
Like gold of pure essence and natural luster, adorned with the thirty-two marks and the two [minor signs],
he gazes upon the throngs of men and women, yet he never experiences satiety from seeing them.

"Who is this being, never seen before, whose radiance causes the entire city to shine? Surely it is because he is wearing garments adorned with jewels set in rows that Avaśiri follows behind him. (Lal 16.4)
Thousands of women stood upon the rooftops, likewise at the gates, and likewise at the windows;
having filled the streets and left the houses empty, they gazed at the Best of Men with undivided attention.
No longer did they engage in buying and selling, nor again did they drink intoxicating liquors;
neither at home nor in the streets did they find pleasure, as they gazed upon the form of the Best of Men.
The man went quickly to the royal palace and spoke to King Bimbisāra, who was pleased: "O Lord, a supreme gain has been obtained for you! Brahmā himself is wandering here in the city for alms."
Some said, "Śakra, the king of the gods," while others spoke of the divine son Suyāma;
likewise, some spoke of Saṃtuṣita, and others spoke of the god Sunirmita among the Nirmita gods.
Some, moreover, say: "It is the moon and the sun, as well as Rāhu, Bali, and Vemacitrī";
others, however, speak these words: "This is he who dwells on the king of mountains, Pāṇḍava."
Having heard these words, the king stood at the window with a most exalted mind;
he gazed upon the Supreme Being, the Bodhisattva, blazing with glory like well-refined gold.
Having given the alms-food, King Bimbisāra said to a man, "Observe where he is going.
Seeing him proceeding toward the excellent mountain, he replied, "Your Majesty, he has gone to the side of the mountain."
Knowing that the night had passed, King Bimbisāra, the lord of men, surrounded by a great multitude, approached the foot of the Pāṇḍava mountain-king; blazing with splendor, he beheld that mountain.
Having descended from his chariot, he went upon the earth; with the utmost reverence, he gazed upon the Bodhisattva.
Like Mount Meru, indeed, remaining unshaken, he spread out some grasses and sat down in the auspicious posture.
Having bowed his head at the feet of the prince and engaged in various conversations, the king said:
"I shall give you half of my entire kingdom; enjoy yourself here with the qualities of sensual pleasure, and I too shall partake of the alms-food."
The Bodhisattva spoke these gentle words: "O Lord of the Earth, may you protect your long life for a long time!
As for me, having renounced my beloved kingdom, I have gone forth as a wanderer, indifferent [to worldly things] for the sake of peace."
"You are young, endowed with fresh youth, possessing a beautiful complexion and full of vigor.
Accept vast wealth and this multitude of women; dwell here in my kingdom and enjoy sensual pleasures."
"I am supremely delighted at the sight of you," the King of Magadha said to the Bodhisattva:
"Be my companion; I shall give you my entire kingdom. Enjoy abundant sensual pleasures."
Do not dwell again in the empty forest; do not dwell any longer on the ground among the grasses.
Your body is most delicate; dwell here in my kingdom and enjoy sensual pleasures.
The Bodhisattva, compassionate for their welfare, spoke these gentle, straightforward, and pleasing words:
"O Protector of the Earth, may you always have well-being; nor am I one who seeks after the qualities of sensual pleasure."
Sensual desires are like poison, possessing endless faults; they cause one to fall into hell, and into the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.
They are censured by the wise and are ignoble; O Kāma, abandon me as one would a lump of spittle.
Like the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree falling, like clouds moving according to their course,
or like the wind that moves unsteadily and fleetingly, they scatter all that is auspicious and are deceptive. (Lal 16.21)
Not obtaining sensual pleasures, they burn with longing; even when obtained, they find no satisfaction.
But when they must consume them against their will, those terrible sensual desires produce great and horrific suffering. (Lal 16.22)
O protector of the earth, even if a single man were to obtain all the divine and human pleasures that are most excellent,
he would find no satisfaction, but would continue to seek more.

But those who, O protector of the earth, are peaceful and self-controlled, noble ones filled with the perception of the untainted Dharma—those wise ones, satisfied by wisdom, are truly satisfied; there is no satisfaction for them again in the qualities of sensual desire.
O Protector of the Earth, for one who indulges in sensual pleasures, no prior limit to conditioned existence can be found;
for just as one who drinks salt water finds their thirst increases all the more, so it is when one indulges in sensual pleasures.
Moreover, O protector of the earth, behold this body: it is unstable, devoid of essence, and a machine of suffering;
it constantly flows from nine openings of wounds. Therefore, O lord of men, I have no desire or passion for sensual pleasures.
I too, having abandoned vast sensual pleasures as well as three thousand beautiful women,
have gone forth, finding no delight in worldly existences, desiring to attain supreme, auspicious, and excellent enlightenment.
The king said:
"In which direction have you come from, monk? Where was your birth, and where are your father and mother?"
Whether he be a kṣatriya, a brahmin, a king, a counselor, or a monk, if he does not perceive it as a burden.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Listen, O Protector of the Earth! There is the city of Kapilavastu of the Śākyas, supremely prosperous and flourishing.
My father there is named Śuddhodana; desiring virtue, I have gone forth from that place."
The king said:
"Excellent! Your vision is well-seen; since you have taken birth, we too shall be your disciples.
Moreover, forgive me for my intention, as I also desire to invite one who is free from passion."
"If you attain enlightenment, then it shall be mine, O Lord of Dharma.
Furthermore, "I have long ago obtained a great gain, since you, O Self-Existent One, dwell here within my realm."
Once again, having paid homage at his feet and performed circumambulations with reverence, the king, the lord of men,
surrounded by his own people and retinue, re-entered Rājagṛha.
Having entered the city of Magadha and dwelt there with a peaceful mind according to his desire, the Lord of the World,
the Sovereign of Men, having accomplished the welfare of gods and humans, approached the banks of the Nirañjanā river.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter of the *Śrī-lalitavistara*, titled "The Visit of Bimbisāra."

Furthermore, monks, at that time Rudraka Rāmaputra was dwelling near the great city of Rājagṛha together with a large assembly of disciples, seven hundred in number;
he was teaching them the Dharma for the sake of attaining the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, monks, the Bodhisattva saw Rudraka Rāmaputra, who was the head of a community, a teacher of a group, renowned, esteemed, honored by many people, and regarded as wise.
Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to him: "This Rudraka Rāmaputra is indeed the head of a community, a teacher of a group, renowned, esteemed, honored by many people, and regarded as wise.
If I were to approach him and undertake ascetic practices under him..."

"Let him not form a notion of superiority toward me, nor let him know me through direct perception, nor let him perceive the fault in conditioned, out-flowing, and grasping states such as the meditations, concentrations, and attainments.
What if I were to demonstrate such a means by which these would become directly perceived?"
"The lack of deliverance would have been shown for worldly meditative concentrations, which have the spheres of meditation as their domain and the objects of attainment as their focus.

Suppose I were to go into the presence of Rudraka Rāmaputra, accept discipleship in order to manifest the excellence of my own special qualities of concentration, and demonstrate the insubstantiality of conditioned concentrations. Then, monks, with this purpose in mind, the Bodhisattva approached where Rudraka Rāmaputra was.
Having approached Rudraka Rāmaputra, he said this to him: "Who, friend, is your teacher, or whose taught Dharma do you understand?
When this was said, Rudraka Rāmaputra spoke thus to the Bodhisattva: "Friend, I have no teacher at all."
"Moreover, indeed, this has been correctly realized by me myself.
The Bodhisattva asked, "What have you realized? He replied, "The path to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
The Bodhisattva said, "May we receive from you the path to the samādhi of instruction and admonition? He replied, "So be it. Thereupon, the instruction was given.

Then the Bodhisattva went to a secluded place and sat down, having folded his legs crosswise. As soon as the Bodhisattva had sat down, by virtue of the excellence of his merit, the excellence of his knowledge, the excellence of the fruit of his previous conduct in good deeds, and the excellence of his mastery of all meditative concentrations, all mundane and supramundane qualities— headed by the dhyānas— [arose].

Hundreds of meditative attainments (samāpatti) became manifest before him, with their specific forms and details, because he had attained mastery over his own mind. Then the Bodhisattva, mindful and clearly comprehending, rose from his seat and approached Rudraka Rāmaputra.
Having approached, he said this to Rudraka Rāmaputra: "Friend, is there any other path superior to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
He replied, "There is none."
Then this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "It is not only Rudraka who possesses faith, energy, mindfulness, and wisdom;
I too possess faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Then the Bodhisattva said to Rudraka Rāmaputra: "Friend, this very Dharma has been realized by me as well, that in which you have attained liberation."
He said: "In that case, come;
both you and I shall lead this group.
And he spoke to the Bodhisattva regarding their common purpose.
And he established him in the position of a teacher.

The Bodhisattva said: "This, friend, is not the path that leads to extinction, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to tranquility, nor to direct knowledge, nor to full awakening, nor to the state of a śramaṇa, nor to the state of a brāhmaṇa, nor to nirvāṇa."
Thus, monks, the Bodhisattva, having failed to win over Rudraka Rāmaputra along with his disciples—even though he had practiced as much as they did—departed, thinking, "Enough for me of this."
Now at that time, the five of the auspicious group were practicing the holy life under Rudraka Rāmaputra.
This thought occurred to them: "For the sake of what we have long striven and exerted ourselves, yet we have not been able to reach its end or its limit."
That was realized and directly witnessed by the ascetic Gautama with little difficulty;
yet it did not please him,
and so he sought further.
"Without doubt, he will become a Teacher in the world;
and whatever he shall realize,
he will share that with us."
Having reflected thus, the group of five auspicious companions departed from the presence of Rudraka Rāmaputra and followed after the Bodhisattva.
Thus, monks, after the Bodhisattva had stayed in Rājagṛha as long as he desired, he set out on a journey through Magadha together with the group of five auspicious companions.
Now at that time, between Rājagṛha and Gayā, a certain group was holding a festival;
that group invited the Bodhisattva, together with the five of the auspicious company, for lodging and a meal.

Then, monks, while the Bodhisattva was practicing his course of conduct in Magadha, he followed toward Gayā of the Magadhans and arrived there. There, monks, the Bodhisattva dwelt on Mount Gayāśīrṣa, intent upon exertion. While he was dwelling there, three similes occurred to him, never heard before and never known before.
What are these three?
They are those ascetics and brahmins who dwell with their bodies not withdrawn from sensual pleasures,
and they dwell with their minds not withdrawn from sensual pleasures.

Furthermore, whatever delight they have in sensual pleasures, whatever passion for sensual pleasures, whatever desire for sensual pleasures, whatever craving for sensual pleasures, whatever thirst for sensual pleasures, whatever infatuation with sensual pleasures, whatever feverish longing for sensual pleasures, and whatever fixation upon sensual pleasures— that too has not been stilled. Moreover, although they experience painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations that are self-inflicted and tormenting to the body.

In that case, they are indeed incapable of realizing the superhuman state, the unsurpassed noble knowledge and vision of distinction. It is just as if, for example, a man seeking fire, searching for fire, and looking for fire, were to take a piece of wet wood and a wet upper fire-drill, place them in water, and attempt to churn them—
he would be incapable of producing fire or manifesting heat.

In the same way, those ascetics and brahmins who dwell with their bodies and minds not withdrawn from sensual pleasures— even though they experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations that are self-inflicted and tormenting to the body—

their delight in sensual pleasures, their passion for sensual pleasures, their desire for sensual pleasures, their craving for sensual pleasures, their thirst for sensual pleasures, their infatuation with sensual pleasures, their fever for sensual pleasures, and their obsession with sensual pleasures remain unappeased. Furthermore, although they undergo such painful, sharp, rough, and agonizing sensations that involve self-mortification and bodily affliction, [their underlying defilements persist].
"In that case, they are indeed incapable of realizing the further states of a human being—that is, the distinguished noble knowledge and vision.
This was the first simile that occurred to the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, this thought occurred to him: "As for these ascetics and brahmins who dwell with their bodies and minds withdrawn from sensual pleasures—
even that delight they have in those pleasures— all must be abandoned," and so on, up until, "he sought out the light."
If one were to take a piece of wet wood, place it on dry ground, and churn it with a wet upper fire-drill, that person would be incapable of producing fire.

In the same way, regarding those ascetics and brahmins—everything should be understood as previously stated—up until: they are incapable of realizing the superhuman state, the excellence of noble knowledge and vision.
This second simile occurred to him, one never heard or known before.
Furthermore, as for those venerable ascetics and brahmins who dwell with their bodies and minds withdrawn from sensual pleasures—
even that delight of theirs in sensual pleasures [is abandoned]; and so on for everything else in detail.
Even that [affliction] of theirs has been stilled.
Furthermore, although they experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations— self-inflicted and tormenting to the body—
they are nevertheless truly capable of realizing the distinction of noble knowledge and vision that transcends human conditions.

It is just as if, for example, there were a man here who, desiring fire and seeking light, while searching for light, took dry wood and a dry upper fire-drill, placed them on dry ground, and churned them; he would be capable of producing fire and manifesting heat.
In the same way, regarding these worthy recluses and brahmins— everything from "those who experience feelings" up to that point—
they are indeed capable of realizing the superhuman state, the unsurpassed noble knowledge and vision of distinction.
This third simile occurred to him, one never heard before and never known before.

Then, monks, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "Indeed, at this time I dwell with my body withdrawn from sensual pleasures and my mind withdrawn from them. Whatever delight I had in sensual pleasures—all that has been stilled for me.
Furthermore, although I experience painful sensations—[the full passage] including those resulting from self-inflicted violence and bodily mortification."
Indeed, I am capable of realizing the distinction of noble knowledge and vision that transcends human conditions.

Thus, monks, having stayed at Gayā for as long as he desired, the Bodhisattva, while walking about on a walking-path on Mount Gayāśīrṣa, followed the road toward Urubilvā, the village of Senāpati, and arrived there.
There he saw the river Nairañjanā with its clear water and beautiful landing-stairs, adorned on all sides by lovely trees and shrubs, and surrounded by villages providing his range of alms.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva’s mind became exceedingly serene: "Ah, how level, delightful, and suitable for solitary retreat is this spot!
This is sufficient for a son of good family who seeks to abandon [defilements], and I am one who seeks such abandonment."
What if I were to remain right here?

Thus, monks, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "I have descended here into Jambudvīpa at a time of the five corruptions, amidst beings of inferior inclinations, crowded with hosts of non-Buddhist teachers, fallen into various views, and obsessed with grasping the body as a solid mass; they seek purity of the body through various kinds of mortifications and austerities."

And the deluded prescribe [such practices], namely: those who investigate mantras, those who lick their hands, those who do not beg, those who do not invite [alms], those who use many roots, those who abstain from fish and meat, those who do not follow the rainy season retreat, those who are like people with wine,

bran-water, and dregs, those who accept alms from one, three, five, or seven families, and those who subsist on roots, fruits, algae, *kuśa* grass, leaves, cow dung, cow urine, rice-gruel, curd, and ghee.
By means of drinking molasses and eating unground flour; by means of the "crane," the "young pigeon," the "tongs," and the "washing-aside" [methods of begging];
by means of livelihoods both village-based and forest-based;

by means of the vows of the cow, the deer, the dog, the boar, the monkey, and the elephant; and by means of standing postures, silence, the hero’s posture, and speaking only one word up to seven words.

They subsist on a single meal a day, or observe fasts of one day and night, four days, five days, or six days; they practice the *pakṣakṣapaṇa* (fasting for a fortnight), the *māsakṣapaṇa* (fasting for a month), and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance; they wear the feathers of vultures and owls; they dwell in huts made of fruit-stalks, *muñja* grass, bark, *darbha* grass, *balbaja* grass, camel-hair blankets, goat-hair blankets, hair-blankets, or animal skins; they sleep on wet clothes, straw mats, or nets; and they lie upon ashes, gravel, stones, wooden planks, thorns, grass, pestles, or on the bare ground in a prone position, in a squatting posture, or while standing upright.

[They appear] with one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or many garments, or in a state of nakedness; by rules regarding proper and improper places; by wearing long hair, nails, and beards, or by wearing matted locks and crowns; by subsisting on a single jujube fruit, sesame seed, or grain of rice; by smearing themselves with ashes, soot, discarded flower-garlands, darkness, dust, or mud;
by carrying hair, muñja-grass, locks, nails, rags, cages, or skulls; and by drinking hot water, rice-water, strained kāmbalika broth, or water from cooking-pots.
Deluded as they are, they believe that purity is attained by carrying charcoal, minerals, decoctions, triple staves, shaven heads, water-pots, skull-bowls, and *khaṭvāṅga* staffs;
and they accumulate ascetic merit through inhaling smoke, drinking fire, not looking at the sun, the five fires, standing on one leg with arms raised, and walking on one foot.
They seek a desired destination through the burning of husks and charcoal, the use of *nikumbha* plants, cooking on heated stones, entering fire or water, and death at sacred fords (*tīrtha*).

They understand purity through the utterance of *oṃ*, *vaṣaṭ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*; through benedictions, hymns of praise, ritual piling of fire, invocations, recitation, and the memorization and application of mantras.
Considering themselves pure, they take refuge in these [deities], namely:

Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Devī, Kumāra, the Mātṛkās, Kātyāyanī, Candra, Āditya, Vaiśravaṇa, Varuṇa, Vāsava, the Aśvins, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Asuras, Garuḍas, Kiṃnaras, Mahoragas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, Bhūtas, Kumbhāṇḍas, the Gaṇapatis who are attendants, and Piśācas.
They pay homage to the celestial sages, royal sages, and brahmin sages,
and they perceive them as their essence;
they take refuge in earth, water, fire, air, and space.

They take refuge in mountains, rivers, streams, springs, lakes, pools, oceans, ponds, puddles, lotus-pools, wells, trees, shrubs, creepers, grass, stumps, cow-pens, cremation grounds, crossroads, triple-forked roads, and the entrances to marketplaces;
they pay homage to houses, pillars, stones, pestles, swords, bows, axes, arrows, spears, and tridents;
and they regard curd, clarified butter, mustard seeds, barley, amulets, dūrvā grass, gems, gold, silver, and so forth as auspicious.
Such are the practices these non-Buddhists perform, and they resort to them out of fear of the cycle of existence.

And here, some people, thinking that heaven and liberation will be achieved for us from these [practices] in this world and the next, have set out upon false paths; perceiving a refuge where there is no refuge, perceiving auspiciousness in what is inauspicious, and imagining purity through impurity,
they daily undertake such specific vows and austerities so that all the proponents of other doctrines may be refuted.
I shall demonstrate the non-destruction of the activity of karma for those beings whose karmic activity has been lost;
and I shall effect the conversion of the gods who dwell in the realm of form and whose sphere is meditative concentration, by showing them the distinctions within meditation.
Thus, monks, having reflected in this way, the Bodhisattva undertook for six years a most terrible practice of vows and austerities—difficult practices that were exceedingly difficult.
For what reason is it called "difficult practice"?
Because it is a performance of what is difficult to do.
Therefore, it is called "the practice of difficult deeds.
There is no being whatsoever to be found among the classes of beings— whether human or non-human— who is capable of performing such difficult deeds.
Except for a bodhisattva in his final existence who has entered the *āsphānaka* meditation,
for what reason is it called "all-pervading" (*āsphānaka*)?
Entering the fourth dhyāna from the very beginning, he suppresses and brings to cessation inhalation and exhalation.
That dhyāna is without conceptualization, free from discrimination, immovable, removed from agitation, unwavering, all-pervading, and yet not dependent on anything.
Furthermore, that dhyāna has never before been entered by anyone—neither by a disciple, nor by one who is not a disciple, nor by a pratyekabuddha.
Or by a bodhisattva who has entered upon the practice;
for this reason it is called "all-pervading" (*āsphānaka*). Space is non-expanding, non-acting, and non-transforming, yet it pervades everything; thus that meditation is equal to space.
Therefore, it is called "āsphānaka."
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva— for the purpose of displaying a marvel to the world, for the purpose of shattering the pride of the heretics,

for the purpose of subduing the proponents of other doctrines, for the purpose of winning over the gods, for the purpose of introducing beings who hold views of annihilationism or eternalism and who have lost their way regarding action and its performance back to the practice of action, for the purpose of manifesting the fruit of merit, and for the purpose of demonstrating the fruit of wisdom— [proceeded].
For the purpose of analyzing the factors of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*), for the purpose of demonstrating bodily strength and power, and for the purpose of generating mental courage,
he sat down cross-legged upon the unconditioned earth. Having sat down, he restrained his own body with his mind.
He squeezed it.
Then, monks, during the eight nights of the winter season, as I thus restrained and tormented my body, sweat flowed from my armpits;
sweat also flowed from my forehead.
It fell upon the ground, freezing, steaming, and evaporating.
Just as if a strong man were to seize a much weaker man by the neck and squeeze him, even so, monks, as he restrained and squeezed this body with his mind, sweat flowed from his armpits;
sweat also flowed from his forehead.
They fell upon the ground, becoming like frost, emitting heat, and shedding tears.

Monks, this thought occurred to me: "What if I were to practice the breath-holding meditation (āsphānaka-dhyāna)? Then, monks, as I was practicing the breath-holding meditation, the inhalation and exhalation were completely stilled through my mouth and nose;
yet from my two ear-cavities there issued forth loud sounds and great noises.

Just as, for example, when a blacksmith’s bellows are being blown, a loud and great sound issues forth, even so, monks, when my inhalation and exhalation were obstructed through my mouth and nose, a loud and great sound issued forth from the openings of my ears.

Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: "What if I were to practice the breath-holding meditation (āsphānaka-dhyāna) even further? Thereupon, monks, my mouth, nose, and ears were closed off; when they were thus closed, the wind struck upward against the skull of my head.
"Monks, it was just as if a man were to strike the skull with a blunt spear;
even so, monks, when my mouth, nose, and ears were blocked, the inhalations and exhalations struck upward against the skull."
Seeing that state of the Bodhisattva, some gods there said, "Alas! It is a tragedy; Prince Siddhārtha has indeed passed away.
Others said, "He has not passed away; rather, this is the kind of meditative abiding (dhyānavihāra) characteristic of Arhats."
And at that time, they spoke this verse:
"May this scion of the Śākya king not, with his purpose yet unfulfilled, pass away right here in the forest;
for having left the three worlds suffering and without a protector, he would depart without having accomplished his aim."

"Alas, O Essence of Beings, you who were firm in your vow and invited by the sacrifice of the True Dharma! Formerly, O Protector, we were among the Tuṣita gods; where now is that vow of yours, O Pure Being? (Lal 17.2)
Then those sons of the gods, having gone among the gods of the Thirty-three, announced this matter to Queen Māyā: "The prince has passed away.
Then Queen Māyā, surrounded by a host of apsarases, approached the bank of the Nairañjanā River at the hour of midnight, where the Bodhisattva was;
there she beheld the Bodhisattva with his limbs withered.
Seeing him as if he were dead, her throat choked with tears, she began to weep;
and at that moment, she spoke this verse:
"When you were born to me, my son, in the grove called Lumbinī..."
Like a lion, you have set out on your own, taking seven steps without being grasped.
Having surveyed the quarters, those four uttered these auspicious words:
"This is my final birth; that [vow] of yours has not yet been fulfilled."
"By Asita you were designated: 'You shall become a Buddha in the world.
His prophecy has been fulfilled; by him, permanence was not seen."
O son, you did not enjoy even the delightful glory of a universal monarch, nor did you attain awakening; instead, you have gone to your death in the forest.
"For the sake of my son, whom shall I approach? To whom shall I cry out in my distress?
Who can grant even a moment of life to my only son, whose life is as fragile as a breath?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"Who is this that weeps so piteously for you, with disheveled hair and her beauty destroyed?
For she stands upon the surface of the earth, writhing and lamenting excessively for her son."
Queen Māyā said:
"For ten months indeed I carried you in my womb like a thunderbolt;
O dear son, I am that mother of yours, and I lament, deeply afflicted by sorrow."
Then the Bodhisattva, comforting him, said: "Do not be afraid, O you who cherish your son;
you shall make your toil fruitful.
The renunciation of the Buddha is never in vain."
I shall make the prophecy of Asita clear,
and I shall also clarify the prediction of Dīpaṃkara.
Even if the earth were to shatter into a hundred pieces, and Mount Meru, with its jeweled peak, were to float upon the waters.
The moon, the sun, and the hosts of stars may fall to the earth, and ordinary people may likewise perish, yet I shall not die; therefore,
you should feel no grief for me here, for before long you shall behold the enlightenment of a Buddha.

Upon merely hearing this, Queen Māyā’s hair stood on end with joy; she scattered māndārava flowers over the Bodhisattva, circumambulated him three times, and, as divine musical instruments were being played, she departed for her own abode.
"Monks, this occurred to me: 'There are some ascetics and brahmins who believe that purity comes through eating little food; what if I were to practice eating little food?
Monks, I recall consuming only a single jujube fruit as my sole meal."
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that the raft at that time was larger;
however, it should not be viewed in this way.
Indeed, the raft at that time was exactly this much."
Monks, as I took only a single jujube fruit as food and no second, my body became exceedingly emaciated and weak.
Monks, it was just like the joints of the *āsītakī* plant or the joints of the *kālā* plant;
even so were my limbs and members.
Just as the ribs of a crab,
even so were my ribs;
just as in a dilapidated carriage shed or an elephant stable, with both sides open, the rafters appear and shine forth from within.
In the same way, my ribs shone and radiated light on both sides within my body.
Just as a bamboo pole in a workshop is uneven, with its high and low parts,
so too was my spinal column uneven, with its high and low parts.

Just as a young bitter gourd, once harvested, becomes withered, shriveled, and covered in blisters, even so his head became withered, shriveled, and covered in blisters. Just as in the last month of summer, the stars in a well become distant and are only visible with great difficulty, [so too was his vision].
In the same way, my pupils became sunken and were revealed with great difficulty,
just like the hoofprint of a goat or a camel;
likewise, my armpits, belly, and chest became sunken.
Then, monks, when I thought, "I shall touch my belly with my hand," I touched only my backbone;
and though I made an effort, thinking, "I shall stand up," I fell forward just as before, face down.
Even when I had risen with great difficulty, as I rubbed my dust-covered limbs with my hands, the putrid hairs fell away from my body.
Even that former body of mine, which was of beautiful complexion, vanished, just as this [present body] is preeminent in its coarseness due to my self-exertion.
And the neighbors living in the villages within my range of activity perceived me thus: "Alas, the ascetic Gautama has become dark! Alas, the ascetic Gautama has become sallow!"
Alas, O friends, the ascetic Gautama has the complexion of a madgura fish!
That former, beautiful, radiant hue which he once possessed has vanished.
"Monks, this thought occurred to me: 'What if I were to practice with an even greater degree of moderation in food?
Monks, I recall taking only a single grain of rice as my sole meal, without a second.
Monks, you might think that the grain of rice at that time was larger."
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
Rather, at that time there was only this much rice.
Monks, as I was eating that single grain of rice, my body quickly became as described before, up until: "Alas, the ascetic Gautama has become like the color of a madgura fish!"
That former body of his, which was of auspicious complexion, has also vanished.
"Monks, this thought occurred to me: 'What if I were to practice eating even less food?
Monks, I recall that I took only a single sesame seed as my sole meal, without a second."
And so on,
until even his body of beautiful complexion had disappeared.

Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: "There are some ascetics and brahmins who believe that purity comes through abstaining from food; what if I were to practice total abstinence from food? Thereupon, monks, I remained without food.
Monks, because I was without food, my body became exceedingly dry, emaciated, and weak, just like the joints of an *āsītaki* plant or the joints of a *kālā* plant.
Consequently, my major and minor limbs became twice, three times, four times, five times, or even ten times more emaciated than before.
For example, the ribs are like the claws of a crab; the spinal column is like a braid of hair that has been doubled over in a carriage shed or along the side of a roof-beam;
and the skull is like a bitter gourd.
"O monks, my two pupils were like the pupils of a well;
as I was exerting my limbs with the thought, 'I shall rise up properly,' I fell down face-downward.
Even when I had risen with great difficulty and was wiping my dust-covered limbs, my hair, rotten at the roots, fell away."
That beautiful complexion and radiance which I once possessed also vanished,
just as it does for one whose self is intent upon harsh and austere practices.
And the people living in the villages within my range perceived me thus: "Alas, the ascetic Gautama is black! Alas, the ascetic Gautama is dark-complexioned!
Alas, the ascetic Gautama has the hue of a madgura fish!"
That former, auspicious appearance of his complexion which he once possessed has also vanished.
At that time, King Śuddhodana also sent a messenger to the presence of the Bodhisattva every single day.

Thus, monks, for the sake of demonstrating wonderful deeds to the world, as previously described, up until: for the sake of leading beings who have lost the practice of karma back to the practice of karma; for the sake of manifesting the accumulation of merit; for the sake of demonstrating the qualities of great wisdom; and for the sake of distinguishing the factors of meditative concentration, the Bodhisattva [lived] for six years on a single sesame seed, a single kola-fruit, and a single grain of rice.
He displayed himself as practicing austerities;
for six years, with an undepressed mind, the Bodhisattva remained seated just as he had sat down in the cross-legged posture, and he did not deviate from that mode of conduct.
He did not go from the sunlight into the shade, nor from the shade into the sunlight; he provided no protection against wind, sun, or rain, nor did he ward off gadflies, mosquitoes, or reptiles;
and he did not discharge excrement, urine, phlegm, or snot.
He did not perform the actions of contracting or extending [his limbs],
nor did he remain in a position with his side, belly, or back [pressed against anything].
And as for those great clouds— those of stormy weather, rain, thunderbolts, autumn, summer, and winter—
They too fell upon the body of the Bodhisattva;
yet, in the end, the Bodhisattva did not even shield himself with his hand,
nor did he close his sense faculties.
And he did not perceive the sense objects.
Furthermore, whatever village boys or village girls, cowherds, shepherds, grass-gatherers, wood-gatherers, or dung-collectors came there,
they thought the Bodhisattva was a dust-demon (pāṃśupiśāca).
And they played with him,
and they smeared him with dust.

There, during those six years, the Bodhisattva’s body became so emaciated, worn down, and weak that a blade of grass or a tuft of cotton, when inserted into his ear canals, would emerge from his nostrils;
and when inserted into his nostrils, it would emerge from his ear canals.
It was being expelled;
having been inserted through the ear canals, it was expelled through the opening of the mouth;
having been inserted through the opening of the mouth, it was expelled through the ear canals and the nostrils.
Having been cast into the nose, it was expelled through the openings of the ears, nose, and mouth.

And those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who had direct perception of the Bodhisattva’s virtues, empowered themselves day and night and performed worship of the Bodhisattva,
and they also made aspirational prayers.
There, while the Bodhisattva was demonstrating his practice of austerities for those six years, twelve full *nayutas* of gods and humans were brought to maturity by means of the three vehicles.
Regarding this, it is said:
"And of that virtuous Bodhisattva, who had gone forth from the city..."
His reflection, joined with skillful means, arose for the benefit and welfare of sentient beings.
In this world of the five corruptions, debased and inclined toward unrighteousness,
I have been born in Jambudvīpa, in a world where the performance of Dharma has become rare.
Crowded with throngs of heretics and filled with curious rites for good fortune,
these fools believe that purity is attained through such bodily mortifications.
Entering fire, leaping from cliffs, falling into pits, and smearing themselves with dust and ashes, they remain naked;
for the sake of tormenting the body, they are devoted to the practice of the five fires.
Some fools, lacking discernment regarding mantras, lick their hands;
they do not take [the food] from the mouth of the jar, nor from a skull-bowl, nor from the interior of a vessel that is not skillfully held.
And yet, where he does not experience [this] for himself, nor has it been established by him through his own speech, those who live on alms from noble families consider themselves pure. (Lal 17.16)
They avoid ghee and oil, molasses, curd, milk, fish, and meat;
they subsist on millet and vegetables, or consume lotus roots, *garḍula* stalks, and long pepper.
Subsisting on roots, fruits, and leaves, some wear garments of kusha grass, bark, or woolen blankets;
others wander about naked, deluded fools who think, "This alone is truth, everything else is delusion. (Lal 17.18)
They hold their hands aloft, with hair standing erect and matted locks;
utterly lost on the path, they stand upon a wrong path while desiring to go to a happy rebirth.
Some lay on beds of grass, clubs, or ashes; some slept on beds of thorns; some practiced meditation while squatting; and some stood on one foot, gazing upward at the moon and sun.
They pay homage to the dry land, the lakes, the ponds, the oceans, and the rivers; to the moon and the sun;
to the trees, the mountains, and the mountain peaks; and they bow to the jar and the earth.
Deluded and enveloped by false views, they purify their bodies through various means, yet they quickly fall into the lower realms. (Lal 17.22)
"What if I were now to undertake vows, austerities, and difficult practices that are formidable—difficult practices which cannot be performed even by gods or humans? (Lal 17.23)
And may I practice the *āsphānaka* meditation, the adamantine state that is firm like a kalpa;
a meditation which even the Pratyekabuddhas are not capable of demonstrating.
There are gods and humans here who rejoice in the coarse vows of the heterodox;
for the sake of bringing them to maturity, he undertook extremely intense vows and austerities that were difficult to perform.
Having assumed the cross-legged posture, he sat upon the bare ground;
he demonstrated the manner of taking food with jujube fruits, sesame seeds, and rice grains.
Free from inhalation and devoid of exhalation, the powerful one did not move;
for six years he meditated upon the supreme, all-pervading concentration (āsphānaka-dhyāna).

For an eon, he meditates on the "all-pervading" meditation, which is without conceptualization, without discursive thought, without movement, nor any activity through another; it is a pervasion of the realm of space.
Moving from the sunlight into the shade, yet not from the shade back into the sunlight,
he remained as unshakable as Mount Meru and meditated upon the "all-pervading" concentration (*āsphānaka-dhyāna*).
Having no shelter against wind and rain, nor protection from gadflies, mosquitoes, and reptiles,
he meditates upon the all-encompassing absorption (*āsphānaka-dhyāna*) with unshakable conduct.
And he does not meditate on the all-pervading meditation (āsphānaka-dhyāna) solely for his own sake;
rather, with a compassionate heart, he practices it for the vast benefit of the world.
The village boys, cowherds, wood-gatherers,
and grass-cutters regarded him as a dust-demon and smeared him with dust.
They showered him with various impurities and subjected him to diverse tortures;
yet he did not stir or waver, but remained absorbed in the immovable meditation (*āsphānaka-dhyāna*).
He neither bends nor stoops, nor does he touch his body for protection;
he has no need for excrement or urine, and among sounds he is not startled, nor does he look about at others.
The flesh and blood were completely dried up, and only skin, sinews, and bones remained;
from the belly, the backbone was visible like a twisted braid of hair.
Those gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas who have performed their duties pay homage day and night to him who possesses manifest virtues.
And they make this vow: "May we also quickly become like him, just as this Gaganacitta meditates upon the all-pervading meditation."
And he will not act for his own sake alone, nor out of a relish for meditation, nor with the thought of mere pleasure;
rather, out of a mind of compassion, he will accomplish vast benefit for the world.
The doctrines of others have been defeated; the heretics, devoid of wisdom, have been eclipsed. And the performance of karma has been demonstrated, as it was proclaimed by the words of Kāśyapa.
The enlightenment of Krakucchanda is very difficult to attain here even over many eons;
for the sake of the people, he meditates upon the immovable meditation (*āsphānaka-dhyāna*).
Twelve full *niyutas* of gods and humans were disciplined by means of the three vehicles;
with this in mind, O Sumati, he meditated on the *āsphānaka* meditation.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Chapter on the Practice of Austerities."
START Chapter 18 (Vaidya 191):
The Eighteenth Chapter, "The Nairañjanā."

And, monks, Māra the Evil One followed closely behind the Bodhisattva for six years while he was practicing austerities, watching for a lapse and seeking an opportunity; yet he never found any lapse whatsoever. Failing to find such an opportunity, he departed despondent and full of regret.
In this regard, it is said: Delightful are the forests, the groves, and the shrubs, To the east of Urubilvā, where the river Nairañjanā flows. (Lal 18.1)
There he was constantly exerting himself for the sake of abandonment, with firm prowess,
striving with vigor to attain security and well-being.
Speaking sweet words, Namuci approached him and said:
"Son of the Śākyas, arise! What is the use of this exhaustion of your body?"
Life is better for one who lives; while living, you shall practice the Dharma.
