For it is while alive that one performs those deeds by doing which one does not grieve.
"You are emaciated, discolored, and dejected; death is near for you.
Death shall occupy a thousand parts, while life remains but a single part."
"For one who constantly gives gifts and offers the fire-sacrifice, there will be great merit; what will you achieve by renunciation? *Lalita-vistara* 18.6.
"Suffering is the path; the restraint of the mind is difficult to accomplish"—at that time, Māra spoke these words to the Bodhisattva.
To Māra, who was speaking thus, the Bodhisattva then said:
"O Evil One, friend of the heedless, you have come here for your own sake."
"O Māra, I have no need for even an atom's worth of merit.
You should speak in this manner only to those who have a need for merit."
I do not consider death to be [the end], for life indeed ends in death;
I shall remain irreversible, devoted solely to the holy life.
For this wind could dry up even the currents of the rivers;
how much more would it dry up the blood of those who have directed their minds toward the body?
When the blood has indeed dried up, then the flesh withers;
as the flesh wastes away, the mind becomes further clarified.
Furthermore, zeal, vigor, and meditative concentration remain steadfast.
As I dwell thus, having attained supreme consciousness, my mind does not regard the body; behold the purity of a being!
I possess desire, as well as vigor, and wisdom is also found in me;
I see no one in the world who could shake me from my vigor.
Death that takes away life is better; fie upon a vulgar existence! Death in battle is better than a life lived as a vanquished man. (Lal 18.15)
"One who is not a hero does not conquer an army, nor, having conquered it, does he take pride in it;
but the hero conquers the army. O Māra, I shall quickly conquer yours. (Lal 18.16)
Sensual desires are your first army; likewise, discontent is the second;
hunger and thirst are your third, and craving is your fourth army.
The fifth is sloth and torpor; the sixth is declared to be fear;
the seventh is doubt for you; and the eighth is anger and hypocrisy.
Greed, flattery, and the mental formations [of pride], as well as fame acquired through falsehood; whoever exalts himself and whoever indeed disparages others. (Lal 18.19)
For this is the army of Namuci, the powerful kinsman of Darkness;
these ascetics and brahmins are seen to have plunged into it.
That army of yours which assails this world together with its gods, I shall shatter it with my wisdom, like an unbaked clay vessel with water. (Lal 18.21)
Having established mindfulness well and having thoroughly cultivated wisdom, I shall proceed with full awareness; what will you do, O evil-minded one?
When this was said, Māra the Evil One, suffering, dejected, displeased, and full of remorse, vanished right there.

Then, monks, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "Whatever ascetics or brahmins, in the past, future, or present times, experience painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations that involve self-inflicted violence and torment the body— they experience no suffering beyond this limit."

"Monks, this thought occurred to me: 'Indeed, by this conduct and by this practice, I have not realized any superhuman state, any excellence of noble knowledge and vision; this is not the path to enlightenment.'"
"This path does not lead to the cessation of the occurrence of birth, aging, and death in the future.
There must be another path for the cessation of the arising of the suffering of birth, aging, and death in the future, which leads to awakening."

Then, monks, this occurred to me: "When I sat in the shade of a rose-apple tree in my father’s park, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion; and so on, up to entering and dwelling in the fourth dhyāna."
"Could that be the path to awakening, for the non-arising and the subsiding of the mass of suffering consisting of birth, old age, and death?
And my consciousness followed after that thought:
"That is the path to awakening."
Then this thought occurred to me: "That path cannot be fully realized by one who has reached such a state of weakness.

If, however, I were to approach the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) while my body is still emaciated and weak, merely through the power of the knowledge of supernormal faculties, I would not be showing compassion for future generations."
"And this is not the path to awakening;
what if I were to take solid food, generate strength and vigor for my body, and only then approach the seat of awakening?"

Thereupon, monks, those sons of the gods who were inclined toward the coarse, having understood with their own minds the reflection in my mind, approached me and said this to me: "O noble being, do not take solid food;
we shall infuse vitality into you through the pores of your skin."

Monks, this occurred to me: "I indeed profess to myself that I am fasting, yet the people living in the surrounding villages where I go for alms perceive me as such, thinking, 'The ascetic Gautama is fasting.
Thus, sons of the gods who were devoted to austerity were infusing vital energy into me through my pores."
"That would be a supreme falsehood for me.
Thereupon, in order to avoid speaking a falsehood, the Bodhisattva rejected those sons of the gods and directed his mind toward taking solid food.

Thus, monks, having completed the ascetic practices of his six-year vow, the Bodhisattva rose from that seat and uttered these words: "I shall partake of substantial food," namely, parched flour, mung-bean soup, pea soup, and boiled rice with sour gruel.

Then, monks, this thought occurred to the group of five auspicious ones: "Even by that practice and even by that path, the ascetic Gautama was not able to realize any superhuman state, any distinction in noble knowledge and vision;
how much less so now, as he dwells consuming substantial food and devoted to the pursuit of pleasure?"
Thinking, "This boy is unrefined," they departed from the presence of the Bodhisattva;
having gone to Vārāṇasī, they took up residence in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.

There, while the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities from the very beginning, ten young daughters of village headmen approached him for the purpose of seeing, saluting, and attending upon him. He was also attended by those five companions of the auspicious group,
through their offerings of a single jujube fruit, sesame seed, and grain of rice.
And he was instructed [in this way].
There were also the daughters of village headmen named Balā, Balaguptā, Supriyā, Vijayasenā, Atimuktakamalā, Sundarī, Kumbhakārī, Uluvillikā, Jaṭilikā, and Sujātā.
All those various kinds of broth were prepared by these young girls and offered to the Bodhisattva.
Having consumed them, the Bodhisattva gradually became endowed with excellent complexion, form, and strength as he wandered for alms in the village of Gocara.
Because of that, they called the Bodhisattva "the handsome ascetic" and "the great ascetic."
And there, monks, Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman, from the very beginning while the Bodhisattva was practicing his difficult austerities,
fed eight hundred Brahmins every day for the sake of bringing him out of his vows and penances, and for the purpose of nourishing his body.
And he made this aspiration: "May the Bodhisattva, having eaten my food, awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Monks, when six years had passed for me, my saffron-colored robes had become completely worn out.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: "If I were to obtain something to cover my private parts, it would be excellent."
Furthermore, monks, at that time the maidservant of Sujātā, the village headman’s daughter, named Rādhā, passed away.
She was wrapped in hempen cloths, carried out to the cemetery, and abandoned there.
It was I myself who saw that rag-robe.
Then, having stepped upon that rag-robe with my left foot and extended my right hand, I bent down to take it up.
Thereupon, the gods of the earth caused a cry to resound among the gods of the intermediate space: "A marvel, friends! A wonder, friends!
That the mind of one born into such a great royal family, who has renounced the sovereignty of a universal monarch, should be inclined toward a rag-robe!"
The gods of the intermediate space, having heard the sound of the terrestrial gods, raised a cry to the gods of the Four Great Kings;
the gods of the Four Great Kings [raised it] to the Trāyastriṃśa gods;
and the Trāyastriṃśa gods [raised it] to the Yāma gods.
The Yāma gods [are the retinue] of the Tuṣita gods;
the Tuṣita gods [are the retinue] of the Nirmāṇarati gods;
the Nirmāṇarati gods [are the retinue] of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.

"From the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods up to the Brahmakāyika gods—thus, monks, at that very moment, at that very instant, at that very second, a single sound, a single resonance, arose as far as the Akaniṣṭha realm: ‘O friends, this is marvelous! This is extraordinary!
That one born of such a great royal lineage, having renounced the sovereignty of a universal monarch, should incline his heart toward a rag from a dust-heap!’"
Then it occurred again to the Bodhisattva: "I have obtained this rag from a dust-heap;
if I could obtain water, it would be excellent."
Then, right there, the deity struck the earth with her hand;
a lotus pond appeared there,
and even today that pond is known by the name Pāṇihata.
Again, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "I have obtained water; if only I could find a stone upon which I might wash this rag-robe."
"That would be excellent.
Then, at that very moment, Śakra deposited a rock right there.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva washed that rag-robe.
Then Śakra, the king of the gods, said this to the Bodhisattva: "O noble being, give this to me;
I shall wash it.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, in order to demonstrate that his renunciation was performed by his own hand, did not give that rag-robe to Śakra, but washed it himself.
Exhausted and with a weary body, he descended [to the water] thinking, "I shall cross over to the lotus pond.
Then Māra, the Evil One,
overcome by the nature of envy, manifested the banks of the lotus pond as being exceedingly high.
And on the bank of that lotus pond stood a great *kukubha* tree.
There, the Bodhisattva, in conformity with worldly custom and for the sake of favoring the deity, spoke to the goddess: "O goddess, bring down a branch of the tree.
By her, a branch of the tree was brought down.
The Bodhisattva took hold of it and crossed over;
having crossed, he spread out that rag-robe beneath that *kakubha* tree and sewed it together as a double-layered outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*).
Even today, that rag-robe is known by the name "the Sewing."
Then a son of the gods named Vimalaprabha, belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host,

presented to the Bodhisattva divine robes dyed with the color of saffron, which were suitable, appropriate for a recluse, and in keeping with the appearance of a śramaṇa. Having accepted them, the Bodhisattva dressed himself in the forenoon, put on his outer robe, and set out toward the village where he was to seek alms.

There, at the hour of midnight, the deities announced to Sujātā, the daughter of Nandika the village headman in the village of Urubilvāsenāpati: "He for whose sake you perform this great sacrifice has emerged from his vow;
that fortunate one will partake of substantial food."
And you previously made this vow: "Having eaten my food, may the Bodhisattva awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Do now whatever must be done by you.

Then, monks, Sujātā, the daughter of the village of Nandika, having heard those words of the deities, quickly took the foremost, most potent essence— the cream— from the milk of a thousand cows that had been repeatedly skimmed seven times.
Having taken that fresh milk, she...
Having smeared a new hearth, he prepared that meal in a new pot using fresh rice grains.
While it was being cooked, these preliminary signs appeared: in that very milk, auspicious marks such as the śrīvatsa, svastika, nandyāvarta, lotus, and vardhamāna became visible.

Then this thought occurred to her: "From the way these preliminary signs are appearing, there is no doubt that after eating this food, the Bodhisattva will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that moment, a fortune-teller skilled in the methods of maritime knowledge arrived at that place.
He, too, likewise prophesied the attainment of the Deathless itself.

Then Sujātā, having cooked that milk-rice, smeared a level spot of ground, scattered flowers over it, sprinkled it with scented water, and prepared a seat, honored him and addressed her maidservant named Uttarā:
"Go, Uttarā, and bring the brahmin."
"I shall look for this honeyed milk-rice.
Having assented with "Very well, Noble One," Uttarā went toward the eastern direction.
There she saw the Bodhisattva.
In the same way,
he saw only the Bodhisattva in the south;
likewise, he went toward the western and northern directions as well.
In each instance, he saw only the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, at that time, all the followers of other sects had been subdued by the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm;
not a single one of them was to be seen.
Then, having returned, she said this to her mistress: "Indeed, Noble Lady, no other ascetic or brahmin is seen;
wherever I go, there I see only the handsome ascetic."
Sujātā said: "Go, Uttara; he is that very brahmin, he is that very śramaṇa.
It was for his sake alone that this undertaking was begun."
"Bring him here. "Very well, noble lady," said Uttarā; she went and, prostrating at the feet of the Bodhisattva, invited him by the name of Sujātā.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva went to the residence of Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman, and sat down on the seat that had been prepared for him.
Then, monks, Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman, offered to the Bodhisattva a golden bowl filled with honeyed milk-rice.

Then this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "Since Sujātā has offered me such food as this, there is no doubt that today, having eaten this meal, I shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Then the Bodhisattva, having accepted that food, said this to Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman: "Sister, here is this golden bowl; what shall be done with it?
She replied, "Let it remain yours alone."
The Bodhisattva said, "I have no need for such a vessel.
Sujātā said, "Do as you wish;
however, I do not give food to anyone without a vessel."
Then the Bodhisattva, taking that alms-bowl, departed from Uruvilvā and, at the time of forenoon,
approached the river Nairañjanā. Having set down that alms-bowl and his robes in a secluded spot, he descended into the river Nairañjanā to cool his limbs.
Furthermore, monks, while the Bodhisattva was bathing, many hundreds of thousands of sons of gods stirred the river with divine powders and ointments of aloe-wood and sandalwood,
and they scattered various kinds of divine flowers of many colors into the water— that is to say, as an act of worship for the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, at that time, the river Nairañjanā flowed filled with divine perfumes and flowers.

And hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sons of gods took up that scented water with which the Bodhisattva had bathed and carried it to their respective abodes for the sake of shrines and for worship.
And whatever hair and beard the Bodhisattva had, Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman, took them all for the sake of a shrine and for the sake of worship, considering them to be auspicious.
Having crossed the river, the Bodhisattva looked toward the sandy bank, desiring to sit down.
Then, the Naga maiden who dwelt in the Nairañjanā River rose from the surface of the earth and presented a beautiful, jewel-encrusted throne to the Bodhisattva.
There the Bodhisattva sat down and, out of compassion for Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman, partook of that honeyed milk-rice as much as he required.
Having eaten, he cast the golden bowl into the water without regard for it.
As soon as it was thrown in, Sāgara, the king of the nāgas, filled with affection and great respect, thinking, "This is worthy of worship," took it and set out toward his own abode.
Then Purandara, the thousand-eyed one, having manifested the form of Garuḍa and become one with a vajra-beak, began to seize that golden vessel from the presence of Sāgara, the king of the nāgas.
When he was unable to do so,
he then respectfully entreated him in his own form and led [the vessel] to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven for the purpose of worship and for the sake of a reliquary monument (caitya).
Having brought it back, he inaugurated the festival known as the *pātrīyātrā* on the day of the full moon;
even today, among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the *pātrī-mahotsava* is celebrated annually.
Furthermore, that auspicious throne (*bhadrāsana*) was taken up by that very Naga maiden for the sake of a shrine and for worship.
Monks, when the Bodhisattva had fully consumed that substantial food,
at that very moment, through the power of his merit and the power of his wisdom, the former beautiful complexion and lotus-like radiance of his body reappeared.

The thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty secondary characteristics, and the fathom-wide aura: regarding this, it is said— Having completed the six-year vow, the Blessed One reflected thus in his mind: "I possess the power of meditative concentration, supernormal knowledge, and wisdom; even though my body is thus emaciated,"
I would go to the branches at the foot of the king of trees to awaken to omniscience; for if I were not to have compassion for the people, this would be my final existence.
Having consumed this excellent, abundant food, may I strengthen my body and go to the foot of the king of trees to awaken to omniscience;
lest gods and men of meager merit, seeing knowledge through such austerity, be unable to awaken, their bodies too weak to realize the Deathless.
And that village girl, Sujātā by name, who had practiced her former conduct and was constantly performing sacrifices, thus resolved in her mind upon the vow for the Leader:
"Having observed the exhortation of the gods, I shall then take home the honeyed milk-rice."
Having approached the bank of the Nairañjanā river, she stood there with a joyful mind.
Having practiced his conduct for a thousand eons, with his faculties stilled and perfectly tranquil, he—
having crossed over himself and being capable of ferrying others across, wise and intent on bathing— approached the Nairañjanā River surrounded by gods, hosts of nāgas, and sages.
Having descended and bathed in the river, the sage, compassionate toward the world, became pure and stainless.
Thousands of millions of gods, with joyful minds, descended and stirred the water with perfumed waters and powders for the sake of bathing the Supreme Being.
Having bathed, the stainless Bodhisattva stood upon the bank, gentle and serene.
Thousands of gods rejoiced at the bathing water for the sake of worshipping the Supreme Being.
The sons of the gods gave him spotless, beautiful, and suitable saffron robes; having put them on, the Blessed One stood upon the bank of the river.
Then the daughter of the Naga, her heart uplifted and joyful, offered him a noble seat.
There he sat down, his mind at peace, bringing sight to the world.
Having given the food from a golden vessel, that wise and well-born woman,
being delighted, bowed at his feet and said: "O charioteer, please partake of my meal."
Having eaten as much food as he required, the wise one washed that bowl in the water;
Purandara, the preceptor of the gods, seized it, thinking, "I shall perform worship with this."
When the Jina had consumed that excellent, substantial meal, at that very moment his physical strength, splendor, and majesty were restored exactly as they had been before.
Having delivered a discourse on the Dharma to Sujāta and having accomplished great benefit for the gods, he remained there.
Having the gait of a lion, the stride of a swan, and the movement of a lordly elephant, he stood at the Bodhi tree.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Chapter on the Nairañjanā."
START Chapter 19 (Vaidya 199):
The Nineteenth Chapter, "The Departure for the Seat of Enlightenment" (Bodhimaṇḍagamanaparivarta).

Thus, monks, having bathed in the river Nairañjanā and eaten, the Bodhisattva generated physical strength and vigor, and set out with a victorious gait toward the foot of the great king of trees, the Bodhi tree, at that spot on earth endowed with sixteen characteristics.

That which is the gait of the Great Beings— the gait that does not waver, the gait that is not drawn by the senses, the well-established gait, the gait like the king of mountains, the straight gait, the non-crooked gait, the unassailed gait, the unhurried gait, the undisturbed gait, the unfaltering gait, the unclashing gait, the non-attached gait, the non-fickle gait,

the graceful gait, the stainless gait, the auspicious gait, the faultless gait, the delusion-free gait, the passion-free gait, the lion’s gait, the gait of the king of swans, the gait of the king of elephants, and the gait of Nārāyaṇa.

His gait does not touch the surface of the earth; his movement upon the ground is as variegated as a thousand-spoked wheel; his gait is characterized by webbed fingers and copper-colored nails; his movement causes a resonant sound upon the surface of the earth; his stride is like the collision of the king of mountains; his feet and hands are level whether on high ground or in low places; his gait touches beings with rays of light emitted from between the webs of his fingers, leading them to happy rebirths; and his stride is the setting down of his steps upon pure lotuses.

The gait that proceeds from former virtuous and well-performed conduct; the gait of approaching the lions that were former Buddhas; the gait of an adamantine, firm, and indivisible intention; the gait of all skillful means;

the gait that closes off all states of woe and miserable rebirths; the gait that generates happiness for all sentient beings; the gait that reveals the path to liberation; the gait that renders the power of Māra powerless; the gait that suppresses through the Dharma the assemblies of bad factions and rival disputants; the gait that disperses the mass of darkness that is the afflictions; the gait that renders the side of saṃsāra powerless; and the gait that surpasses Śakra, Brahmā, Maheśvara, and the world-protectors.

He possessed the gait of a solitary hero throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system; the self-arisen, unconquerable gait; the gait of attaining the knowledge of the omniscient one;

the gait of mindfulness and intelligence; the gait of proceeding toward a happy rebirth; the gait that pacifies aging and death; and the gait leading to the city of Nirvana—auspicious, stainless, pure, and fearless.
With such a gait, the Bodhisattva set out for the seat of awakening.
Thus, monks, from the river Nairañjanā as far as the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), the area in between was swept clean by the sons of gods who were wind-clouds;
it was sprinkled with perfumed water by the sons of gods who were rain-clouds, and strewn with flowers.
Furthermore, all the trees throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system bent their tops toward the seat of awakening.
Even the young girls born on that day slept with their heads toward the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
Furthermore, all the mountains in this great trichiliocosm, headed by Mount Sumeru, bowed down toward where the seat of awakening was located.
And from the Nairañjanā River as far as the seat of awakening, a path one krośa in width was prepared in that interval by the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire.
On both the left and right sides of that path, an altar made of the seven precious gems was constructed.

It was seven palm trees in height and covered above with a net of jewels, adorned with divine parasols, banners, and flags. Within the range of an arrow-shot, seven palm trees made of the seven precious gems were manifested, rising up from that altar.
And from every palm tree, a jeweled cord hung down to the second palm tree;

and between every two palm trees, a lotus pond was constructed, filled with scented water, strewn with golden sand, covered with blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses, surrounded by jeweled railings, and provided with steps made of beryl and precious gems.
Resounding with the cries of cranes, herons, swans, ruddy geese, and peacocks,
eighty thousand apsarases sprinkled that path with scented water;
eighty thousand apsarases scattered loose flowers, divine and fragrant, upon it.
In front of every palm tree, a jeweled canopy was established.
Within each jeweled canopy, eighty thousand apsarases stood, holding caskets of sandalwood and agallochum powder and carrying incense burners that emitted fragrant smoke following the wind.
Within each jeweled canopy, five thousand apsarases stood, performing divine musical concerts.
Thus, monks, while the world-systems were trembling, the Bodhisattva emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays of light; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded,
a great rain rich with flowers fell, and hundreds of thousands of celestial garments fluttered about.
With hundreds of thousands of drums being beaten;
with horses, elephants, and bulls roaring and thundering;
and with hundreds of thousands of parrots, mainas, cuckoos, sparrows, jīvaṃjīvaka birds, swans, cranes, peacocks, and ruddy geese circumambulating [the Buddha].
With hundreds of thousands of auspicious offerings being presented,
the Bodhisattva proceeded toward the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) by means of such an array of the path.
And on the very night that the Bodhisattva became desirous of fully awakening to enlightenment,

On that very night, the Brahmā named Vaśavartin, the lord of the great trichiliocosm and the sovereign of the Sahā world, addressed the assembly of Brahmās and said: "O worthy ones, you should know this: this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has donned the great armor; he has not relinquished his great vow; he is clad in firm armor; his mind is untiring; he has emerged victorious in all the practices of a Bodhisattva; he has reached the further shore in all the perfections (pāramitās); and he has traversed all the stages (bhūmis) of a Bodhisattva."

Having attained mastery, his intention is perfectly purified like that of all bodhisattvas; he has entered into accordance with the faculties of all sentient beings, has thoroughly entered all the secret places of the Tathāgatas, and has completely transcended all paths of Māra’s activity. Not dependent on others regarding any roots of virtue, he is empowered by all the Tathāgatas;
as a great caravan leader, he teaches the path of liberation to all sentient beings.
He is the destroyer of the entire mandala of Māra, the sole hero of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system;
he is the Great King of Physicians, who has brought forth the medicine of all dharmas;
he is the Great King of Dharma, bound with the turban of liberation.

He is the one who emits the light of great wisdom, the great king of banners, unstained by the eight worldly dharmas, become like a great lotus, never forgetting any of the dhāraṇīs of all dharmas, become like a great ocean, free from attraction and aversion, immovable and unshakable, become like Mount Sumeru, perfectly stainless, thoroughly pure, possessing a stainless intellect as firm as a diamond, become like a great precious jewel, and having mastery over all dharmas.

With a mind made entirely pliant, the Bodhisattva, having become like Great Brahmā, approaches the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), desiring to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening in order to overwhelm the armies of Māra;
for the sake of fulfilling the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and for the sake of setting in motion the great wheel of Dharma.

For the purpose of uttering the great lion’s roar; for the purpose of satisfying all sentient beings with the gift of Dharma; for the purpose of purifying the Dharma-eye of all sentient beings; for the purpose of refuting all opposing disputants in accordance with the Dharma; for the purpose of demonstrating the fulfillment of his previous vow;
and for the purpose of attaining mastery and sovereignty over all phenomena.
"In this matter, friends, you all must be eager to perform acts of worship and service for the Bodhisattva.
Then, at that time, the Great Brahmā Vaśavartin spoke this verse:
"By whose splendor, merit, and glory the Brahma-path is known—namely, loving-kindness, compassion, equanimity, sympathetic joy, as well as the meditative concentrations and the superknowledges."
He, who has practiced his conduct for a thousand eons and has now set out toward the tree of awakening—
perform well the worship of that Sage, who is established in his auspicious vow!
Having gone for refuge to whom, one encounters neither the fear of miserable rebirths nor the lack of leisure;
and having attained vast, desired happiness among the gods, one goes to the abode of Brahmā.
Having practiced the difficult austerities for six years, he proceeds to the tree of awakening.
Excellent! All of us, with uplifted and joyful minds, shall perform worship for him.
This king is the supreme lord of the triple-thousandfold world system, a sovereign of the Dharma and a ruler of the earth;
in the realms of Śakra and Brahmā, and among the sun and moon, there is no one equal to him.
At his birth, billions of nayutas of fields trembled in six ways.
This very one today proceeds toward the excellent great tree to conquer the armies of Māra.
The crown of whose head cannot be seen even by those dwelling here in the abode of Brahmā;
whose body bears the most excellent primary marks and is adorned with the thirty-two [secondary marks];
whose speech here is charming, elegant, sweet, possessing the voice of Brahmā, and melodious.
His mind is perfectly tranquil and free from defects; let us go to worship him.
Or those whose minds desire to spend eternal happiness in the abodes of Brahmā and Śakra,
or rather, to sever that ensnaring creeper of all the bonds of affliction—
may I, without hearing it from another, realize the deathless and auspicious state of Pratyekabuddhahood.
If Buddhahood is desired, let him worship this Leader throughout the three worlds.
By him the earth, together with the oceans, was renounced— along with infinite jewels,
as well as palaces with their windows, turrets, and balconies, and various vehicles and carriages; and the beautiful gardens, wells, and lakes, adorned with the earth and garlands of flowers.
With his hands, feet, head, and excellent eyes, he was directed toward the seat of awakening.
Thus, monks, at that very moment, Mahābrahmā of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system established this triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system in perfect evenness.

It became like the palm of a hand, free from pebbles and gravel, abounding in jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, and soft blue *kuṇḍala* grass, which was right-spiraling, curling to the right, as soft to the touch as *kācilindika* cloth, and covered with such grass.
He stood pervading the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system;
at that time, all the great oceans were situated upon the surface of the earth,
and there was no harm whatsoever to the beings who dwell in the water.

Having seen this very world-system thus adorned, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors in the ten directions, for the purpose of honoring the Bodhisattva, made hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields beautifully adorned;

and by means of celestial and human offerings that surpassed [the mundane], immeasurable Buddha-fields in the ten directions were likewise embellished by Bodhisattvas for the purpose of honoring the Bodhisattva.
And all those buddha-fields appeared as if they were a single buddha-field,
adorned with various magnificent arrays; furthermore,
no more world-intervals, nor black mountains, nor the Cakravāla and Mahācakravāla mountain ranges were perceived.
And all those buddha-fields were seen to be filled with the light of that bodhisattva.
Also present were sixteen sons of gods who protect the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), namely:
the son of god named Utkhalī, the son of god named Sūtkhalī, Prajāpati, Śūrabala, and Keyūrabala.
Supratiṣṭhita, Mahīndhara, Avabhāsakara, Vimala, Dharmeśvara, Dharmaketu, Siddhapātra, Apratihatanetra, Mahāvyūha, Śīlaviśuddhanetra, and Padmaprabha—

these sixteen sons of the gods who protect the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), all of whom had attained irreversible patience (avaivartikakṣānti), adorned the seat of awakening for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva.
Extending eighty *yojanas* on all sides, it was surrounded by seven jeweled railings, seven rows of palm trees, seven nets of jeweled bells, and seven jeweled cords;

it was strewn with cloths of Jāmbūnada gold inlaid with the seven precious gems, with golden threads, and with Jāmbūnada gold lotuses, perfumed with the finest essential incense, and covered by a canopy of jewel nets.

And whatever various trees there were in the diverse world-systems throughout the ten directions—those born of noble lineage and honored by gods and humans—all of them appeared there at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
And whatever kinds of flowers, whether grown in water or on land, there were in the ten directions, all of those also appeared there at the seat of awakening.

Furthermore, whatever bodhisattvas in the diverse world-systems throughout the ten directions were adorning the seat of awakening with arrays of immeasurable accumulations of merit and wisdom, they too appeared there at the seat of awakening.
[They] were.
Thus, monks, such arrays were manifested by the sons of the gods who protect the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa),
upon seeing which the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras conceived the perception of their own palaces as charnel grounds;
and having seen those arrays, they felt an exceeding sense of wonder.
And they uttered this inspired utterance: "Excellent indeed! How inconceivable is the outflow of the ripening of merit!
And there were four deities of the Bodhi tree, namely:
Veṇu, Valgu, Sumana, and Ojāpati.

These four deities of the Bodhi tree constructed the Bodhi tree for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva; it was endowed with a perfect root, a perfect trunk, and perfect branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; it was perfect in its height and circumference, beautiful, lovely to behold, and vast, eighty *tāla* trees in height and proportionate in circumference, variegated and pleasing to the sight.

It was enchanting, surrounded by seven railings of jewels, seven rows of jewel-palm trees, seven nets of jewel-bells, and encircled on all sides by seven strings of jewels; it was as radiant as the *pārijātaka* and *kovidāra* trees, a sight for which one could never tire of looking.

And that spot of earth became firm and solid, composed of indestructible diamond, as hard as the vajra of the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, where the Bodhisattva sat down, desiring to fully awaken to enlightenment.

Thus, monks, as the Bodhisattva was approaching the seat of awakening, such a radiance was emitted from his body that by that radiance all states of woe were pacified and all unfavorable conditions were closed off.
The sensations of all miserable rebirths were dried up as he experienced them;
and those beings who had been deficient in their faculties all attained the perfection of their faculties.
Those who were afflicted by diseases were liberated from their ailments;
those tormented by fear attained consolation;
and those bound in fetters were released from their bonds.
Poor beings became possessed of wealth;
those tormented by afflictions became free from burning anguish;
and hungry beings had their bellies filled.
Those who were thirsty became free from thirst;
those who were pregnant gave birth with ease;
and those who were aged and weak became endowed with strength.

At that time, no sentient being was afflicted by passion, nor hatred, nor delusion, nor anger, nor greed, nor stubbornness, nor malice, nor envy, nor stinginess. At that time, no sentient being died, nor did anyone pass away.
It was not possible [for them to harm one another];
and at that time, all sentient beings possessed minds of loving-kindness and minds of benefit, regarding one another as mothers and fathers.
In this regard, it is said:
As far as the hells of terrifying appearance reaching down to the Avīci hell,
the suffering of sentient beings was stilled and they experienced a feeling of bliss.
O Great Sage, as many beings as there are among the animal births who were mutually destructive have become intent on welfare with minds of loving-kindness, touched by your rays of light.
As many hungry ghosts as there are in the realms of the pretas, who are tormented by hunger and thirst,
they obtain food and drink through the majestic power of the Bodhisattva.
All unfavorable conditions have been closed off and the miserable realms have been dried up;
all sentient beings are happy, endowed with celestial bliss.
Those who were deprived of sight or hearing, and others whose faculties were impaired,
were born with all their senses fully complete and beautiful in every limb.
Those beings who were always oppressed by the afflictions such as passion and hatred all then became free from afflictions and were endowed with happiness.
The insane became possessed of mindfulness, the poor became wealthy,
the diseased were freed from illness, and those bound in fetters were liberated.
At that time, they were established in minds of loving-kindness; they harbored no stubbornness, nor stinginess, nor malice, nor did they engage in mutual strife.
Just as love arises for a mother and father toward an only son,
so then did the love of children arise among beings for one another.
Indeed, inconceivable realms, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, throughout all ten directions, were suffused by the networks of light from the Bodhisattva.
No longer are the Cakravāla mountains or the Kāla mountains seen;
all those vast fields appear as if they were one.
All the buddha-fields were adorned for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva, appearing as bright as the palm of a hand and filled with every kind of jewel.
And sixteen gods likewise, who attend upon the seat of awakening,
adorned the bodhimaṇḍa for an extent of eighty yojanas.
And whatever infinite great arrays there are in millions of fields,
they all appear there by the splendor of the Bodhisattva.
The gods, nāgas, yakṣas, kinnaras,
and mahoragas regarded their own celestial mansions as if they were cremation grounds.
Beholding those military arrays here, gods and men were struck with wonder: "Excellent!
This is the outflow of merit; such is the perfection of his fortune."
He does not exert any effort whatsoever through body, speech, or mind;
yet all his goals, those desired aspirations of his heart, are accomplished.
Just as the intentions of others were fulfilled by him in the past through his conduct,
such is the ripening of that karma that has now come to fruition.
The seat of awakening was adorned by the four deities of awakening;
it excelled even the Pārijāta tree in heaven.
All those qualities cannot be fully proclaimed by speech—
the magnificent arrays of the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) that have been fashioned by the deities.

Thus, monks, by that radiance emitted from the body of the Bodhisattva, the palace of the Naga king Kālika was illuminated— a radiance that was pure and stainless, producing refreshment and exhilaration for body and mind, removing all afflictions, and generating happiness, joy, serenity, and gladness for all sentient beings.
And having seen this, at that moment the Naga king Kālika stood before his own retinue and spoke these verses:

"Just as the beautiful radiance was seen in Krakucchanda, and just as it was seen in the one named Kanaka, and just as the stainless light was seen in the sinless Dharma-king Kāśyapa; [so too is it now]."
Without doubt, one endowed with excellent marks, a benefactor, has arisen as the light of wisdom,
by whom this abode of mine shines forth, adorned with a golden radiance.
In this palace, the vast radiance of the moon and sun is not seen,
nor that of fire, nor of jewels, nor the stainless light of lightning, nor the brilliance of the stars;
neither the splendor of Śakra, nor the splendor of Brahmā, nor even the splendor of the Asuras is seen there.
My home was previously filled with total darkness due to my past evil deeds.
Today this auspicious palace shines brilliantly like the sun in its center;
it generates joy in the mind, the body is happy, and the limbs are wonderfully cool.
The hot sand that falls upon my body has become cool;
it is quite evident that he who has practiced for many millions of eons is proceeding toward the Bodhi tree.
Quickly take up the *nāgapuṣpa* flowers, the beautiful, fragrant, and auspicious garments, the pearl necklaces, the bracelets, the powders, and the finest incenses!
Perform songs and play various musical instruments, such as the auspicious kettledrums and clay drums!
Come then, go to the Benefactor, who is worthy of worship by all the world!
Having risen up together with the Naga maidens, he gazed toward the four directions;
then he beheld one who resembled Mount Meru, beautifully adorned with splendor,
surrounded by gods, tens of millions of Dānavas, as well as Brahmās, Indras, and Yakṣas.
With joyful minds they pay him honor, for they show that this is indeed the path.
For that king of nāgas was indeed thrilled and exceedingly joyful; having honored the Supreme among Men and bowed at his feet with reverence, he stood before the Sage.
The nāga maidens, their minds uplifted and delighted, performed worship for the Sage.
They scattered flowers, perfumes, and ointments, while sounding musical instruments.
Having joined his palms in reverence, the Naga king, greatly delighted, praised the virtuous one with truthful qualities:
"O you who possess a face like the full moon, O supreme leader of the world!
Just as those signs were seen by me previously through the ancient seers, so do I now behold them in you."
Today, having utterly defeated the forces of Māra, you shall attain the desired state.
For whose sake you were formerly a renunciant, practicing self-control, generosity, and restraint;
for whose sake you cultivated the power of self-control, virtuous conduct, loving-kindness, compassion, and patience;
and for whose sake you were devoted to self-control, vigor, and meditative concentration, and made the lamp of wisdom.
This very fulfillment of all your vows—today you shall become a Jina.
Just as trees with leaves, flowers, and fruit bow down toward the Bodhi tree;
just as thousands of jars filled with water perform a circumambulation;
and just as throngs of apsarases, greatly delighted, utter sweet sounds—
Just as flocks of swans and cranes move gracefully through the sky, those with joyful minds circumambulated the Sage; today you shall become one worthy of honor.
Or as a beautiful golden radiance spreads through hundreds of kṣatriyas,
so too do all lower realms become stilled, and all beings are liberated from sufferings.
Just as from the rain, the moon, or the sun, a gentle breeze blows today, so shall you become a caravan leader who liberates beings from birth and old age within the three worlds.
Just as the gods, having abandoned their delight in sensual pleasures, have come here to worship you—
Brahmā and the Brahmapurohita deities, and the immortals, having relinquished their meditative bliss—
all those who exist within the three realms, as well as those in the city, have likewise come here.
Today you shall become the King of Physicians, the liberator from birth and old age within the three worlds.
And the path by which you go today has been purified by the gods;
by this very path came the Blessed One Krakucchanda, the one named Kanaka, and Kāśyapa.
Just as pure, stainless, and beautiful lotuses, having burst through the earth, have emerged.
Upon whomsoever you place your exceedingly powerful steps, he shall become worthy today.
Māras numbering many thousands of koṭis and nayutas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
are not capable of moving or shaking you from the seat of enlightenment;
nor are the various kinds of sacrifices, numbering thousands of nayutas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Having performed sacrifices for the welfare of the world while wandering [the earth], you shine brilliantly here because of that.
The stars together with the moon and the host of constellations might fall from the sky to the earth; the greatest of great mountains might move from their own places; and the ocean might dry up;
yet a wise man could point out each of these four elements individually.
Having approached the foot of the king of trees, you shall certainly not rise up without having attained awakening.

Great gain has been well-obtained by me; my increase is vast, since you have been seen, O charioteer, and worship has been performed, virtues have been proclaimed, and I have been encouraged toward awakening.
May all the Naga women and I, along with my sons, be liberated from this womb.
Just as you go with the gait of an elephant in rut, may we likewise proceed in that same manner.
Thus [it is said].
Thus, monks, Kālika the Nāga king’s chief queen, named Suvarṇaprabhāsā,

was surrounded and escorted by many Nāga maidens who held various jeweled parasols, various garments, various strings of pearls, various precious gems, divine and human garlands, ointments, and powders, as well as various incense burners.
They showered the Bodhisattva as he proceeded with rains of various jewel-flowers and the sounding of various musical instruments and songs.
And with these verses they praised him:
"Unconfused, fearless, undaunted, unshaken, neither dejected nor depressed, joyful, and invincible."
Unattached, undeluded, unconfused, free from greed, dispassionate, and liberated—homage to you, O Great Seer!

A physician who removes the arrow, a guide who leads others across, a skilled healer who liberates the world from sufferings; having recognized those who are without shelter, without protection, and destitute, you have been born as a refuge and a protector in the three worlds.
Clear-minded and overjoyed like hosts of gods, they rained down a great shower of flowers from the sky;
throwing up magnificent garments, they cried, "Since you shall become a Jina today, let there be great rejoicing!"
Approach the king of trees and sit down without fear; O Victor, shake off Māra’s army and the web of afflictions!
Awaken to the supreme, peaceful, and excellent enlightenment, just as it was awakened to by those former Lords of Victors.

For the sake of which you have performed difficult austerities for many millions of eons for the purpose of liberating the world—your aspiration is now fulfilled; this is the time that has arrived. Approach the King of Trees and touch supreme enlightenment!
Thus it is said.

Then, monks, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "Seated where did those previous Tathāgatas awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Thereupon, it occurred to him: "Seated upon a bed of grass."

Then, indeed, hundreds of thousands of gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm, situated in the sky, having known with their own minds the reflection in the mind of the Bodhisattva, spoke these words: "So it is, O noble son! So it is!
It was by sitting upon a bed of grass, O noble son, that those former Tathāgatas fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

Furthermore, monks, the Bodhisattva saw on the right side of the road a grass-cutter named Svastika who was cutting grass that was blue, soft, delicate, and beautiful; it grew in curls, turning to the right,
resembling the neck of a peacock, as pleasant to the touch as kācilindika cloth, fragrant, colorful, and delightful.
Having seen him, the Bodhisattva again stepped off the path and approached Svastika the grass-cutter;
having approached him, he addressed Svastika the grass-cutter with sweet words.
That speech of his is commanding and informative, distinct, bringing joy to all people through its single tone, lovely, worth hearing, smooth, memorable,
exhortative, satisfying, endearing, not harsh, not faltering, not rough, not restless, polished, sweet, pleasant to the ear,
causing exhilaration of body and mind, dispelling the stains of passion, hatred, delusion, strife, and impurity, and possessing a voice like the song of the kalaviṅka bird.

It possesses a resonance like the song of the kuṇāla and jīvañjīvaka birds; it has the sound of the music of celestial drums; it is unassailable, true, clear, real, and possesses a resonance like the voice of Brahmā; it resembles the forceful roar of the ocean and the clashing of mountain peaks;
it is praised by the lords of gods and asuras; it is profound and difficult to fathom; it renders the power of Namuci powerless and crushes the arguments of adversaries.

It has the speed of a lion’s roar; it possesses the resonance of the trumpeting of horses and elephants; it is the thundering of a dragon; its voice booms like the rumbling of clouds. It pervades all Buddha-fields in the ten directions and exhorts sentient beings who are to be trained. It is not hurried, unimpaired, unhindered, harmonious, appropriate, timely in its utterance, and never misses the right moment. It is well-composed with hundreds of thousands of dharmas, gentle, unattached, and sustained by inspired eloquence. It is a single sound that fashions all sounds.

Making known all intentions, generating all happiness, showing the path to liberation, teaching the provisions for the path, not overstepping the assembly, satisfying all assemblies, and conforming to what has been spoken by all Buddhas—
with such speech, the Bodhisattva addressed Svastika the grass-cutter with these verses:
"O Svastika, give me grass quickly; today my need for grass is very great.
Having slain Namuci along with his army, I shall touch the unsurpassed peace of enlightenment."
"For whose sake thousands of eons of generosity, self-restraint, discipline, renunciation,
virtuous conduct, vows, and austerity have been well-practiced by me— his perfection shall come to pass this very day."
The power of patience as well as the power of vigor, the power of meditative concentration as well as the power of knowledge,
and the power of merit, supernormal faculties, and liberation— today my perfection of these shall be accomplished.

The power of wisdom and the power of skillful means, the power of supernatural success and the power of unattached loving-kindness, and the power of the analytical knowledges and absolute truth— today their perfection shall be achieved.
The power of your merit is also infinite, since you will give me grass today;
let this not be the final sign for you, for you too shall become an unsurpassed Teacher.
Having heard the leader’s words, which were most beautiful and sweet, Svastika was satisfied, uplifted, joyful, and his mind was filled with gladness;
he took up a handful of grass that was soft, fresh, auspicious, and pleasant to the touch.
Standing before him, he spoke these words with a joyful heart.
If even by means of straw mats the supreme state, the immortal, the unsurpassed, peaceful, and difficult-to-behold awakening— the path of the former Victors—
can be attained, then let it be so, O ocean of great qualities, you of immeasurable fame!
I alone, indeed, first awaken to the supreme nectar of the path.
O Svastika, this awakening is not attained merely by lying on a bed of excellent grass,
without having practiced various difficult vows and austerities for many eons;
it is attained when one becomes wise, exalted through wisdom, merit, and skillful means.
Then, O Jina, the Sages prophesy: "You shall become free from dust."

If this enlightenment could be given away as a gift to others, I would give it to all living beings in its entirety; let there be no doubt in this regard. When I have attained enlightenment, you shall know that I distribute the nectar of immortality.
"Come and listen; you shall become endowed with the Dharma and free from passion."
Taking a handful of grass that was exceedingly soft,
the Leader, with the gait of a lion or a swan, set forth; as he moved, the earth trembled,
and the hosts of gods and nāgas, their minds filled with joy, joined their palms in reverence.
Today, having destroyed the army of Māra, he shall touch the deathless.

Thus, monks, as the Bodhisattva was approaching the Bodhi tree, eighty thousand Bodhi trees were adorned by sons of gods and Bodhisattvas with the thought: "Sitting here, the Bodhisattva will attain and fully awaken to enlightenment.
Among them, there were some Bodhi trees made of flowers, rising a hundred thousand yojanas in height.
Some Bodhi trees were made of incense, rising two hundred thousand yojanas in height; some Bodhi trees were made of sandalwood, rising three hundred thousand yojanas in height.
Some bodhi trees were made of cloth, five hundred thousand yojanas in height;
some bodhi trees were made of jewels, one million yojanas in height;
and some bodhi trees were made of every kind of jewel, ten quadrillion yojanas in height.

Some of the Bodhi trees were made of jewels, rising up hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of leagues in height. At the foot of all those Bodhi trees, lion thrones appropriate to each were prepared, spread with various divine cloths.
At some Bodhi trees, a lotus throne was prepared.
In some places there were seats of fragrance, and in others seats of various kinds of jewels;
and the Bodhisattva entered the samādhi called Lalitavyūha.

And as soon as the Bodhisattva had entered this bodhisattva-samādhi called *Lalitavyūha*, at that very moment the Bodhisattva was seen seated upon lion-thrones at the foot of all those bodhi-trees, his body adorned with the primary and secondary marks.
And each individual Bodhisattva, together with the sons of the gods, perceived it thus: "The Bodhisattva is seated on my very lion-throne, and not on those of others."

And just as they perceived it— by the power of this very Bodhisattva-samādhi called Lalitavyūha— all those in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, as well as all gods and humans, and indeed all beings born in any state of existence, beheld the Bodhisattva seated upon the lion throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Then, moreover, for the sake of satisfying the minds of those beings who were inclined toward inferior aspirations, the Bodhisattva took a handful of grass and approached the Bodhi tree.
Having approached, he circumambulated the Bodhi tree seven times and himself spread out a seat of grass that was auspicious on all sides, with the tips pointing inward and the roots outward.

Like a lion, like a hero, like one who is powerful, like one of firm vigor, like one possessed of strength, like an elephant, like one possessing sovereignty, like the Self-Existent One, like a man of knowledge, like one who is unsurpassed, like one distinguished, like one who has emerged, like one with renown, like one with fame, like a donor, like one endowed with ethical conduct, like one endowed with patience, like one endowed with vigor, like one endowed with meditation, like one endowed with wisdom, like one endowed with knowledge, like one endowed with merit, and like one who has struck down Māra and his adversaries— he sat down upon that grass mat, having folded his legs crosswise, facing the east, holding his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him. And he made this firm vow:
On this seat let my body wither away; let skin, bone, and flesh go to destruction.
Until I have attained enlightenment—so difficult to reach even in many eons—this body shall not move from this seat.
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Departure for the Seat of Enlightenment."
START Parivarta 20 (Vaidya 211):
The twentieth chapter, "The Array of the Seat of Enlightenment" (Bodhimaṇḍavyūha).

Thus, monks, when the Bodhisattva was seated at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), the six classes of gods belonging to the realm of desire stood in the eastern direction, thinking: "May no one cause any obstacle for the Bodhisattva.
In this same way, the southern, western, and northern directions were likewise protected by the gods.
Thus, monks, at that time, the Bodhisattva, seated upon the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), emitted a ray of light called "the Exhortation to the Bodhisattvas.

By that ray, all Buddha-fields—immeasurable and incalculable, extending throughout the ten directions, reaching the limits of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and the realm of space (ākāśadhātu)—were illuminated.

Then, indeed, from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Vimalaprabhāsa in the world-system Vimalā in the eastern direction, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Lalitavyūha, being exhorted by that radiance and surrounded and preceded by bodhisattvas beyond counting, approached the seat of awakening where the Bodhisattva was.
Having approached, at that very moment, he performed such a miraculous feat for the purpose of honoring the Bodhisattva,

by means of which miraculous feat, once performed, he displayed all the Buddha-fields in the ten directions, extending to the limits of the realm of space, as a single mandala made of pure blue beryl.
He manifested the Bodhisattva seated upon the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) before all sentient beings born within the five realms of existence;
and those beings pointed toward the Bodhisattva with their fingers, saying to one another, "Who is this being of such a form, so graceful? Who is this being of such a form, so radiant?"
And before those beings, the Bodhisattva manifested emanations of Bodhisattvas;
there, those forms of Bodhisattvas spoke these verses:
"For one from whom every stain of passion and hatred has been uprooted, along with its latent tendencies (*vāsanā*)."
He by whose bodily radiance all other lights in the ten directions are rendered lusterless;
he whose accumulation of merit, meditative concentration, and wisdom has been nurtured through a flood of eons—
this Śākyamuni, the supreme among great sages, illuminates every direction.
Thus it is said.

Then, monks, from the world-system called Ratnavyūhā in the southern direction, the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratnārcis, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Ratnacchatrakūṭasaṃdarśana was impelled by that radiance;
surrounded and escorted by a retinue of bodhisattvas beyond counting, he proceeded toward the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
He approached where the Bodhisattva was;
having approached, for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva, he covered that entire circle with a single jewel-canopy.
There, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors said this to one another: "Whose fruit is this?"
"By whom has this array of precious parasols (*ratnacchatra-vyūha*) of such a form been manifested? Then, from that precious parasol, this verse issued forth:
"By whom [this] thousands of billions of trillions of parasols, perfumes, and jewels..."
Having given [gifts] with a mind of loving-kindness toward those who are peerless, they abide in nirvāṇa;
he is this very one, endowed with excellent marks, acting for the welfare of others, and possessing the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
This possessor of virtues has come to the root of enlightenment; this is the worship offered to him.
Thus [it is said].

Then, indeed, from the world-system called Campakavarṇā in the western direction, from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Puṣpāvalivanarājikusumitābhijña, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Indrajālī— having been exhorted by that radiance—
surrounded and escorted by bodhisattvas beyond counting, proceeded toward the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and toward where [the Lord was].
The bodhisattva approached him;
having approached, for the sake of performing an act of worship toward the bodhisattva, he covered the entire area of the mandala with a single net of jewels.
Thereupon, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas in the ten directions said to one another: "Whose is this such magnificent array of light?"
Then, from that net of jewels, this verse issued forth:

"The Mine of Jewels, the Banner of Jewels, the Delight of the three worlds, the Supreme Jewel, the Renown of Jewels—he who delights in the sublime Dharma and has attained vigor shall not be severed from the Three Jewels; he shall attain supreme enlightenment, and this is his worship."
Thus it is said.

Then, indeed, from the world-system called Sūryāvartā in the northern direction, from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Candrasūryajihmīkaraprabha, the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Vyūharāja— being impelled by that radiance— approached the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and the Bodhisattva, surrounded and escorted by bodhisattvas beyond counting.

Having approached, for the sake of making an offering to the Bodhisattva, he manifested within that very circle all the arrays of qualities of the Buddha-fields, as many as exist in all the world-systems throughout the ten directions.
There, some bodhisattvas said: "To whom do such arrays belong?"
Then, from all those arrays, this verse issued forth:
"By whom the body has been purified many times over through merit and wisdom, and by whom speech has been purified through vows, austerities, truth, and the Dharma."
He by whom the mind has been purified through shame, steadfastness, compassion, and loving-kindness— he,
this bull of the Śākyas, has arrived at the foot of the king of trees and is now worshipped.
Thus it is said.

Then, indeed, from the world-system called Guṇākarā in the southeastern direction, from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Guṇarājaprabhāsa, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Guṇamati— being impelled by that radiance— approached the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and the Bodhisattva, surrounded and escorted by a retinue of bodhisattvas beyond counting.
Having approached, for the purpose of making an offering to the Bodhisattva, he miraculously manifested a gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra) adorned with all virtues within that very circle.
His retinue asked, "To whom does this kind of magnificent gabled chamber belong?
Then, from that gabled chamber, this verse issued forth:
He by whose virtues the gods, asuras, yakṣas, and mahoragas are constantly made fragrant with virtue—
he, the virtuous one, born of the royal family of virtues, an ocean of qualities, is seated at the foot of the tree of awakening.
Thus [it is said].

Then, indeed, from the world-system called Ratnasaṃbhavā in the southwestern direction, from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratnayaṣṭi, the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Ratnasaṃbhava, being impelled by that radiance, surrounded and escorted by bodhisattvas beyond counting, approached the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) where the bodhisattva was.
Having approached, for the sake of making an offering to the Bodhisattva, he miraculously produced immeasurable and incalculable jeweled celestial palaces within that circle;
and from those jeweled celestial palaces, this verse issued forth:
"By him the earth, together with the oceans, was surrendered, as well as manifold jewels."
Palaces with excellent windows and turrets, vehicles and carriages,
beautiful flower-garlands adorning the sky, gardens, wells, and assembly halls—
these were his hands, feet, head, limbs, and eyes as he stood at the seat of awakening.
Thus [it is said].

Then, indeed, from the world-system called Meghavatī in the northwestern direction, from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Megharāja, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Meghakūṭābhigarjitasvara, being exhorted by that radiance, approached the seat of awakening and the Bodhisattva, surrounded and escorted by bodhisattvas beyond counting.

Having approached, for the sake of making an offering to the Bodhisattva, he miraculously manifested a cloud of black agallochum and rained down a shower of powdered uragasāra sandalwood upon that circle of the mandala.
And from that circle of the black agallochum cloud, this verse issued forth:
"Having pervaded the entire triple world with the cloud of Dharma, you shine with the light of knowledge and resolute faith."
And he will rain down the true Dharma— the nectar that leads to dispassion and the attainment of Nirvana—

and with the power of meditation and the faculties in full bloom, he will sever all the creepers of the bonds of passion and afflictions along with their latent tendencies, and bestow the fruit of faith.
Thus it is said.

Then, indeed, from the world-system called Hemajālapraticchannā belonging to the Tathāgata Ratnacchatrābhyudgatāvabhāsa in the northeastern direction, from that Buddha-field, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Hemajālālaṃkṛta, being impelled by that radiance,
surrounded and escorted by bodhisattvas beyond counting, [proceeded] toward the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).

He approached where the Bodhisattva was; having approached, for the sake of making an offering to the Bodhisattva, he manifested within all those gabled pavilions with jeweled canopies the forms of Bodhisattvas adorned with the thirty-two marks.
And all those bodhisattva-forms, holding divine and human flower garlands, bowed their bodies toward where the Bodhisattva was and let those flower garlands hang down.
They spoke this verse:
"By whom millions of Buddhas were previously praised with great reverence, having generated faith..."
I bow my head to him who has reached the seat of enlightenment, whose speech is the resonance of Brahmā and whose voice is sweet.
Thus.

Then, indeed, from the world-system called Samantavilokitā in the direction below, the Tathāgata Samantadarśin’s buddha-field, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Ratnagarbha was impelled by that radiance.
Surrounded and escorted by bodhisattvas beyond counting, he approached the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and the place where the Bodhisattva was.
Having arrived, for the purpose of honoring the Bodhisattva, he manifested Jāmbūnada-gold lotuses rising up from that lapis lazuli circular terrace;
and upon the pericarps of those lotuses, he manifested women appearing from their waists upward, endowed with perfect complexion and form, and adorned with every ornament.
With their left and right hands, they held various ornaments such as bracelets, armlets, golden threads, and pearl necklaces;
and while hanging down garlands of flowers and silk ribbons, they leaned their bodies forward toward the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and toward the Bodhisattva.
And they spoke this verse:
He who always bows down to the gurus—the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas; he who is well-disciplined, ever upright, and foremost in virtue—bow down to that possessor of qualities.
Thus it is said.

Then, indeed, from the world-system called Varagaganā in the zenith direction, from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Gaṇendra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Gaganagañja, being impelled by that radiance, surrounded and preceded by bodhisattvas beyond counting, approached the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) where the bodhisattva was.

Having approached for the purpose of making offerings to the Bodhisattva, while remaining in the expanse of the sky, he [produced] as many flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, garments, ornaments, parasols, banners, flags, victory standards, jewels, gems, gold, silver, pearls, necklaces, horses, elephants, chariots, infantry, mounts, flowering trees, leaves, blossoms, fruits, boys, and girls as exist throughout all the Buddha-fields in the ten directions— things never before seen or heard.
Gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, humans, and non-humans—
all of them rained down a great shower of flowers from the expanse of the sky, generating joy and happiness for all sentient beings;
yet it caused neither fear nor oppression to any being whatsoever.
In this regard, it is said:

"O sons of the Conqueror, listen to a mere illustration of those sons of the Conqueror who, having attained awakening, have come to honor the Benefactor throughout these directions with their arrays, strides, and noble steps. *Lalitavistara* 20.10.
And some have arrived, thundering like clouds in the sky, trailing down millions of necklaces;
and some have arrived with crests adorned by dangling jewel-crests, displaying flowery celestial palaces in the firmament.
And some have arrived roaring like lions upon the earth, emitting the sounds of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and some have arrived rejoicing like bulls, scattering beautiful flowers such as have never been seen before. (Lal 20.12)
And who are these who have arrived, thundering like clouds in the sky, displaying thousands of colors within their own bodies;
and who are these who have arrived, like the full moon in the firmament, proclaiming the garland of virtues of the Son of the Sugata?
And who have arrived, emitting radiance like the sun, making all the abodes of Māra appear dim?
And who have arrived at that seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), O Vimalaketu, like Indra’s banners, heaped with the merit of their accumulations?

Some cast nets of precious jewels from the sky; O Sucandra, like moons shining brilliantly, they scatter mandārava, sumana, vārṣika, and campaka garlands upon the Bodhisattva as he stands at the king of trees.
And who have arrived, shaking the earth with their feet, causing the ground to tremble and bringing joy to the people?
And who have arrived, holding Mount Meru in the palms of their hands, with handfuls of flowers released and suspended in the air?

And some arrived having taken the four oceans upon their heads, pouring them out over the earth with waters of exquisite fragrance; and some arrived holding wonderful jeweled staffs, standing at a distance to point toward the Bodhisattva.
And some Brahmās have arrived, possessing peaceful forms; they are tranquil, with minds perfectly calmed, abiding in meditative concentration.
From their pores issues forth a delightful voice, [proclaiming] the immeasurables of loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and sympathetic joy.
And those Maruts who had arrived like Śakra, just as they had been ordained of old by the gods with thousands and millions of them,
approached the Bodhi tree; with palms joined in reverence, they cast down various wonderful jewel-ornaments that were fastened upon Śakra.
And those who have come from the four directions, like the world-protectors surrounded by gandharvas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras,
raining down flowers as radiant as flashes of lightning, praise the Hero with the voices of gandharvas and kinnaras.
And some arrived, having grasped trees in full bloom that were laden with fruit and emitting the finest fragrance of flowers;
when those had appeared, the Buddhas of pure bodies remained among them, and while being adorned by them, they scattered flowers as they hung down.
And some arrived, having taken flowering lotus ponds with blossoming *padma*, *utpala*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers;
bearing the thirty-two marks, they stood within the heart of the lotuses and praised the wise Bodhisattva whose mind was unstained.
And some who had arrived with vast bodies likewise stood in the sky like Mount Meru and cast themselves down;
as soon as they were cast down, they became garlands of fresh flowers and covered the three-thousandfold world-system of the Jina’s field.

And those who have arrived before his two eyes, demonstrating the burning of the aeon as well as dissolution and manifestation—their bodies resound with many teachings on happiness; hearing them, millions of beings abandon craving.

And those who had arrived, with voices like the singing of *kinnaras*, with beautiful faces and lips like the *bimba* fruit and full countenances—like maidens well-adorned with variegated necklaces, whom the hosts of gods never tire of beholding—gazed upon her. (Lal_20.25)
And some have arrived, indestructible like a diamond body, being supported from below by the hooves of their hindquarters;
and some have arrived with faces full as the moon and radiant as the sun, emitting moonlight and radiance, having destroyed the faults of the afflictions.

And those who have arrived, O Jewel-Adorned One, with jewels in their hands, covering many billions of fields, rain down excellent jewels and fragrant flowers for the sake of satisfying, benefiting, and bringing happiness to many beings. *Lal_20.27*
And those who have arrived, great treasuries of the jewel-like dhāraṇīs, proclaiming millions of sūtras from their pores;
possessed of eloquence, intelligence, and excellent wisdom, they awaken the people who are intoxicated or heedless.
And some have arrived, having taken up drums like Mount Meru, which produce a most delightful sound as they are struck in the sky;
their resonance travels through the ten directions across millions of realms, so that today the Teacher may awaken to the deathless and be fully realized.
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Array of the Seat of Enlightenment," in the glorious Lalitavistara.
START Chapter 21 (Vaidya 218):
The Twenty-first Chapter, "The Subduing of Māra" (Māragharṣaṇaparivarta).
Thus, monks, these kinds of arrays were prepared by the Bodhisattvas at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) as an act of worship for the Bodhisattva.

And the Bodhisattva himself manifested upon that seat of awakening all the arrays of ornaments for the seat of awakening belonging to as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, throughout all the Buddha-fields in the ten directions.
Then, monks, as the Bodhisattva sat upon the seat of enlightenment, this thought occurred to him: "In this realm of desire, Māra the Evil One is the sovereign lord and ruler who wields power.
It would not be fitting for me to awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without being known by him.
What if I were to issue a challenge to Māra the Evil One?"
When that realm is conquered, all the gods and others belonging to the desire realm will be subdued.
Consequently, those sons of the gods from Māra’s host who have previously planted roots of merit will, upon seeing my lion-like play, resolve their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva, having reflected thus, at that moment emitted from the circle of hair between his eyebrows a single ray of light called "The Destroyer of All Māra’s Mandalas."
By that ray, all the abodes of Māra throughout the entire trichiliocosm were illuminated, eclipsed, and violently shaken;
and this entire trichiliocosm was filled with a great radiance.
And from that light, Māra the Evil One heard this kind of voice:

Having practiced his conduct throughout a flood of eons, this perfectly pure being, the son of Śuddhodana, has renounced his kingdom and gone forth as a benefactor seeking the deathless nectar; he has now approached the tree of awakening—exert yourself!
Having crossed over himself, he shall ferry others across as well; having himself been liberated, he shall liberate others.
Having attained consolation, he shall console others as well; and having entered final nirvāṇa, he shall cause others to attain it.
He will leave the three lower realms entirely empty and fill the cities of gods and humans;
having touched the deathless, this benefactor will bestow the supreme nectar of bliss consisting of meditative absorptions and superknowledges.
"O friend of Kṛṣṇa, he will leave your city empty—he who is powerless though called 'Powerful,' who is devoid of strength, and whose own side has no partisans.
When the Self-Existent One himself pours down the rain of Dharma, you will not know where to go nor what to do. (Lal_21.4)
Thus it is said.
Thus, monks, Māra the Evil One, having been exhorted by these inciting verses, saw a dream in thirty-two forms.
What are the thirty-two forms? They are as follows: he saw his own abode enveloped in darkness.
He saw his own palace filled with dust and strewn with gravel and pebbles;
he saw himself fleeing in all ten directions, terrified, trembling, and agitated;
and he saw himself with his crown fallen off and his earrings cast away.
He saw himself with his lips, throat, and palate parched;
he saw himself with a burning heart;
and he saw gardens whose leaves, flowers, and fruits were withered.
He saw lotus ponds that were devoid of water and completely dried up;
he saw flocks of birds such as swans, cranes, peacocks, sparrows, kuṇālas, and jīvaṃjīvakas with their wings withered;
and he saw musical instruments—drums, conchs, clay drums, kettledrums, flutes, lutes, vallakīs, and tāḍas—broken, shattered, and fallen upon the ground.
He saw his beloved attendants, having abandoned Māra with dejected faces, go to one side and remain lost in thought.
He saw the chief queen, Māriṇī, fallen from her bed upon the ground, pressing her head with both hands.

And he saw those sons of Māra who were most heroic, most powerful, most majestic, and most wise, paying homage to that Bodhisattva as he sat at the supreme and excellent seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
He saw his own daughters crying out, "Alas, father! Alas, father!
He saw himself with soiled garments and limbs;
he saw himself with his head covered in dust, pale and discolored, and robbed of his vital energy.
He saw the turrets, gabled chambers, windows, and archways being covered in dust and falling down;
and he saw all those generals of his— the lords of the yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, and gandharvas— with their hands placed upon their heads, weeping, wailing, and fleeing.
And as for those lords of the gods among the gods of the desire realm—
namely Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, Vaiśravaṇa, Śakra, Suyāma, Saṃtuṣita, Sunirmita, Vaśavartin, and so forth—
the Evil Māra saw them all listening attentively and facing toward the Bodhisattva.
In the midst of the battle, his sword was no longer unsheathed;
he saw himself crying out inauspiciously,
and he saw himself abandoned by his own retinue.
He saw auspicious jars full of water fallen at the gate;
he saw the Brahmin Nārada proclaiming inauspicious sounds;
and he saw the delighted gatekeeper proclaiming sounds of joylessness.
He saw the expanse of the sky overwhelmed by darkness;
he saw Śrī, who dwells in the abode of desire, weeping;
and he saw his own sovereignty turned into non-sovereignty.
He saw his own side rendered wingless; he saw the nets of jewels and pearls become silent, severed, shattered, and fallen;
and he saw the entire abode of Māra trembling.
He saw trees being cut down and their trunks falling;
he beheld the entire array of Māra’s army being cast down toward him.
Thus, monks, Māra the Evil One saw a dream of thirty-two aspects.
