Having woken up, he was afraid, terrified, and agitated; he assembled all his household, and perceiving that they were gathered together with his forces, retinue, generals, and gatekeepers, he addressed them with these verses:
(Vaidya 220)
Having seen that dream, Namuci, afflicted by grief, addressed his sons and his courtiers;
Namuci, the kinsman of darkness, questioned them all, including the commander-in-chief named Siṃhahanu.
Today, a song composed of verses has been heard from the sky: "He whose limbs are adorned with the most excellent marks was born among the Śākyas;
having practiced terrible austerities for six years, he has indeed approached the Bodhi tree—exert yourself! (Lal 21.6)
If that Bodhisattva, once awakened, should awaken many millions of billions of beings,
he will leave my abode entirely empty when he attains the state of the cool touch of immortality.
"Come, let us go together with a great army; let us strike down that solitary ascetic at the foot of the king of trees!
Quickly mobilize the fourfold army if you wish to do what is pleasing to me; do not delay! (Lal 21.8)
Even if the world were filled with Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats passing into nirvāṇa, my power would not become weak;
moreover, he alone shall become a Jina, a King of Dharma, and the lineage of the Jinas, which transcends all calculation, shall never be severed.
Then, monks, a son of Māra named Sārthavāha addressed Māra the Evil One in verses:
"Father, why is your face downcast and your countenance discolored? Your heart leaps up and your limbs tremble."
"Have you heard this, or have you seen it? Tell us quickly; having reflected upon the truth, we shall apply ourselves accordingly. (Lal 21.10)
The emanated Māra said: "Listen to me, my child; I have seen a most terrible and dreadful dream.
I shall tell you all of it here in this assembly today, lest you all faint and fall to the surface of the earth."
The caravan leader said:
"If victory is attained at the time of battle, there is no fault; however, he who is slain right there—that is the fault."
But if such omens as these appear to you even within a dream, it is better for you to desist from battle, lest you suffer defeat.
Māra said:

"O man of resolute intellect, by relying on courage in battle, if one achieves success through well-executed deeds, what power do I have—along with my retinue—to prevent his victory? He shall rise up and prostrate himself at my feet. *Lal_21.13*
The caravan leader said: "Indeed, there is both vast strength and very feeble strength; there is the solitary hero, powerful and a vanquisher in battle.
If the three thousandfold world-system were filled with fireflies, a single sun swallows them all and renders them lusterless."
Moreover:
"He in whom pride, delusion, and even critical inquiry are no longer found—if such a wise one acts contrary [to reason], he cannot be cured. (Lal 21.15)

Thus, monks, Māra the Evil One, disregarding the words of the Caravan Leader, mobilized a vast fourfold army— mighty, skilled in the arts of war, terrifying, and hair-raising— a sight never before seen or heard of by gods or humans; it displayed hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various facial contortions,

its bodies coiled and entwined by hundreds of thousands of serpents, and it bore swords, bows, arrows, spears, lances, axes, sharp-edged spears, *bhuśuṇḍi*-missiles, clubs, staffs, nooses, maces, wheels, thunderbolts, and iron bolts.

Her body was armored with excellent shields and mail; her head, hands, feet, and eyes were distorted; her head, eyes, and face were ablaze; her belly, hands, and feet were misshapen; her face possessed fierce radiance; her appearance was supremely hideous;

she had terrifyingly deformed fangs; her tongue was thick, vast, wide, and long-hanging; her tongue resembled a *suṇḍika* or a blade of straw; and her blood-red eyes were like fire and filled with the venom of black serpents.
For some there were vomiting venomous serpents; others, seizing venomous serpents with their palms, were devouring them;
and like Garuḍas emerging from the ocean, some were lifting up and devouring human flesh, blood, hands, feet, heads, liver, entrails, excrement, and so forth.

Some had blazing, tawny, black, blue, red, or brownish-brown forms that were terrifying and variegated; some had distorted mouths, blazing uprooted fangs, and distorted side-glances; others had eyes that were turned back, blazing, and distorted.
Some, having seized blazing mountains, came sporting as they ascended other mountains;
some, having uprooted trees with their roots, ran toward the Bodhisattva;
some had ears like those of goats, *kaṇa*-grass, winnowing baskets, elephants, or boars.
Some had ears like those of wolves;

some had dropsical bellies and feeble bodies, having conjured up skeletons of bones; others had broken noses, pot-bellies, and feet like skulls; their skin, flesh, and blood were withered away; and some—with their ears, noses, hands, feet, eyes, and heads severed—were hacking at one another's heads out of a thirst for blood.
Some, with voices that were harsh, distorted, terrifying, and coarse, made sounds of *phuṭ-phuṭ*, *picut-kāra*, *phulu-phulu*, and shrieks.
Some said: "Seize him! Carry him off! Strike him! Kill him! Bind him! Grasp him! Cut him! Split him! Crush him! Throw him up! Destroy this ascetic Gautama along with the Dravidian!
Thus they spoke.

Some had faces that were terrifying, fierce, and deformed, resembling those of *bheruṇḍakas*, jackals, pigs, donkeys, cows, elephants, horses, camels, mules, buffaloes, rabbits, *camaras*, rhinoceroses, *śarabhas*, and various other [beasts];

some had bodies resembling lions, tigers, bears, boars, monkeys, leopards, cats, goats, sheep, snakes, mongooses, fish, crocodiles, porpoises, tortoises, crows, vultures, owls, *garuḍas*, and so forth;
and some had misshapen forms.
Some had one head, some two heads, up to a hundred thousand heads; some were headless. Some had one arm, up to a hundred thousand arms.
Some were armless; some had only one leg;
some even had as many as a hundred thousand legs.
Some were footless;
some emitted venomous serpents from the streams of their ears, mouths, noses, eyes, and navels.

Others brandished various weapons—swords, bows, arrows, spears, pattis, axes, discs, tomara-lances, kanaya-javelins, vajras, bhushundis, bhindipalas, and so forth—and while dancing, they threatened the Bodhisattva.
Some men, having cut off their fingers, made them into garland strings and wore them;
others, having made their heads, bones, hand-basins, and skull-bowls like garland strings, wore them.
Some had their bodies encircled by venomous serpents;
some, clutching iron helmets, were mounted upon elephants, horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, and buffaloes;
and some had their heads downward and their feet upward.
Some had hair like needles;

some had hair like that of cows, donkeys, boars, mongooses, goats, sheep, cats, monkeys, wolves, and jackals; they were vomiting venomous serpents, spitting out iron balls, emitting comets, raining down showers of blazing copper and iron, and raining down flashes of lightning.

Hurling thunderbolts, releasing showers of heated iron sand, bringing forth dark clouds, producing wind and rain, discharging showers from clouds of arrows, manifesting the night of doom, and raising a great roar, they rushed toward the Bodhisattva.

Some, whirling their nooses, causing great mountains to fall, agitating the great oceans, leaping over them, shaking the great mountains, and running about Meru, the king of mountains; fleeing, tossing their limbs and members, brandishing their bodies, laughing loud laughs, slapping their chests, and beating their breasts.
Shaking their hair, with yellowed faces, blue bodies, flaming heads, and upstanding locks, they ran hither and thither with great speed;
and with terrifying eyes like those of a *bheruṇḍa*, they sought to frighten the Bodhisattva.
Then aged women, weeping, approached the Bodhisattva and spoke thus: "O son!"
Alas, my son! Arise, arise;
flee away quickly!

Taking the forms of *rākṣasas* and *piśācas*, as well as emaciated *pretas* who were one-eyed, lame, and weak, with eyes hollowed by hunger, arms upraised, and distorted faces, they ran toward the Bodhisattva from the front, crying out, manifesting fear, and generating terror. And by that assembled army of Māra, the area for eighty *yojanas* in length and breadth all around was completely filled.

And just as it was for a single Māra, so too were the regions below, above, and across completely filled with the armies of hundreds of millions of evil Māras included within the triple-thousandfold world system.
In this regard, it is said:
They take the forms of yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and mahoragas; they take the forms of rākṣasas, pretas, and piśācas.
However many hideous and most fierce beings there are in the world, they were all created there by those who are deceitful.
Some had one head, two heads, three heads, and up to a thousand heads; they had many faces.
Some had one arm, two arms, three arms, and up to a thousand arms; they had many arms.
Some had one foot, two feet, three feet, and up to a thousand feet; there were many others besides.
With blue faces and yellow bodies, and yellow faces and blue bodies;
with various faces and various bodies, the army of servants approached as one.
The wind blows, the rain pours down, and hundreds of thousands of lightning bolts fall;
the god thunders and the trees shake, yet not a single leaf of the Bodhi tree stirs.
The god rains, he pours down rain; floods carry away the earth made turbid by water. Such are the many terrifying calamities where senseless trees fall.
And having seen them all of such extremely terrifying form, distorted and misshapen,
the mind of him who possesses the splendor, virtues, marks, and majesty did not waver, just like Mount Meru.
He beholds all phenomena as equal to an illusion, equal to a dream, and resembling a cloud;
reflecting upon such a system of phenomena, he dwells well-established, meditating while firmly established in the Dharma.

Whoever should have the notions "I" and "mine," being established in the reality of the physical body, should fear the unawakened state; remaining fixed in grasping at a self, he goes into delusion—look closely and proceed [from that]. (Lal 21.23)
But the Son of the Śākyas has awakened to the fact that all phenomena arise dependently, being by nature non-existent;
with a mind well-composed like the sky, he does not waver even upon seeing the entire host of Māra and his deceit.
Thus, monks, there were one thousand sons of Māra, the Evil One. Among them, those sons of Māra who were devoted to the Bodhisattva, led by Sārthavāha, stood on the right side of Māra.
Those who were on the side of Māra stood on the left flank of Māra, the Evil One.
There, Māra the Evil One addressed his own sons: "With what kind of force shall we subdue the Bodhisattva?"
There, on the right side, was a son of Māra named Sārthavāha.
He addressed his father in verse:
"He who wishes to awaken the sleeping king of serpents, he who wishes to awaken the sleeping lord of elephants."
He who wishes to awaken the sleeping lion wishes to awaken the sleeping king of men.
On his left side was a son of Māra named Durmati, who spoke thus: "By a mere glance, the hearts of even the most solid trees in the world burst asunder;
what power does he have to remain alive in this world once he has been struck down by my gaze, like one already slain by death? (Lal 21.26)
To the south, the one named Madhuranirghoṣa said:
"What essence is there in trees that you speak thus after seeing them? What state would there be among men?
Even if you were to shatter Mount Meru with a single glance, your eyes would not even be able to open again."
Moreover:
"It might be possible for a man to cross the ocean with his two arms, or even to drink its waters; but I say that it is more difficult than this for one to gaze upon his stainless face. (Lal 21.28)
On the left, the one named Śatabāhu said: "In this body of mine there are a hundred arms, and with a single [hand] I discharge a hundred arrows."
"I shall shatter the body of the ascetic, my dear; be at ease and go, do not delay! (Lal 21.29)
To the south, Subuddhi said:

"If there were a hundred arms, what would be the distinction? Why would the arms not become hairs? Likewise, one could pierce with a single spear; even with many, it would accomplish nothing for him."

What is the reason? Because poison, weapons, or fire do not affect the body of that Sage who possesses loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Weapons thrown at him turn into flowers, for his loving-kindness is supramundane. (Lal 21.31)
Moreover: Whether they be powerful beings in heaven, on earth, or in the water— be they *guhyakas* or men bearing swords and axes—
once they encounter this King, the strength of patience, they all become those whose great power has become diminished.
From the left, Ugratejas said:
"Having entered his auspicious body, I shall consume him from within,
just as a forest fire subtly burns a withered tree full of hollows."
To the south, Sunetra said:

"Even if you were to burn Mount Meru in its entirety, or enter deep within the earth itself, you could not burn him whose intellect is like a diamond; he cannot be overcome by those like you, even if they were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Moreover:
All the mountains might move, the great ocean might go to destruction, the sun and moon might fall to the earth, and the world itself might go to ruin. (Lal 21.35)
Having set out for the sake of the world and being firm in his resolve regarding his vow,
he will not rise from this great tree until he has attained supreme enlightenment.
From the left, Dīrghabāhu, full of pride, said:
"Remaining here in your palace, I shall crush with my hand the abode of the moon, the sun, and all the stars."
And from the four oceans, I shall take water as if in play;
having seized that ascetic, father, I shall cast him beyond the sea.
"Stay, dear father; let this army remain. Do not be overcome by grief.
Having uprooted the Bodhi tree itself, I shall cast it in all ten directions with my hand."
On the right, Prasādapratilabdha said:
"Intoxicated with pride, you might even crush with your two hands the entire earth, including its gods, asuras, gandharvas, oceans, and mountains."
Thousands of beings like you, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges,
could not move even a single hair of that wise Bodhisattva.
To the left, Bhayaṃkara said:
"O father, why do you have such great fear while standing in the midst of an army?
You have no army; from where could there be allies? Why, then, does this fear arise in you here?"
Dakṣiṇa, with one-pointed mind, said:
"In this world there is no herd of moons or suns, nor of universal monarchs or lions;
O Father, there is no herd of Bodhisattvas here, for a single one is capable of slaying Namuci."
Looking for an opening on the left, he said:
"There are no spears, no tridents, no maces, no swords; no elephants, no horses, no chariots, and no infantry.
Today I shall slay that single intoxicated ascetic as he sits there; do not be anxious, father, do not worry at all. *Lal 21.44*
(Vaidya 227) On the right, Puṇyālaṃkāra said:
"Just as the body of Nārāyaṇa is indestructible and impenetrable, armored with the powers of patience and wielding the sword of firm vigor;"
He possesses the vehicle of the three liberations and the bow of wisdom; O father, by the power of his merit, he shall indeed conquer the army of Māra.
To the left, Anivartī said:
"A forest fire consuming the grass does not turn back; an arrow shot by a skilled archer does not turn back;
and a thunderbolt fallen from the sky does not turn back. Likewise, there is no place for me to go without having conquered the son of the Śākyas."
To the south, Dharmakāma said:
"Fire turns back upon encountering moist grass; an arrow turns back upon hitting a mountain peak;
a thunderbolt, having reached the earth, goes downward; but this [arrow] does not turn back until it has attained the peaceful, deathless state."
What is the reason?
It might be possible, dear father, to paint a picture in the sky, or to fix all sentient beings, however many there may be, in a single state of mind;
it might be possible to bind the moon, the sun, and the wind with a rope, but it is not possible, dear father, to move a Bodhisattva from the seat of awakening.
From the left, Anupaśānta said:
"With the great poison of my gaze, I shall burn Mount Meru and reduce the waters of the great oceans to ashes!
Behold, O Śramaṇa, and behold me, O Father; for today, with my gaze, I shall indeed turn both of these into ashes. (Lal 21.49)
To the south, Siddhārtha said:
"Even if this entire excellent trichiliocosm were filled with poison and set ablaze,
by the mere glance of the Mine of Virtues, that poison would become completely non-toxic."

Whatever fierce poison exists here in the three worlds— namely passion, hatred, and likewise delusion— these are not present in his body or his mind, just as mud and dust do not exist in the sky. (Lal 21.51)
"Therefore, father, let us all turn back."
From the left, the one named Ratilola said:

"With thousands of musical instruments being played and thousands of millions of adorned apsarases, having enticed him, I shall lead him to the supreme city; for I shall bring the delight of sensual pleasure under your control. *Lalita-vistara* 21.53.
To the south, Dharmarati said:
"Dharmarati is always his delight; he delights in meditation and delights in the goal of the deathless.
He delights in the liberation of sentient beings and in loving-kindness; he does not take pleasure in the delight of passion."
On the left, the one named Vātajava said:
"By my speed I could swallow the sun and moon, and the wind blowing through the sky.
This very day, father, having seized the ascetic, I shall scatter him like a handful of chaff before the wind. *Lalita-vistara* 21.55.
To the south was a son of Māra named Acalamati; he spoke thus:
"If gods and humans possessed a swift force as fierce as this of yours, even all of them together would not be able to cause pain to one who is peerless."
From the left, Brahmamati said:
"Even a multitude of such as these could not inflict even the slightest blow to your pride; how much less could he alone? For all tasks are indeed accomplished by a multitude. *Lalitavistara* 21.57.
To the south, Siṃhamati said:
"A herd of lions has never been seen before on this earth, nor is there even a herd of those whose very glance is poisonous."
Even among those who are radiant, whose valor is truth, and who are bulls among men, there is no multitude.
On the left, the one named Sarvacāṇḍāla said:
"Father, have you not heard these blazing words as they cry out:
'Endowed with heroism, speed, and strength, let us go quickly to slay the śramaṇa'? *Lal 21.59*
To the south, the one named Siṃhanādī said:
"Indeed, many jackals howl their cries within the depths of the forest when the lion is not present here;
but upon hearing the lion’s terrifying roar, they flee in terror in the ten directions."

In the same way, these unwise sons of Māra, having not heard the roar of the Supreme Person, bellow with excessive arrogance according to their own opinions; yet once the Lion of Men has roared, they no longer exist.
From his left side, Duścintitacintin said:
"Whatever I think of happens here immediately; why does he not look at this?
Is he a fool, or perhaps ignorant, that having stood up, he does not flee quickly? *Lal 21.62*
From the right side, the one named Sucintitārtha said:
"This man is neither foolish nor lacking in prowess; rather, it is you who are foolish and unrestrained.
You do not know his vigor; by the power of his wisdom, you have all been conquered."
Even if there were as many sons of Māra as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and they possessed the same vigor as you,
they would not be able to move even a single hair, let alone one who intends to slay me.
Do not let your minds be distressed here; be of serene heart and full of reverence.
Do not turn back, and do not engage in conflict; he shall become the king within these three worlds.
And so on; thus all those sons of Māra—those thousand sons in their entirety, both those of the white faction and those of the black faction—addressed Māra the Evil One individually with verses.
Then indeed Bhadrasena, by name, the commander-in-chief of Māra the Evil One, addressed Māra the Evil One with verses:

To him who has you as his followers—Śakra, the world-protectors, the hosts of kinnaras, the lords of the asuras, and the lords of the garuḍas—all bow with palms joined in reverence. *Lalita-vistara* 21.66.
How much more so Brahmā, who has no followers, and the sons of the gods from the Ābhāsvara realm,
and the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens— all of them also bowed down before him.
And these sons of yours, who are wise, intelligent, and powerful—
they have entered the heart of the Bodhisattva and pay him homage.
This army of Māra, though it extends for eighty yojanas and is filled with yakṣas and other beings,
is indeed faultless before one who looks upon all with a mind full of serene faith.
Having seen this army—so terrifying, fierce, deformed, and formidable—he is neither astonished nor shaken; surely his victory shall be today.
Wherever this army is stationed, there the owls and jackals howl;
with the cawing of crows and the braying of donkeys, it is fitting to retreat quickly.
Behold at the seat of awakening the skillful curlews, swans, cuckoos, and peacocks;
they perform circumambulations to the right, for his victory today is certain.
Wherever this army stands, there ink and dust rain down;
O Mahimaṇḍi, there is a shower of flowers—heed my words and turn back!
"Where this army stands upon ground uneven with rises and hollows, strewn with thorns and brambles—
it is fitting for the wise to turn back from the stainless golden orb of the earth."
"You have seen this in a dream before; it will come to pass if you do not go.
He will reduce the army to ashes, just as the regions were turned to ash by the seers."
Since King Brahmadatta had provoked the wrath of that preeminent seer,
the Daṇḍaka forest was utterly consumed by fire, and for many years not even a blade of grass grew there.
Whosoever in the entire world are seers who observe vows and are devoted to asceticism,
he is indeed the foremost among them, for he is non-violent toward all living beings.
Have you not heard before that he whose body is ablaze with auspicious marks goes forth from the home and becomes a Buddha who has conquered the afflictions?
Such is this splendor created for the sake of worship by the sons of the Conqueror;
surely that Supreme Being is the recipient of the foremost offering.
Just as the perfectly pure *ūrṇā* hair shines forth across millions of billions of buddha-fields, we have been eclipsed by it; without a doubt, this is the slayer of Māra’s forces.
Just as his crown cannot be seen even by the gods dwelling at the peak of existence,
he will surely attain omniscience without it being taught by others.
Just as Mount Meru, the Cakravāla mountains, the moon and sun, Śakra and Brahmā, the trees, and the best of mountains— all bow down toward the circle of the earth.
Without doubt, he is powerful through merit, powerful through wisdom, and powerful through knowledge;
he is powerful through patience and powerful through vigor—the one who renders the faction of Namuci powerless.
Just as an elephant crushes a clay vessel, just as a lion [devours] jackals,
and just as the sun outshines a firefly, so shall the Sugata shatter this army.
Having heard this, another son of Māra, his eyes bloodshot with extreme rage, said:
"You speak with excessive affection for the praises of only one; you speak of that single individual alone.
For what indeed is one person capable of doing? Do you not see those who are possessed of great power and are terrifying?"
Then, from the right side, a son of Māra named Mārapramardaka said:
"In this world, there is no need for assistance for the sun, nor for the moon, nor for the lion, nor for a universal monarch;
likewise, there is no need for assistance for a Bodhisattva who is seated at the site of awakening and is resolute."
Then the Bodhisattva, for the purpose of weakening Māra, moved his face, which resembled a blooming hundred-petaled lotus;
seeing which, Māra the Evil One fled, thinking, "Māra’s army has taken refuge in the Bodhisattva’s face."
Thinking thus, he fled, but then returned once more with his retinue and hurled various weapons upon the Bodhisattva, as well as mountains as large as Mount Sumeru.
Those which were thrown over the Bodhisattva remained suspended in the air as canopies of flowers and celestial palaces.
And those venomous serpents with poisonous gaze, poisonous fangs, and poisonous breath that emitted flames of fire—
And that circle of fire remained like the circle of light of a bodhisattva.
Then the Bodhisattva once again wiped his head with his right hand;
and Māra, seeing a sword in the Bodhisattva’s hand, fled away facing the south.
Thinking "nothing at all," he turned back once more.

Having returned, he hurled various kinds of weapons at the Bodhisattva—swords, bows, arrows, spears, javelins, axes, *bhuśuṇḍi* missiles, clubs, *kaṇaya* darts, maces, discuses, thunderbolts, hammers, trees, stones, nooses, and iron balls—extremely terrifying things;
yet, as soon as they were thrown, they remained suspended like various garlands of flowers or canopies of flowers.
And scattering loose flowers upon the earth and hanging down garlands of blossoms, they adorned the Bodhi tree.
Seeing those arrays and the splendor [of the display], Māra the Evil One, his mind struck by envy and avarice, said to the Bodhisattva: "Arise, arise, O prince!
Enjoy the kingdom!"
"Your merit is only that much; how then can you attain liberation?

Then the Bodhisattva, with a voice that was courageous, profound, noble, smooth, and sweet, said this to Māra the Evil One: "O Evil One, by means of a single unobstructed sacrifice, you have attained the sovereignty over the realm of desire."
It has been attained.
By me, indeed, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of unimpeded sacrifices have been performed;
and hands, feet, eyes, and heads have been repeatedly cut off and given to those who asked for them.
Seeking the liberation of all beings, he bestowed upon beggars his house, wealth, grain, beds, clothing, walkways, and gardens many times over.
Then Māra, the Evil One, addressed the Bodhisattva in verse:
"I have performed sacrifices; you are my witness here in this matter—sacrifices that were unobstructed and blameless in my previous lives."
There is no witness here for you at all; you have been defeated by this mere prattle.
The Bodhisattva said: "O Evil One, this earth, the supporter of beings, is my witness."
Then the Bodhisattva, having suffused Māra and his assembly with a mind preceded by loving-kindness and compassion,

remained like a lion— fearless, undaunted, unhesitating, not dejected, not cowed, unperturbed, and unshaken; free from fear and horripilation, he stood with a hand whose palm was marked with the conch, banner, fish, vase, svastika, goad, and wheel, which was covered by a web-like membrane and adorned with beautiful copper-colored nails.

Having stroked his entire body with his right hand— which was soft, youthful, and delicate, and had been accumulated through a store of roots of merit over immeasurable infinite eons— he playfully struck the earth.
And at that moment, he spoke this verse:
This earth is the foundation of the entire world; impartial toward all that is moving and unmoving, she is equal to all.
She is my authority, for there is no falsehood in me; let her grant me witness in this matter.
As soon as this great earth was touched by the Bodhisattva, it shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways; it resounded, reverberated, and echoed,
just like a Magadhan bronze vessel struck with a wooden mallet, which rings out and resonates.
In this very way, when this great earth was struck by the Bodhisattva’s hand, it resounded and reverberated.
Then, indeed, in that great trichiliocosm world-system, the great earth deity named Sthāvarā,

accompanied by a retinue of a hundred million earth deities, caused the entire great earth to tremble; she split the surface of the earth not far from the Bodhisattva, raised her upper body, adorned with all ornaments, and bowed her body toward where the Bodhisattva was.
With palms joined in reverence, she said this to the Bodhisattva: "It is so, Great Being; it is so, just as you have declared.
We are witnesses to this here.
Nevertheless, Blessed One, you alone are the supreme witness and the authoritative standard for the world including its gods."
Having spoken thus, the great earth goddess Sthāvarā, after rebuking Māra the Evil One in many ways, praising the Bodhisattva, and displaying her various personal powers,
vanished on the spot along with her retinue.
Hearing that roar of the earth, that rogue fled with his army, his heart shattered by terror;
for like jackals hearing the lion's roar in the forest, or crows at the falling of a clod of earth, they suddenly vanished.
Then indeed, Māra the Evil One, suffering, dejected, displeased, and appearing ashamed, neither went forth out of his pride and arrogance,
nor did he turn back,
nor did he flee.

Standing with his face turned toward the west, he addressed the army once more: "Remain all together and united for a moment, while we determine whether it is possible to rouse him through conciliation, lest there be a sudden destruction of such a jewel among beings."
Then Māra, the Evil One, addressed his own daughters: "Go, you maidens, approach the seat of awakening and test the Bodhisattva—whether he is still possessed of passion or free from passion;
whether he is mute or wise."
"Is he blind, or one who knows the way, or intent on his goal;
is he wretched, or steadfast?
Having heard these words, those apsarases approached the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and the Bodhisattva.
Having approached and stood before the Bodhisattva, they displayed the thirty-two forms of feminine illusion. What are these thirty-two forms? They are as follows: [list follows].
Some there covered half their faces;
some displayed their high and firm breasts;
some revealed their rows of teeth with half-smiles.
Some, raising their arms and yawning, revealed their side-long glances;
some displayed lips resembling the bimba fruit;
and some gazed at the Bodhisattva with half-closed eyes.
Upon seeing him, some quickly closed their eyes;
others displayed their half-covered breasts; and some loosened their garments.
Some displayed their hips adorned with girdles;
some displayed their hips covered by fine silken garments and adorned with girdles;
and some made a jingling sound with their anklets.
Some displayed single-string necklaces between their breasts;
some displayed their naked, priceless thighs;
and some displayed green parrots and mynas perched upon their heads and shoulders.
Some gazed at the Bodhisattva with side-long glances; some, though well-dressed, made themselves appear ill-dressed;
and some caused the girdles on their hips to jingle.
Some wandered here and there with graceful gestures as if in a state of agitation;
some danced;
and some sang.
Some were sporting and felt bashful;
others, like plantain trees shaken by the wind, made their thighs tremble.
Some roared with deep sounds;
some, draped in fine silken garments and wearing girdles of bells, wandered about while laughing;
others cast their clothes and ornaments upon the ground.
Some displayed all their ornaments, both secret and manifest; some displayed arms smeared with fragrant unguents;
and some displayed earrings and fragrant ointments.
Some covered their faces with veils, yet revealed them again and again;
others recalled to one another their former laughter, dalliance, and play.
Once again, they stood as if ashamed;
some displayed the forms of young maidens, those who had not yet given birth, and those of middle-aged women. Some invited the Bodhisattva with gestures imbued with passion.

Some scattered loose flowers over the Bodhisattva; standing before him, they examined his intention and gazed upon his face, wondering: "Does he look with impassioned senses, or does he cast them aside?"
Whether their eyes were directed toward it or not,

they beheld the Bodhisattva’s face— pure and stainless like the orb of the moon released from Rāhu, like the sun rising in splendor, like a sacrificial pillar made of gold, like a blossomed thousand-petaled lotus, and like a fire into which the oblation has been poured.
Like Mount Meru, immovable; like the Cakravāla range, risen high; with senses guarded, like an elephant whose mind is well-subdued.
Then those daughters of Māra, for the sake of further enticing the Bodhisattva, spoke these verses:
"Now that the excellent season of beautiful spring has arrived, we delight in this lovely place where the trees are in full bloom.
O you of beautiful form, most handsome one, who possess sovereign power and are adorned with auspicious marks!"* *Lalitavistara 21.90*

O you who are well-born, of noble birth, and perfectly formed, the cause of happiness for gods and men, and the source of great contentment—arise quickly and enjoy this excellent youth! Do not let your mind turn back from awakening, which is so difficult to attain. (Lal 21.91)
Behold these celestial maidens, so beautifully adorned; they have come here for your sake, arrayed and decorated.
Who, upon seeing this form, would not be filled with passion—even one who is as withered as a piece of old wood, his life-force dried up? (Lal 21.92)
Whose hair is soft, fragrant, and of excellent scent; whose face is adorned with a crown, earrings, and leaf-patterned ornaments;
whose forehead is beautiful and whose face is well-anointed; whose large eyes are as pure and clear as a lotus.
Behold, O beloved, her face resembling the full moon, her lower lip like a perfectly ripe bimba fruit,
and her beautiful teeth as white as a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or snow— she who longs for the pleasure of love.
O Lord, behold this beautiful woman of great desire, whose breasts are firm and full, whose waist is exquisitely lovely with its three folds, and whose hips are charmingly broad.

Behold, O Lord, this female servant of yours, whose thighs resemble the trunks of elephants, whose arms are adorned with a continuous array of bracelets, and whose hips are beautifully decorated with a fine girdle.
She whose gait was as slow and graceful as that of a swan, who spoke with a charming and lovely voice full of passion,
who was adorned with such beauty of form, and who was highly skilled in divine delights.

If you do not desire her—who is well-trained in song, instrumental music, and dance; who possesses a beautiful form born for the sake of pleasure; and who is intensely longing for love—then you have indeed been thoroughly deceived in this world.

Just as a certain man, his mind deluded and ignorant of the happiness wealth brings, flees upon seeing a treasure, so too are you; for, being ignorant of passion, you do not enjoy this lovely woman who has come to you of her own accord.
Thus [it is said].

Then, monks, the Bodhisattva—with unblinking eyes, a smiling face, and a cheerful countenance; with senses undisturbed and limbs composed; straight, unattached, uncorrupt, and undeluded; unshakable like the king of mountains; neither dejected nor disheartened, nor oppressed, but firmly established—(Vaidya 236).

Because the afflictions had been utterly abandoned through the gateway of knowledge mastered by his own intellect, he addressed Māra’s daughters with verses, using smooth and sweet speech, with a voice exceeding that of Brahmā, resonant like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, lovely and pleasing to the mind:
"O sir, sensual desires are a mass of manifold suffering, rooted in suffering, and they cause the ruin of meditation, supernatural powers, and asceticism for the ignorant.
The wise say there is no satisfaction through the qualities of feminine desire; I shall become one who brings wisdom-satisfaction to the ignorant. (Lal 21.100)
For one who indulges in sensual desires, craving increases further, just as a certain man who drinks salt water [only becomes more thirsty].
I have not set out for my own sake nor for the sake of others; rather, I shall be one who is eager for both my own welfare and the welfare of others.
Your form is like a bubble on foam, manifested by your own will as if upon a stage of illusion;
it is indeed unstable like a play or a dream, impermanent, and always a deluder of the minds of the foolish and the ignorant.
The eyes are like bubbles, similar in nature, covered by skin; the body is a hard mass of blood, like a swelling.
The belly is a collection of urine and excrement, impure and foul, a machine of suffering arisen from karma and afflictions.

When those of childish intellect, being utterly deluded and not wise, falsely imagine a basis as being pure, they wander for a long time in *saṃsāra*, the root of suffering, experiencing many painful sensations in the hells. (Lal 21.104)
The hips flow with foul-smelling fluids, repulsive; the thighs, shanks, and feet are positioned like a mechanical device.
I behold you as you truly are, like a magical illusion, proceeding through causes and conditions in a false manner.

Having seen that the qualities of sensual desire are devoid of virtue and lacking in merit, being byways and detours from the path of noble knowledge; and seeing them as like poisonous leaves, fire, or enraged great serpents—yet fools here are deluded, perceiving them as pleasure. (Lal 21.106)

That man who, out of desire for women, exists in them—meditating on a pathless way regarding virtue and being devoid of wisdom—is indeed far removed from knowledge; he who, having abandoned delight in the Dharma, finds pleasure in sensual desires.

I do not dwell with passion, nor with hatreds; I do not dwell together with impermanence, impurity, or non-self. My mind is liberated from the power of both aversion and attraction, like the wind in the sky. (Lal 21.108)
If this entire world were filled with such as these, I would dwell for an eon together with them;
yet for me there would be no harshness, no passion, and no delusion, for they have become Jinas whose minds are equal to space.

Although here the divine apsarases are free from blood and bone, exceedingly pure, auspicious, and beautiful, they too all abide in great fear; they are devoid of permanent existence and are impermanent.

Then indeed those daughters of Māra, highly trained in the illusions of women, having generated even more passion, intoxication, and pride, displayed various gestures, adorned their limbs, exhibited feminine wiles, and sought to entice the Bodhisattva.
In this regard, it is said: O best of men, the delights of craving and pleasure, accompanied by sweet intoxication,
impelled by Māra, most alluring, have swiftly approached.
The young shoots of the tender trees, stirred by the wind, seemed to beckon the prince with their dancing as he stood among the branches of the forest trees.
This is the season of spring, the most excellent of seasons,
which brings joy to men and women and has destroyed darkness and dust.
The season has arrived, thick with flocks of birds— the sound of cuckoos, swans, and peacocks— to experience the delight of the qualities of passion.
Devoted to the observance of precepts for a thousand eons, practicing vows and ascetic penances,
as immovable as the king of mountains, with a body like the rising sun,
his voice was as melodious as the roar of clouds and like the cry of the lord of beasts.
He, who brings benefit to the world, spoke words endowed with meaning.
This world is full of sensual desires, disputes, enmity, and strife; it causes fear of death, is always frequented by the foolish, and is forever devoid of the wise.
It is in this very age that the Sugatas have attained the nectar of immortality.
Today, having conquered Māra, he will become the Arhat endowed with the ten powers.
Displaying her illusory power, she said, "Listen, O lotus-faced one:
you shall become a king, a supreme lord, a powerful ruler of the earth," as thousands of musical instruments resounded amidst a multitude of excellent women.
What is the use of this ascetic’s garb? Cease from this and enjoy pleasure!
The Bodhisattva said:
"I shall indeed become a king honored throughout the three worlds, in heaven and on earth;
a sovereign whose feet turn the wheel of Dharma, possessing the ten powers and great strength."
Constantly and perpetually saluted by millions of sons, both those in training and those beyond training, he delights in the Dharma; his mind does not delight in nor take pleasure in sense objects.
They said:
"As long as youth has not faded, while you still possess the first stage of life, and as long as disease does not assail you and old age has not darkened you."
"As long as you possess beauty and youth, and as long as we too are happy, enjoy the delights of desire with a smiling face."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Since this excellent moment, so difficult to find, has been obtained today;
and since the suffering of the moment has been avoided in the cities of both asuras and devas."
Until old age, sickness, and death appear in their wrathful forms, I shall cultivate the excellent path that leads to the city of fearlessness.
They said:
"Like the Lord of the Thirty-three surrounded by apsarases in the celestial city of Devapura, you are praised by the best of immortals in the Suyāma, Saṃtuṣita, and other heavens."
And in the city of Māra, being under the sway of intoxication, enjoy the delights of the senses together with us, experiencing vast pleasures.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Sensual pleasures are as fickle as dewdrops on grass, like autumn clouds, and resemble the wrath of a serpent maiden—causing intense fear.
Even Śakra, Suyāma, and the gods of Tuṣita fall under the power of Namuci. Who would find delight in that which is desired by women, yet is encompassed by calamity?"
They said:
"Behold these excellent trees in bloom, with their young sprouts, resounding with the cries of cuckoos and jīvañjīvaka birds and the humming of bees;
O lion among men, why do you not enjoy this forest frequented by women, where the ground-grown grass is glossy, deep blue, and soft? *Lal_21.121*
The Bodhisattva said:
"These young trees have blossomed by the power of the season; the bees, parched with hunger and thirst, have come to the flowers.
When the sun shall dry up the moisture of those growing from the earth, my resolve here will be to partake of the nectar enjoyed by the former Victors."
The daughters of Māra said:
"Behold first, O moon-faced one, those who resemble fresh lotuses, whose speech is charming and gentle, and whose teeth are like snow and silver!
Such as these are difficult to find even in the city of the gods; how much more so in the city of men? Yet you have obtained them—those who are always desired by the best of gods."
The Bodhisattva said: "I see this body as impure and unclean, filled with swarms of worms, decaying and transient, fragile and pervaded by suffering."
May I attain that infallible state, honored by the wise, which brings supreme happiness to the entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
Having experienced those sixty-four kinds of graceful amusements, with their anklets and girdles clashing, their garments fell away.
Struck by the arrows of desire, filled with passion, and with smiling faces, [the women said]: "O noble son, what is wrong with you that you do not accept us? *Lalita-vistara* 21.125.

The faults in all states of existence have been recognized and declared by me, who has shaken off passion: they are like the blades and spears of the god of love, yet equal to honey and sugarcane juice;
they are well understood by me here as being like the heads of serpents or pits of fire.
Therefore, O assembly of women, I abandon you—you who steal away my virtues.
Though they attempted to entice the Sugata— who moves with the gait of a young elephant— with many millions of kinds of seductive charms, they were unable to do so;
out of shame and modesty, they fell at the feet of the Sage.
Having generated reverence, joy, and love, he praised him who is the benefactor.
With a face like the autumn moon, resembling the interior of a stainless lotus,
possessing a splendor like the flame of an oblation of ghee, and appearing like the Golden Mountain— may this aspiration, practiced throughout hundreds of existences, be fulfilled as intended.
Having crossed over yourself, ferry across the world that is overwhelmed by calamity.
Having praised him in many ways, he who resembled a *karṇikāra* or a campaka flower, and having performed circumambulations with supreme devotion like an immovable mountain,
he went before his father, prostrated with his head, and spoke these words:
For there is no fear, O dear one, nor any resentment toward the Teacher of gods and men.
With eyes like lotus petals and a smiling countenance, he does not look at people with redness of anger nor with a frown;
even if Mount Meru were to shake, the ocean were to dry up, or the moon and sun were to fall.
Seeing the faults in the three realms of existence, he will certainly not fall under the power of passion.

Then indeed, Māra the Evil One, having heard these words, became even more distressed, dejected, dispirited, and ill-tempered; he addressed his own daughters: "How is it, sirs, that he cannot be made to rise from the seat of awakening?
Is he not truly a fool, ignorant, or does he simply not see your beautiful forms?"
Then those daughters of Māra replied to their father in verses:
"He speaks gently and sweetly, yet he is not lustful; he looks upon the venerable and the secret with reverence, yet he is not wicked."
He observes his posture and his movements, yet he is not deluded; his intention regarding the entire body is profoundly deep.
Without a doubt, he has thoroughly understood the manifold faults of women; his mind is detached from desires and he is not stained by passion.
There is no man, whether on earth or in heaven, nor even a god, who could fully comprehend the movements of his mind.
O father, were the illusions of women displayed before him, the heart of one who still possessed passion would surely melt away;
yet even upon seeing her alone, his mind did not tremble, for he stands unshakable like the king of mountains.
Filled with the splendor of a hundred merits, replete with the brilliance of virtues, and having practiced ethical conduct and austerity for many millions of eons—
to him, Brahmā and the gods of pure essence and auspicious radiance bow their heads and pay homage at his feet.
Without doubt, having utterly defeated Māra’s army, he will attain supreme enlightenment as approved by the former Victors.
Father, we do not approve of this; indeed, combat and dispute are unpleasant, and this undertaking involves conflict with the powerful and is fraught with great hardship.
"Behold, dear father, in the sky millions of Bodhisattvas standing with reverence, their crests adorned with jewels and gems;
they have come from the mines of jewels, their bodies variegated with garlands of flowers, and are being gazed upon here by the Ones Possessing the Ten Powers for the sake of worship."

O Father, whether they are sentient or insentient—trees, mountains, the lords of the Garuḍas, the lords of the gods, and the yakṣas—all bow down before this mountain of virtues; it would be better to turn back today for the sake of our welfare.
Moreover:
One should not cross over that for which there is no further shore to reach; one should not dig up that for which there is no root to be extracted.
One should not provoke him; rather, one should forgive him again, and act in such a way that he does not become dejected.
Then, monks, at that time there were eight tree-deities of the Bodhi tree, namely:
Śrī, Vṛddhi, Tapā, Śreyasī, Vidu, Ojobalā, Satyavādinī, and Samaṅginī.
Having honored the Bodhisattva, they caused the Bodhisattva’s splendor to increase in sixteen ways.
They praised him, saying:
"O Being of Pure Essence, you are resplendent like the moon in its bright fortnight;
O Buddha of Pure Intelligence, you shine forth like the sun as it rises."
O Being of Pure Essence, you are in full bloom like a lotus in the midst of water;
O Being of Pure Essence, you roar like a lion roaming through the forest king.
You shine forth, O supreme being, like the king of mountains in the midst of the ocean;
you have arisen, O pure being, like the Cakravāḍa mountain range.
O Supreme Being, you are difficult to fathom, like an ocean filled with jewels;
O Lord of the World, your vast intelligence is boundless, like the sky. (Lal 21.142)
O being of pure essence, you are one whose intellect is firmly established; like the surface of the earth, you are the source of livelihood for all beings.
O supreme being, your intellect is untroubled; like the Anavatapta lake, you are ever serene.
O Supreme Being, you have no fixed abode; like the wind, you are ever unattached throughout the entire world.
O Supreme Being, you are difficult to approach; like a king of splendor, you are free from all anger.
You are powerful, O supreme being, as invincible as Nārāyaṇa;
you are firm in your resolve, O Lord of the World, and shall not rise from the seat of awakening.
"You are irreversible, O Supreme Being, like a thunderbolt released from Indra's hand.
You have well-attained your gain, O Supreme Being; you shall before long become one endowed with the full array of the ten powers."
Thus it is said.
In this way, monks, the deities of the Bodhi tree caused the Bodhisattva to increase in glory through sixteen aspects.
There, monks, the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host weakened Māra the Evil One in sixteen ways.
What are these sixteen? They are as follows:
"O Evil One, you are ruined; you brood like a decrepit crane."
"You are weak, O Evil One, like an old elephant stuck in the mud."
"You are alone, O Evil One, like a man who prides himself on his heroism but has been defeated;
you are without a companion, O Evil One, like one afflicted by disease abandoned in the wilderness."
"You are weak, O Evil One, like an ox burdened by a load;
you are cast down, O Evil One, like a tree blown by the wind."
O evil one, you stand upon a wrong path like a merchant who has lost his way;
O evil one, you are wretched and lowly like a poor man full of envy. (Lal 21.150)
"You are talkative, O most sinful one, as bold as a crow; you are overcome by pride, O most sinful one, as ill-behaved as an ungrateful man. (Lal 21.151)
Today you shall flee, O evil one, like a jackal at the roar of a lion;
today you shall be cast about, O evil one, like a bird scattered by the Vairambha wind.
"You do not know the right time, O evil one; like a beggar whose merit is exhausted, you shall today be cast aside, O evil one, like a broken vessel filled with dust. (Lal_21.153)
"O Evil One, today you shall be subdued by the Bodhisattva, as serpents are by a mantra;
you are utterly stripped of all power, O Evil One, like a cripple with severed hands and feet."
In this way, monks, the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm weakened Māra, the Evil One, by means of sixteen aspects.
In that regard, monks, the sons of the gods who attend upon awakening reproached Māra, the Evil One, in sixteen ways.
What are these sixteen? They were as follows:
"O Evil One, today you shall be defeated by the Bodhisattva, just as an enemy army is by a hero."
"O wicked one, today you shall be subdued by the Bodhisattva, like a weak wrestler by a great wrestler."
"O Evil One, today you shall be overcome by the Bodhisattva, as a firefly is by the orb of the sun;
O Evil One, today you shall be destroyed by the Bodhisattva, as a handful of muñja grass is by a great wind. (Lal 21.156)
"O most wicked one, today you shall be terrified by the Bodhisattva, like a jackal by a lion;
O most wicked one, today you shall be cast down by the Bodhisattva, like a great sāl tree cut at its roots. (Lal 21.157)
"O wicked one, today you shall be destroyed by the Bodhisattva, as a hostile city is by a great king;
O wicked one, today you shall be dried up by the Bodhisattva, as the water in a cow's footprint is by a great heat."
"O wicked one, today you shall flee from the Bodhisattva like a rogue man released from execution;
O wicked one, today you shall be scattered by the Bodhisattva like a swarm of bees by a forest fire. (Lal 21.159)
Today, O most wicked one, you will be filled with rage by the Bodhisattva, like a righteous king deprived of his kingdom;
today, O most wicked one, you will brood in sorrow by the Bodhisattva, like an aged crane whose wings have been plucked.
Today, O most wicked one, you shall be abandoned by the Bodhisattva like a traveler whose provisions are exhausted in a vast wilderness;
today, O most wicked one, you shall lament before the Bodhisattva like one whose ship has been wrecked in the great ocean.
"O evil one, today you shall be crushed by the Bodhisattva, like grass and forest trees in the conflagration at the end of an eon;
O evil one, today you shall be scattered by the Bodhisattva, like a mountain peak struck by a great thunderbolt."
Thus indeed, monks, the sons of the gods who attend upon Bodhi discouraged Māra by means of sixteen modes;
yet Māra, the Evil One, did not turn back.
In this regard, it is said:
Having heard this true exhortation, the hosts of deities do not turn back; "O End-maker, cut them down, kill them, plunder them! Do not give him his life!"
Having himself crossed over, he will also ferry others across the objects of my domain;
I do not speak of any other liberation. Let no other ascetic rise up or set forth [to challenge him]. *Lal_21.163*
The Bodhisattva said:

"O King of Mountains, Meru, even if you were to move from your place, the entire world would not be destroyed; all the hosts of stars, along with the moon and the luminaries, might fall from the sky to the earth."
"May all sentient beings become of one mind; the great ocean might dry up, but one who has approached the foot of the king of trees like us would never be moved."
Māra said:
"I am the lord of desires, the master here in all the world—gods together with the hosts of Dānavas, humans, and even animals.
I pervade them all, and they all move according to my will. Arise, you who dwell within my domain, and do as I say!"
The Bodhisattva said:
"If you are truly the lord of desire, then you are clearly not the lord of Dharma; see me as the lord of Dharma in reality.
If you are the lord of desire, you shall not go to an evil rebirth; yet, while you look on helplessly, I shall attain enlightenment."
Māra said:
"O ascetic, you are all alone; what are you doing in the forest? That which you seek is indeed difficult to attain through union.
Even by those such as Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras, despite their efforts in austerity, that supreme state was not reached; how much less so by you, a mere mortal?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"Austerities were practiced by the sages preceded by ignorance, their minds overcome by anger and desiring the heavenly worlds."
By those who rely on the self as being both eternal and non-eternal, and by those who rely on liberation as consisting in going to a specific place; Lal_21.168 //
In reality devoid of any objective referent, they speak of a "Person" (puruṣa); some say he is all-pervading, others that he is localized and eternal;

likewise, some say he is embodied, others that he is formless; some say he possesses qualities, others that he is quality-less; and still others declare him to be both an agent and a non-agent. (Lal 21.169)
Having attained awakening today while seated here upon this throne, and having conquered you, Māra, along with your power and your army,
I shall demonstrate to this world the source of its arising, as well as nirvāṇa— the pacification of suffering and the state of coolness.
Māra, enraged, wicked, and furious, spoke again with harsh words: "Seize Sugautama! For he is alone; having cast him into the forest, seize him and go quickly before me. Bring him under my control!
Having gone swiftly to my home, make him a gatekeeper, deformed by a pair of shackles and fetters!"
I shall see my own son afflicted by suffering, crying out with many various cries of distress, like a servant of the gods in the desert.
The Bodhisattva said:
"It might be possible to paint various diverse and manifold figures upon the sky, word by word and individually;
or it might be possible for a man, through great effort, to bind with nooses the wind that rushes with speed through the cardinal and intermediate directions."
The moon and the sun, which dispel the darkness and gloom, can be moved from the sky to the surface of the earth today;
even by many beings like you, crying out in calculation, I cannot be moved from this tree.
The powerful army of Namuci rose up with the sounds of shouts of "Ha!", conchs, drums, and kettledrums:
"O son! O dear child! Why have you perished upon seeing this most terrifying army of Namuci? *Lalita-vistara* 21.173.

O you who are fair as the interior of a Jāmbūnada gold Campaka flower, so delicate, praised and worshiped by gods and men—today you shall go to your destruction in this great battle; you will fall under the power of Māra, like the moon [eclipsed] by Rāhu.
With a voice like that of Brahmā, with a voice like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, the Sugata addressed those hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas:
"The ignorant man who wishes to terrify space would likewise wish to seize one such as me from this best of trees."
Even one who could split a great trichiliocosm with a hair, or draw up the waters of the ocean,
or scatter a mountain of adamant in an instant— even such a person would not harm me as I sit beneath this tree.

At that moment, Māra, with a malevolent mind, stood nearby; drawing his sharp sword from its scabbard and grasping it in his hand, he said: "Arise quickly, Śramaṇa! Go away against my will, lest I cut you today like a green bamboo stalk!"* Lal_21.176 *In the original Sanskrit, "veṇuyaṣṭi" refers to a bamboo pole. I have translated it as "bamboo stalk" for clarity. I hope this meets your requirements. Let me know if you need further assistance.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Even if this entire trichiliocosm were filled with Māras, and if every one of them held in their hands a sword as massive as Meru, the best of mountains;"
They are not even capable of making a single hair on my body quiver, let alone killing me;
do not be corrupted, for you burn excessively with passion—I shall remind you of your own lack of firmness.
They pierce mountain peaks blazing with the color of fire; they cast down trees along with their roots, as well as copper and iron.
There are those with the faces of camels, cows, and elephants, with terrifying eyes, and fierce venomous serpents whose very glance is poison.
Like clouds arisen in the four directions, thundering and raining down thunderbolts, lightning, and iron balls;
with swords, spears, sharp axes, and poisoned arrows, they split the surface of the earth and crush the trees.
Some, with hundreds of arms, hurl hundreds of arrows; some emit venomous serpents and fires from their mouths;
others, having seized sea-monsters and other aquatic creatures from the ocean, pierce them; and some, having become Garuḍas, [pierce] serpents. *Lalita-vistara* 21.180.
Some, enraged, hurl iron balls resembling Mount Sumeru with peaks glowing like heated fire;
having reached the surface of the earth, they agitate the ground and churn the waters below from the depths of the ocean.
Some fall before him, and likewise behind him; they fall on his left and on his right, crying out, "O, child!
With their hands and feet contorted, their heads ablaze, lightning flashes seem to issue from their eyes as if burning. (Lal 21.182)
Having seen Namuci’s army transformed by its distortions, the Pure Being regards it as if it were a magical illusion;
herein there is neither Māra, nor an army, nor a world, nor a self—the three worlds revolve like the form of the moon in water.
The eye is neither woman nor man, nor is it "mine"; the ear, the nose, and likewise the tongue and the body are the same.
These phenomena are empty internally and empty externally, born through dependence; they have transcended both the agent and the experiencer.

Thus that speaker of truth always made a declaration of truth; by this word of truth, O gentle one, may all those who are well-disposed toward the Vinaya perceive these empty phenomena as garlands of flowers, even while looking upon those with weapons in their hands.
With his right palm, its fingers webbed at the tips and adorned with beautiful copper-colored nails like a thousand-spoked wheel,
resembling the luster of Jāmbūnada gold and graced by auspicious merit, he playfully touched the crown of [his father's] head down to his feet.
Stretching out his arm like a flash of lightning in the sky, he said: "The Earth herself is my witness;
I have performed hundreds of thousands of diverse sacrifices in the past, yet never before have I been a beggar, nor shall I ever become a slave to a creditor. (Lal 21.187)

The waters are my witness, as are fire and likewise wind; Brahmā, Prajāpati, along with the luminaries, the moon and the sun; and the Buddhas residing in the ten directions are my witnesses—those whose moral conduct, vows, and factors of enlightenment have risen high for me. *Lal_21.188*
Generosity is my witness, and likewise morality and patience; energy too is my witness, as are meditation and wisdom.
The four immeasurables are my witnesses, as well as the superknowledges; my entire gradual practice for awakening is here my witness.
Whatever merit, power, virtue, and likewise wisdom all sentient beings throughout the ten directions possess;
and whatever unobstructed sacrifices have been offered by the deceitful in the Kali age—all these do not equal even a hundredth part of a single hair on my body.

He playfully struck the earth with his hand, and this earth resounded like a bronze vessel. Hearing the noise of the ground, Māra was cast down and heard these words: "Kill him! Seize the kinsman of Kṛṣṇa! *Lal_21.191*
With his limbs perspiring, his splendor destroyed, and his face discolored, Māra perceived himself struck down by old age;
beating his breast, he cried out, afflicted by fear and rendered helpless, while the mind of Namuci wandered and his heart fell into delusion.
Cast down upon the ground from their elephants, horses, vehicles, and chariots, the *rākṣasas*, *kubhāṇḍas*, and *piśācas* run about, terrified;
bewildered, they find no path, having neither refuge nor protection, as if scorched by the sight of a bird falling into a forest fire.

"Mother, sister, father, son, and likewise brother, ask there: 'Where has she been seen? Where has she gone? They will quarrel with one another and suffer distress, crying, 'We have met with calamity; there is no hope for our lives. (Lal 21.194)
That vast, great, and unshakeable army of Māra has been utterly shattered; all its ranks have fallen apart and no cohesion remains.
For seven days we have recognized one another; if you are seen alive, you will surely be greeted with joy.
Then that tree deity, having felt compassion, took a water-jar and sprinkled the Kinsman of the Śākyas, saying:
"Arise quickly, go, O Master; do not delay further, for such is the way of those who lift up their teachers."
Māra said:
"Suffering, fear, calamity, grief, and destruction; the sound of reproach, humiliation, and wretchedness."
Having today committed an offense against the perfectly pure being, I have arrived here without having heard the sweet and beneficial words of my sons.
The deity said:

"Fear, suffering, calamity, wretchedness, the sound of reproach, execution, and imprisonment—the ignorant man indeed incurs these many evils, he who seeks to harm even those who are innocent. *Lalita-vistara* 21.198.

The gods, asuras, lords of the garuḍas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras, as well as Brahmā, Śakra, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin and Akaniṣṭha deities, proclaim his victory: "Victory, O hero of the world! For by you, such an army of Namuci has been cast down."

Giving necklaces, crescent moons, banners, parasols, and flags, and raining down flowers, agallochum, tagara, and sandalwood powder, they beat musical instruments and uttered these words: "O pure one, O tree, you have conquered the enemy-lion, O hero! *Lalitavistara* 21.200.
Right here upon this supreme seat, today you shall attain awakening— the unique qualities, the ten powers,
and the analytical knowledges— and today, O Hero, having conquered the vast factions of the deceitful Māra with your loving-kindness, you shall attain the entire domain of a Buddha.

In this battle that was waged for the sake of subduing Māra, those who witnessed the power and prowess of the Bodhisattva numbered thirty-six quadrillion, four hundred and twenty million; and by them, their minds were set upon the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha.
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Subduing of Māra."
START Parivarta 22 (Vaidya 250):
The Twenty-second Chapter, "The Manifest Complete Enlightenment."

Thus, monks, the Bodhisattva—having struck down his adversaries, the Māras; having trampled the thorns; having achieved victory after victory on the field of battle; with his parasols, banners, and flags raised high—dwelt, having attained and entered the first dhyāna, which is secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, and is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with joy and happiness.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he entered and dwelt in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by rapture and bliss.
Through detachment from rapture, he dwelt in equanimity, mindful and clearly conscious, experiencing bliss with the body—of which the Noble Ones say: "He who is equanimous and mindful."

He entered and dwelt in the third dhyāna, which is free from joy. Then, through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of mental ease and distress, he entered and dwelt in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

Then, when the Bodhisattva’s mind was thus concentrated— purified, cleansed, luminous, stainless, free from secondary afflictions, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability— he, during the first watch of the night, directed his mind toward the realization through direct knowledge of the vision and wisdom of the divine eye.
He directed [his mind] toward it.

Then, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Bodhisattva beheld beings passing away and being reborn—fair and ugly, in happy states and in miserable states, lowly and exalted;
he understood how beings fare according to their karma: "Alas, these beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct of body..."
Endowed with misconduct of speech and mind, revilers of the noble ones, and holders of wrong views, they—

on account of their undertaking of actions and dharmas characterized by wrong view— after the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a downfall, in the hells.
Furthermore, these beings, sirs, are endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech and mind,
do not revile the noble ones, and possess right view.
By reason of their undertaking the dharma of actions characterized by right view, upon the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly worlds.

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he beheld beings passing away and being reborn— fair and ugly, in happy states and miserable states, lowly and exalted, according to their karma. In this way, monks, the Bodhisattva realized the knowledge during the first watch of the night.
It dispelled darkness and produced light.

Then, when his mind was thus concentrated— purified, cleansed, luminous, stainless, free from secondary afflictions, supple, wieldy, established, and attained to imperturbability— the Bodhisattva, during the middle watch of the night, directed his mind toward the realization of the knowledge and vision that recollects past lives.
He directed his attention and recollected the various kinds of former existences of himself and of other beings;
namely— one birth, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and a hundred births.
He recollects a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, even many hundreds of thousands of births, a ten million births, a billion births, a ten billion births, a hundred billion births;
even many thousands of ten-billion births, many hundreds of billions of births, and many hundreds of thousands of ten-billion births;
up to an eon of dissolution, an eon of evolution, an eon of both dissolution and evolution, and even many eons of both dissolution and evolution.
"I was there, with such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such an appearance, such food, such a lifespan, remaining for such a long time,
and experiencing such pleasure and pain.
Having passed away from there, I was reborn in that other place."
Having passed away from there and been reborn here, he recollected his own and that of all sentient beings' various former abodes in their many aspects, with their specific details and locations.

Then, during the last watch of the night, at the time when the dawn was breaking— the "Joyous Face" of the night— the Bodhisattva, with his mind thus concentrated, completely pure, cleansed, luminous, stainless, free from secondary afflictions, supple, workable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, [perceived it].
He directed and applied his mind toward the realization of the knowledge and vision that leads to the destruction of the outflows, for the sake of the cessation of suffering and its origin.
Then this occurred to him: "Alas, this world has fallen into hardship, in that it is born, grows old, dies, passes away, and is reborn."
And yet, he does not clearly understand the escape from this entire great mass of suffering consisting of old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
Alas! An end to this entire great mass of suffering—of all that consists of old age, sickness, death, and so forth—is not perceived.

Then this occurred to the Bodhisattva: "When what exists do aging and death come to be? And what is the condition for aging and death? It occurred to him: "When birth exists, aging and death come to be."
Conditioned by birth, there is aging and death.
Then this further thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "What being present does birth come to be, and what is the condition for birth?
To him it occurred: "When existence is present, birth comes to be; furthermore, existence is the condition for birth."
Then this occurred to the Bodhisattva: "What being present does existence come to be, and what is the condition for renewed existence?
It occurred to him: "When grasping is present, existence comes to be."
For existence has grasping as its condition.
Then this occurred to the Bodhisattva: "When what exists does grasping come to be, and what is the condition for grasping?
It occurred to him: "When craving exists, grasping comes to be."
For clinging has craving as its condition.
Then this further thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "When what exists does craving come to be, and with what as its condition does craving arise?
To him it occurred: "When sensation exists, craving comes to be."
And craving has feeling as its condition.
Then this further thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "What being present does feeling come to be? With what as its condition does feeling arise?
It occurred to him: "Contact being present, feeling comes to be."
For feeling has contact as its condition.
Then this further thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "When what exists does contact come to be? And what is the condition for contact?
It occurred to him: "When the six sense bases exist, contact comes to be."
For contact has the six sense bases as its condition.
Then it occurred again to the Bodhisattva: "What being present does the sixfold sense-base come to be, and what is the condition for the sixfold sense-base?
It occurred to him: "Name-and-form being present, the sixfold sense-base comes to be."
For the six sense bases have various forms as their conditions.
Then, this further thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "What being present does name-and-form come to be, and what is the condition for name-and-form?"
This occurred to him: "When consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be; for name-and-form has consciousness as its condition."
Then this further thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "When what exists does consciousness come to be?
With what as its condition does consciousness arise?
It occurred to him: "When volitional formations exist, consciousness comes to be."
And consciousness has volitional formations as its condition.
Then this further thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "What being present do volitional formations come to be, and what is the condition for volitional formations?
It occurred to him: "When ignorance is present, volitional formations come to be."
For the formative forces have ignorance as their condition.
Thus, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisattva: "Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces;
conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness;
conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form."
With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises.
With feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises.
With existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
"Arising, arising."
Thus, monks, through wise attention and repeated cultivation regarding dharmas previously unheard, knowledge arose in the Bodhisattva, vision arose, and wisdom arose.
Abundant [wisdom] arose, cloud-like [wisdom] arose,
and wisdom arose.
Light appeared:
"In the absence of what do aging and death not come to be?
Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of aging and death?"
This occurred to him: "When birth does not exist, aging and death do not occur; from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death."
Then this further thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "In the absence of what does birth not come to be?
Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of birth? It occurred to him: "In the absence of becoming, birth does not come to be."
From the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth.

Then it occurred again to the Bodhisattva: "In the absence of what, and so on in detail, do the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) not come to be; or through the cessation of what is there the cessation of the formative forces?
It occurred to him: "When ignorance (*avidyā*) is absent, the formative forces do not come to be."
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;
with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases, and so on, until with the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Thus, monks, through wise attention and repeated cultivation regarding dharmas previously unheard, knowledge arose in the Bodhisattva; vision arose, science arose, and vast understanding arose.
Wisdom arose, insight arose, and light appeared.

Monks, at that time I understood, as it truly is, "This is suffering"; I understood, as it truly is, "This is the origin of the outflows, this is the cessation of the outflows, and this is the practice leading to the cessation of the outflows. I understood, as they truly are: "This is the outflow of sensual desire, this is the outflow of existence, this is the outflow of ignorance, and this is the outflow of views."
"Here, the outflows are ceased without remainder;
here, the outflow goes to its disappearance and sets without remainder.
Thus I have known, as it truly is: "This is ignorance, this is the origin of ignorance, this is the cessation of ignorance, and this is the practice leading to the cessation of ignorance."
In this regard, ignorance goes to its setting without remainder and without appearance—this is the abbreviated formula.

"These are the volitional formations; this is the origin of volitional formations; this is the cessation of volitional formations; this is the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations"—I understood this as it really is.
"This is consciousness; this is the origin of consciousness; this is the cessation of consciousness; this is the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness"—I understood this as it really is.
"I understood, as it truly is: ‘This is name-and-form; this is the origin of name-and-form; this is the cessation of name-and-form; this is the practice leading to the cessation of name-and-form.

I understood, as it truly is: ‘This is the six sense-bases; this is the origin of the six sense-bases; this is the cessation of the six sense-bases; this is the practice leading to the cessation of the six sense-bases.’"

"I understood, as it truly is: 'This is contact; this is the origin of contact; this is the cessation of contact; this is the practice leading to the cessation of contact. I understood, as it truly is: 'This is feeling; this is the origin of feeling; this is the cessation of feeling; this is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling. I understood, as it truly is: 'This is craving; this is the origin of craving; this is the cessation of craving; this is the practice leading to the cessation of craving.'"
I understood, as it truly is, that "this is clinging, this is the origin of clinging, this is the cessation of clinging, and this is the practice leading to the cessation of clinging.

I understood, as it truly is, that "this is existence, this is the origin of existence, this is the cessation of existence, and this is the practice leading to the cessation of existence. I understood, as it truly is, that "this is birth, this is the origin of birth, this is the cessation of birth, and this is the practice leading to the cessation of birth."
"I understood, as it truly is: 'This is aging; this is the origin of aging; this is the cessation of aging; this is the practice leading to the cessation of aging.
I understood, as it truly is: 'This is death; this is the origin of death; this is the cessation of death; this is the practice leading to the cessation of death.
These are sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."
Thus I understood, as it really is, the origin of this entire great mass of suffering, as well as its cessation;
