I understood, as it really is, that "this is suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."

Thus indeed, monks, during the last watch of the night, at the time of the breaking of dawn, in the night called Nandīmukhī, by the Bodhisattva— whatever [is achieved] by a man, a true man, a transcendent man,
a great man, a bull among men, an elephant among men, a lion among men, a hero among men, a bull among men, a hero among men, a steadfast man, a wise man, a lotus among men— was accomplished.
By that lotus among men, the leader of men, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed— by such a Noble One, through such noble knowledge,
whatever is to be known, understood, attained, seen, and realized,
all that was fully awakened to as unsurpassed perfect enlightenment by means of wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind, and thus the three knowledges were achieved.
Then, monks, the gods said, "Scatter flowers, friends!
The Blessed One has attained perfect awakening!
Those sons of the gods who had previously seen other Buddhas and were assembled there said, "Friends, do not scatter flowers until the Blessed One manifests a sign."
The previous Perfectly Awakened Ones also manifested signs; they created emanations and further transformed them.
Then, monks, the Tathāgata, knowing that those sons of the gods were filled with doubt, rose into the air to the height of seven palm trees; standing there, he uttered this inspired utterance:
"The path is severed, passion is stilled, the outflows are dried up and flow no more.
When the path is cut, one moves [freely]; this is called the end of suffering. (Lal 22.1)
Thus [it is said].
Then those sons of the gods scattered divine flowers over the Tathāgata,
and there arose a carpet of divine blossoms reaching up to the knees.
Thus, monks, when the Tathāgata had attained perfect enlightenment, the darkness of ignorance was dispelled,
craving was purified,
and false views were overturned.
The afflictions have been agitated,
the thorns have been dispersed, and the knot has been released.
The banner of pride has been cast down;
the banner of Dharma has been raised high;
the latent tendencies have been opened up.
The suchness of phenomena has been known;
the limit of reality has been realized;
the realm of phenomena has been fully understood.
The realm of sentient beings has been established;
the group destined for rightness has been praised,
and the group destined for falsehood has been disparaged.
The indeterminate group has been embraced;
the faculties of sentient beings have been established; and the conducts of sentient beings have been fully understood.
The disease of sentient beings has been understood; the application of the ambrosial medicine, perfected through the emergence of sentient beings, has been realized;
and the King of Physicians has appeared—the liberator from all sufferings and the establisher in the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Seated upon the great Dharma-king’s throne within the Tathāgatagarbha,
having bound all the factors conducive to liberation,
he has entered the city of omniscience where all Buddhas converge.

"O monks, because he had realized the unimpeded expanse of the *dharmadhātu*, the Tathāgata remained seated on that very seat of awakening during the first week, thinking: 'Here I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
here I have brought an end to the suffering of birth, old age, and death, which is without beginning or end.'"
Monks, as soon as the Bodhisattva had attained omniscience, at that very moment,
at that instant, at that second, all sentient beings in all world-systems throughout the ten directions were endowed with supreme happiness;
and all world-systems were illuminated by a great radiance.
Furthermore, those intermediate spaces between worlds—void, filled with calamity, and shrouded in darkness—as described previously;
and all the world-systems in the ten directions shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways; they were agitated, violently shaken, and thoroughly convulsed.
It shook, it shook violently, it shook intensely;
it trembled, it trembled violently, it trembled intensely;
it resounded, it resounded loudly, it resounded intensely.
He roared, he roared forth, he roared completely; and all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas who have attained perfect enlightenment, gave their approval, saying "Excellent!",
and they sent down canopies of Dharma.
By those canopies of Dharma, this trichiliocosm great thousandfold world-system became covered with many jewels;
and from those jeweled canopies issued forth such networks of light rays that immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions were illuminated.
In the ten directions, the bodhisattvas and the sons of the gods uttered a cry of joy: "A wise being has arisen!

A lotus born in the lake of primordial wisdom, unsullied by worldly conditions, having spread a great cloud of universal compassion in every direction, will rain down upon the abode of the realm of phenomena."

In the Vinaya, which is a rain of Dharma, it causes the sprouts of the medicinal herbs for beings to grow, increases the seeds of all roots of merit, bestows the sprouts of faith, and grants the fruits of liberation.
Regarding this, it is said:
Having conquered Māra along with his army, that Lion among Men, the Teacher, turned his face toward the gateway of meditative absorption.
When he attained the state of the Three Knowledges through the Ten Powers, the ten directions and many millions of world-systems trembled.
Those Bodhisattvas who previously came desiring the Dharma, having prostrated at his feet, spoke thus: "Are you not weary?
I have witnessed firsthand what kind of army it was—so terrifying—but it has been shattered by the power of wisdom, merit, strength, and vigor."
O virtuous one, O Great Being who has conquered the army of Māra, these parasols have been sent by the Buddhas from millions of fields.
You have attained the supreme state, the deathless and sorrowless; quickly rain down the rain of the True Dharma upon the three worlds.
Stretching out their arms toward the ten directions, those who are the essence of beings addressed him with voices like the song of the kalaviṅka bird:
"Just as pure awakening has been realized by you, you are equal and the same as the cream of ghee is to ghee."

Then, monks, the celestial nymphs of the desire realm [beheld] the Tathāgata seated at the seat of awakening— one who had attained supernormal knowledge, whose resolve was fulfilled, who had won the battle, who had utterly defeated Māra and his adversaries, who had raised high the parasols,
banners, and flags, who was a hero, a man risen in victory, a Great Man, the supreme physician, the remover of the great thorn, a lion free from fear and horripilation.

He is a Nāga with a well-tamed mind, stainless and free from the three impurities; a physician who has attained the state of the three knowledges, one who has reached the further shore and crossed over the four floods; a Kṣatriya who bears the single jewel-parasol, a Brāhmaṇa of the three worlds who has cast off evil karma;
a Bhikṣu who has burst the shell of ignorance, a Śramaṇa who has completely transcended all attachments, and a Śrotriya from whom the afflictions have emerged.

Recognizing him as a hero whose banner has not been cast down, the most powerful one who possesses the ten powers, like a mine of jewels filled with the jewels of all dharmas, they faced the Tathāgata at the seat of awakening and praised him with these verses:
"Here at the foot of the king of trees, having conquered the army of Māra, he stands unshakable like Mount Meru, fearless and free from idle chatter."
Having fully realized awakening through giving, self-control, and restraint over many millions of countless eons, he shines resplendent today.
For many millions of eons, while seeking the supreme enlightenment, he has eclipsed Śakra and Brahmā through his moral conduct, vows, and austerities;
for many millions of eons, armored with the power of patience, he has endured sufferings, and by that merit, his radiance is the color of gold.
By this power of vigor and prowess throughout many millions of eons, he has turned back the army of Māra;
by him, through meditations, superknowledges, and wisdoms, the Lord of Munis was worshipped for many millions of eons, and thus he is worshipped today.
By this accumulation of wisdom and learning throughout many millions of eons, he has uplifted millions of beings; therefore, he has swiftly attained awakening.
By him the Māra of the Aggregates has been conquered, as well as the Māras of Death and the Afflictions; by him the Māra of the Son of a God has been conquered, and thus for him there is no sorrow.
For he is indeed the God of gods (worthy of worship even by the gods), deserving of honor in the three worlds,
a field for those seeking merit, and the giver of the fruit of immortality.
This one, worthy of the most excellent offerings, has arisen; there shall be no destruction of the merit from those offerings, for he has attained supreme enlightenment.
His *ūrṇā* hair-tuft shines brilliantly, radiating across many millions of fields; it eclipses the sun and moon, bringing light to the darkness.
Thus indeed is he of beautiful form, of excellent form, of perfect form, endowed with the finest marks, seeking the welfare [of others], and worthy of worship by the three worlds.
This Self-Existent One, with his perfectly pure eyes, beholds for himself the bodies of beings, their thoughts, and their volitions;
this one, with his perfectly pure ears, hears infinite sounds—both divine and human, as well as the words of the Victors and the words of the Dharma.
He has a broad tongue and a voice as melodious as the kalaviṅka bird; we shall hear his Dharma, which leads to the deathless peace.
And having seen the army of Māra, his mind is not disturbed.
Furthermore, upon seeing the hosts of gods, the wise one did not feel joy.
He has not been conquered by weapons nor even by arrows; rather, he has conquered Māra’s army through his vows of truth and asceticism, and thus defeated that wicked wrestler.
He was not shaken from his seat, nor was his body pierced.
And neither affection nor any fault arose immediately thereafter.
Great gain has been well-obtained by those gods and humans who,
having heard the Dharma from you, shall indeed practice it; whatever merit there is in praising you, O Jina, heap of the splendor of merit!
May we all quickly become like you, O Moon among Men!
Having awakened to enlightenment, the Leader, the Bull among Men, caused millions of worlds to tremble and conquered Māra;
then, with a voice like that of Brahmā and the song of the kalaviṅka bird, the Leader spoke these first verses: Lal_22.16 //
The ripening of merit is happiness that removes all suffering; the intention of the meritorious man is fulfilled.
Having struck down Māra, he quickly touches enlightenment and, having traveled the peaceful path, he goes to the state of the coolness of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, who would not be satiated in performing meritorious deeds? And who, hearing the Dharma which is like nectar, would ever be satiated?
Who would be satiated while dwelling in the solitary forest? For what being would ever be satiated in working for the welfare of others? ||| Lal_22.18 |||
Extending his hand, he said to the Bodhisattvas, "The worship has been performed; depart each to your own respective fields.
Having all paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata, they departed for their own respective fields with various arrays of splendor.

And having seen that great condition of the Namucis and the Sugata’s playful sport so full of grace, they made an incomparable vow for enlightenment, thinking: "Having conquered Māra along with his army, may we touch the deathless state for the sake of all beings."

Monks, at that moment when the Tathāgata had attained perfect awakening and was seated upon the lion throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree, there occurred immeasurable displays of the Buddha’s miraculous power, which would not be easy to describe even in an eon.
Regarding this, it is said:
This earth became as level as the palm of a hand; lotuses with a hundred petals arose, radiant with masses of rays;
hundreds of thousands of immortals bowed toward the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa). This first sign was seen by the Lion’s Roar. (Lal_22.21)
Three hundred thousand trees bowed at the seat of awakening, as did many excellent mountains and Meru, the king of peaks;
having encountered the One of Ten Powers, Brahmā and Śakra also bowed—this too was the play of the Lion among Men at the seat of awakening.
Hundreds of thousands of rays of light radiated from the Blessed One’s own physical body, O Best of Jinas, and the three realms were pervaded; the lower worlds became peaceful.
Then, in that very instant and moment, the unfavorable conditions were purified, and neither stubbornness nor the fault of pride afflicted any sentient being.
This divine splendor of the lion among men, seated upon his throne—a radiance like that of the moon, the sun, jewels, fire, and lightning—is a mere plaything.
Overwhelmed by it, the tuft of hair between his brows does not shine, just as the sun’s rays do not outshine its own halo; nor can anyone in this world behold the crown of the Teacher's head.
This earth, too, was shaken by the touch of the palm of Narasiṃha as he sat upon his throne;
by him the army of Namuci was agitated until it became like a tuft of cotton.
Even if Namuci were to take up a bow and scratch the earth with it,
this too would be but a plaything upon the throne of the Lion among Men.
Thus [it is said].

The Twenty-third Chapter, "On Familiarity" (Saṃstava-parivarta).

Then indeed, the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm, having circumambulated the Tathāgata seated at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and having showered him with divine rains of sandalwood powder, praised him with these appropriate verses:
"The Light of the World has arisen, the Lord of the World, the Maker of Radiance;
he is the giver of eyes to the world that had become blind, the Abandoner of Strife. (Lal 23.1)
Having conquered all battles, your desires fulfilled by merits,
and perfected in pure virtues, you shall bring satisfaction to the world.
For Gautama has crossed over the mire and stands on dry land, free from affliction;
having emerged from the great flood yourself, you shall ferry other beings across as well.
You have arisen, O one of great wisdom, without rival among all beings in the worlds;
you are unstained by worldly conditions, like a lotus situated in the water.
This world has long been asleep, shrouded by a mass of darkness;
you alone are capable of awakening it with the lamp of wisdom.
In this world of living beings who have long been ill and tormented by the diseases of affliction,
you have arisen as the King of Physicians, the liberator from all maladies.
When you have arisen as our protector, the inopportune states will become empty;
both humans and gods shall be endowed with happiness.
O gentle one, O bull among men, those to whom you shall appear upon being seen will never,
for thousands of aeons, fall into an evil rebirth.
Those who hear this Dharma shall also be wise and free from disease;
they shall become profound, have exhausted the substrata of existence, and be confident.
And having severed the bonds of the afflictions, they shall all swiftly be liberated;
free from grasping, they will go forth to the supreme, auspicious attainment of the fruit.
They are the ones worthy of offerings in the world, the recipients of oblations;
no gift given to them is ever deficient in being a cause for the nirvāṇa of sentient beings.
Thus, monks, the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm, having praised the Tathāgata, stood to one side with palms joined,
paying homage to the Tathāgata with their palms joined.

Then indeed, the sons of the gods from the Ābhāsvara realm, having honored the Tathāgata seated at the seat of awakening with various kinds of divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, umbrellas, banners, and flags, and having circumambulated him three times, praised him with these verses: (Vaidya 260)

O Sage of profound wisdom, O Muni of sweet voice, O you whose song is like the voice of Brahmā, O you who have attained the supreme, excellent enlightenment and the ultimate truth; homage to you, who have reached the further shore of all sounds!
You are the protector, you are the lamp, you are the final refuge, and you are the lord in the world, possessing a mind of compassion and love.
You are indeed the supreme physician, the remover of the thorn, the healer who brings about the highest benefit.
O Protector, as soon as you beheld Dīpaṃkara, you gathered a cloud-mass of loving-kindness and compassion;
release now the stream of the Deathless and quench the fever of gods and humans!
You are like a lotus, unsullied by the three worlds; you are like Mount Meru, indeed immovable and unshakable.
You are like a diamond, O you of unwavering vow; you are the moon, the bearer of the foremost of all virtues.
Thus, monks, the Ābhāsvara gods, having praised the Tathāgata, stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata.

Then indeed, the gods of the Brahma-realm, headed by the divine son Subrahman, having covered the Tathāgata seated at the seat of awakening with a net of jewels inlaid with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of precious gems, and having circumambulated him three times, praised him with these appropriate verses:
"O you who possess the splendor and majesty of pure, stainless wisdom; O you who bear the most excellent and supreme thirty-two marks!"
Possessed of mindfulness and intelligence, upholders of virtue and knowledge, and untiring—upon your head I bow.
Stainless and pure, purified from the three impurities, renowned throughout the three worlds, and attained to the three knowledges;
you who bestow the supreme eye of the threefold liberation—I bow to you, the stainless one with three eyes.
Having uprooted the defilements of the Kali age, his mind is perfectly subdued; arisen with compassion, he acts for the sake of the world.
The Sage has risen in joy, his mind profoundly tranquil; he is the liberator from dualistic thought and delights in equanimity.
Exalted through vows and asceticism, you act for the benefit of the world;
having reached the further shore of the purity of your own conduct, you reveal the Four Truths. Delighting in liberation, being yourself liberated, you liberate other beings as well.

O Namuci, you have come here with strength and vigor, but you have been conquered by your own wisdom, vigor, and loving-kindness. You have attained the supreme state of the deathless; we pay homage to you, the crusher of the host of the wicked.
Thus, monks, the gods of the Brahma-realm, headed by the divine son Subrahma, having praised the Tathāgata with these verses, stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata.
Then those sons of Māra belonging to the side of light approached the place where the Tathāgata was;
having approached, they covered the Tathāgata with canopies of great jeweled parasols and, with palms joined, praised the Tathāgata with these appropriate verses:
I have witnessed your exceedingly vast power, in that you, in a single moment, conquered Māra’s terrible army— that most fearsome host of Māra;
yet you did not rise, nor was your body shaken, nor was a word uttered.
We pay homage to you, the Sage honored by all the worlds, who has accomplished all aims.
Māras numbering many thousands of millions of billions, equal to the atoms of the Ganges,
are not capable of moving or shaking you from the seat of enlightenment;
nor are sacrifices numbering many thousands of millions of billions, like the sands of the Ganges.
Because you have performed sacrifice beneath the Bodhi tree, you shine brilliantly today.
Wives most cherished, sons beloved, female and male servants as well; gardens, cities, kingdoms, provinces, and royal palaces;
even hands, feet, the head—the best of limbs—as well as eyes and tongues.
Having abandoned those [worldly things] while practicing the sublime conduct of awakening, you shine forth brilliantly today.
As for those words spoken by you many times— "I shall become a Buddha; I will deliver many millions of billions of beings who are being swept away by the ocean of suffering"— [that was said].
Armored with meditations, the faculties, and wisdom, this very ship of the True Dharma is now fully prepared for you; through your own vow, you shall ferry across living beings.
Whatever merit there is from praising the Bull among Orators, who bestows the eye upon the world— having all become uplifted in heart, may we pray for omniscience,
having fully realized that incomparable, supreme, and excellent awakening so well extolled by the Buddhas.
Thus, having utterly destroyed that host of Māra, may we awaken to omniscience.
Thus, monks, having praised the Tathāgata, the sons of Māra stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata.
Then the son of the gods from the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm, surrounded and honored by many hundreds of thousands of sons of gods,

scattered lotuses with the color of Jāmbūnada gold over the Tathāgata and praised him to his face with these verses: "Unoppressed, unagitated, one whose speech is not false, free from the dust of darkness, you have gone to the state of the deathless."
O you who possess incomparable splendor and surpassing brilliance, mindfulness, and wisdom, worthy of honor in heaven and on earth, I bow my head to you.
O bringer of delight, O conqueror of strife, O destroyer of the impurities of passion, you gladden gods and men with your most lucid words;
with the rays from your blossoming, vast, and excellent body, you triumph over this world like a lord of gods and men.
O crusher of rival assemblies, skilled in the conduct of others, be dear to humans and gods by shaking off false views;
you who possess most subtle intelligence, analyze the conduct of others as you travel here on the path leading to the state of the Ten-Powered One.
You have abandoned the vast grasping at existence and its false sufferings; you discipline gods and men according to their respective capacities through your great discipline.
You wander in the four directions like the moon in the sky, O Eye of the World, the ultimate refuge here on earth within the three realms of existence.
O beloved of gods and men, you do not wallow in the objects of sense; you delight in virtue and are detached from sensual pleasure.
Appearing daily before the assembly, you are not equal to anyone in the three worlds; O Lord, you alone are the refuge and the ultimate goal for this world.
Thus, monks, the sons of the gods of the Parinirmitavaśavartin realm, headed by Vaśavartin, having praised the Tathāgata, stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata.
Then the son of the gods Sunirmita, surrounded and escorted by a host of gods, covered the Tathāgata with various jeweled silk streamers and praised him to his face with these verses:
“O Light of Dharma, you have arisen as the destroyer of the threefold stains.”
The destroyer of delusion, wrong views, and ignorance, filled with the glory of moral shame (hrī),
he has arisen here in this world as a monument (caitya) honored in heaven and on earth, having established these people— who delight in false paths— in the deathless state. (Lal 23.31)
You are indeed a physician, a skillful healer, the giver of the bliss of immortality;
you remove all the diseases of embodied beings— the afflictions of wrong views, the accumulation of ignorance, and former latent tendencies— following the path of the former Victors.
Therefore, O Leader, you are the supreme physician as you traverse the earth.
The radiance of the moon and sun, the light of the stars and likewise of jewels and fire,
and the splendor of Śakra and Brahmā do not shine before the one who is a mass of glory;
he is the maker of the light of wisdom, the creator of radiance, filled with the glory of light.
Your kinsmen have witnessed this wonder; they bow their heads in prostration.
Speaking of both truth and untruth, O Leader, you possess most sweet speech;
self-restrained, with a peaceful mind, having conquered the senses and calmed the heart,
as a Teacher you instruct the assembly of humans and gods in that which is to be taught.
I pay homage to Śākyamuni, the bull among men, who is honored by gods and humans.

O Knower, you who uphold the foremost discourse on wisdom, you make yourself known throughout the three worlds as the teacher of the three types of knowledge and the three liberations, the remover of the stains of the three impurities.
O Sage, you understand the capacity and incapacity of beings according to their respective inclinations within the discipline.
I pay homage to you, the wonder of the triple-thousand world system, who are honored in heaven and on earth.
Thus, monks, the devaputra Sunirmita, together with his retinue, having praised the Tathāgata, stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata.
(Vaidya 264) Then the divine son Saṃtuṣita, together with the gods belonging to the Tuṣita host, approached the Tathāgata.
Having approached, he completely covered the Tathāgata seated at the seat of awakening with a great net of celestial garments and praised him face-to-face with these verses:
When you dwelt in the Tuṣita abode, you taught the sublime Dharma there;
and that instruction has not been interrupted even today as the sons of the gods practice the Dharma.
We find no satiety in beholding you, nor do we find satiety in hearing the Dharma; O ocean of virtues, lamp of the world, we bow to you with our heads and our minds.
When you departed from the Tuṣita abode, all the states of misfortune were then dried up by you;
when you sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the afflictions of the entire world were stilled.
For whose sake you have attained this sublime awakening after conquering Māra—
since your vows have been fulfilled through asceticism, quickly set in motion the sublime wheel!

In many directions, thousands of living beings are devoted to the Dharma; therefore, having mastered the Dharma, swiftly turn the sublime wheel and liberate thousands of beings from their worldly existences.
Thus, monks, the divine son Santuṣita, together with his retinue, having praised the Tathāgata, stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata.
Then, indeed, the Suyāma gods, headed by the divine son Suyāma, approached the place where the Tathāgata was.

Having approached and honored the Tathāgata seated at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) with various flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments, they praised him face-to-face with these appropriate verses:
"There is no one equal to you anywhere within the realms, whether in ethical discipline, meditative concentration, or likewise in wisdom."
Skilled in the liberations of resolute faith, we bow our heads in homage to you, the Tathāgata.
This magnificent array, which has been created by the gods at the seat of enlightenment,
is not worthy of anyone else other than you, who are honored by gods and men.
You did not arise for nothing, for whose sake you have performed many difficult austerities;
indeed, the deceitful one along with his army has been conquered, and unsurpassed awakening has been attained by you.
Light has been made in the ten directions by the lamp of wisdom; the three worlds have been set ablaze.
You shall dispel the darkness and bestow the unsurpassed eye upon the world.
Though they praise you for many eons, there is no end to the description of even a single pore of your skin;
O Ocean of Virtues, renowned throughout the world, we bow our heads in homage to you, the Tathāgata.
Thus, having praised the Tathāgata, those gods, headed by the divine son Suyāma, stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, together with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa realm, having honored the Tathāgata with arrays of various flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags, praised him with these verses: "O Sage, you are unerring, faultless, always well-established, and like Mount Meru."
O Sage, your radiance of wisdom was proclaimed throughout the ten directions, endowed with the splendor of merit;
you were honored by hundreds of thousands of Buddhas in the past, and it was through this excellence that the army of Māra was defeated by you at the tree of awakening.
O Sage, you are the creator of ethical conduct, learning, concentration, and wisdom; you are the banner and standard of knowledge;

you are the destroyer of old age and death; you are the supreme physician who bestows the eye of the world; you have abandoned the three impurities and all obstructions, with senses stilled and mind at peace.
O Bull of the Śākyas, King of Dharma in the world, we go to you for refuge.
His conduct for awakening became infinite and peerless, arising from the station of vigor;
he possessed the power of wisdom, the power of skillful means, the power of loving-kindness, and the power of brahmic merit.
He who possesses the power of the Ten Powers has now truly arrived at the seat of awakening today, having set out for existence with a strength equal to the infinite.
Seeing the army of infinite beings, the gods became terrified and alarmed,
thinking, "May the King of Śramaṇas, stationed at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), not be harmed! Yet, no fear arose from them, nor did there even be a movement of their bodies.
Struck by the heavy burden, Māra’s army was shaken and defeated.

Just as supreme enlightenment was attained by those of former times upon the lion-throne, so too has it been realized by you; it is equal and identical, for you are not otherwise. With an even mind and an even heart, you have attained the power of omniscience.
Therefore, O Self-Existent One, you are the supreme being in the world and a field of merit for the universe.

Thus, monks, Śakra, the lord of the gods, together with the sons of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa realm, having praised the Tathāgata, stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata.
Then the four Great Kings, together with the sons of the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings, approached the place where the Tathāgata was;
having approached, they were surrounded by hundreds of thousands of apsarases and held garlands and wreaths of abhimukta, campaka, sumana, vārṣika, and dhānuṣkāri flowers.

Having performed worship of the Tathāgata with the sounding of divine music, they praised him with these appropriate verses: "O Sage, salutations to you! Your words are most sweet and your voice is pleasing; like the moon, you bring tranquility to those with serene minds. With a smiling face and a long tongue, you bring supreme joy. (Lal 23.51)
Whatever sweet and lovely sounds there are in all the world of men and gods, let your voice,
released as a gentle resonance, surpass all those who speak.
The passion, hatred, delusion, and afflictions of those who have reached tranquility give rise to a pure, superhuman joy;
having heard the Dharma with untroubled hearts, they all indeed attain noble liberation.
O Bhava, you do not despise the ignorant, nor are you ever intoxicated by the pride of knowledge;
neither haughty nor humble, you stand firm like a mountain in the midst of the ocean.

A great gain has been well-attained here by human beings, for such a being as you has indeed appeared in the world; like the lotus that bestows wealth upon Fortune, you shall likewise bestow the Dharma upon all the world.

Thus, indeed, the gods of the retinue of the Four Great Kings, headed by the Four Great Kings themselves, having praised the Tathāgata seated at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata. Then, the gods from the intermediate space approached the presence of the Tathāgata; for the purpose of honoring his perfect awakening, they covered the entire firmament with nets of jewels, nets of tinkling bells, jeweled parasols, jeweled banners, jeweled silk streamers, and jeweled ear-ornaments, as well as with various pearl necklaces, flower garlands, and crescent-shaped ornaments held by deities who had manifested half their bodies.
Having adorned them, they offered them to the Tathāgata. Having offered them, they praised him to his face with these verses:
"O Sage, we see our own dwelling fixed in the sky, just as beings perceive the conduct in the world."
O Pure Being, having observed your conduct, we do not see any lapse in you who are single-minded.
The Bodhisattvas who have come to offer worship—those leaders of men—have filled the sky;
yet there was no decrease in the celestial palaces, for they indeed have space as their very nature.
The flowers that rained down from the sky, as numerous as those bound in the crest-ornaments of the great trichiliocosm,
fell entirely upon your body, just as rivers enter the ocean.
We see the gods casting down parasols, earrings, strings of garlands, wreaths of campaka flowers, necklaces, full moons, and likewise crescent moons, yet they do not construct them. (Lal_23.59)
In this [assembly], there was clearly no space for Bāla on all sides because of the gods;
yet they perform worship to the Supreme among Men, and in him neither pride nor astonishment arises. (Lal 23.60)
Thus, having praised the Tathāgata seated at the seat of awakening, the gods of the intermediate space stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata.
Then, indeed, the terrestrial gods, for the purpose of making an offering to the Tathāgata, having made the entire surface of the earth thoroughly swept,
smeared with plaster, sprinkled with scented water, and strewn with flowers, and having spread canopies of various fine cloths, presented them to the Tathāgata. They praised him with these verses:
Impregnable like a diamond, this triple-thousandfold world-system stands firm; by means of my diamond-like footing, I am established here at the seat of awakening.
Let my skin and flesh wither away here, and let my bones and marrow dry up, yet I shall not rise from this place until I have touched enlightenment.
All these three thousandfold world-systems, together with their sovereign lords, would not have been able to withstand it without being shattered;
such Bodhisattvas of great speed have arrived, by the soles of whose feet millions of realms were shaken.
A great gain has been well-acquired here by the gods of the earth, wherein this supreme being walks upon the ground;
for by him all the dust of the world is illuminated, as are the shrines throughout the triple-thousandfold world system—how much more so, then, your own body?
"Today we offer you a hundred thousand [gold pieces], as much as the mass of water upon the surface of the earth, and as much as the world's means of subsistence;
we bear all this wind and the three-thousandfold earth—we give it all to you, so enjoy it as you wish."

Wherever you may stand, walk, or lie down, O Bhava, and wherever those sons of the Sugata— the disciples of Gautama— preach the discourse on Dharma, or wherever they hear it, we dedicate all those roots of merit toward awakening.
Thus, indeed, the gods of the earth, having praised the Tathāgata seated at the seat of awakening, stood to one side with palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Chapter on Praise."
START Chapter 24 (Vaidya 269):
The Twenty-fourth Chapter, "Trapuṣa and Bhallika"
Thus, monks, having attained perfect awakening, the Tathāgata—being praised by the gods, without breaking his cross-legged posture and with unblinking eyes—gazed at the king of trees.
Sustained by the food of meditative joy and experiencing bliss, he remained inclined toward the foot of the Bodhi tree for seven nights.
Then, when seven days had passed, the sons of the gods belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) approached the Tathāgata, taking ten thousand jars of scented water.
The sons of the gods belonging to the form realm (rūpāvacara) also approached the Tathāgata, taking ten thousand jars of scented water.
Having approached, they bathed the Bodhi tree and the Tathāgata with the scented water.

Countless gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas smeared their respective bodies with that perfumed water which had fallen upon the body of the Tathāgata, and they resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Even after entering their own abodes, those sons of the gods and others remained never parted from the fragrance of that perfumed water.
And they did not conceive a longing for that fragrance;
rather, through that very joy and gladness born from the mental attention of reverence for the Tathāgata, they became irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then, monks, a son of the gods named Samantakusuma was present, gathered in that very assembly.

He prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and, with palms joined, addressed the Tathāgata thus: "Blessed One, what is the name of this samādhi endowed with which the Tathāgata remained for seven nights in this manner?

Monks, the Tathāgata said to that son of the gods: "Son of the gods, this samādhi is called the Array of the Food of Joy (prītyāhāravyūha), endowed with which the Tathāgata remained for seven nights."
He spoke while remaining in the unbroken cross-legged posture.
Then, monks, the divine son Samantakusuma praised the Tathāgata with these verses:

“I bow my head to the feet of the one who is a mass of glory— feet adorned with wheels, possessing the splendor of the petals of a thousand-petaled lotus, and whose soles have been rubbed by the crowns of the gods.”
Then that son of the gods, with a joyful heart, having paid homage at the feet of the Sugata, spoke these words which dispel doubt and bring peace to humans and gods: *Lalita-vistara 24.2*
Bringer of joy to the Śākya clan, you who bring an end to passion, hatred, and delusion;
with a mind that has withered away all defilements, dispel the doubts of gods and men.
For what reason do the Jinas, the possessors of the ten powers, having realized immeasurable omniscience,
not break their cross-legged posture on the seat of enlightenment for seven days?
But why indeed, O Lion among Men, do you gaze for seven days with an unblinking eye;
you of pure vision, whose eyes are like blossoming hundred-petaled lotuses?
But was this the vow of you alone, or rather that of all the lions among speakers,
by which you did not break your cross-legged posture for seven days at the foot of the king of trees?
Excellent! O you with even, pure teeth, whose mouth has a fragrant scent, speak words that are unfailing for the One Possessed of the Ten Powers; bring joy to men and gods.
The son of the immortals, whose speech was like the moon, said to him: "Listen to me as I speak, O son of the immortals;
I shall explain a small portion of this question."
Just as when a king is consecrated by a host of kinsmen, he does not leave that region for seven days; such indeed is the nature of kings.
In the very same way, the Ten-Powered Ones also become consecrated when their vows are fulfilled;
for seven days, the Victors do not break their cross-legged posture upon the circle of the earth.
Just as a hero gazes upon the hosts of his enemies, completely conquered and leaving none remaining,
so too do the Buddhas gaze upon the afflictions destroyed at the seat of enlightenment.
Here, those desires, anger, and delusions— the very power of which resembles the world—
have been utterly destroyed without remainder, like thieves caught with their stolen goods.
Here, by my wrath, various types of Māras dwelling in the cities have been slain;
all outflows (āsravas) are abandoned, and supreme knowledge has arisen within me.
Here, that craving for existence which performs improper deeds and likewise ignorance—
born from the root of latent tendencies— have been consumed by the sharp fire of knowledge.
Here, this noose of conceptual proliferation— “I” and “mine”— which has its roots deeply embedded and is difficult to follow,
and which is a hard knot of hindrances, has been severed by me with the weapon of wisdom.
"Here, these aggregates, long extended for you, deceptive and ending in destruction, along with their fuel of grasping, have been fully understood by me through wisdom."
"Here, these two-fold delusions and false graspings of yours, which culminate in the great hells, have been extracted by me entirely; furthermore, they shall never arise again."
Here, the forest of the hindrances has been burned away by the power of my roots of virtue;
and the four perversions have been incinerated by me without remainder.
Here, that garland of discursive thoughts is strung upon the threads of perception, forming a noose.
All [of them] have been turned back by the various garlands of the factors of enlightenment.
On this circle of the earth, I have severed sixty-five difficult-to-cross delusions, thirty impurities, and forty evils. (Lal 24.20)
The sixteen unguarded states and the eighteen elements within this great mandala—
these twenty-five hardships have been severed by me while remaining here.
Twenty Rajastaras and twenty-eight Vitrāsas of the world have been transcended by me here, having exerted the power and prowess of my vigor.
In this way, I have fully realized five hundred of the lion's roars of the Buddhas;
I have fully realized a full hundred thousand dharmas.
"Here, my ninety-eight latent tendencies, together with their roots and all their extensions,
have been utterly consumed by the fire of gnosis, along with the sprouts of their active outbursts."
The river of craving, which arises from doubt and indecision, is born of the dullness of false views and has its root in the unwholesome—
this river with its threefold current has been dried up by the sun of wisdom.

The abandonment of hypocrisy and flattery, along with the faults of deceit, stinginess, and envy—here, that forest of afflictions has been cut down and consumed by the fire of the Vinaya. *Lalitavistara* 24.26.
Here, those roots of dispute of yours—which lead to dragging one into miserable and perilous states—have been vomited out by the excellent purgatives of the speech of the Noble Ones. (Lal 24.27)
"Here, by means of the attainment of knowledge, qualities, and meditative concentration, I have reached the end of all weeping, crying out, grieving, and lamenting without exception."
The floods, the bonds of attachment, the knots, the sorrows, the thorns, and intoxication and negligence—
all these have been conquered by me here, having attained the samādhi of the method of truth.
Here, by me, the trees of existence— with their roots grown deep through conceptualization and their thickets of afflictions—
have been cut down entirely with the axe of mindfulness and burned by the fire of wisdom.

Right here, indeed, that exceedingly powerful Māra, who holds the three worlds in his sway, has been struck down by me with the sword of wisdom— this deceitful-souled one— just as the lord of the Daityas was slain by Indra.
Here, this entire web that moves through twenty-six realms upon the circle of the earth has been cut by the powerful sword of wisdom and consumed by the fire of knowledge.
"Here, those root afflictions of yours, together with their latent tendencies, which give rise to suffering and grief,
have been uprooted by me without remainder by means of the plowshare of the power of wisdom."
Here, my eye of wisdom has been purified for the sake of beings who are pure by nature;
by the great ointment of knowledge, the vast film of delusion has been shattered.

Here, these oceans of existence— consisting of the four elements, churned by the sea-monsters of intoxication and possessing vast cravings— have been dried up by me with the rays of the sun of mindfulness and tranquility. (Lalita-vistara 24.35)
Here, the great fire of passion, with its fuel-heap of sense objects and its smoky fumes of discursive thought,
though blazing intensely, has been extinguished by the cool water of the essence of liberation.

Here, these layers of latent tendencies—flashes of relish and the thunder of discursive thoughts—have been shaken off and brought to dissolution by the force of the wind of the power of my vigor. *Lalitavistara* 24.37.

For here, by means of the powerful sword of wisdom and having attained the stainless concentration of mindfulness, I have slain this enemy who follows through existence— the adversary that is the movement of my own mind— without exception.
Here, that army of Namuci— bearing banners on its crest, elevated with elephants, horses, and chariots, and possessing deformed shapes— was utterly destroyed upon encountering loving-kindness.

Here, having attained the auspiciousness of meditative concentration, I have bound all these steeds of the six sense-faculties— which are ever intoxicated with passion and enriched by the five qualities— without exception.
"Here, by means of unimpeded samādhi, I have attained the complete and total abandonment of attraction and aversion, ending all strife and disputes."
In this state, all things cherished by me, both internal and external, have been completely exhausted;
having attained the meditative absorption that perceives that both the imagined and the discriminated are empty.
In this world, all mortals, from the gods up to the peak of existence, were cherished by me;
yet, having attained the irreversible samādhi, I have abandoned them all without exception.
And all those bonds of existence have been liberated by me here;
having attained the threefold liberation through the power of wisdom, they are entirely freed in this world.
"Here, by perceiving the [true] cause, I have indeed conquered the three types of causalists:
the notion of permanence and impermanence, and the notion of pleasure, pain, and the self."
Here, this accumulation of my karmic dispositions, which had arisen and was rooted in the six sense-bases,
has been severed at the foot of the king of trees by the blow of universal impermanence.

Here, having pierced the long-standing darkness within the field of existence— which was turbid with the gloom of delusion, corrupted by wickedness, and filled with pride and anger— the sun of knowledge has shone forth.

Here, by means of the ship of the power of vigor, I have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, which has passion and intoxication as its crocodiles, craving as its waves and water, and wrong views as its sharks.
In this regard, I have realized that which the Buddha burns away—passion, hatred, and delusion—as well as the discursive thoughts of the mind, like moths fallen into a forest fire. (Lal 24.49)
"Here I have indeed traveled for a long time— through immeasurable billions of trillions of eons—
afflicted by the path of saṃsāra, now rested and with my fever of suffering extinguished. (Lal 24.50)
Here, I have realized that which was not attained by any other proponents;
it is the nectar for the sake of the world's welfare, the end of old age, death, sorrow, and suffering.
Wherein suffering arises from the aggregates and suffering born of craving through the sense-bases shall no longer arise— here I have entered the city of fearlessness.
"Here, these internal enemies of yours, vast and all-encompassing, have been recognized by me;
they have been bound, utterly consumed by fire, and their abodes of rebirth have been destroyed by me."
In this world, I have realized that for whose sake I have, throughout millions of billions of eons,
sacrificed my own flesh and eyes, as well as many jewels, for the sake of the deathless.
Here, I have realized that which was realized by the immeasurable Victors of the past—
He whose sweet and charming voice is renowned throughout the worlds.
Here, I have realized that this world, which arises dependently, is empty;
it follows every moment of thought and is like a mirage or a city of the Gandharvas.
Indeed, this pure and excellent eye of mine here is such that I behold all world-systems as if they were fruits placed in the palm of my hand.
I have attained here these three sciences: the recollection of former existences;
I remember [them] for immeasurable millions of eons, as one who has awakened remembers a dream. (Lal 24.58)
By which gods and men, whose perceptions were perverted and who were deluded, were set ablaze;
even that very nectar-essence, which is thus and not otherwise, has been drunk by me here.
For the sake of which the Ones Possessing the Ten Powers cultivate loving-kindness toward all beings—
having conquered by the power of that loving-kindness, I have drunk this essence of the nectar in this place.
For the sake of which the possessors of the ten powers cultivate compassion toward all sentient beings;
having conquered by the power of that compassion, this essence of nectar has been drunk by me here.
For the sake of which the Ten-Powered Ones cultivate joy toward all sentient beings;
having conquered by the power of that joy, I have drunk this essence of nectar here.
For the sake of which the Possessors of the Ten Powers cultivate equanimity for millions of eons—
having conquered that with the powers of equanimity, this essence of nectar has been drunk by me here.

That which was drunk by the Lions among Jinas of the past— by those endowed with the ten powers, more numerous than the sands of the river Gaṅgā— that very essence of nectar has indeed been drunk by me here.
Whatever words were spoken by Māra here as he arrived with his army—
"I shall not break this cross-legged posture until I have reached the further shore of old age and death. (Lal 24.65)
For ignorance has been shattered by me with the blazing, firm vajra of wisdom;
and the state of the Ten Powers has been attained—therefore, I break this cross-legged posture.
Arhatship has been attained by me; my outflows are exhausted without remainder.
The army of Namuci is shattered; therefore, I break this cross-legged posture.
All five door-panels of the hindrances have been shattered by me here;
the creeper of craving has been cut asunder—indeed, I shall now break this cross-legged posture.
Then that moon among men, rising slowly from his seat and sitting upon the auspicious throne, accepted the great consecration.
With thousands of precious jars filled with various scented waters,
the hosts of gods bathe the Friend of the World, who has attained the perfection of the qualities of the Ten Powers.
With thousands of musical instruments on all sides, millions of billions of gods,
together with myriads of apsarases, perform incomparable worship in their entirety.
Thus indeed, O sons of gods, with its cause, its condition,
and its basis, the Jinas do not break their cross-legged posture upon the circle of the earth for seven days.

Thus, monks, having realized awakening, the Tathāgata remained on that very seat for the first seven days, thinking: "Here I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; here I have brought an end to the suffering of birth, old age, and death, which is without beginning or end.
During the second seven days, the Tathāgata practiced long walking meditation, encompassing the entire trichiliocosm great thousandfold world system.

During the third week, the Tathāgata gazed unblinking at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), thinking: "It is here that I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and brought an end to the suffering of birth, old age, and death, which has no beginning or end.
During the fourth week, the Tathāgata walked back and forth on the short promenade, extending from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.
Then indeed Māra, the Evil One, approached the place where the Tathāgata was;
having approached, he said this to the Tathāgata: "May the Blessed One pass into parinirvāṇa;
may the Sugata pass into parinirvāṇa."
"It is now the time for the Blessed One’s final nirvāṇa.

When this was said, monks, the Tathāgata spoke thus to Māra, the Evil One: "I will not enter final nirvāṇa, O Evil One, as long as my elder monks have not become disciplined, proficient, well-trained, confident, learned, and practitioners of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma."

They are capable themselves of illuminating the knowledge of the Teacher, and of suppressing the intentions of whatever opposing disputants arise through the Dharma, and having inspired confidence in them, they shall teach the Dharma accompanied by miracles. O Evil One, I will not pass into final nirvāṇa until the lineage of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha has been established by me in the world.

"Immeasurable bodhisattvas will not yet have received their predictions of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. I, the Evil One, shall not enter final nirvāṇa until my fourfold assembly has become disciplined, trained, proficient, and confident, and until they are able to teach the Dharma with miraculous displays."

Then indeed, Māra the Evil One, having heard these words, stepped aside and stood there, suffering, dejected, and full of remorse, with his head cast down, scratching the earth with a stick, thinking, "He has transcended my domain."

Then those three daughters of Māra—Rati, Arati, and Tṛṣṇā—addressed Māra, the Evil One, with this verse: "Why are you dejected, father? Tell us, if that man can be caught with the snare of passion, we shall lead him away like an elephant. (Lal 24.73)
"And having brought him here quickly, we shall bring him under your control.
Māra said:
"The Sugata is an Arhat in the world; he would not fall under the power of passion."
For he has indeed transcended my domain; therefore, I grieve most bitterly.
Then, out of feminine fickleness, even though they were unaware of the Tathāgata’s power while he was still a bodhisattva, they disregarded their father’s words;
having reached the prime of youth and possessing full maturity, they approached the presence of the Tathāgata with the intent of deceiving his vision and employed all the wiles of women.
And the Tathāgata did not take them to heart;
moreover, they became even more decrepit with old age.
Then, having gone into the presence of their father, they spoke thus:
"You speak the truth to us, dear one; he is not led away by passion, for he has already transcended my domain; therefore, I grieve most bitterly."
If he were to behold that form which has been created by us for the purpose of destroying Gautama, then his heart would burst asunder.
Therefore, dear father, it would be well if you were to cause this body, worn out by old age, to vanish.
Māra said:
"I do not see any man in this world, including the realms of the moving and the unmoving,
who could otherwise alter the empowerment of the Buddha."
"Go quickly and confess your own transgression to the Sage;
he will restore your entire body to its former state, according to his wish."
Then, having approached, they asked the Tathāgata for forgiveness: "May the Blessed One accept our transgression;

may the Sugata accept our transgression—[the transgression] of us who were like children, like fools, like the ignorant, unskilled, and lacking in worldly knowledge, in that we thought the Blessed One was to be reviled.
Then the Tathāgata addressed them with a verse:
You might scratch a mountain with your claws, or chew iron with your teeth;
you might split a mountain with your head, or seek a footing in the bottomless deep.
Therefore, daughter, I accept your transgression.
Why is that? Noble one, in the Dharma and Vinaya, it is an increase [in merit] for one who, having seen a transgression as a transgression, confesses it and undertakes restraint for the future.

In the fifth week, monks, the Tathāgata was dwelling in the abode of the nāga king Mucilinda during a week of great stormy weather. Then the nāga king Mucilinda, having emerged from his own abode, coiled his body seven times around the body of the Tathāgata and covered him with his hoods, thinking: "Lest cold winds should strike the body of the Blessed One."

From the eastern direction as well, many other nāga kings arrived, coiled their bodies seven times around the body of the Tathāgata, and covered him with their hoods, thinking: "May cold winds not strike the body of the Blessed One.
Just as they did from the eastern direction, so too did the nāga kings arrive from the southern, western, and northern directions [to do the same] for the Tathāgata.
Coiling their bodies seven times around him, they covered the Blessed One’s body with their hoods, thinking, "May cold winds not strike the Blessed One’s body.
And that mass of the serpent king's coils stood as high as Meru, the lord of mountains.
And those dragon kings had never before experienced such happiness as they did during those seven days and nights from being in close proximity to the body of the Tathāgata.

Then, at the end of the seven days, those dragon kings, perceiving that the foul weather had passed, withdrew their coils from the body of the Tathāgata; having bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata and circumambulated him three times to the right, they each departed for their own respective abodes.
The Naga King Mucilinda, too, having bowed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata and circumambulated him three times, entered his own abode.
In the sixth week, the Tathāgata went from the abode of Mucilinda to the foot of the Nyagrodha tree belonging to the cowherd [Ajapāla].

And on the way, between the abode of Mucilinda and that of the cowherd, on the bank of the river Nairañjanā, the Carakas, Parivrājakas, Vṛddhaśrāvakas, Gautamas, Nirgranthas, Ājīvikas, and others, seeing the Tathāgata, addressed him: "Has this unseasonable storm been spent by the Blessed Gautama in perfect comfort?"
Then, monks, at that time the Tathāgata uttered this inspired utterance:
"For one who is contented and sees the Dharma as it has been heard, solitude is blissful;
for one who is self-restrained toward living beings in the world, there is the bliss of being free from harm."
Detachment from the world is happiness, the complete transcendence of evils;
in this human realm, this indeed is the supreme happiness.
Monks, the Tathāgata beheld the world ablaze, burning with birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata uttered this inspired utterance: "This world is born of torment by means of sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells."
Terrified by fear, one seeks further fear through the thirst for existence.

In the seventh week, the Tathāgata was dwelling at the foot of the Tārāyaṇa tree. Now at that time, two brothers from the northern region named Trapuṣa and Bhallika, who were wise and skillful merchants, having taken various goods and having gained great profit, were traveling from the southern region toward the northern region.
They were traveling with a great caravan consisting of five hundred fully laden wagons.
Of those two, there were two noble oxen named Sujāta and Kīrti;
they had no fear of being caught or held up.
Where other oxen could not pull, there those two were yoked;
and wherever there was danger ahead, there they went.
They stood as if pinned by stakes;
they were not driven by a goad,
but were driven instead by a handful of blue lotuses or a garland of jasmine flowers.
Near the Tārāyaṇa tree, through the empowerment of a deity dwelling in the Kṣīrikā forest, all those carts came to a standstill and would not move;
furthermore, the cloths and all the parts of the carts were being torn and shattered.
The wheels of the carts sank into the ground up to their hubs, and despite all their efforts, those carts would not move.
They were struck with wonder and fear, thinking: "What indeed could be the cause here?
What is this transformation that these carts have come to a standstill on dry land?"
They yoked those two oxen, Sujāta and Kīrti;
yet even they would not pull, though being led by Sotpalahasta and Sumanādāmaka.
This thought occurred to them: "Without a doubt, there is some danger ahead, since even these two will not pull."
Horse messengers were dispatched ahead; the horse messengers returned and reported,
"There is no danger whatsoever."
That deity also revealed her true form and comforted them, saying, "Do not be afraid.

Those two oxen then pulled the cart toward where the Tathāgata was, until they beheld the Tathāgata blazing like Vaiśvānara, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, appearing as if he had just risen.

Seeing the Sun blazing with splendor, they were struck with wonder and thought: "Who indeed is this? Is it Brahmā who has arrived here, or Śakra the Lord of the Devas, or Vaiśravaṇa, or the Sun and Moon, or perhaps some mountain deity or river deity?"
Then the Tathāgata displayed his saffron-colored robes.
Thereupon they said, "This man is indeed a renunciant clothed in saffron; there is no fear from him.
Having gained confidence, they said to one another, "This renunciant will surely be one who eats only at the proper time."
"Is there anything?
They replied, "There is honey for refreshment and sugar-cane stalks. Taking that honey for refreshment and the sugar-cane stalks, they approached the place where the Tathāgata was.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, circumambulated him three times, and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, they said this to the Tathāgata: "May the Blessed One accept this alms-bowl out of compassion for us."
Then, monks, this thought occurred to the Tathāgata: "It would indeed be excellent if I were to accept it with my two hands.
But in what manner was it accepted by the previous Tathāgatas, the perfectly enlightened ones?
He then understood: "By means of a bowl."

Thus, monks, knowing that it was the time for the Tathāgata’s meal, at that very moment the four Great Kings came from the four directions, took four golden bowls, and presented them to the Tathāgata, saying:
"May the Blessed One accept these four golden [bowls]."
"Out of compassion for us, [the Tathāgata] did not accept those bowls,
considering that they were not suitable for a śramaṇa.
In this same way, there were four made of silver, four made of beryl, four made of crystal, four made of musāragalva, and four made of emerald."
Then, taking four bowls made entirely of precious gems, they offered them to the Tathāgata; however, considering that they were not suitable for a śramaṇa, the Tathāgata did not accept them.
Then, monks, it occurred again to the Tathāgata: "In what kind of bowls did the previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones accept [alms]?
He knew: "In stone bowls.
And such a thought arose in the Tathāgata.

(Vaidya 278) Then indeed, the Great King Vaiśravaṇa addressed the other three Great Kings: "Friends, these four stone bowls were given to us by the sons of the gods belonging to the blue host; regarding this, the thought occurred to us:"
"We shall enjoy ourselves among these.
Then a son of the gods named Vairocana, belonging to the blue-bodied class, spoke thus to us: "You shall eat from these vessels; you should maintain them as being honored as *caityas*."
There will be a Victor named Śākyamuni; you should present these bowls to him.

"O noble ones, this is the time and the occasion to present the vessels for Śākyamuni; having performed our worship, we shall give the bowls accompanied by the sounding of songs and musical instruments. (Lal 24.85)
For he possesses an indestructible vessel made of Dharma, whereas these vessels made of stone are fragile;
no other is capable of receiving [this gift]. Come, let us go for the sake of making him a recipient.

Then the four great kings, together with their respective retinues and followers, approached the Tathāgata with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, and the sounding of musical instruments, cymbals, and songs; taking those bowls with their own hands, they went to where the Tathāgata was.
Having approached and performed worship to the Tathāgata, they offered those bowls, filled with divine flowers, to the Tathāgata.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Tathāgata: "These four great kings, full of faith and confidence, are offering me four stone bowls.
Yet, four stone bowls are not appropriate for me;
I shall accept only one."
"The three of them would feel dejected, thinking:
'What if I were to take these four bowls and empower one of them?
Then, monks, the Tathāgata extended his right hand and addressed the Great King Vaiśravaṇa in verse:"
"Offer this vessel to the Sugata; you shall become a vessel for the Supreme Vehicle.
For by giving a vessel to those like us, one's mindfulness and intelligence never fail."
Then, monks, the Tathāgata, out of compassion, accepted that bowl from the great king Vaiśravaṇa.
Having accepted it, he addressed the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra with a verse:
(Vaidya 279)
Whoever gives a vessel to the Tathāgata never loses mindfulness or wisdom;
having passed the time in great happiness, they eventually awaken to the state of coolness.
Then, monks, the Tathāgata, out of compassion, accepted that bowl from the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Having accepted it, he addressed the great king Virūḍhaka with a verse:
"Since you give this pure vessel to the Tathāgata whose mind is pure,"
"You shall soon become one of pure mind, praised in the world of gods and men."
Then, monks, the Tathāgata, out of compassion, accepted that bowl from the great king Virūḍhaka. Having accepted it, he addressed the great king Virūpākṣa with a verse:
"The Tathāgata, whose conduct is flawless and whose behavior is flawless, has a flawless vessel."
With an unbroken mind you give with faith; thus your merit and reward shall be unbroken.
Monks, the Tathāgata, out of compassion, accepted that bowl from the great king Virūpākṣa.
Having accepted it, he empowered it to become a single bowl through the power of his resolve.
And at that moment, he uttered this inspired utterance:
In a previous existence, I gave away alms-bowls, filling them with fruit and making them beautiful;
because of that, these four well-proportioned bowls are now being offered by the four gods of great supernatural power.
In this regard, it is said:
Having gazed for seven nights at the excellent Bodhi tree, that steadfast one, the seer of ultimate reality,
shook the earth in six ways and rose up with the gait of a lion, he who is the lion among men.

Moving with the slow, majestic gait of a lordly elephant, the Sage gradually arrived at the foot of the Tārāyaṇa tree; there he sat down, as immovable as Mount Meru, and applied himself to meditation and samādhi.
And at that time, Trapuṣa and Bhallika, the two brothers, together with a caravan of merchants,
entered the flowering Sāla grove with five wagons filled with wealth.
And by the power of the great seer, the wheels sank into the earth to the depth of an axle-hole in an instant;
seeing her in such a state, a great fear arose among the group of merchants.

With swords in hand and arrows and spears in their grasp, searching for a deer in the forest, they beheld him—this who was the Jina with a face like the autumn moon, like the thousand-rayed sun released from the clouds. *Lal_24.96*
Having abandoned anger and removed pride, they bowed their heads and reflected, "Who is this?
Then a voice from the sky spoke: "This is indeed a Buddha, who acts for the benefit of the world."
For seven days and nights, this compassionate one has not partaken of food or drink.
If you desire the pacification of your own afflictions, feed him whose body and mind have been cultivated.
Having heard that sweet sound and having bowed to and circumambulated the Jina, they were filled with joy; then, together with their companions, they resolved to offer alms to the Jina.
At that time, monks, there was a herd of cattle belonging to the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika living in a frontier village.
Then, at that very time and on that occasion, those cows yielded cream-of-ghee (*sarpiṣmaṇḍa*).
Thereupon, the cowherds took that cream-of-ghee and approached the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika.
Having approached, they reported this matter: "Venerable sirs, you should know that all those cows have yielded ghee-cream (*sarpiṣmaṇḍa*).
Is this auspicious or not?
Thereupon, the Brahmins, being by nature greedy, said: "This is inauspicious for Brahmins."
"The great sacrifice is to be performed."
Furthermore, monks, at that time there was a brahmin named Śikhaṇḍin, a paternal kinsman from a previous birth of the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika, who had been reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having manifested the form of a brahmin, he addressed those merchants with verses:
"In the past, the Tathāgata who fulfilled your aspiration made this vow:
'Having eaten our food, he shall turn the wheel of Dharma.'"
And this very vow has been fulfilled; having attained awakening, the Tathāgata would have food presented to him, and having eaten it, he would set the Wheel of Dharma in motion.
It is a great auspiciousness and a favorable star for you that cows yield ghee;
this is the power of that great seer who performs meritorious deeds.
Having thus exhorted the merchants, Śikhaṇḍin returned to his palace;
all those called Trapuṣas became uplifted in spirit.
When the milk from a thousand cows had been collected in its entirety,
they took the finest essence from it and prepared that food with great reverence.
The jewel bowl named Candana, which was worth one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] for a single pala,
having been made clean, well-washed, stainless, and level at its rim, was filled with food.
Taking the honey and the jewel bowl, they approached the root of the Tārāyaṇī tree where the Teacher was;
"Accept this out of compassion, favor us, and partake of this exquisite food. *Lalita-vistara* 24.106.

Out of compassion for both brothers, and knowing their former aspirations as they were set forth toward awakening, the Teacher accepted [the food] and partook of it; having eaten, he cast the bowl into the expanse of the sky.
Indeed, the king of the gods named Subrahman, who took that bowl of excellent jewels,
even now, accompanied by other deities, continues to worship it in the Brahma-world.
Then, at that time, the Tathāgata inspired these merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika with this [verse]:
"It is divine, auspicious, a bringer of well-being to the quarters, and an accomplisher of goals."
May all your purposes be successful as you govern, and may everything quickly turn auspicious for you.
May prosperity be in your right hand; may prosperity be established in your left.
May prosperity be in all your limbs, standing upon your head like a garland.
For the merchants seeking wealth who have set out toward the ten directions,
may great profits arise, and may they experience the dawn of happiness.
Whatever business you have that leads you toward the eastern direction,
may the constellations situated in that quarter protect you.
Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, and likewise Aśleṣā— these belong to the eastern direction and the others.
Thus, these seven illustrious constellations, the guardians of the world, stationed in the eastern quarter— may the gods protect [them] on all sides.
And their sovereign king, renowned as Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the lord of all gandharvas, shall protect [her] together with the Sun.
He also has many sons, wise and of one name—eighty-one in total, all named Indra and possessed of great strength. May they also protect you with health and auspiciousness. (Lal 24.116)
In the eastern quarter, indeed, are eight divine maidens:
Jayantī, Vijayantī, Siddhārthā, and Aparājitā; Lal_24.117 //
Nandottarā, Nandiṣeṇā, Nandinī, and Nandavardhanī—
may they also protect you with health and auspiciousness.
In the eastern quarter, there is a shrine named Cāpāla;
it was inhabited by the Jinas, the Arhats, and the Protectors. May they also protect you with health and auspiciousness!
May the directions be safe for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, return protected by all the gods.
If you should travel to the southern direction for any purpose whatsoever, may the constellations that preside over that direction protect you. (Lal 24.121)
Maghā, the two Phālgunīs, Hastā, Citrā as the fifth,
Svāti, and Viśākhā— these belong to the southern direction. (Lalita-vistara 24.122)
Thus, these seven illustrious lunar mansions, the guardians of the world, have been assigned to the southern quarter; may they protect you from all sides.
And their sovereign king is known as Virūḍhaka;
may he, the lord of all kumbhāṇḍas, protect [the world] together with Yama.
He also has many sons, wise and of one name—ninety-one in all, named Indra, possessed of great strength. May they also protect you with health and auspiciousness. (Lal 24.125)
In this southern quarter of the world, there are eight divine maidens:
Śrīmatī, Yaśomatī, Yaśasvatī, Yaśaprāptā, and Yaśodharā.
Well-risen, foremost, well-awakened, and bringing happiness—
may they also protect you with health and auspiciousness.
In this southern quarter, there is a divine monastery named Padma,
which is eternally ablaze with splendor and illumines all things;
may they also protect you with health and auspiciousness.
May the directions be secure for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, return, protected by all the gods.
If you must go to the western direction for any purpose whatsoever,
may the constellations that preside over that direction protect you.
Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, and Dṛḍhavīryatā;
the two Āṣāḍhas, Abhijit, and Śravaṇa is the seventh.
Thus, these seven illustrious constellations, the guardians of the world, have been assigned to the western quarter; may they protect you at all times.
And their sovereign king is known as Virūpākṣa;
may he, the lord of all nāgas, together with Varuṇa, protect [you].
He also has many sons, wise and of one name—ninety-one in total, all named Indra and possessed of great strength. May they also protect you with health and auspiciousness. (Lal 24.134)
In this western quarter, there are eight divine maidens:
Alambuṣā, Miśrakeśī, Puṇḍarīkā, and likewise Aruṇā.
Ekādaśā, Navamikā, Śītā, Kṛṣṇā, and Draupadī—
may they also protect you with health and auspiciousness. (Lal 24.136)
In this western quarter of the world stands the mountain named Aṣṭāṅga,
the foundation of the moon and sun; may it grant you the eightfold aim,
and may it protect you with health and auspiciousness.
May the directions be secure for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, return home protected by all the gods.
If you must go to the northern direction for any purpose whatsoever,
may the constellations presiding over that direction protect you.
Dhaniṣṭhā and Śatabhiṣā, the two [asterisms] Pūrvā and Uttarā,
Revatī, Aśvinī, and Bharaṇī is the seventh.
Thus, these seven illustrious constellations, the guardians of the world, have been assigned to the northern quarter; may they protect you at all times.
And may their sovereign king, Kubera, who is borne by men,
the lord of all yakṣas, together with Māṇibhadra, protect them.
He also has many sons, all of one name, wise and of great strength, numbering ninety-one, each named Indra; may they also protect you with health and auspiciousness. (Lal 24.143)
In this northern direction, there are eight divine maidens:
Ilādevī, Surādevī, Pṛthvī, and Padmāvatī.
O Great King, Hope, Faith, Modesty, and Splendor are present; may they also protect you with health and auspiciousness. (Lal 24.145)
In this northern quarter of the world is the Gandhamādana mountain,
the abode of yakṣas and spirits, variegated and beautiful to behold;
may they also protect you with health and auspiciousness.
May the directions be secure for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, return protected by all the gods.
There were twenty-eight constellations, seven in each of the four directions,
and thirty-two divine maidens, eight in each of the four directions.
There are eight types of ascetics, eight types of brahmins, and eight types of merchants in the countryside.
May those eight gods, together with Indra, protect you from all sides.
May there be well-being for you as you go; may there be well-being for you as you return.
May there be well-being as you behold your kinsmen; may your kinsmen behold you with well-being.
May the Yakṣas together with Indra and the Great Kings, out of compassion for the Arhat, grant you well-being everywhere; may you go forth and attain the auspicious nectar of immortality.
O Brahmin, you have been protected by Vāsava, by those with minds liberated from outflows, and by those free from taints;
you have always been shown compassion by the Nāgas and Yakṣas. May you protect your life for a full hundred autumns.
The peerless Guide, the Lord of the World, circumambulated them from the right and said:
"By this wholesome deed, you shall become Jinas named Madhusambhava."
This was the first prediction of the Jina, the Leader of the World, given by him without attachment;
afterwards, infinite and numerous bodhisattvas were predicted, saying, "They shall not fall back from awakening."
Having heard this prophecy of the Jina, those two brothers, with uplifted hearts and supreme joy, together with their companions, took refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma.
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Chapter on Trapuṣa and Bhallika."
