Thus, monks, while the Tathāgata was staying at the foot of the Tārāyaṇa tree, having just attained perfect awakening, alone, in seclusion, and in meditative absorption, there occurred within him this reflection in accordance with the ways of the world: "Alas, this Dharma that I have realized and fully awakened to is profound— peaceful, utterly tranquil, completely stilled, sublime, difficult to see, and difficult to understand."
This is beyond the sphere of reasoning; it is not accessible to discursive thought.

It is noble, to be experienced by the wise and the learned—namely, the relinquishing of all substrates of existence, which is neither felt nor caused to be felt, the cessation of all that is felt, the ultimate truth, and without abode.
It is the state of cooling, without grasping, without appropriation, unmanifest, incapable of being made manifest, unconditioned, and transcending the six sense objects.
It is without conceptualization, without discursive thought, and inexpressible; it is without sound, without noise, and beyond verbal description;
it is invisible, non-obstructive, and transcends all objects of perception; it is the cessation of the phenomena of tranquility.
Emptiness is non-apprehension;
the exhaustion of craving is dispassion, cessation, and nirvana.
If I were to teach this Dharma to others, [they would not understand it].
If they were not to understand,
that would be for me a fruitless exhaustion and a mistaken exertion, as well as a failure in teaching the Dharma at the proper time;
what if I were instead to dwell with little concern, in silence?
And at that time, he spoke this verse:
"I have attained a Dharma that is profound, peaceful, stainless, luminous, immortal, and unconditioned.
Yet, I do not know how another might understand it if I were to teach it; therefore, I shall surely dwell in silence within the forest. (Lal 25.1)
For the nature of phenomena is free from the path of speech and words, and like the sky, it is unstained;
liberated from mind, intellect, and discursive thought, the Supreme One knows that which is most wondrous.
Furthermore, this entry that is free from the application of meaningless words cannot be entered by means of syllables;
for those beings who have performed their duties under previous Victors, having heard this Dharma, they indeed place their faith in it.
Furthermore, there is no phenomenon here whatsoever, nor does that exist for which non-existence could be predicated;
for one who understands the succession of causes and actions, there is neither existence nor non-existence in this world.

For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, I practiced in the presence of former Jinas; yet I had not attained this patience wherein there is no self, no sentient being, and no life-principle. (Lal 25.5)
When I attained this patient acceptance— that here no one dies and no one is born—
and that all these phenomena are by nature selfless, then the Buddha named Dīpaṃkara prophesied my destiny.
My compassion for the entire world is infinite; I do not wait for others to entreat me.
But when the people are filled with faith, O Brahmā, at their request I shall set the wheel of Dharma in motion.
And this Dharma should be accepted by me only if Brahmā, having prostrated at my feet, should entreat me:
"Proclaim the stainless, sublime Dharma; there are beings who understand it and are worthy vessels. (Lal 25.8)
Thus, monks, at that time the Tathāgata emitted a radiance from the circle of hair between his eyebrows, by which radiance the great trichiliocosm was suffused with a vast, golden-colored light.
Then indeed, Śikhin, the Great Brahmā, lord of the ten trichiliocosms, through the very power of the Buddha and by means of the Tathāgata’s own mind,
understood the reflection in the Tathāgata’s mind: that the Blessed One’s mind was inclined toward inactivity and not toward teaching the Dharma.
This thought occurred to him: "What if I were to approach the Tathāgata and entreat him to set the wheel of Dharma in motion?"

Then, at that time, the Great Brahmā Śikhin addressed the other sons of the gods belonging to the Brahma-realm: "Alas, friends, this world is perishing; it is truly being destroyed, in that the Tathāgata, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, inclines his mind toward inaction rather than toward teaching the Dharma.
What if we were to approach the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, and entreat him to turn the wheel of the Dharma?"
Then, monks, the Great Brahmā Śikhin, surrounded and escorted by six million eight hundred thousand brahmins, approached the Tathāgata.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata and, with palms joined, addressed the Tathāgata thus: "Alas, Blessed One, this world is perishing!
Alas, Blessed One, this world is being destroyed!"
Since the Tathāgata, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, inclines his mind toward a lack of exertion rather than toward teaching the Dharma,
it would be well if the Blessed One would teach the Dharma.
"May the Sugata teach the Dharma!
There are beings who are of good disposition, easy to instruct, capable, worthy, and able to understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken.
And at that time, he spoke this verse:
Having fully realized the great and supreme mandala of wisdom and having emitted rays of light into the ten directions,
you now stand as the sun among speakers, the one who awakens the lotuses of men with the rays of wisdom, remaining in equanimity.
Having invited beings with the wealth of the noble ones and having comforted many millions of living creatures,
it is not fitting for you, O Kinsman of the World, that you should neglect the world through silence.
Beat the drum of the supreme Dharma and quickly blow the conch of the true Dharma!
Raise high the great sacrificial pillar of the Dharma and kindle the great lamp of the Dharma!
Rain down the supreme water of Dharma; ferry across those who stand in this ocean of existence.
Liberate these beings afflicted by great disease; bring peace to those scorched by the fire of the afflictions.
Do indeed show us the path of peace—secure, auspicious, free from decay, and without sorrow.
O Protector, have compassion for those who stand on the wrong path, protectorless, because they have not entered the way to Nirvāṇa.
Open the doors of liberation and proclaim that unshakable method of Dharma;
O Protector, purify the supreme eye of Dharma for people who have been born blind.
Neither in the world of Brahmā, nor in the world of the gods, nor in the world of yakṣas, gandharvas, and humans,
is there anyone other than you, O Moon among Men, who can remove birth and old age from the world.
I am your petitioner, O King of Dharma, having surpassed all the gods by my conduct;
by this merit, may I too swiftly set in motion the supreme wheel of Dharma. (Lal_25.16)
Monks, the Tathāgata, out of compassion and for the sake of favoring the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, consented to Śikhin Brahmā by remaining silent.

Then, monks, the Great Brahmā Śikhin, perceiving through the Tathāgata’s silence that his request had been granted, scattered divine sandalwood powder and aloe-wood powder over the Tathāgata. Filled with joy and rapture, he vanished right there.

Then, monks, for the sake of generating reverence for the light of the Dharma of the Tathāgata, for the purpose of increasing the roots of merit of the Great Brahmā Śikhin through his repeated entreaty of the Tathāgata, and on account of the extreme profundity and sublimity of the Dharma—

Furthermore, while he was alone in seclusion and withdrawn in meditation, this kind of reflection arose in his mind: "Truly, this Dharma I have fully awakened to is profound, subtle, precise, difficult to understand, beyond logic, not within the sphere of logic, to be realized by the wise and the learned, contrary to the whole world, hard to see, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, and the stilling of all conditioned formations."
The complete cutting off of all darkness is emptiness, non-apprehension, the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation, and nirvana.
If I were to teach this Dharma, and others were not to comprehend it, [it would be a weariness for me].
That would be a supreme vexation for me;
what if I were to dwell instead in a state of complete lack of concern?

Then, monks, Śikhin the Great Brahmā, through the power of the Buddha, once again perceived with his own mind this very reflection of the Tathāgata’s mind. Having understood it, he approached Śakra, the lord of the gods, and having approached him, he said to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "O Kauśika, you should know that the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, is inclined toward a lack of exertion and not toward teaching the Dharma.
Alas, O Kauśika, this world will perish!"

"Alas, Kauśika, this world will perish! Alas, Kauśika, this world will be cast into the great darkness of ignorance, since the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has inclined toward a lack of exertion rather than toward the proclamation of the Dharma."
"Why do we not go to entreat the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, to turn the wheel of Dharma?
For what reason?
Because Tathāgatas do not turn the wheel of Dharma unless they have been entreated."

"Excellent, O worthy one! said Śakra, Brahmā, the terrestrial gods, the gods of the intermediate space, those of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Ābhāsvara, Bṛhatphala, and Śubhakṛtsna gods,
as well as many hundreds of thousands of sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm, all of surpassing beauty.
When the night had passed, illuminating the foot of the Tārāyaṇa tree with a divine color and a divine radiance, they approached the place where the Tathāgata was;
having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, circumambulated him, and stood to one side.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, bowed with palms joined toward the Tathāgata and praised the Tathāgata with a verse:
"Arise, O victor in battle! Dispel the darkness in the world with the light of wisdom!
For your mind is liberated, like the full moon released from the grasp of Rāhu."
When this had been said, the Tathāgata remained silent.

Then Śikhin, the Great Brahmā, said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones are not requested to turn the wheel of Dharma in the manner that you have requested."

Then indeed, the Great Brahmā Śikhin, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and placed his right knee upon the ground, bowed with palms joined toward the Tathāgata and addressed the Tathāgata in verse:
"Arise, O victor in battle! Open the door of wisdom for the darkness in the world!"
"O Sage, teach the Dharma; there will be those who understand it."

When this had been said, monks, the Tathāgata spoke thus to the Great Brahmā Śikhin: "O Great Brahmā, this Dharma awakened by me is indeed profound, subtle, and precise... [and so on] ...lest it should cause me supreme vexation.
Moreover, O Brahmā, these two verses have frequently appeared to my mind:"
My path goes against the current; it is profound and difficult to see.
Those blinded by passion will not perceive it; therefore, it is enough that I have revealed it.
Beings fallen into sensual pleasures are carried away with the current;
this [truth] has been attained by me with great difficulty, therefore it is enough to reveal it.

Then, monks, Śikhin the Great Brahmā and Śakra, the lord of the gods, perceiving that the Tathāgata remained silent, became distressed and dejected along with those sons of the gods; they vanished from that very spot, and for a third time, Śikhin directed his mind toward the Tathāgata’s lack of enthusiasm [for teaching].
Furthermore, monks, at that time such evil and unwholesome views as these arose among the people of Magadha.
For example, some said: "The winds will not blow."
Some said thus: "The fire will not burn.
Some said: "The god will not send rain.
Others said: "The rivers will not flow."
Some said: "The crops will not grow.
Others said: "Birds will no longer fly through the sky.
Still others said: "Pregnant women will not give birth in good health."

Then, monks, Śikhin the Great Brahmā, having understood such a reflection in the mind of the Tathāgata and having perceived these views of the people of Magadha, approached the Tathāgata during the night, illuminating the entire foot of the Tārāyaṇa tree with a divine radiance that surpassed [all other] light.

Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Tathāgata, addressed him with these verses:
In Magadha, there was formerly a doctrine conceived by the impure, an unclean teaching. O Sage, reveal that nectar; they are listening to the Dharma awakened by the stainless one.

You have accomplished your own purpose and attained freedom; you have drawn away the stains of the conditioning of suffering. There is neither decrease nor increase for your virtue; you have reached the perfection here in the supreme dharmas. (Lal 25.22)

O Sage, there is no one equal to you here in this world; how then could there be anyone superior to you, O Great Seer? You shine supreme here within the three realms of existence, like that mountain situated in the abode of the asuras.
Conceive great compassion for beings who suffer; those like you are never indifferent.
You are endowed with the powers of fearlessness; you alone are capable of leading the people across.

May these beings—including the gods, the ascetics, the twice-born, and all others—though long afflicted and pierced by many thorns, become healthy and free from the fever of disease; for no other refuge exists for them here.
Devas and humans have long followed you, possessing virtuous minds and seeking the deathless.
Whatever Dharma the Jina shall realize, he will proclaim exactly as it is, without omission.

Therefore, with your wisdom, exert yourself among these beings whose path has long been lost; they are ignorant of the goal, longing for tranquility, utterly weak, or yearning for nourishment. (Lal 25.27)
O Great Sage, this people, afflicted by thirst, gazes toward you for the water of the Dharma;
O Leader, like a cloud to the parched earth, satisfy them with the rain of the Dharma. *Lalita-vistara* 25.28.
For a long time lost, human beings wander in this existence, which is a thicket of evil views and full of thorns.
Please point out to me that straight path free from thorns, by cultivating which I may indeed attain the deathless.
For these beings, leaderless, have fallen into a blind abyss and cannot be rescued by others here;
lift them up as they fall into the great precipice! Arouse your zeal, for you are a bull among men and possessed of wisdom.

O Sage, there is never an opportunity for you to meet; the Jinas, the leaders on earth, appear only rarely, like the flowers of the udumbara tree. O Protector, since this moment of leisure has been attained, liberate all sentient beings!

And in your previous lives, this was your resolve: "Having crossed over myself, may I become a savior of others. Without doubt you have now reached the further shore; O you of true valor, fulfill your vow!
O Sage, dispel the darkness with the torch of Dharma; raise high the banner of the Tathāgata!
This is the time to proclaim what you have attained; roar like a lion-king with the voice of a drum.

Then, monks, the Tathāgata, surveying the entire world with his Buddha-eye, beheld sentient beings—those who were inferior, middling, and superior; high, low, and middle; those of good disposition and easy to purify, and those of bad disposition and difficult to purify; those of instantaneous understanding and those of analytical understanding;
and those for whom words are the ultimate limit. He saw these three groups of beings: one fixed in falsehood, one fixed in truth, and one that was undetermined.
"Monks, it is just as if a man standing on the bank of a lotus pond were to see some water-born flowers submerged within the water, some level with the water, and some rising above the water;
even so, monks, the Tathāgata, surveying the entire world with his Buddha-eye, saw sentient beings established in three groups."
Then, monks, this thought occurred to the Tathāgata: "Whether I teach the Dharma or do not teach it, this group fixed in falsehood will certainly not understand the Dharma;
whether I teach the Dharma or do not teach it."

This group which is fixed in rightness will certainly understand the Dharma; and as for this group which is not yet fixed, they too will certainly understand the Dharma. Indeed, as for this group which is not yet fixed...
If I were to teach him the Dharma, he would understand it;
but if I do not teach it,
he will not understand it.
Then, monks, the Tathāgata directed his great compassion toward those beings who were situated in the group of the undetermined.
Then the Tathāgata, having taken account of this perfect knowledge of his own and having understood the request of the Great Brahmā Śikhin, addressed the Great Brahmā Śikhin in verses:
"O Brahmā, the gates of the Deathless have been opened for those who are constantly possessed of ears."
Entering with faith and free from thoughts of malice, the beings in Magadha listen to the Dharma.

Then indeed, Śikhin, the Great Brahmā, perceiving the Tathāgata’s assent, was satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; he bowed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata and vanished right there.
Then, monks, at that time the terrestrial gods raised a cry to the gods of the intermediate space and made this proclamation:
"Friends, today the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, has promised to turn the wheel of Dharma.
This will be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
"Alas, friends, the hosts of asuras will diminish;
the divine hosts will reach fullness,
and many beings in the world will attain parinirvāṇa."
In the same way, having received the word from the terrestrial gods, the gods of the intermediate space raised a cry to the Cāturmahārājika gods;
the Cāturmahārājikas [raised it] to the Trāyastriṃśa gods,
and the Trāyastriṃśas to the Yāma gods.
The Yāma gods [proclaimed it] to the Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati,
and Paranirmitavaśavartin gods;
those [latter] also raised their voices to the Brahmakāyika gods.
They proclaimed these words: "Today, friends, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has promised to turn the wheel of Dharma.

This will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, the welfare, and the happiness of the great multitude of beings—both gods and humans.
Alas, friends, the hosts of asuras will surely diminish!"
The divine bodies will increase,
and many sentient beings in the world will attain parinirvāṇa.
Thus, monks, at that very moment, at that very instant, at that very second, from the gods of the earth up to the gods of the Brahma-realm,
there arose a single voice, a single sound, a single resonance: "Friends, today the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One,
has pledged himself to set in motion the Wheel of Dharma!"

Then, monks, the four deities of the Bodhi tree—namely Dharmaruci, Dharmakāya, Dharmamati, and Dharmacārī—prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and said: "Where will the Blessed One turn the wheel of Dharma?
When this was said, monks, the Tathāgata spoke thus to those deities: "In Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣipatana in the Deer Park."
They said: "Lord, the great city of Vārāṇasī has a small population, and the Deer Park has little shade from trees.

There are other great cities, Lord, that are prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, delightful, crowded with many people and inhabitants, and adorned with gardens, groves, and mountains."
"May the Blessed One turn the wheel of Dharma for one among them.
The Tathāgata said, "Not so, gentle sirs. Why is that?"
There, sixty sextillion sacrifices were performed by me;
there, sixty sextillion Buddhas were fully honored.
This excellent abode of the ancient seers is here, known by the name Vārāṇasī.
Praised by the gods who have arrived, he is the protector of the earth, always inclined toward the Dharma.
I remember ninety-one thousand million Buddhas of the past who turned the supreme wheel of Dharma in that excellent forest called Ṛṣisāhvaya—
a place peaceful, oriented toward tranquil meditation, and constantly frequented by deer.
For this purpose, I shall abide in the excellent forest named after the Ṛṣis, [turning] the supreme wheel.
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Chapter on the Exhortation."

The Twenty-sixth Chapter, "The Turning of the Wheel of Dharma."
Then, monks, the Tathāgata— having accomplished what was to be done, having performed his task, having severed all bonds,
having uprooted all afflictions, having extinguished the stains of defilement, having struck down Māra and adversaries, having entered the method of all Buddha-dharmas,
being omniscient and all-seeing, endowed with the ten powers, attained the four grounds of self-confidence, and perfected the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— [remained].

Endowed with the five eyes, he surveyed the entire world with his unobstructed Buddha-eye and reflected thus: "To whom should I first teach the Dharma? Which being is pure, of good character, easy to discipline, easy to instruct, and capable of purification; one who has little passion, hatred, and delusion, possesses direct knowledge, and yet, having not heard the Dharma, is falling away?"
Therefore, I should first teach the Dharma to one who would understand the Dharma taught by me and would not cause me any trouble.

Then, monks, it occurred to the Tathāgata: "Rudraka Rāmaputra is indeed pure, of good character, easy to instruct, and easy to purify; he has little passion and delusion, and his knowledge is not obscure.
Yet, due to not hearing the Dharma, he is falling away.
He teaches the Dharma to his disciples for the sake of the practice leading to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
He perceived where he was dwelling at that time, [realizing] that he had passed away seven days ago.
The deities also, prostrating themselves at the feet of the Tathāgata, said this: "It is even so, Blessed One."
"So it is, Sugata;
Rudraka Rāmaputra passed away seven days ago.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: 'A great loss has befallen Rudraka Rāmaputra.'"
If someone has passed away without having heard this very well-expounded Dharma,
were they to have heard this Dharma, they would have understood it;
and I would have been the first to teach that Dharma to them.
And he would not have harmed me.
Furthermore, monks, this thought occurred to the Tathāgata: "Who else is a pure being, easy to discipline, as previously described, up to one who would not obstruct the teaching of the Dharma?
Then, monks, this thought occurred to the Tathāgata: "This Ārāḍa Kālāma is indeed pure, up to one who would not obstruct my teaching of the Dharma.
Monks, the Tathāgata then reflected: "Where is he now?"
Reflecting upon it, he knew that three days had passed since his death;
and the deities belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm also informed the Tathāgata of this matter: "It is so, Blessed One; it is so, Sugata."
"Today is the third day since Ārāḍa Kālāma passed away.
Then this thought occurred to the Tathāgata: "A great loss has befallen Ārāḍa Kālāma, in that he has passed away without having heard this Dharma so well-expounded."
Furthermore, monks, this thought occurred to the Tathāgata: "Who else is a being who is pure and of good character, such that he would not find fault with my teaching of the Dharma?"

Then, monks, this thought occurred to the Tathāgata: "Those five of the auspicious group are indeed pure, well-disposed, easy to instruct, easy to purify, with little passion, hatred, and delusion, and possessing direct knowledge;
yet they are falling away because they have not heard the Dharma.
It was for their sake that I attended upon them while practicing austerities."
They will understand the Dharma taught by me,
and they will not cause me any harm.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Tathāgata: "What if I were to teach the Dharma first to the group of five auspicious ones?"
Then, monks, it occurred again to the Tathāgata: "Where are the group of five auspicious ones living now?
Then the Tathāgata, surveying the entire world with his Buddha-eye, beheld them;
he saw the group of five auspicious ones dwelling at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
And having seen this, it occurred to the Tathāgata: "What if I were to teach the Dharma first of all to the group of five auspicious ones?
For they will understand the Dharma taught by me first of all.
Why is that?"
For those monks have practiced the holy life; they possess the most perfected and pure dharmas, are oriented toward the path of liberation, and have been freed from all bonds.

Then, monks, the Tathāgata, having reflected thus, rose from the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and, after causing the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system to tremble, proceeded in due order, wandering through Magadha and traveling on a journey through the country of Kāśi.
Then, between Gayā and the seat of enlightenment, a certain Ājīvika saw the Tathāgata approaching from afar.
Having seen him, he approached the Tathāgata;
having approached, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, monks, the Ājīvaka engaged in various friendly greetings with the Tathāgata and said this: "Venerable Gautama, your faculties are very serene."

Your complexion is perfectly pure, radiant, and golden-hued; just as in the autumn season the color of a white lotus becomes luminous and golden-hued, even so are the faculties of you, Gautama, perfectly pure, and your facial circle is perfectly pure and radiant.
Just as the stalk-base of a ripe palm fruit that has just fallen from its stem is golden-hued, perfectly pure, and radiant, so too is yours.
In the very same way, the faculties of the venerable Gautama are completely pure, and his facial orb is perfectly pure and radiant.

It is just as if there were a gold coin of Jāmbūnada hue, refined by a skilled smith’s son at the forge, well-polished and placed upon a white woolen cloth; it would be brilliant, perfectly pure, radiant, glowing with a golden luster, and exceedingly luminous.
In this very way, the faculties of the venerable Gautama are serene,
his complexion is perfectly pure, and the circle of his face is radiant.
"In what, venerable Gautama, is the holy life lived?
When this was said, monks, the Tathāgata replied to that Ājīvika in verse:
"I have no teacher whatsoever; there is no one equal to me."
I alone am the perfectly awakened one, become cool and free from outflows.
He said: "Gautama, you indeed claim yourself to be an Arhat.
The Tathāgata said:
"I alone am the Arhat in the world; for I am the unsurpassed Teacher."
In the world including its gods, asuras, and gandharvas, there is no rival to me.
He said: "Gautama, do you indeed claim yourself to be a Victor?
The Tathāgata replied:
"Those like me who have attained the destruction of the outflows should be known as Victors."
"Evil states have been conquered by me; therefore, Upaga, I am indeed a Jina."
He said: "Then, venerable Gautama, where will you go?
The Tathāgata replied:
"I shall go to Vārāṇasī; having gone to the city of the Kāśis, I will create an incomparable light for this world that has become blind."
"I shall go to Vārāṇasī; having gone indeed to the city of the Kāśis, I will beat the drum of immortality for the world that is devoid of sound."
"I shall go to Vārāṇasī; having gone indeed to the city of the Kāśis, I will set in motion the Wheel of Dharma, which has never been turned before in the worlds."
"Then you shall become [a Buddha], Gautama," said that Ājīvika, and having spoken, he set out facing south;
the Tathāgata also set out facing north.
Thus, monks, the Tathāgata was invited by the nāga king Sudarśana at Gayā for lodging and a meal.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata went to Rohitavastu; from there he went to Urubilvākalpa, and from there he went to Anāla.
Then [he went] to Sārathipura.
And in all these places, monks, the Tathāgata, being invited by householders for meals and lodging, arrived in due course at the bank of the river Gaṅgā.
Furthermore, monks, at that time the great river Gaṅgā flowed completely full, with its banks level.
Then, monks, the Tathāgata approached the boatman for the purpose of crossing to the other shore. He said, "Give me the fare, Gautama.
Having replied, "Sir, I have no fare," the Tathāgata went from this shore to the further shore by way of the sky.
Then that ferryman, seeing him, became deeply remorseful, thinking, "I have not ferried across such a worthy recipient of offerings.
Crying out, "Alas, what a tragedy!", he fainted and fell to the ground.

Thereupon, the ferryman reported this matter to King Bimbisāra: "Lord, the ascetic Gautama, when asked for the fare for crossing, said, 'There is no fare,' and [having crossed] from this bank to the other by means of the sky—"
"He has reached the shore.
Upon hearing this, King Bimbisāra, following that lead, abolished the ferry-toll for all renunciants.

Thus, monks, the Tathāgata, wandering on his gradual journey through the countryside, approached the great city of Vārāṇasī. Having arrived there, he dressed early in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered the great city of Vārāṇasī for alms. Having walked for alms in that city and finished his meal, he returned from his alms-round after his meal and proceeded toward the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, where the group of five auspicious disciples were staying.

Then the group of five auspicious ones indeed saw the Tathāgata approaching from afar. Upon seeing him, they made a pact among themselves: "Venerable sirs, here comes that ascetic Gautama, who is lax, indulgent, and fallen away from his exertion."
Indeed, even by means of that former practice of austerities, she was not able to realize any superhuman state, any excellence of noble knowledge and vision;
how much less so now, while consuming coarse food and dwelling devoted to the pursuit of pleasure?
This person is truly incapable, being lax and indulgent.
No one should go out to meet him, nor rise up for him;
his bowl and robe should not be received, nor food given to him, nor water for consumption, nor a footstool—except for extra seats.
And he should be told: (Vaidya 298)
"Venerable Gautama, there are these extra seats available;
if you wish, please sit down.
The venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya assented with his mind.
And he did not reject him with his speech.
Monks, in whatever manner the Tathāgata approached the group of five auspicious ones,
in that very manner they found no pleasure in their respective seats.
They desired to rise up,
just as if a winged bird were inside a cage and a fire were burning beneath that cage.
Just as one scorched by fire would desire to rise up quickly and flee,
even so, in whatever manner the Tathāgata approached the five companions of the auspicious group,
in that same manner those five companions of the auspicious group found no pleasure in their respective seats.
They desired to rise.
Why was that? Because there is no being whatsoever to be found among the classes of beings who, upon seeing the Tathāgata, would not rise from their seats.
And in whatever manner the Tathāgata approached the group of five auspicious ones, so did they respond.

In this manner, the group of five auspicious ones, unable to endure the splendor and majesty of the Tathāgata, began to tremble on their seats; breaking their agreement, they all rose from their seats—
some went out to meet him, and some, having gone out to meet him, received his bowl and robe.
One person brought forth a seat;
another provided a footstool; another set out water for washing the feet.
And he spoke thus: "Welcome to you, venerable Gautama!"
"Welcome to you, venerable Gautama! Here is a seat prepared; please sit down.
Monks, the Tathāgata then sat down upon the very seat that had been prepared.
The group of five auspicious ones also sat down to one side after the Tathāgata had engaged them in various pleasant and delightful conversations.
Seated to one side, those five auspicious ones said this to the Tathāgata: "Venerable Gautama, your faculties are serene;
the color of your skin is perfectly pure"—thus everything was as before.
"Venerable Gautama, do you possess any superhuman state, any excellence of noble knowledge and vision, that has been realized?

When this was said, monks, the Tathāgata spoke thus to the group of five auspicious ones: "Monks, do not address the Tathāgata by the title 'Venerable. Let it not be for your long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness."
"O monks, I have realized the deathless and the path leading to the deathless.
O monks, I am a Buddha— omniscient, all-seeing, cooled, free from outflows,
and master over all phenomena."
"Monks, I shall teach the Dharma;
go quickly, listen, and practice! Apply your ears; I am instructing and exhorting you."

Just as you have been correctly instructed and correctly exhorted by me, so too shall you, having realized and attained in this very life the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom from the outflows, declare: "Birth is exhausted for us; the holy life has been lived;
what was to be done has been accomplished."
"We know no further existence beyond this.
Now, monks, did it not occur to you: "Venerable ones, here comes the ascetic Gautama—he is lax, indulgent in luxuries, and fallen from his exertion," as before?
"If you wish, sit down."
And when he said to them, "Come, monks," whatever sectarian marks or sectarian banners they possessed all vanished at that very moment;
the three robes and the alms bowl appeared.
Thereupon their hair was shorn;
indeed, their deportment became like that of a monk who had been ordained for a hundred years.
That itself was their going forth, that was their full ordination, and that was their state as monks.
Then, monks, at that time, the five monks of the auspicious group fell at the feet of the Tathāgata and confessed their transgressions.

In the presence of the Tathāgata, they conceived the perception of him as their Teacher, as well as love, serene faith, and reverence. Having become reverent, they performed the service of bathing the Tathāgata in the Bahuvicitra lotus pond.

And when the Tathāgata had emerged from his bath, monks, this thought occurred to him: "Upon what spot, indeed, did the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones sit and set in motion the Wheel of Dharma?
And, monks, upon that very spot of earth where the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones had previously set in motion the Wheel of Dharma...
Then, on that spot of earth, a thousand seats made of the seven precious gems appeared.

Then the Tathāgata, out of reverence for the previous Tathāgatas, circumambulated the three seats and sat down cross-legged on the fourth seat like a fearless lion; the five monks also, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, sat down before him.
Then, monks, at that time the Tathāgata emitted such a radiance from his body that by this radiance this great trichiliocosm world-system was filled with a vast light.
And by that light, even those intermediate spaces between worlds— voids filled with nothingness, regions of blinding darkness where these two, the moon and the sun [do not shine]— were illuminated.

Possessing such great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), such great majesty (*mahānubhāva*), and such great authority (*maheśākhya*), they do not scorch one another with their radiance, nor do they outshine one another with their color or their splendor.
Furthermore, those beings born there cannot even see their own arms when extended.
At that time, a great and sublime radiance appeared in the world;
and those beings who were born there, being suffused by that radiance, saw one another and recognized one another.
And they spoke thus: "O friends, it seems other beings have also been reborn here;
O friends, it seems other beings have also been reborn here!

And this great trichiliocosm world-system underwent six types of movement and eighteen great omens: it shook, it shook violently, it shook intensely; it quaked, it quaked violently, it quaked intensely; it trembled, it trembled violently, it trembled intensely; it rattled, it rattled violently, it rattled intensely; it crashed, it crashed violently, it crashed intensely; it roared, it roared violently, it roared intensely.
It shook, it shook violently, it shook intensely;
it quivered, it quivered violently, it quivered intensely;
it trembled, it trembled violently, it trembled intensely.
It resounded, it resounded loudly, it resounded intensely;
it roared, it roared loudly, it roared intensely; at the end, it bowed down.
It rose in the middle;
it sank in the middle and rose at the edges;
it sank in the eastern direction.
The western direction rose up,
the western direction sank down,
and the eastern direction rose up.
It sank down in the southern direction and rose up in the northern direction;
it sank down in the northern direction.
The southern direction rose up,

and at that time, sounds were heard— sounds that were gladdening, satisfying, affection-inspiring, clarifying, worthy of being beheld, refreshing, indescribable, beyond description, never-tiring to hear, agreeable, and not causing terror.
And at that moment, no sentient being experienced any affliction, terror, fear, or paralysis.
Furthermore, at that moment, the radiance of the sun and moon, as well as that of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, was no longer perceived.
And all sentient beings born in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama became free from suffering and were endowed with every happiness at that very instant.
And no sentient being was afflicted by passion,

nor by hatred, delusion, envy, stinginess, pride, hypocrisy, arrogance, anger, malice, or burning resentment. At that moment, all sentient beings possessed minds of loving-kindness and minds of benevolence, regarding one another as mothers and fathers.
Then, from that array of light, these verses issued forth: "He who, having descended from the Tuṣita abode, entered the mother’s womb,
and was born in the Lumbinī grove, was received by the Lord of Śacī."
He who possesses the gait and prowess of a lion, taking seven strides without confusion,
then uttered a voice with the sound of Brahmā: "I am the most excellent in the world."
Having renounced the four continents, he went forth for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings;
having practiced austerities difficult to perform, he approached the seat of enlightenment.
Having subdued Māra along with his army, he attained awakening for the benefit of the world;
having arrived at Vārāṇasī, he shall set in motion the wheel of Dharma.
Requested by the Brahmās along with the gods, "Turn the wheel of peace," the Sage consented,
having generated compassion for the world.
Thus, this one of firm resolve has arrived at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī;
for that glorious one shall set in motion the unsurpassed and most wonderful Wheel.
Whoever desires to hear the Dharma, which was acquired by the Jina through tens of millions of eons— let that person come quickly and with haste for the hearing of the Dharma.
Human birth is difficult to obtain; the appearance of a Buddha is very hard to encounter; faith is rare;
hearing the sublime Dharma and being free from the eight inopportune states are difficult to attain.
Today you have all obtained the appearance of a Buddha, the opportune moment, and likewise faith;
you have also obtained the excellent hearing of the Dharma—therefore, abandon all heedlessness!
There may occasionally arise a state in which a Dharma that has not been heard for ten million eons is attained;
and since that has been reached today, abandon all heedlessness.
He exhorts the hosts of gods, from Bhauma up to Brahmā:
"Come quickly, all of you; for the Leader is about to turn the Wheel of Immortality."
Urged on at that very moment by the great sound of the gods' voices, they all abandoned their divine splendor and arrived at the side of the Buddha.

Thus, monks, by the terrestrial deities, a great maṇḍala was established for the Tathāgata at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī for the purpose of turning the wheel of Dharma; it was variegated, beautiful to behold, vast, and extensive, measuring seven hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
And above, the surface of the sky was adorned by the gods with parasols, banners, flags, and canopies.

The sons of the gods belonging to the desire realm and the form realm presented eight million four hundred thousand lion-thrones to the Tathāgata, saying: "May the Blessed One sit here and turn the wheel of Dharma, out of compassion for us."

Then, monks, at that time, many millions of bodhisattvas from the east, south, west, north, above, below, and from all ten directions— endowed with their former vows— having arrived and prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata, entreated him to turn the wheel of Dharma.

And all those in this trichiliocosm— the Śakras, the Brahmās, the world-protectors, or other sons of the gods, whether of great power or of lesser power— who bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, entreated the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma, saying: "May he turn it!"

May the Blessed One turn the wheel of Dharma; may the Sugata turn the wheel of Dharma for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of gods and humans.
O Blessed One, perform the sacrifice of Dharma;
rain down the great rain of Dharma;
raise high the great banner of Dharma.
Fill the great conch of the Dharma;
beat the great drum of the Dharma!
In this regard,
it is said: From here, many Brahmās, Sureśvaras, and Pālas from the three-thousandfold world system approached the Jina, prostrated at his feet, and spoke thus:
Remember your former vow, O Great Sage; recall the word you spoke:
"I am the eldest and most distinguished; for the sake of all beings, I shall bring about the end of suffering. (Lal 26.19)

O Sage, standing at the king of trees, you have subdued Māra along with his army and awakened to supreme enlightenment in perfect peace; you have felled the trees of the afflictions and fulfilled every intention you conceived throughout hundreds of eons.
Beholding the people who are without a leader, turn the supreme wheel!
Many hundreds of thousands of fields were illuminated by the Sugata’s radiance,
and many hundreds of sons of the Buddhas arrived with the power of their supernatural faculties;
having performed various kinds of vast offerings to the Sugata, they gathered in great numbers.
They praised the Tathāgata with his true qualities and entreated the Compassionate One.
O Cloud of Compassion, with wisdom as lightning and insight as the wind, you have thundered for thousands of eons, inviting the entire world.
O Holder of the Water of the Eightfold Path, rain down equally upon the world and quench its thirst.
Increase the wealth of the harvests through the powers, faculties, meditations, and liberations.
Well-trained in the reality of emptiness for many thousands of eons,
you have attained the medicine born of the Dharma and understood the conduct of sentient beings;
this generation is afflicted by hundreds of diseases, the multitude of defilements.
O Physician of Jinas, set us free; turn the supreme wheel of Dharma!
For a long night you have increased the treasury of the six perfections; you have incomparably and immovably accumulated this sublime and well-heaped treasure of Dharma.
Having seen all these people—helpless, poor, and leaderless—you [have gathered it].
O Guide, bestow the seven treasures and set the wheel of Dharma in motion!
Wealth, grain, silver, and gold, as well as fine garments, excellent flowers, ointments, incense, powders, and superior dwellings;
Having renounced the inner apartments, the kingdom, and your beloved son, you gladden [the world] while seeking the awakening of a Jina; O most awakened one, set in motion the supreme wheel!

Likewise, O Sage, you have always guarded your morality for hundreds of eons—unbroken and stainless; your patience was well-cultivated, and your vigor was never weary. You possess supreme meditative concentration, supernormal knowledges, insight, wisdom, and equanimity.
O you whose desires are fulfilled and who are free from fever, turn the supreme wheel!

Then, monks, at that moment, the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Sahacittotpādadharmacakrapravartī [produced] a wheel inlaid with all kinds of jewels, adorned with all kinds of jewels, embellished by an array of various jewel ornaments, having a thousand spokes, a thousand rays, a hub, and a rim; it was accompanied by garlands of flowers, a golden net, and a network of tinkling bells.
It was adorned with fragrant hands, full vases, *nandikāvarta* motifs, and *svastika* symbols; beautified by divine garments dyed in various colors;

anointed and strewn with divine flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ointments; endowed with the excellence of all aspects; brought forth by the former vows for the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma; purified by the intention of the Bodhisattvas; worthy of worship for the Tathāgata; and attended by the mindfulness of all Tathāgatas.

He presented the wheel of Dharma— which had been previously accepted and set in motion by former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and which is never to be revoked through the empowerment of all Buddhas—
and having presented it, with palms joined in reverence, he praised the Tathāgata with these verses:

When Dīpaṃkara prophesied that this pure being would indeed become a Buddha, a lion among the lions of men, at that time I made this very vow: "Upon attaining perfect awakening, may I request him to teach the Dharma."
And it is not possible to enter into the calculation of all these supreme beings who have come here from the ten directions;
O Joy of the Śākya clan, we entreat you to turn the wheel of Dharma, bowing low with palms joined in reverence and falling at your feet.

Whatever array was prepared for the seat of enlightenment by the gods, or whatever arrays were created by all the sons of the Victors—all those arrays remain present at the wheel of Dharma; even if one were to speak of them for a full eon, they would not reach exhaustion.
The sky of the triple-thousandfold world-system was filled with hosts of gods, and the surface of the earth with asuras, kinnaras, and humans;
for that moment, even the sound of a cough was not heard, as everyone gazed upon the Jina with serene minds.
Thus, monks, the Tathāgata remained in silence during the first watch of the night;
during the middle watch of the night, he engaged in a discourse that inspires affection.
During the last watch of the night, having addressed the group of five auspicious monks, he said this to them: "Monks, these two extremes are not to be pursued by one who has gone forth:

that which is devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires—low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—which does not lead to the holy life in the future, nor to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to higher knowledge, nor to awakening."
It does not lead to nirvāṇa.
And this middle way—which is the pursuit of self-mortification, painful, unbeneficial, involving suffering in the present life and resulting in suffering in the future—[is what he avoids].
Monks, without approaching these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of the middle way itself.
Namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
These, monks, are the four noble truths.
Which four?
Suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is suffering?
Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the unpleasant is suffering, and separation from the pleasant is suffering.
Furthermore, not obtaining what one desires and seeks after is also suffering.
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
This is called suffering.
In that regard, what is the origin of suffering?
It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and passion, finding delight here and there; this is called the origin of suffering.
In that regard, what is the cessation of suffering?

It is the complete fading away and cessation of this very craving—which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, finds delight here and there, and gives rise to and brings about [rebirth]—this is the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
This is precisely the noble eightfold path; namely,
right view up to right concentration.
This is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
These, monks, are the four noble truths.
Thus, monks, regarding the Dharma unheard of before, through wise attention and repeated cultivation, knowledge arose in me: "This is suffering."
"Vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, broad understanding arose, insight arose, and light appeared.

'This is the origin of suffering,' monks— regarding these teachings unheard of before, through proper attention and repeated cultivation, knowledge arose, vision arose, knowledge arose, broad understanding arose, insight arose, and light appeared."
"‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ monks—[all as before]—until light appeared to me.
‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ monks—as before, and so forth—until light appeared to me.
‘That which is this suffering must be fully understood,’ monks—as before, and so forth—until light appeared to me."

"Monks, regarding this origin of suffering, it was previously unheard by me that it must be abandoned; thus, monks, there arose in me, as before, even unto light. Regarding this cessation of suffering, monks, it was previously unheard by me that it must be realized; thus, monks, as before, even unto light. Regarding this path leading to the cessation of suffering, it was previously unheard by me that it must be cultivated; thus, monks, as before, even unto light."

"Indeed, monks, 'this suffering has been fully understood by me'—this, monks, was unheard of by me before... [and so on]. Indeed, monks, 'this origin of suffering has been abandoned by me'—this, monks, was unheard of by me before... [and so on]. Indeed, monks, 'this cessation of suffering has been realized by me'—this, monks, was unheard of by me before... [and so on]."

"Monks, regarding this cultivation of the path leading to the cessation of suffering: through wise attention and repeated practice toward these teachings unheard of before, knowledge arose in me; vision arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, intelligence arose, discernment arose, and light became manifest."

"Thus, monks, as long as this knowledge and vision— consisting of three revolutions and twelve aspects— did not arise in me through proper mental attention toward these four noble truths, for that long, monks, I did not claim to have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
And yet, no knowledge or vision arose in me. But when, monks, this knowledge and vision regarding these four noble truths had arisen in me in this way— three turnings and twelve aspects—
and my liberation of mind became unshakable, [then I knew that I had attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment].
And liberation through wisdom was directly realized;
therefore, monks, I claimed, "I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment," and the vision of knowledge arose within me.
Exhausted is my birth; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished.
I do not cognize existence from another.
In this regard, it is said:

With a voice like the Brahma-sound, the roar of the Kinnaras, and arisen from thousands of millions of melodic tones, Śākyamuni, the Self-Existent One, who has always cultivated truth for many millions of eons, personally addresses Kauṇḍinya: *Lalita-vistara 26.31*
The eye is impermanent and unstable; likewise the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are suffering, selfless, and empty.
They are insentient by nature, inactive like grass or a wall; herein there is no self, no person, and no living being.
All these phenomena have arisen in dependence upon causes; they are utterly free from [extreme] views and are as luminous as space.
There is no agent, nor likewise is there any experiencer; yet one does not fail to see that unwholesome or wholesome karma has been performed.
For suffering indeed arises dependent upon the aggregates; thus they come into being, increasing through the water of craving.
When one perceives them through the path of the equality of phenomena, they are utterly exhausted and ceased by their very nature of decay.
Ignorance arises from improper mental application born of conceptual construction, yet there is no one who produces it;
the formative forces provide its cause, and there is no transmigration, for consciousness arises in dependence upon that transition.
Consciousness arises together with name-and-form; from name-and-form, the six sense-faculties arise.
That which is encountered by the six sense-faculties is called contact; through contact, the threefold feeling follows. *Lalita-vistara* 26.36.
Whatever is felt, all that is said to be accompanied by craving; from craving, this entire mass of suffering arises.
From grasping, there occurs the entire process of becoming; and with becoming as a condition, birth indeed emerges for this person. (Lal 26.37)
Birth is the cause of the sufferings of old age and disease; there are many various rebirths within this cage of existence.
Thus, all this world arises from conditions; there is no self, no person, and no transmigrating agent whatsoever.
In that which is neither conceptualization nor discursive thought, they say there is no source; where there is such fundamental understanding, there is no ignorance whatsoever.
In that cessation of ignorance which occurs here, all factors of existence are exhausted, worn away, and brought to an end.
Thus, through these conditions, that self-existent Tathāgata has personally prophesied his own Buddhahood.
I do not speak of the Buddha as being the aggregates, the sense-bases, or the elements; rather, it is through the realization of causes that one becomes a Buddha in this world.
This ground here is not for those who have departed from other sects; such a union with the Dharma is empty for them as they debate here.
Only those beings who were previously devoted to the conduct of the Buddhas and are utterly pure are capable of understanding these teachings.
Thus was the Wheel of Dharma set in motion in its twelve aspects;
Kauṇḍinya understood it, and the Three Jewels were established.
"The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—this is the Triple Gem; its sound has spread from one to another as far as the abode of the Brahma-world. (Lal 26.43)
The dustless wheel has been set in motion by the Protector of the World, the Savior;
the Three Jewels, most difficult to obtain, have arisen in the world.
Having first [taught] Kauṇḍinya and the five monks,
the Dharma-eye was purified for sixty million deities.
And there were another eighty koṭis of deities from the realm of form;
their eyes were purified for the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
Eighty-four thousand humans gathered together;
their eyes were purified, and they were all liberated from the miserable states of existence.
At that moment, the infinite Buddha-voice reached throughout the ten directions,
and a sweet, charming, and auspicious sound was heard in the sky:
"This supreme Wheel of Dharma has been turned by the Śākya Sage, who possesses the Ten Powers."
Having reached Ṛṣipatana, he turned back toward Vārāṇasī; it was not otherwise.
In the ten directions, all the hundreds of Buddhas remained silent;
their attendants, following the way of the Sages, all asked the Jinas:
"Why have the Discourses on Dharma been cut off by the Ten-Powered Ones? having heard this sound.
"Speak quickly, it is well; for what reason do you remain in silence?"
Through the power of his vigor over hundreds of previous existences, he fully realized awakening; many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas were turned back from their course by him.
By that benefactor, through intense application, auspicious awakening was attained.
The wheel of the three turnings was set in motion by him; therefore, they became silent.
Having heard these words of theirs, hundreds of millions of beings among the sages,
generating the power of loving-kindness, set out for supreme, auspicious enlightenment;
we too shall train ourselves according to that Sage, rising up in the station of vigor.
May we quickly become the supreme ones in the world, bestowing the eye of Dharma.
Thus [it is said].

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas assembled here from the world-systems of the ten directions desire to hear from the presence of the Blessed One the entry into the miraculous manifestation of setting the wheel of Dharma in motion.
Therefore, it would be well if the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, would explain: in what manner has the wheel of Dharma been set in motion by the Tathāgata?"

The Blessed One said: "Maitreya, the wheel of Dharma is profound because it is ungraspable; that wheel is difficult to see because it is free from duality; that wheel is difficult to realize because it is beyond both mental attention and non-attention."
That wheel is difficult to comprehend because it is bound up with the equality of gnosis and consciousness;
that wheel is untroubled because it has attained the liberation that is free from obscuration;
that wheel is subtle because it is devoid of any comparable illustration.
That wheel is essential because it has attained knowledge that is like a diamond;
that wheel is indivisible because it has existed since the beginningless past;
that wheel is free from conceptual proliferation because it is devoid of all attempts at conceptual proliferation.
That wheel is unshakable because it is ultimately final;
that wheel pervades everywhere because it is like space.
Furthermore, Maitreya, that wheel of Dharma is the wheel that demonstrates the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
The wheel of non-arising, non-ceasing, and non-occurrence; the wheel of non-abiding; the wheel that extensively expounds the method of phenomena free from conceptualization and discrimination;

the wheel of emptiness; the wheel of signlessness; the wheel of wishlessness; the wheel of non-conditioning; the wheel of seclusion; the wheel of dispassion; the wheel of cessation; the wheel of the Tathāgata’s awakening; and the wheel of the indivisibility of the realm of phenomena.

The wheel that does not disturb the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); the wheel of non-attachment and non-obstruction; the wheel that enters into dependent origination and transcends the views of both extremes;

the wheel that does not disturb the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) which is without end or middle; the wheel that never ceases its effortless buddha-activity; the wheel of non-arising and non-manifestation; the wheel of absolute non-apprehensibility; the wheel of neither accumulation nor dispersal.

It is the wheel of the ineffable, the wheel of the nature of things as they truly are, the wheel that enters into the equality of all phenomena within a single sphere, the wheel of non-retrogression through the empowerment that disciplines beings in unfavorable states, the wheel that enters the method of the ultimate truth free from dualistic superimposition, and the wheel of convergence into the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
That wheel is immeasurable, transcending all measures.
That wheel is incalculable, transcending all calculation;
that wheel is inconceivable, having transcended the path of the mind; that wheel is incomparable, having transcended all comparison.
That wheel is ineffable, transcending the path of speech and all sounds and noises;

it is immeasurable, incomparable, yet accessible through comparison; equal to and like space; neither annihilated nor eternal; entered through dependent origination, non-contradictory, peaceful, and utterly quiescent; it is reality (*tattva*), suchness, non-falsity, non-alteration, and the state of non-differentiation—the movement of the voices of all sentient beings.

It is the subduing of Māras, the defeat of the heretics, the transcending of the realm of saṃsāra, and the entry into the realm of the Buddhas; it is fully understood by noble persons, adhered to by pratyekabuddhas, embraced by bodhisattvas, praised by all Buddhas, and undifferentiated from all Tathāgatas.
It is in such a manner, Bhaisajyaraja, that the wheel of Dharma has been turned by the Tathagata, through the turning of which he is called "Tathagata," "Samyaksambuddha," and "Svayambhu."
He is called the Lord of Dharma;
he is called the Leader;
he is called the Guide.
He is called the leader;
he is called the caravan leader;
he is called the one who has mastery over all phenomena.
He is called the Lord of Dharma; he is called the Turner of the Wheel of Dharma;
he is called the Master of the Gift of Dharma.
He is called the Lord of Sacrifice;
he is called one who has well-sacrificed;
he is called one whose vows are perfected.
He is called one whose intentions are fulfilled;
he is called a guide;
he is called one who provides consolation.
He is called the Maker of Security;
he is called the Hero; he is called the Abandoner of Battle.
He is called "Victorious in Battle";
he is called "One with Raised Parasols, Banners, and Flags";
he is called "Light-Maker."
He is called the Light-Maker;
he is called the Dispeller of Darkness;
he is called the Bearer of the Torch.
He is called the Great King of Physicians;
he is called the Healer of Reality;
he is called the Great Extractor of Arrows.
He is called the one whose vision of knowledge is free from darkness;
he is called the all-seeing;
he is called the one who gazes everywhere.
He is called Samantacakṣus;
he is called Samantaprabha;
he is called Samantāloka.
He is called Samantamukha;
he is called Samantaprabhākara;
he is called Samantacandra.
He is called "universally serene";
he is called "without abiding, without exertion, and without withdrawal";
he is called "equal to the earth" because of being neither elevated nor depressed.
He is called "Equal to the Lord of Mountains" because he is unshakable;
he is called "The Glory of All the World" because he is endowed with all the virtues of the world;
he is called "One Whose Crown Cannot Be Seen" because he has transcended the entire world.
He is called "resembling the ocean" because he is profound and difficult to fathom;
he is called "a mine of the jewels of Dharma" because he is completely filled with the jewels of all the factors conducive to enlightenment;
he is called "equal to the wind" because he has no fixed abode.
He is called "one of unattached intellect" because his mind is unattached, unbound, and liberated.
He is called "one of irreversible nature" because he possesses the knowledge that penetrates all phenomena.
He is called "equal to fire" because he is difficult to approach and stands ready to burn away all afflictions, having abandoned all conceits.
He is said to be "equal to water" because he has washed away all evil through a body and mind that are stainless due to his untroubled resolve.
He is said to be "equal to space" because he has attained the superknowledges of gnosis whose range is the dharmadhātu—vast without center or periphery—and whose object is unattached knowledge.
He is said to "dwell in the liberation of unobstructed gnosis" because he has thoroughly abandoned all obstructive phenomena.
He is called "one whose body extends throughout the entire realm of phenomena" because he has transcended the range of vision like space;
he is called "the supreme being" because he is undefiled by the spheres of all worlds;
he is called "the unattached being."
He is called one of immeasurable intelligence;
he is called a teacher of supramundane dharmas;
he is called a teacher of the world.
He is called the Physician of the World; he is called the One Transcending the World; he is called the One Untainted by Worldly Dharmas.
He is called the Lord of the World;
he is called the Eldest of the World;
he is called the Best of the World.
He is called the Lord of the World; he is called the One Honored by the World; he is called the Ultimate Refuge of the World.
He is called one who has gone beyond the world;
he is called the lamp of the world;
he is called the transcendent.
He is called the Teacher of the World;
he is called the One who Acts for the Benefit of the World;
he is called the One who Conforms to the World.
He is called the Knower of the World;
he is called the One who has attained sovereignty over the world;
he is called the Great Object of Veneration.
He is called one worthy of worship;
he is called a great field of merit;
he is called a Great Being.
He is called the foremost being;
he is called the excellent being;
he is called the most sublime being.
He is called the supreme being;
he is called the unsurpassed being;
he is called the peerless being.
He is called a peerless being;
he is called one who is constantly and perpetually in meditative equipoise;
he is called one who dwells in the equality of all phenomena.
He is called one who has attained the path;
he is called a showman of the path;
he is called a teacher of the path.
It is called the well-established path;
it is called that which has transcended the realm of Māra;
it is called that which destroys the mandala of Māra.
It is called the state of coolness, free from old age and death; it is called the departure of the darkness of ignorance;
it is called the removal of thorns.
He is said to be free from doubt;
he is said to be free from afflictions;
he is said to have his uncertainties dispelled.
He is said to have emerged from doubt;
he is said to be dispassionate;
he is said to be liberated.
He is called "pure";
he is called "free from passion";
he is called "free from hatred."
He is called one who has departed from delusion;
he is called one whose outflows are exhausted;
he is called one free from afflictions.
He is called one who has attained mastery;
he is called one whose mind is well-liberated;
he is called one whose wisdom is well-liberated.
He is called a thoroughbred;
he is called a great elephant;
he is called one who has accomplished what was to be done.
He is said to have accomplished what was to be done;
he is said to have laid down the burden;
he is said to have attained his own goal.
He is called one whose fetters of existence are completely exhausted;
he is called one liberated through the knowledge of equality;
he is called one who has attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states.
He is called one who has reached the further shore of generosity;
he is called one who is preeminent in ethical discipline;
he is called one who has reached the further shore of patience.
He is called one who has risen through vigor;
he is called one who has attained the meditative absorptions and the superknowledges;
he is called one who has gone to the perfection of wisdom.
He is called one whose vows are accomplished;
he is called one who dwells in great loving-kindness;
he is called one who dwells in great compassion.
He is called one who dwells in great sympathetic joy; he is called one who dwells in great equanimity;
he is called one who is devoted to the gathering of sentient beings.
He is said to have attained the unobstructed analytical knowledges;
he is said to be a source of refuge;
he is said to possess great merit.
He is called one of great wisdom;
he is called one endowed with mindfulness, intelligence, comprehension, and awakening;

he is called one who has attained the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, the analytical knowledges, and the light of insight.
He is said to have crossed the ocean of saṃsāra;
he is said to have reached the further shore; he is said to have arrived at dry land.
He is said to have attained security; he is said to have attained fearlessness;
he is said to have crushed the thorns of the afflictions.
He is called a person;
he is called a great person;
he is called a lion among persons.
He is called "one whose fear and horripilation have vanished";
he is called "an elephant" (nāga);
he is called "stainless."
He is said to have abandoned the stains of the three impurities; he is said to be a knower; he is said to have attained the three types of higher knowledge.
He is called one who has crossed over the four floods;
he is called one who has reached the further shore;
he is called a kṣatriya.
He is called a brahmin;
he is called one who holds the single jewel-parasol;
he is called one who has carried out the dharma that leads beyond.
He is called a bhikṣu; he is called one who has shattered the eggshell of ignorance; he is called a śramaṇa.
He is said to have completely transcended the path of attachment to objects;
he is called a *śrotriya*;
he is called one who has emerged from the afflictions.
He is called the Powerful One;
he is called the Possessor of the Ten Powers;
he is called the Blessed One.
He is called one who has cultivated the body;
he is called a king beyond kings;
he is called a King of Dharma.
He is called the one who turns the most excellent wheel of Dharma and instructs others; he is called the teacher of the unshakable Dharma;
he is called the one consecrated with the wisdom of the omniscient one.
He is said to be one who has bound on the crown of his head the pure, radiant turban of unattached great gnosis;
he is said to be one endowed with the jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment;
he is said to have attained the distinction of all dharmas.
He is called one whose facial orb is gazed upon by all the noble śrāvaka ministers; he is called one who has a retinue of sons who are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
he is called one who is well-disciplined in the discipline.
He is called a well-expounded bodhisattva;
he is called one who resembles Vaiśravaṇa;
he is called one whose treasury is filled with the distribution of the seven riches of the noble ones.
He is called one who has renounced all that is to be renounced; he is called one endowed with every excellence of happiness;
he is called the giver of all intentions.
He is called the protector of the welfare and happiness of all the world;
he is called equal to Indra;
he is called the wielder of the vajra of the power of gnosis.
He is called Samantanetra;
he is called the one who possesses unobstructed knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena;
he is called the one who manifests universal transformations of wisdom.
He is said to have entered the viewing of the vast drama of the Dharma;
he is said to be equal to the moon;
he is said to be one whose appearance leaves the entire world insatiable.
He is called "The Light of Universal, Vast, and Pure Radiance";
he is called "The Light that Produces Joy and Delight";
he is called "The Manifestation Appearing Face-to-Face with All Sentient Beings."
He is called "one who has attained the manifestation of the mental dispositions and intentions of all living beings as a vessel";
he is called "the Great Array";
he is called "one whose retinue consists of the hosts of luminaries among those in training and those beyond training."
He is called "Equal to the Solar Disk";
he is called "One Who Has Dispelled the Darkness of Delusion";
he is called "The Great King of Banners."
He is called "The One Whose Rays Are Immeasurable and Infinite";
he is called "The One Who Manifests Great Illumination";
he is called "The One Unconfused in Explaining and Teaching the Answers to All Questions."
He is called the one who destroys the darkness of great ignorance;
he is called the one whose non-conceptual intellect surveys with the light of great wisdom;
he is called the one whose immeasurable range is released like rays of light that are equal toward all the world through great loving-kindness, compassion, and pity.
He is called the one whose maṇḍala is profound, unassailable, and difficult to behold through the perfection of wisdom;
he is called equal to Brahmā;
he is called one whose deportment is perfectly tranquil.
He is said to be endowed with the excellence of all modes of conduct and behavior; he is said to possess supreme beauty; he is said to be of such a form that one can never tire of beholding him.
He is called one whose faculties are stilled;
he is called one whose mind is stilled;
he is called one who has fulfilled the equipment for tranquility.
He is called one who has attained the supreme tranquility; he is called one who has attained the highest self-control and tranquility;
he is called one whose equipment for tranquility and insight is fully perfected.
He is said to be protected and one who has conquered the senses; like a well-tamed elephant, he is clear, undisturbed, and serene like a lake.
He is said to have completely abandoned the obscurations of all afflictions and habitual tendencies.
He is said to be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
He is called the Supreme Person;
he is called one whose body is adorned with the variegated array of the eighty secondary marks;
he is called the Bull among Men.
He is called "endowed with the ten powers";
he is called "the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed who has attained the four grounds of self-confidence";
he is called "the Teacher."
He is said to be one who has fulfilled the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
he is said to be one whose bodily, vocal, and mental actions are beyond reproach;
and because his circle of knowledge and vision is endowed with the excellence of all aspects and is perfectly purified, he is said to be a dweller in emptiness.
Because of the perfect awakening to the equality of dependent origination, he is called one who dwells in the signless;
because of the penetration of the method of ultimate truth, he is called one who dwells in the wishless;
because of being unstained by any undertaking, he is called one whose sphere is the unconditioned.
Because all conditioned phenomena have been completely stilled, he is called a speaker of reality (*bhūtavādī*).
Because his object of knowledge is the unshakeable limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), he is called a speaker of that which is non-false and non-otherwise.

Because his object is suchness, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and the characteristicless characteristic of space, he is called one who has well attained the dharma of the wilderness (*araṇyadharma*).

Because he dwells in the equality of all phenomena—which are like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, the moon reflected in water, an echo, and a reflection—he is called "One whose Sight and Hearing are Unfailing.

Because he generates the cause for parinirvāṇa, he is called "One Who Takes Unfailing Steps. Because he has displayed valorous prowess in training sentient beings, he is called "One Who Has Cast Off Weariness."

Because he has completely severed ignorance and the craving for existence, he is called "one who has established the transition. Because he well teaches the path leading to liberation, he is called "one who has conquered the adversary Māra and the afflictions. Because he is unsullied by conduct within the domain of all Māras, he is called "one who has crossed over the mire of desire."
Because he has transcended the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), he is called "one who has cast down the banner of pride.
Because he has transcended the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), he is called "one who has raised the banner of wisdom.
Because he has transcended the realm of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), he is called "one who has transcended all worldly objects."
Because his body is the wisdom-body of the *dharmakāya*, he is called the "Great Tree.
Because he is perfectly endowed with the fruit of liberation, which is like a flower in full bloom through the jewels of infinite qualities and wisdom, he is said to be "like the *udumbara* flower.
And because his appearance and sight are difficult to encounter, he is said to be "equal to the jewel-king of the *cintāmaṇi* gem."
Because he has perfectly fulfilled his intention regarding the vehicle of Nirvāṇa, he is said to have "well-placed feet.

Because for a long time he has maintained with firm resolve and remains unshakable and immovable in renunciation, ethical discipline, austerity, vows, celibacy, and meditative concentration, he is said to have "soles of the feet marked with various svastikas, nandyāvartas, and a thousand-spoked wheels.

Because for a long time he has protected and guarded his parents, śramaṇas, brahmins, gurus, those worthy of offerings, and those who have come for refuge in accordance with the Dharma, and because he has never abandoned them, he is said to have "long heels."
Because he has abstained from taking life for a long time, he is said to have long fingers.
Because he has caused other beings to undertake the abstention from taking life for a long time, he is said to be a protector of many people.
Because he has proclaimed the praise of the virtues of abstaining from taking life for a long time, he is said to have soft and youthful hands and feet.

Because for a long time he has undergone the exhaustion of personally attending to and serving his parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gurus, and those worthy of offerings— bathing them, anointing them, massaging them with ghee and oil, and performing physical care with his own hands— he is said to have webbed fingers and toes. Because for a long time he has been well-trained in the skill of gathering sentient beings through the net of the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)— namely, generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful action, and consistency between words and deeds— he is said to have high-arched feet.

Because for a long time he has taken as his object roots of merit that are increasingly more distinguished, he is said to have body hairs that curl upward and to the right from each pore.
