Because for a long time he has practiced circumambulating his parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gurus, those worthy of offerings, and the reliquaries (caitya) of the Tathāgata; because he has listened to the Dharma with reverence, experienced horripilation, gladdened other beings, and applied himself to teaching the Dharma, he is said to have shanks like those of an antelope (eṇeya).
Because for a long time he has honored the skillful means of listening to, grasping, retaining, reciting, understanding, determining the meaning and words, and mastering the Dharma;

and because, toward sentient beings facing old age, sickness, and death, he has provided refuge and taught the Dharma with honor, never regarding them with a sense of contempt, he is said to have the private organ withdrawn into a sheath.
Because for a long time he has [served] ascetics, brahmins, and others who lead the holy life...

He is called "Long-Armed" because he supports the holy life (*brahmacarya*), provides all requisites, bestows strength upon the naked, praises the virtues of celibacy and avoiding the wives of others, and maintains a firm commitment to the observance of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).

He is called "Symmetrical as a Nyagrodha Tree" because for a long time he has been endowed with physical actions, verbal actions, and mental actions characterized by friendliness, and because he practices non-harming toward beings through restraint of the hands and restraint of the feet.

Because for a long time he has known the proper measure of food, practiced moderation in eating, provided medicine for the sick, refrained from despising lowly people, did not oppress the helpless, repaired dilapidated shrines of the Tathāgata, established stūpas, and granted fearlessness to beings afflicted by fear, he is said to have skin that is soft, tender, and delicate. Because for a long time he has [provided] bathing, ointments, and anointing with ghee and oil for his parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, teachers, and those worthy of offerings during the cold...

He is said to have a golden complexion because for a long time he provided warm water in the heat and cool water in the cold, and offered the enjoyment of shade, sunlight, and the comforts of the seasons; because he provided beds and seats spread with soft, fresh cotton and delicate fabrics; because he offered fragrant oils for the shrines of the Tathāgatas, and provided fine silk banners and flags as offerings;

and because he practiced the yoga of cultivating loving-kindness toward all beings without resentment, and because he encouraged others to practice patience and gentleness, and proclaimed the virtues of freedom from enmity and ill-will.

Because of his offering of gold inlay for the reliquaries of the Tathāgata and the images of the Tathāgata, as well as his scattering of golden flowers and golden powder, and his provision of golden-colored silk banners, flags, ornaments, golden vessels, and golden garments, he is called "one whose every single pore is filled with gold."

Because for a long time he has engaged in approaching wise men to inquire about what is wholesome and unwholesome, and to inquire about and investigate the meaning of the dharmas that are blameworthy or blameless, to be practiced, inferior, middling, or sublime; and because he has been devoted to removing insects, spiders, cobwebs, discarded flowers, and various grasses and pebbles from the shrines of the Tathāgatas, he is called "one with seven protuberances.
Because for a long time he has [rendered service] to his mother and father, to elders, superiors, those worthy of honor, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the destitute, beggars, and so forth...

Because he respectfully provides to those who have approached food, drink, seats, clothing, shelter, lamps, and the requisites for livelihood according to their wishes; and because he provides wells, lotus ponds, and large reservoirs filled with cool water for the enjoyment of the great multitude, he is called "one whose upper body is like that of a lion. Because for a long time he has bowed down, prostrated, saluted, and granted fearlessness to his parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, teachers, and those worthy of offerings; and because he does not despise the weak, does not abandon those who have come for refuge, and never relinquishes his firm resolve to give, he has "rounded shoulders."
Thus it is said:

because for a long time he has avoided the mantras that cause division among others— the root of disputes consisting in weighing one's own faults, observing the faults and lapses of others, and finding their vulnerabilities— and because his verbal activity is well-guarded through the thorough relinquishing [of such mantras], he is called "one whose shoulders are well-rounded."
For a long time, they have desired to rise from their seats, go forward to meet, and pay homage to their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, teachers, and those worthy of offerings;

through confidence in all treatises, they have sought to restrain beings who desire dispute, while conforming to their own Dharma and Vinaya; they have established and caused to flourish the righteous paths of wholesome qualities for kings and ministers who act rightly, and have undertaken the practice of all wholesome deeds by upholding and maintaining the teaching of the Tathāgata.

Because he is the precursor [to all virtues], he is called "Lion-Jawed. Because for a long time he has delighted in the abandonment of all things and in speaking kindly to supplicants according to their wishes, and because he has never insulted, deceived, or distracted those who approached him, but has fulfilled the wishes of all through his firm commitment to the renunciation of giving, he is called "Having Forty Even Teeth."
Because for a long time he has avoided divisive speech, refrained from taking up secret counsel intended to cause dissension, and delighted in promoting harmony and unity;
and because he applied himself to censuring divisive speech and proclaiming the virtues of harmony and unity even with his mind, he is said to have "very white teeth.

Because for a long time he has avoided the dark side, accumulated wholesome qualities on the bright side, avoided black actions and their black maturation, praised white actions and their white maturation, offered milk-food, given white garments, and [made offerings] at the shrines of the Tathāgatas...
Because he gave gifts of ambrosia, milk, jasmine, *vārṣikī*, *dhānuṣkāri*, garlands, strings of flowers, and white-colored blossoms, he is said to have teeth that are closely set.

Because for a long time he avoided laughter and levity, guarded his speech so as to bring joy, uttered speech that brings joy, did not seek out the lapses or faults of others, established all beings in the adoption of an even mind, practiced with equanimity, taught the Dharma with impartiality, and never abandoned his firm commitments, he is said to possess the supreme sense of taste.

Because for a long time he has refrained from harming or injuring any sentient being, has attended to those afflicted by various diseases, has provided medicine to the sick, and has tirelessly bestowed all kinds of flavors upon those seeking them, he is called "Brahma-voiced."

Because he has for a long time avoided speech that is false, harsh, rough, deceitful, bitter toward others, offensive, unpleasant, or extremely abrasive; and because he has practiced loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and the production of gladness; and because his speech is affectionate, sweet, gentle, heart-pleasing, and gladdening to all the sense-faculties through the correct application of right words—he is called "one with deep blue eyes."

Because for a long time he has practiced toward all sentient beings with eyes free from obstruction, like those of a mother and father, and with the regard for a beggar as if for an only son; because he is preceded by love and compassion, and because he gazes without frowning, with serene faculties, at the reliquaries (*caitya*) of the Tathāgata with unblinking eyes, and because he firmly undertakes the task of inducing other beings to behold the Tathāgata, he is called "one whose eyes are like a cowherd."

Because for a long time he has avoided inferior states of mind, fulfilled vast and expansive resolute intentions, incited sentient beings toward the desire for the unsurpassed Dharma, avoided frowning faces and maintained a smiling countenance, approached all spiritual friends with a forward-facing and leading attitude, and accumulated all roots of virtue without turning back, he is called "one with a broad tongue. Because for a long time he has avoided all faults of speech, proclaimed the immeasurable virtues and praises of all *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and Dharma-preachers, and has caused the Tathāgata’s sūtras to be written, recited, read, and made known.
And because he possesses skill in analyzing the meaning and phrasing of those dharmas and in bringing them to other beings, he is called "the one with the uṣṇīṣa and invisible crown of the head.

This is due to his long-standing practice of prostrating with his head at the feet of his parents, śramaṇas, brahmins, teachers, and those worthy of offerings; his bowing, saluting, and honoring those who have gone forth; his shaving of hair; his pouring of fragrant oils upon the heads [of others];
and his giving to all beggars powders, garlands, wreaths, strings of flowers, and head-ornaments.
Between his eyebrows is the *ūrṇā*, which is said to be well-formed, curling to the right, and possessing the luster of a pure, refined color;

this results from having for a long time encouraged the performance of all unimpeded sacrifices, followed the instructions of all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and acted as a messenger for Dharma-preachers who were not being rescued.

Because he is tireless in traveling to and from all directions; because he dispels the darkness of ignorance for all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, noble Śrāvakas, Dharma-preachers, parents, gurus, and those worthy of offerings; because he provides oil-lamps, grass torches, and lamps of various fragrant oils; because he fashions images of the Tathāgata endowed with the excellence of all forms and possessing a serene majesty; because he adorns them with jewel-encrusted cases shining like milk; because he is skilled in causing other beings to turn toward the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*); and because of his preeminence in the accumulation of merit—therefore he is called Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Because he is endowed with the strength of Mahānārāyaṇa, he is called Mahānārāyaṇa.
Because he possesses the power to subdue hundreds of millions of Māras, he is called "the crusher of all adversaries.
Because he possesses the ten powers of a Tathāgata, he is called "endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

Because he is skilled in the knowledge of what is possible and impossible, because he possesses the power to abandon inferior and limited vehicles while gathering the qualities of the Mahāyāna, and because he applies himself with insatiable effort, he is called "endowed with the power of the knowledge of what is possible."

Because he is endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the causes and the maturation of all past, future, and present undertakings of karma, he is said to be "endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the causes and the maturation of all past, future, and present undertakings of karma.

Because he is endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the differences in the faculties and vigor of all sentient beings, he is said to be "endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the differences in the faculties and vigor of all sentient beings. Because he is endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the entry into the world of many elements and various elements, he is said to be "endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the entry into the world of many elements and various elements."

Because he is endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the inclinations of many, the inclinations of various kinds, and all inclinations without exception—having attained liberation—he is said to be "endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the inclinations of many, the inclinations of various kinds, and all inclinations without exception.
Because he is endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the path leading everywhere—he is said to be "endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the path leading everywhere.

Because he is endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the establishment of all meditations, liberations, concentrations, attainments, defilements, and purifications—he is said to be "endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the establishment of all meditations, liberations, concentrations, attainments, defilements, and purifications."
Thus it is said:
because he is endowed with the power of unimpeded knowledge that recollects manifold former abodes, he is called "endowed with the power of unimpeded knowledge that recollects manifold former abodes.

Because he is endowed with the power of divine-eye knowledge that perceives all forms without exception and without obstruction, he is called "endowed with the power of divine-eye knowledge that perceives all forms without exception and without obstruction."

Because he is endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the destruction of all outflows, together with their latencies and connections, without exception, he is called "endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the destruction of all outflows, together with their latencies and connections, without exception. Because he has attained the fearlessness of a claim that cannot be surpassed by the world including the gods— a claim having ascended to the realization of all phenomena without exception— he is called "one who has attained the fearlessness of a claim having ascended to the realization of all phenomena without exception, which cannot be surpassed by the world including the gods."

Because he has attained the fearlessness of an unassailable vow regarding his claim that all defiled and obstructive factors create an obstacle to *nirvāṇa*, and because he has ascended to that claim before the world with its gods, he is said to have attained the fearlessness of an unassailable vow regarding his claim that all defiled and obstructive factors create an obstacle to *nirvāṇa*.

One who practices the path leading to liberation will attain *nirvāṇa*; because he has attained the fearlessness of a claim that cannot be challenged in the world including the gods regarding this assertion— that one practicing the path leading to liberation will attain *nirvāṇa*— he is said to have attained the fearlessness of a claim that cannot be challenged in the world including the gods regarding his ascent to the assertion that one practicing the path leading to liberation will attain *nirvāṇa*.

Because he has attained the fearlessness of an irreversible claim in the world including the gods, having ascended to the claim of the knowledge of the destruction of all outflows and the knowledge of abandonment, he is called "one who has attained the fearlessness of an irreversible claim in the world including the gods regarding the knowledge of the destruction of all outflows and the knowledge of abandonment.
Because he teaches the Dharma with unerring words, he is called "one who teaches the Dharma with unerring words."
Because he has awakened to the nature of dharmas that are soundless and inexpressible, he is called "one who has awakened to the nature of dharmas that are soundless and inexpressible.
Because he does not cease [his activity], he is called "one who does not cease.

Because he possesses the power to empower the resonance of the sounds of all sentient beings with the resonance of the immeasurable sounds of the Buddha-dharmas, he is called "one who possesses the power to empower the resonance of the sounds of all sentient beings with the resonance of the immeasurable sounds of the Buddha-dharmas."
Because his mindfulness is undeluded, he is called "one whose mindfulness is undeluded.
Because he is free from perceptions of diversity, he is called "one free from perceptions of diversity.
Because his mind is concentrated and perfectly concentrated in all respects, he is called "one whose mind is concentrated and perfectly concentrated in all respects."

Because he is equanimous without analytical discernment, he is called "one who is equanimous without analytical discernment. Because he is not deficient in the concentration of the formative force of desire, he is called "one who is not deficient in the concentration of the formative force of desire. Because his vigor is uninterrupted and not deficient due to the concentration of the formative force of vigor, he is called "one whose vigor is not deficient in the concentration of the formative force of vigor."
Because he is not deficient in mindfulness, he is called one whose mindfulness is undiminished;
because he is not deficient in wisdom, he is called one whose wisdom is undiminished;
because he is not deficient in liberation, he is called one whose liberation is undiminished.
Because the knowledge and vision of liberation have not been abandoned, he is said to be "one whose knowledge and vision of liberation are unimpaired.

Because he is endowed with all bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge, he is said to be "endowed with the knowledge that precedes and follows all bodily, vocal, and mental actions."

Because he is endowed with knowledge and vision that are unattached and unimpeded regarding the past, future, and present time-periods, he is said to be "endowed with knowledge and vision that are unattached and unimpeded regarding the three time-periods.

Because he has attained unobstructed liberation, he is said to be "one who has attained unobstructed liberation. Because he abides in skillfulness for entering into the conduct of all sentient beings through his empowerment, he is said to be "one who abides in skillfulness for entering into the conduct of all sentient beings through his empowerment."
Because he is skilled in teaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each individual, he is called "skilled in teaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each individual.
Because he has attained the supreme perfection of the entire circle of vocal qualities, he is called "one who has attained the supreme perfection of the entire circle of vocal qualities.
Because he has attained skill in producing all sounds and echoes, he is called "one who possesses the voices of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas."
It is called the resonance of the sound of Brahmā’s voice;
it is called the voice of the kalaviṅka bird;
it is called the voice of the sound of drums and music.
He is called the one whose voice resounds with a thundering roar across the surface of the earth;
he is called the one whose voice has the resonance of the rumbling roar of clouds from the lord of the nāgas of the ocean;
he is called the one whose voice has the thundering resonance of the lion’s and bull’s bellow.
It is called the voice that satisfies by following the sounds and cries of all sentient beings;
it is called the voice that delights all circles of assemblies through being unattached and unobstructed;
it is called the voice that attains all sounds from a single sound.
He is called "worshiped by Brahmā and Indra"; he is called "honored by the lords of gods";
he is called "revered by the lords of nāgas."

He is called "one whose facial orb is gazed upon by the lords of the yakṣas"; he is called "one praised with song by the lords of the gandharvas"; he is called "one beheld with unblinking eyes by the lords of the rākṣasas, their faculties serene."
He is called "the one to whom the lords of the asuras bow";
he is called "the one gazed upon with non-violence by the lord of the garuḍas";
he is called "the one praised by the lords of the kinnaras."
He is called "one whose sight is longed for by the lords of the mahoragas";
he is called "one highly honored by the lords of men";
he is called "one served by hosts of days."
He is called the one who inspires, rouses, and gladdens all bodhisattvas;
he is called the teacher of the Dharma without worldly motive;
he is called the teacher of the Dharma whose words and syllables are never fruitless.
He is called the teacher of the Dharma who does not let the proper time pass.

This, Maitreya, is the turning of the wheel of Dharma; this is but a mere introduction, a brief exposition of a small portion of the praise of the Tathāgata’s qualities. However, Maitreya, the Tathāgata could describe it in detail for an eon or the remainder of an eon.
And there would be no end to this being described.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"The wheel of Dharma, profound, difficult to see, and subtle, has been set in motion;
wherein Māras do not penetrate, nor do any of the followers of other paths."
The wheel of Dharma has been set in motion— without abode, free from conceptual proliferation, unarisen, non-existent, secluded, and empty by its very nature.
Without accumulation and without dispersion, signless and characterless— this wheel, which is the teaching on the equality of all phenomena, was extolled by the Buddha. (Lal_26.54)
Just as an illusion, a mirage, a dream, the moon reflected in water, and an echo—
so too was that wheel turned by the Lord of the World.
The penetration of the dharma of dependent origination—neither annihilated nor eternal—is known as the Wheel of Dharma, which completely cuts through all views. *Lalita-vistara* 26.56.
Always equal to space, non-conceptual, and luminous;
without end, middle, or description—this is here called the Wheel of Dharma.
Free from existence and non-existence, devoid of self and selflessness,
and described as being by nature unborn— this is what is called the Wheel of Dharma here.
The limit of reality and the absence of a limit, through the suchness of suchness— this non-dual teaching of the Dharma is designated as the Wheel of Dharma.
The eye is empty by its very nature, and so too are the ear and the nose;
the tongue, the body, and the mind are empty of self and devoid of activity.
This is that very wheel, the Wheel of Dharma, which has been set in motion;
because it awakens sentient beings who were unawakened, he is called "Buddha."
This intrinsic nature, the characteristic of phenomena, has been personally realized by me;
without instruction from another, I am thus self-become and possessed of vision.
Having attained mastery over all phenomena, he is called the Lord of Dharma;
because he knows the right and wrong ways regarding all phenomena, he is therefore called the Leader.
Just as there are those to be disciplined, I discipline immeasurable people;
because I have reached the perfection of disciplining others, I am therefore called the Vināyaka (Leader).
For those beings who have lost their way, I teach the supreme path;
I lead them to the further shore, and therefore I am the Guide.
Having gathered the multitude through the knowledge of the means of attraction, I have crossed over the wilderness of saṃsāra; therefore, I am indeed a caravan leader.
Having mastery over all phenomena, he is therefore the Jina, the Lord of Dharma;
having set in motion the wheel of Dharma, he is called the King of Dharma.
The Teacher is the master of the gift of Dharma, the unsurpassed Lord of Dharma;
he has accomplished his purpose through well-performed sacrifices, his hopes are fulfilled, and his auspicious signs have been realized.
He is a source of consolation, one who perceives security, a hero who has conquered the great battle;
having crossed over all conflicts, he is liberated and the liberator of all beings.
He has become the light of the world, creating the radiance of wisdom and knowledge;
he is the destroyer of the darkness of ignorance, a torch-bearer of great splendor.
The great physician, the possessor of great wisdom, the healer of the great afflictions,
he is the unsurpassed remover of the thorns for beings pierced by afflictions.
Endowed with all the primary marks and adorned with all the secondary characteristics,
he possessed a body like that of Samantabhadra, yet he conformed to those who were inferior.
Possessing power through the ten powers, confident in his fearlessnesses,
and endowed with the eighteen unique qualities, the Great Sage is the foremost of those who travel the supreme vehicle.
This is a brief exposition regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma; this praise of the qualities of the Tathāgata has been revealed only in summary.
For the wisdom of a Buddha is indeed infinite, equal to the vastness of space;
even if one were to speak for eons, there would be no exhaustion of the Buddha's qualities.
Thus.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Turning of the Wheel of Dharma."
START Chapter 27 (Vaidya 316): The Twenty-seventh Chapter, "The City" (Nigama-parivarta).

Then, indeed, those sons of the gods who had entreated the Tathāgata for the proclamation of this Dharma-discourse— namely, eighteen thousand sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host, headed by Maheśvara, Nanda, Sunanda, Candana, Mahita, Śānta, Praśānta, Vinīteśvara, and others— who had also assembled at the turning of the Wheel of Dharma by the Tathāgata.

There, the Blessed One addressed those sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm, headed by the divine son Maheśvara: "Friends, this Dharma discourse, the sūtra called the *Lalitavistara*, a great vaipulya text on the playful sport of the bodhisattvas,
an entry into the play of the Buddha's domain, and a personal instruction, has been spoken by the Tathāgata."
You should take it up, maintain it, and recite it.
In this way, this guide to the Dharma will become widespread.
And those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, having heard this Dharma discourse, will exert even firmer vigor.
And those beings who possess noble resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment will produce the force of a great rain of Dharma;
the faction of Māra will be subdued,
and all opponents will find no opportunity for attack.
And your wholesome root from requesting that teaching of the Dharma will be of great significance, great fruit, and great benefit.
Friends, whoever shall join their palms in reverence toward this Dharma discourse, the *Lalitavistara*,
will obtain eight supreme qualities.
What are these eight?
Namely: he will obtain superior form;
he will obtain superior strength;
he will obtain a superior retinue.
He will obtain supreme eloquence;
he will obtain supreme renunciation;
he will obtain supreme purity of mind.
He will attain the state of supreme samādhi;
he will attain the illumination of supreme wisdom.
He will attain these eight supreme qualities.

Friends, whoever shall prepare a Dharma-seat for a Dharma-preacher who desires to recite this *Lalitavistara* discourse on the Dharma, eight attainments of seats are to be expected for him as soon as that seat has been prepared.
What are these eight?
Namely: the attainment of the seat of a merchant-leader, the attainment of the seat of a householder, and the attainment of the seat of a universal monarch.
The attainment of the seat of a world-protector; the attainment of the seat of Śakra;
the attainment of the seat of a Vaśavartin.
One should expect the attainment of the Brahma-throne;

for one who has reached the supreme and excellent seat of enlightenment while still a bodhisattva, the attainment of the lion-throne from which there is no turning back and where the adversaries of Māra have been struck down;
and for one who has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the attainment of the throne for turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
These eight attainments of a seat are to be expected.
Friends, whoever shall give a cry of "Well done! to one who is reciting this Dharma discourse, the Lalitavistara, will obtain eight purities of speech.
What are the eight?
Namely: acting in accordance with what one has spoken through the purity of vocal action that accords with truth;
having speech that is accepted because it overcomes the assembly; and having speech that is taken to heart because it is not arrogant.
He possesses smooth and sweet speech by means of gathering beings through gentleness; he possesses a voice like the song of the kalaviṅka bird by means of causing exhilaration in body and mind;
and he possesses speech that is authoritative because he cannot be overcome by any sentient being.
The quality of a Brahma-voice by way of surpassing all other voices;
the quality of a voice roaring with the sound of a lion’s roar by way of being unsurpassed by any opposing disputants;
and the quality of a Buddha-voice by way of satisfying the faculties of all sentient beings.
He will obtain these eight purifications of vocal action.

Friends, whoever shall have this *Lalitavistara* Dharma-discourse written in a book and shall preserve it, honor it, revere it, respect it, and worship it; and who, with a mind free from envy, shall speak the praise of this Dharma-discourse in the four directions and proclaim that praise, saying: "Come! Preserve this written Dharma-discourse, read it, contemplate it, and recite it!"
He shall obtain eight great treasuries.
What are the eight great treasuries?
Namely, the treasury of mindfulness through non-forgetfulness;
The treasury of intelligence is for the sake of discerning wisdom; the treasury of understanding is for the sake of delighting in the comprehension of the meaning of all sūtras;
the treasury of dhāraṇī is for the sake of retaining all that has been heard.
One obtains the treasury of eloquence by means of conversing with all sentient beings in well-spoken words;

one obtains the treasury of the Dharma by means of discerning the characteristics of the true Dharma; and one obtains the treasury of the bodhicitta by means of ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is not interrupted.
And the treasury of practice, through the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena— he shall obtain these eight treasuries.
Friends, whoever shall uphold this Dharma discourse, the Lalitavistara, having caused it to be well-proclaimed, will fulfill eight provisions.
Which eight?
That is to say: namely, he will fulfill the equipment of generosity by means of a mind free from stinginess;
he will fulfill the equipment of ethical discipline by means of fulfilling all virtuous intentions;
and he will fulfill the equipment of learning by means of bringing forth unattached wisdom.
He will fulfill the equipment of calm abiding by bringing all meditative concentrations and attainments into manifestation;
he will fulfill the equipment of insight by perfecting the three types of higher knowledge;
and he will fulfill the equipment of merit through the purification of the primary and secondary marks and the adornment of the buddha-field.
He will fulfill the equipment of wisdom by satisfying all sentient beings according to their respective inclinations;
he will fulfill the equipment of great compassion by never becoming weary of maturing all sentient beings.
He will thus fulfill these eight equipments.

Friends, whoever shall extensively proclaim this Dharma discourse of the *Lalitavistara* to others with such a thought as this— namely, "How might these beings become recipients of such Dharmas as these?"—
by that root of merit, he shall obtain eight great fortunes.
What are the eight? They are as follows: one becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin); this is the first great merit.
He will exercise sovereignty over the gods of the Four Great Kings;
this is the second great merit.
He will become Śakra, the lord of the gods; this is the third great merit.
He will become the divine son Suyāma;
this is the fourth great merit. He will become the divine son Santuṣita;
this is the fifth great merit.
He will become Sunirmita;
this is the sixth great merit.
He will become Vaśavartin, the king of the gods.
This is the seventh great merit:
one will become a Brahmā, a Great Brahmā;
this is the eighth great merit.
And in the future, he will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, having abandoned all unwholesome qualities and being endowed with all wholesome qualities;
he will obtain these eight great merits.
Friends, whoever shall listen with attentive ears to this Dharma discourse, the Lalitavistara, as it is being spoken, will attain eight purities of mind.
What are these eight?
Namely: he will attain loving-kindness for the sake of destroying all faults;
he will attain compassion for the sake of abandoning all violence;
he will attain sympathetic joy for the sake of removing all discontent.
He will attain equanimity for the sake of relinquishing attachment and aversion;
he will attain the four dhyānas for the sake of mastery over the entire realm of form;
[he will attain] the four... (Vaidya 318)
He will attain the formless attainments for the sake of mastery over the mind;
he will attain the five superknowledges for the sake of traveling to other buddha-fields;
and he will attain the complete eradication of all latencies and their continuities for the sake of attaining the Śūraṅgama samādhi.
He will obtain these eight purities of mind.
And in whatever village, city, town, district, or region, or in whatever walking-path or monastery, this Dharma-discourse of the *Lalitavistara* shall circulate,
there the eight fears shall have no power, with the exception of the ripening of previous karma.
What are these eight?
That is to say: namely, there will be no fear of disturbances caused by kings; there will be no fear of disturbances caused by thieves;
there will be no fear of disturbances caused by wild beasts.
There will be no fear of the disturbances caused by famine or wilderness travel;
there will be no fear of the disturbances caused by mutual strife, disputes, and conflicts;
and there will be no fear of the disturbances caused by celestial beings.
There will be no fear of disturbances caused by nāgas; there will be no fear of disturbances caused by yakṣas;
there will be no fear of disturbances caused by any calamities whatsoever.
Friends, these eight fears will not exist there, except for the ripening of previous karma.

In brief, friends, if the Tathāgata were to remain day and night for the duration of an eon and speak the praise of this Dharma discourse, there would still be no end to the praise of this Dharma discourse, nor would the eloquence of the Tathāgata ever be exhausted.
Moreover, friends, just as the Tathāgata’s morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are immeasurable and boundless, so too is this Dharma discourse.
In the same way, friends, for those who shall take up this Dharma-discourse, uphold it, recite it, write it, cause it to be written, master it, propagate it,
and reveal it in detail in the midst of an assembly— with the thought, "How might these beings come to be recipients of such a sublime Dharma?"—
for them too there is no limit to their merit.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Ānanda, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "O worthy ones, I entrust and transmit into your hands this unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, which has been accomplished over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons, with the highest degree of entrustment."
And you yourselves should likewise uphold this Dharma discourse and reveal it in detail to others.
Having spoken thus, in order to entrust this very Dharma-discourse even more thoroughly, the Blessed One at that time spoke this verse:
"Those beings who have been seen by me with the vision of a Buddha—were they equal to Śāriputra, they would be Arhats.
If someone were to honor them for as many millions of eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges," (Lal 27.1)

But whoever, being joyful, should perform worship for even a single day and night to a Pratyekabuddha with garlands and various other offerings—this person who creates merit is superior to that [previous one]. (Lal 27.2)

If all sentient beings were to become Jinas through conditions, someone here might worship them with flowers, perfumes, and ointments, remaining vigilant and constantly devoted for many eons. (Lal 27.3)
If one were to perform even a single prostration to a single Tathāgata,
or with a devout heart say "Homage to the Arhat," the merit from that would be far superior to this.
Suppose all sentient beings were to become Buddhas, and someone were to worship them just as before—
with divine flowers and the finest human blossoms— in many ways for numerous eons.

And whoever, at a time when the True Dharma is being destroyed, should abandon their own body as well as their very life to recite this sutra for a single day and night—this merit is indeed superior to that. (Lal 27.6)
Whoever desires to worship the Vināyakas, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas and the Śrāvakas,
should firmly generate the thought of awakening and always uphold this supreme sūtra.
For this king is the sovereign of all well-spoken words, who has arisen above all Tathāgatas;
the Tathāgata himself would always abide in the home of one in whose house this jewel of a sūtra resides.
He attains auspicious and infinite eloquence; he shall speak a single word for ten million eons, neither losing its phrasing nor its meaning—this one who gives this sūtra to others.
He is unsurpassed among the leaders of men; no being exists who is his equal. Indeed, he would be like the inexhaustible ocean who, having heard this Dharma, puts it into practice.
Thus [it is said].
The Blessed One spoke thus, and they were uplifted:

the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm headed by the divine son Maheśvara; all the bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas headed by Maitreya; and all the great śrāvakas headed by Mahākāśyapa, together with the world of gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas.
The world rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One.
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter of the *Śrī Lalitavistara*, titled "The Chapter on the Conclusion."
And this "Setting Out upon the Practice of All Bodhisattvas" is completed.

The Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Śrīlalitavistara*, the King of Jewels, is hereby completed. *All phenomena arise from a cause; the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation. Thus speaks the Great Śramaṇa.*
